# SECTION ONE,
## REGARDING
# POLITICAL MA-
## JESTE IN GENERAL,
### TREATING OF THE SUBJECT.

## CHAPTER I.

### *On the Etymology of Majesty: and likewise on*
### *Real Majesty.*

Socrates used to judge—as Xenophon records in his *Memorabilia*—that a noble mind, worthy of every favor, is one to which the political disciplines are dear. <note>Socrates was famously more interested in ethics and the "art of living" together in a city-state than in abstract physics.</note> And for that reason, as I now explain a certain principal head of Politics, I hope no one will stir up a dispute against me; especially since I repeat everything from the decrees of others, and I am ready to yield gladly to anyone teaching better things.

II. The supreme power in a Republic, the description of which completes the greatest part of Politics, is what Aristotle calls in the third book of his *Politics* the "governing power" <note>original Greek: κύριον πολίτευμα (kyrion politeuma)</note>, "absolute power" <note>original Greek: αὐτοκρατεία (autokrateia)</note>, "sovereign rule" <note>original Greek: κυρία ἀρχή (kyria archē)</note>, "power" <note>original Greek: δύναμις (dynamis)</note>, or "political authority" <note>original Greek: ἀρχή πολιτική (archē politikē)</note>, and "supreme power" <note>original Greek: ἄκρα ἐξουσία (akra exousia)</note>. Jean Bodin <note>A French jurist and political philosopher (1530–1596) who was a pioneer in defining the concept of sovereignty.</note> discusses this at the beginning of book 1, chapter 8; see also Tobias Paurmeister in his first book *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 3, number 4. To the Italians, it is called *Signoria* <note>original: "Signoria", meaning lordship or governing body</note> (for this word is also sometimes taken for the supreme Magistrate), according to the *Dictionary of the Crusca* <note>The *Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca* was the first great dictionary of the Italian language, published in 1612.</note>. To the French, it is designated as *Souveraineté* <note>original: "Souveraineté", English: Sovereignty</note>. The Spanish call it *Mayoria* <note>original: "Mayoria", implying seniority or superior power</note>. Commonly, among the Interpreters of the Law, it is the "greatest command" <note>original Latin: Imperium maxumum</note>, as noted by the Doctors of Law <note>The "Dd." refers to the "Doctores," the established legal commentators of the medieval and Renaissance periods.</note> in their commentary on the third law of the Digest regarding Jurisdiction. By the Patriarch Jacob, it is designated as a "rod" or "scepter" in Genesis 49. See Joachim Stephan, book 1 *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 7, number 8. And certainly, the "Scepter" <note>original Hebrew: Schebet (שֵׁבֶט)</note> is taken for the scepter and royal authority in that passage of Genesis by the triple Targum <note>Targums are ancient Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note>; it is also taken this way by the ancient Talmudic Hebrews and very many Rabbis: and therefore, those who interpret it otherwise are in error. This is confirmed by Mr. Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a celebrated Hebraist and scholar of Jewish literature.</note> in his *Lexicon*. I will provide only one Targumic interpretation, namely that of Onkelos <note>The Targum Onkelos is the primary Aramaic translation of the Torah, often treated as a standard authoritative commentary.</note>: "Dominion shall be in the beginning and in the end, the kingdom shall be magnified from the house of Judah: because from the judgment of death, my son, you have withdrawn your soul: he shall rest and dwell in strength like a Lion, and like a Lioness: nor shall there be a kingdom which..." <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

<summary>This page defines the concept of supreme political power (Majesty or Sovereignty) by tracing its terminology across Greek, Latin, Italian, French, Spanish, and Hebrew sources. It establishes the "scepter of Judah" from Genesis 49 as a biblical foundation for royal authority.</summary>

<header>Political-Legal Dissertation</header>

...disturb him. *The one exercising power shall not be taken away from the house of Judah, nor a scribe from the sons of his sons forever, until the Messiah comes, whose is the Kingdom, and the peoples shall obey him.* <note>This is a paraphrase of Genesis 49:10, drawing on the Targum—an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> Israel shall return to its city, and the peoples shall build its temple: the righteous shall be all around it: and those who practice the law shall be in its doctrine: its garment shall be purple: its clothing shall be silk of a crimson color, and various other colors. See Paul Fagius *in his notes on the Targum on the said chapter of Genesis*; Petrus Cunaeus, *On the Hebrew Republic, book 1, chapter 9, page 80*; and Drusius *on the passages of Genesis, chapter 129.*

By a most convenient and by no means new word (although Trebellius Pollio seems to suggest this in his *Lives of the Gallieni, page 253*), we most frequently call it "Majesty," derived from "greatness" <note>original Latin: *magnitudo*</note> (as Festus is the authority); or because it is a "greater" <note>original Latin: *major*</note> status, or the amplitude and magnificence in a Republic. *Law 23 on legacies 3; Law 4; final law of the Code on laws; Law 91 on the institution of heirs; Albericus Gentilis on the Julian Law of Majesty, dispute 2, from the beginning; Henning Arnisaeus, On Majesty, book 2; Bornitius, Treatise on Majesty, chapter 1.* Author of the *Antiquities and Research on the Greatness of the Kings of France, book 3, chapter 2.* Goldast, *On Seniority, book 2, chapter 6, number 5.* It can also be said that "Majesty" is derived from "Greater" <note>original Latin: *Majore*</note>; just as from "honor" comes "honesty," as Priscian notes. And so from Majesty, they called Jove (Jupiter) "Majus." Macrobius, *Saturnalia, book 1.* The wife of Vulcan was also called "Majesta," whom some used to call "Maja." Nevertheless, Etienne Pasquier says in *Research, book 7, chapter 5, page 968* that those forms of address—*Your Majesty, His Majesty, etc.*—were innovations and marks of effeminacy. It was Gallienus <note>A Roman Emperor (reigned 253–268 AD) often criticized by ancient historians for the decline of the empire.</note> who first imposed upon the Romans the necessity of saying "Imperial Majesty" <note>original Latin: *Imperatoriam Maiestatem*</note> instead of "The Emperor"; and this is how Theodorus Marcilius understands Trebellius Pollio in his *Explanation of the Institutes, at the preface, page 5 and following.* So too the Greek Emperors used the word <term>βασιλεία</term> <note>original Greek: *basileia* — meaning kingship or royal majesty</note> in this way: "Your Holy Majesty" <note>original Greek: ἡ ἁγία βασιλεία σου (*hē hagia basileia sou*)</note>. And this title was common to the Emperor and to the Sebastocrator, the Caesar, and the Despot. <note>These were high-ranking titles in the Byzantine hierarchy below the Emperor.</note> However, of those others they simply said "their majesty" <note>original Greek: ἡ βασιλεία αὐτῶν (*hē basileia autōn*)</note>; but for the Emperor, they added "Holy." Meursius, *in his Greek-Barbarous Glossary, under the word* <term>βασιλεία</term>. Elsewhere in Greek, the word that properly corresponds to Majesty is <term>μεγαλοπρέπεια</term> <note>original Greek: *megaloprepeia* — magnificence or "fitting for a great person"</note> according to Aristophanes and St. John Chrysostom, or <term>μεγαλοσύνη</term> <note>original Greek: *megalosynē* — greatness or majesty</note>. On this point, the very learned Andreas Schottus notes in *Tullian Questions, book 5, chapter 19* that Caesar Scaliger falls into error by denying that there is any word for Majesty among the Greeks. But although Majesty is said to refer only to the amplitude and magnificence of the supreme Empire—because by its own greatness it embraces and surpasses all remaining powers; and because it denotes the greatness, honor, command, amplitude, power, dignity, and security of a more eminent or sacred status—nevertheless, sometimes (to increase their esteem and authority) lower magistrates or even Princes lower than the Sovereign are said to possess it. Bodin, *On the Republic, book 1, chapter 8, number 151, and book 3.*

# On Majesty in General

<note>This continues a list of citations from the previous page</note> chapter 3, number 280; for instance, the *Praetor* <note>A high-ranking Roman magistrate</note>, in *the second to last law on justice and law, and the law "if a family" 9, on jurisdiction.* So too **Cicero** says: *Great is the name, great the hope, great the Majesty of the Consul.* And **Pliny**, in *Book 8, Letter 6 of his Epistles*, speaks of the *Majesty of the Senate and of the Judges*, which properly belonged to the people. And if we wish to speak accurately, those who think that the rights of Majesty consist merely in territorial right, <term>Territorial Sovereignty</term> <note>original German: *Landsfürstlicher Oberkeit*</note> or <term>Supreme Jurisdiction</term> <note>original German: *Oberbottmäßigkeit*</note>, are far from the truth. *Bornitius on Majesty, chapter 1 at the end; Thomas Michael, thesis 44, disputation on Jurisdiction.*

III. Now, **Majesty** consists in the Command <note>original Latin: *Imperium*</note> and all the dignity of the Roman people, or of any other body that has no superior. *Cicero in "For Cornelius Balbus"; Quintilian, book 7, chapter 3.* In this Majesty, the right of the entire state consists. It seems correctly divided into **Real Majesty**, or that of the <term>Empire</term> <note>original Latin: *Imperium*—referring here to the state's sovereign power</note> (which consists in the power to constitute or establish the state), and **Personal Majesty** (which consists in administering or governing the Republic). *Hermann Kirchner, Disputations on the Republic 2, thesis 3; Philipp Hoenon, political disputation 3, thesis 37; Johann Camman, disputation on the Rights of Majesty 1, theses 70, 75 and following; Bortius in Arumaeus, volume 9, discourse 30, chapter 1, theses 1 and 2; Mr. Daniel Otto, singular treatise on Majesty, chapter 1, number 8.* However, when they attribute Majesty to the "Empire," they do not assign it to an inanimate thing; rather, it belongs to the state because of the people within it.

IV. **Real Majesty**, or that of the <term>Empire</term>, is as old as the Republic itself; as long as the body of the state lasts, this Majesty remains, and it persists even during interregnums <note>periods between the reigns of rulers</note> and political changes. We can therefore call it the foundation of the Republic. *Christoph Matthias, Dithmarschen Political College 2, disputation 2, thesis 6; Heinrich Velsten, Century of political questions, decade 8, question 2 at the end.* **Personal Majesty**, however, falls with the person of the ruler and returns to the Republic. In view of this Real Majesty, it is said that even after the *Royal Law* <note>The *Lex Regia*, the law by which the Roman people supposedly transferred their power to the Emperor</note>, the Roman people retained some Majesty. *Section 4 of the Institutes on public judgments; Law 7, second to last section: "our Majesty" in the Digest on captives and postliminy; Law 1 and Law 3, the passage "The Julian Law, however," regarding "public Majesty" in the Julian Law of Majesty.* For the *Royal Law* should only be understood as a transfer of **Personal Majesty**; as I argued in my *Treatise on Monarchy, chapter 4, number 4*, the people transferred through it only the power of administration, not the power of constitution <note>the power to create the fundamental laws of the state</note>. It is clear from *Law 2, section 1 of the Digest on the origin of law* that the administration of the Republic—and nothing more—was given to the Emperor. And the Emperor Maximus (as recorded by Herodian) also acknowledged the Sovereignty of the people when he said:
> The Principate <note>the office of the Prince or Emperor</note> is not the private possession of just one man; rather, it has belonged from of old to the whole Roman people. Indeed, in that city [Rome] resides the fortune of the Empire; to us, however, only the distribution and administration of the Principate has been entrusted, together with you.
It should certainly never be thought that the whole and entire Republic is represented by the Prince. He is the head, not the whole body. And just as in the human body, the other parts also have their functions:

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of Majesty (sovereignty), specifically distinguishing between the "Real Majesty" of the state and the "Personal Majesty" of its ruler. # Political-Legal Dissertation,

...thus even now, some Majesty remains with the public body and the people. No one but a flatterer would claim that the name of the Republic—which includes that most sacred title of "Fatherland"—was abolished under the rule of a Prince. From this, it is said that the **Crime of Majesty** <note>original Latin: *Crimen Maiestatis*—often translated as high treason, an offense against the sovereign power</note> is committed against both the people and the State, as well as against the Prince himself. *Book 1, section 1, of the aforementioned title by Lord Doctor Bocerus, treatise on the Crime of Majesty, chapter 1, number 25 etc., and number 55 etc., chapter 2, number 13, number 74 etc.; Vulteius, book 1 of Roman Jurisprudence, chapter 47, from the beginning.* Today, the Emperors are accustomed to speak of those accused of the Crime of Majesty against the Empire in this way: **Those who have acted against us and the Holy Roman Empire.** <note>original German: *Die wider vns vnd das H. Römisch Reich gehandler*</note>

V. To **Real Majesty** <note>This refers to the inherent sovereignty that resides in the state or the "commonwealth" itself, rather than the person of the ruler</note> belong privileges, such as **the Land’s Majesty-Letter** <note>original German: *Landes Maiestatbrief*—referring to the fundamental charters or constitutional documents of a territory</note>; to **Personal Majesty** belong those things which usually pertain to those who command. Therefore, the fundamental laws—under which the State is constituted and rests as if upon a foundation by common consent—comprise this Majesty of the Republic (or Real Majesty). *See Reinkingk, book 2, class 2, chapter 6.* If these laws are removed, the safety and the "state" (the very condition by which the Republic stands and persists) must necessarily be overturned, or at the very least, changed or altered into another form. *Lambert Daneau, Christian Politics, book 1, chapter 6; Johannes Althusius, Politics, chapter 6 of the first edition; Keckermann, Politics, book 1, chapter 6; Bornitius in Arumaeus, discourse 30 on public law, chapter 2, thesis 2; and the same Bornitius, ibid, discourse 33, thesis 9, page 10, section...* Regarding such a **fundamental Law**, it can be properly said that it is the **common pledge of the City**. <note>original Latin: *communis sponsio Civitatis*; original Greek: *πόλεως συνθήκη κοινή*</note>. *Law 2, at the beginning, of the Digest on laws.* Althusius looked to this in Chapter 6 of his *Politics*, asserting that the **Rights of the Kingdom** are twofold: namely, the **Fundamental Law of the Kingdom** and the **Right of Majesty**. He adds a notable distinction: that a Republic or Kingdom can indeed be established, preserved, and passed down to descendants without fundamental laws, but not without Rights of Majesty. However, I do not believe this is without controversy; indeed, every Republic, and even a Lordship, seems to have some Real Majesty. And so also **Samuel**, after the King was elected, wrote down the **Royal Law**. <note>original Latin: *Ius Regium*</note> *1 Samuel chapter 10, verse 25.* A fundamental law was made whenever we read in Holy Scripture that Kings made a **covenant** with their subjects at the beginning of their reign. *2 Samuel 3, verse 21, and chapter 5, verse 3.* In a **Democracy**, although Real and Personal Majesty seem to run together—*see especially Lord Vulteius, book 1 of Roman Jurisprudence, chapter 47, from the beginning, page 254*—Majesty is not held by the people in such a way that a majority part of the people can decree something against it. Rather, in the repeal of fundamental laws, the consent of every individual (if we look at the Law) is required. For a fundamental law has the force of a pact and contract, the rescinding of which requires the consent of all. Thus, the **Religious Peace** <note>Referring to the Peace of Augsburg (1555) or the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which established legal religious rights within the Holy Roman Empire</note> in our Empire cannot be abolished by a plurality of votes, since in that matter, all individuals as well as the group as a whole can claim an acquired...

It argues that fundamental laws act as a binding contract or "common pledge" that cannot be overturned by a simple majority, citing the Religious Peace of the Holy Roman Empire as a prime example.</summary>

# On Majesty in General.

...the question asked. For this reason, not all **Public Law** <term>original Latin: *Ius publicum*—the body of law governing the relationship between the state and its citizens</term> concerns **Real Majesty** <note>original Latin: *Maiestatem realem*—the sovereignty that belongs to the state or people as a whole</note>: for even in Public Law, many things can be changed by those who possess **Personal Majesty** <note>original Latin: *Maiestas personalis*—the sovereignty held by the individual ruler</note>, as I said in my *Commentaries on the first law of the Digest regarding Justice and Law, question 16.* But what I have just said—that the consent of everyone is required in the repealing or establishing of a **fundamental law** <term>original Latin: *lex fundamentalis*—a law that forms the constitutional basis of a state</term>: I understand this to refer to those who represent the whole people: such as the **Estates** <note>original Latin: *Status*—the representative ranks of society, such as nobility and clergy</note> in the **Holy Roman Empire**. Yet, the contradiction of one or two individuals is not taken into account. Sometimes, a change also occurs through **conversion** <note>original Latin: *conversionem*—a fundamental transformation or revolution in the form of government</note>, where the procedure is often extraordinary and violent.

VI. Since the **Majesty of the Ruler** is distinguished from the **Majesty of the Empire**, just as that which is founded is distinguished from the foundation itself. It follows from this that the Majesty of the Ruler is bound to the Majesty of the Empire, as if to a superior. Even he who rules is bound to respectfully observe that Majesty and its laws, **lest the Republic suffer any harm** <note>original Latin: *ne quid Respublica capiat detrimenti*—a traditional Roman legal formula used to justify emergency measures to protect the state</note>; these laws should be changed by no variation. *Jean de Terre Rouge, on the Law of Succession in the Kingdom of France, treatise 1, article 1, conclusion 24;* excellently stated by *Bornitius, on Majesty, chapter 9.* Indeed, a Ruler would be the murderer of his own Majesty if he were to strive to overturn the Republic itself. For the Prince is bound by the laws of the Kingdom. *Jean à Chokier, book 2, chapter 2, page 55;* and a custom that regulates the Prince himself is considered greater than the Prince. *Moditius, in the decision on the section "the law is doubted," number 93, part 4.* Since such laws obtain the force of a **pact and agreement** <note>original Latin: *pacti & conventionis*—implying a contractual relationship between the monarch and the subjects</note>: by which even a Prince, however supreme, is bound. Whence *Bodin, book 1 of the Republic, chapter 8, number 88 at the end:* As far as the laws of the Empire are concerned, he says, since they are joined with Majesty, Princes can neither abolish them nor even deviate from them. Against such laws, no exemption can be granted to the contrary. *Gerlach Buxtorff, dissertation on the Golden Bull <note>The Golden Bull of 1356 was the primary constitutional document of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, thesis 7.* Although, in the meantime, I am not unaware that many are found who, through flattery, write the opposite.

Correctly and prudently, *Bartholomew Keckermann* says in his *Practical Disputations 29, problem 1:* Such things are distinguished from the **Right of Majesty**—and even from that power which is **exempt from other laws** <term>original Latin: *legibus soluta*—a concept where the sovereign is not bound by ordinary civil laws</term>—just as a cause is distinguished from its effect, and they take nothing away from it. For example: Is the rule of women appropriate? Should rule be granted to those chosen from the whole number, or to those succeeding by hereditary right? Should Majesty be offered to a native or rather to a foreigner? These matters (if they have been decided by fundamental law) can no more be in the power of the Prince than his own constitution and his induction into the Kingdom; for they are not the instruments of government like other laws, but the **efficient causes** <note>the primary source or foundation of a thing</note> and foundations etc. Because of this Majesty, it seems correctly said that the Prince is not greater than the whole Republic. *Canonhiero, book 8 of the Introductions, chapter 4, and I have already advised this in book 1 of my Politics, chapter 1, number 37.* In the same sense the Spaniards say: **There is no King who is lord of the office.** <note>original Spanish: *No ay Rey que sea sennor del officio*—indicating that kingship is a public duty, not private property</note> Absolute, and therefore...

It asserts that a ruler cannot unilaterally change the constitution or succession laws, as these are the very foundations upon which their authority rests.</summary>

# A Politico-Legal Dissertation

...thus, even now, there remains some **Majesty** <note>original Latin: *Maiestas*—the supreme power or sovereignty of a state</note> belonging to the public body and the people. Indeed, no one but a flatterer would suggest that the name of the **Republic** <term>original Latin: *Respublica*—literally "the public thing," referring to the state or commonwealth</term>, which includes that most sacred title of "fatherland," was abolished when the rule of a prince began. Therefore, the **Crime of Majesty** <term>original Latin: *Crimen Maiestatis*—the crime of high treason or insulting the dignity of the sovereign state</term> is said to be committed as much against the people and the Republic as against the Prince himself. *See Book 1, Section 1 of the stated title; Lord Doctor Bocerus, Treatise on the Crime of Majesty, Chapter 1, Number 25, etc.; Vulteius, Roman Jurisprudence, Book 1, Chapter 47, at the beginning.* Today, the Emperors are accustomed to speak in this way regarding those accused of the Crime of Majesty against the Empire: <note>original German: *"Die wider vns vnd das H. Römisch Reich gehandlet"*</note> **"Those who have acted against us and the Holy Roman Empire."**

V. To **Real Majesty** <note>sovereignty that resides in the state as an institution</note> belong the privileges and the **Sovereign Charter of the Land** <note>original German: *Maiestätsbrief*—a formal document granting rights or religious freedoms</note>; to **Personal Majesty** <note>sovereignty exercised by the individual ruler</note> belong those powers which are typically granted to those who govern. Therefore, the **fundamental laws** <term>original Latin: *leges fundamentales*—the core constitutional rules of a nation</term> encompass this Majesty of the Republic (or Real Majesty). These are the laws under which the Republic was established and upon which it rests as if on a foundation, arising from common consent. If these laws are removed, the safety and the state—by which the Republic stands and persists—must necessarily be overturned, or at the very least, changed or altered into another form. *See Lambert Danaeus, Christian Politics, Book 1, Chapter 6; Johannes Althusius, Politics, Chapter 6; Keckermann, Politics, Book 1, Chapter 6; Börtius in Arumaeus, Discourse on Public Law 30, Chapter 2.* Of such a fundamental law, it can be truly said that it is a **common covenant of the state** <note>original Greek: *πόλεως συνθήκη κοινή* (poleos synthēkē koinē)</note>. Althusius looked to this in Chapter 6 of his *Politics*, asserting that the rights of a Kingdom are twofold: namely, the **Fundamental Law of the Kingdom** and the **Right of Majesty**. He adds a notable distinction: that a Republic or Kingdom can indeed be established, preserved, and passed down to posterity without fundamental laws, but not without the Rights of Majesty. However, I do not think this is without controversy; for every Republic, even an absolute lordship, seems to possess some form of Real Majesty. And so even **Samuel**, after the King was elected, wrote down the **Law of the Kingdom**. *1 Samuel 10:25.* A fundamental law was also made when we read in Holy Scripture that Kings made a **covenant** with their subjects at the beginning of their reign. *2 Samuel 3:21 and Chapter 5:3.*

In a **Democracy**, although Real and Personal Majesty appear to coincide (see Vulteius, *Roman Jurisprudence*, Book 1, Chapter 47), Majesty is nevertheless not held by the people in such a way that a majority part of the people can decide something against it. Rather, in the abolition of fundamental laws, the consent of **every individual** is required (if we look at the Law). For a fundamental law has the force of a **pact and a contract**; to rescind it, the consent of all parties is necessary. Thus, the **Religious Peace** <note>referring to the Peace of Augsburg (1555) or Westphalia (1648), which granted legal rights to different Christian denominations</note> in our Empire cannot be abolished by a mere plurality of votes, since in that matter, all individuals as well as the whole body can claim their legal right.

<summary>This page explores the dual nature of sovereignty, arguing that fundamental laws act as a binding contract between a state and its people that cannot be overturned by a simple majority. It emphasizes that treason is an offense against the entire commonwealth, not just the individual ruler.</summary>

### Of Majesty in General

...the question at hand. For this reason, not all public law concerns **Real Majesty** <note>sovereignty that resides in the state as an institution</note>; for even within public law, those who hold **Personal Majesty** <note>sovereignty exercised by the individual ruler</note> can change many things, as I have said in my *Commentaries on the first Law of the Digest regarding Justice and Law, Question 16.*

Now, regarding what I just said—that the consent of all is required in the repealing or establishing of a **Fundamental Law** <term>original Latin: *lex fundamentalis*—a foundational law or constitution that defines the core structure and succession of a state</term>—I mean those who represent the entire people, such as the **Estates** <term>original Latin: *Status*—the representative ranks or classes in a political assembly, like a parliament</term> in the **Holy Roman Empire**. However, the opposition of one or two individuals is not taken into account. Sometimes, change also occurs through revolution, where procedures are often extraordinary and violent.

VI. Since the **Majesty of the Ruler** is distinguished from the **Majesty of the Empire**, much like that which is founded is distinguished from the foundation itself, it follows that the Ruler’s Majesty is bound to the Majesty of the Empire as if to a superior. Even he who rules is bound to respectfully observe that Majesty and its laws, **"lest the Republic suffer any harm"** <note>original Latin: *ne quid Respublica capiat detrimenti*—a famous Roman legal formula used to charge leaders with the protection of the state's safety above all else</note>; and these laws ought not to be changed by any variation. 

Jean de Terrevermeille <note>original: *Ioh. de Terrâ Rubeâ*—a 15th-century French jurist</note> in his *First Treatise on the Law of Succession in the Kingdom of France, Article 1, Conclusion 24* and Bornitius in *On Majesty, Chapter 9* express this beautifully. Indeed, a ruler would be the murderer of his own Majesty if he attempted to overturn the Republic itself. For the Prince is bound by the laws of the Kingdom. Jean de Chokier writes in *Volume 2, Chapter 2, Page 55* that a custom which constrains the Prince himself is considered greater than the Prince. Moditius also notes this in his *Decisions, Section "the law is in doubt," 93, Number 4.* 

Since such laws possess the force of a contract and agreement, even the Prince, however supreme he may be, is bound by them. Hence Jean Bodin <note>a famous French political philosopher</note> writes in *On the Republic, Book 1, Chapter 8, Number 88, near the end*: "As far as the laws of the Empire are concerned," he says, "since they are joined with Majesty, Princes can neither repeal nor even diminish them." No dispensation can be granted against such laws. Gerlach Buxtorff, in his *Dissertation on the Golden Bull, Thesis 7.* Although, in the meantime, I am well aware that many are found who, through flattery, write the opposite.

Bartholomäus Keckermann correctly and prudently states in *Practical Disputations 29, Problem 1*: "Such things," he says, "are distinguished from the Right of Majesty—and thus from the power that is otherwise free from the laws—just as a cause is distinguished from its effect, and they take nothing away from it." 

For example: Is the rule of women appropriate? Should power be granted to those elected from the whole number, or to those succeeding by hereditary right? Should Majesty be offered to a native or rather a foreigner? These matters (if they have been decided by fundamental law) can no more be within the Prince's power than his own constitution or his introduction into the Kingdom; for indeed, they are not instruments of governance like other laws, but efficient causes and foundations, etc. Because of this Majesty, it seems correctly said that the Prince is not greater than the whole Republic. Canonhiero says this in his *Introduction, Book 8, Chapter 4*; and I have already noted this in my *Politics, Book 1, Chapter 1, Number 37.* In the same sense, the Spanish say: **"There is no King who is master of the office."** <note>original Spanish: *No ay Rey que sea sennor del officio*—this emphasizes that the kingship is a public duty or office to be administered, not a private piece of property to be used at will</note> Absolute, and therefore...

The author cites various legal authorities to demonstrate that a prince cannot unilaterally change the core rules of succession or state structure.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and political discussion regarding the limits of a ruler's power. It specifically focuses on the relationship between "Real Majesty" (the sovereignty of the state) and "Personal Majesty" (the authority of the individual prince), arguing that the ruler cannot legally dismantle or give away the state he governs.</meta>

# Political-Legal Dissertation

...power belongs only to **Personal Majesty** <note>the authority held by the individual ruler</note>: and this presupposes that a Republic has already been established. However, a Prince, no matter how supreme, can do nothing against the constitution of the Republic. This is just as a human being cannot kill or destroy himself. For such an act should be attributed to a lack of power rather than to any valid authority. Thus, **Real Majesty** <note>the inherent sovereignty of the state or the people as a whole</note> perfects Personal Majesty, and therefore it is not a state of subjection, but rather a state of perfection. Nor is anything taken away from human liberty by the fact that a man is prohibited from killing himself, or even from killing any others without cause.

VII. Thus, the Majesty of the Kingdom, the rights of dignity, and the territory itself prevent **alienation** <term>original Latin: *alienatio*—the legal transfer of ownership or sovereignty to another person or state</term>. See Lancellot Conrad, *Temple of Judges, book 1, chapter 1, section 4, page 454*; Nicolaus Besold, *Treatise on Illustrious Family Pacts, page 72*, and following; Heigius, *part 1, question 19*; Moditius, *in his decisions, section on the plebiscite, doubt 95*; Jean Savaron, *On the Sovereignty of the King, part 1, page 20*, and following; Bartholomaeus Musculus, *Disputation on Confraternities, thesis 20*; Antonius Godofredus, *Feudal Disputation 9, thesis 6*; Lord Bachovius's commentary on Treutler, *disputation 2, thesis 3, letter F, volume 1, page 53*; Lord Lather, *On the Census, book 1, chapter 17*; Bartolomé de las Casas, *Treatise on this Single Question*; and my own work *On the Treasury, chapters 2 and 6*, as well as the *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 2, number 16, page 61*. Neither can subjects be alienated against their will, according to Cravetta, *Counsel 241*, nor can vassals; likewise, subjects cannot be granted as a fief to others, as noted by Cardinal Tuschus, *letter F, conclusion 125*. For this reason, it is even said that a Kingdom falls into **forfeit** <note>original Latin: *in commissum cadere*—a legal term meaning the loss of a right or property due to a violation of duty</note> if a Prince makes himself a subject of another. That is to say, if he hands over to a foreign power the Kingdom which he received as free from his ancestors and the people, and subjects himself along with the Kingdom to a foreign Majesty (as John Balliol, the Scot, submitted himself to Edward I, King of England, see Buchanan, *Scottish History, book 8, regarding Balliol*). See also William Barclay, *On the King, book 3, at the end*. Indeed, such a Prince, even if he did not do this with the intention of overturning the Republic, nevertheless loses that which is the chief essence of rule (namely, that by recognizing a superior, he is no longer supreme in the Kingdom, nor inferior to God alone). By this very act, he deposes himself and ceases to be a Prince. Therefore, it is not without merit—and for the sake of greater caution—that the Kings of Hungary specially promise that they will keep the rights of their Kingdom and the honor of the crown undiminished (see the chapter *Intellecto*, 33, in the *Extravagantes* on oaths); and the Roman Emperors themselves and many other Princes promise the same. See especially Marquard Freher’s notes on Peter von Andlau, *book 2, chapter 8, page 187, letter b*. Lehmann notes in *book 5, chapter 45* that Lothair the Saxon was the first Emperor who sold the rights of the Empire for gold. But certainly, he alienated what he could not preserve without great danger; and Lord Lehmann seems to be somewhat unfair to him, given that the Emperor was quite fair to the Clergy. Jacques Auguste de Thou, in *book 4, page 82*, commends Emperor Charles V for his candid response to Pope Paul III regarding Parma and Piacenza: that if those cities belonged to the Empire, he could not place them under the jurisdiction... <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

<summary>This page argues that a ruler's sovereignty (Personal Majesty) is limited by the state's constitution (Real Majesty) and that a monarch cannot legally sell or transfer the kingdom's territory or subjects to another power. It cites historical examples, such as John Balliol's submission to Edward I, to show that a ruler who acknowledges a superior power effectively deposes himself.</summary>

# On Majesty in General.

...to the prejudice of the Imperial dignity and status. Thus, the recovery of alienated Imperial property was both deliberated upon and desired by the Emperor at the Diet of Worms in the year 1521, in the section "And as we in our Imperial Mind etc." <note>original German: *vnnd als wir in vnser Keyserlich Gemüth rc.*</note>; add also the **Imperial Recess of Augsburg** of the year 1566, the section "after the established articles," and the Imperial Recess of Regensburg of the year 1576, the section "we have also to the sixth article." <note>An "Imperial Recess" (Reichsabschied) was the official published resolution of an Imperial Diet, the deliberative body of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>

And speaking of *Franco-Gallia* <note>a famous political treatise by François Hotman published in 1573</note>, Hotman writes in chapter 9: "The Royal Domain is like the Dowry of the Kingdom, or like the **usufruct** <term>original Latin: *ususfructus*—the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without damaging or transferring it</term> of certain possessions, granted to the King to maintain the splendor of his dignity. I said 'like a usufruct' because the ownership of those possessions remains with the people, and no part of it can be alienated by the King without the people as the author—that is, without the consent of the estates and the public council."

Likewise, it is clear that there is a great difference between *Patrimony* and the *Royal Domain*. For the Patrimony belongs to the King himself, but the Domain belongs to the Kingdom—or as the common people say, to the Crown itself. The former [Patrimony] belongs to the King by full right, and therefore he has full and supreme power to alienate it according to his will. Of the latter [the Domain], the bare ownership lies with the whole body of the people, or the Republic; the usufruct, however, lies with the King. For this reason, he has no power to alienate it. 

And the opinion of the learned doctors on this matter is clearly most true: that the King's right to his Domain is the same as a husband's right to his wife's dowry <note>under Roman law, a husband managed a dowry to support the marriage but was restricted from selling the property it contained</note>. Even the laws of modern France do not permit the alienation of the Domain or the Rights of the Crown unless certain formalities are observed and the Court of Paris approves it. See Jean Papon, *book 5, title 10, articles 2 and 3, and throughout the title passim*; Lord Lansius, *in his Consultations, Oration against France, page 337.* In the German Republic <note>referring to the Holy Roman Empire</note>, however, the alienation of goods is more free, because the subjects lose very little, since the property always remains under the mediate jurisdiction of the Emperor and the Empire.

VIII. There are also fundamental laws regarding successions, which are found to be various in many places, based on the institutions of our ancestors. Especially the law of **primogeniture** <term>the right of the firstborn child to inherit the entire estate or title</term>, and the rule that the Kingdom should not be divided among multiple heirs. See Moditius, *in the said section, doubt 36.* 

In the Roman Empire, the form of Election must also be recognized as a fundamental law, as expressed by the sanction of the **Golden Bull** <term>original Latin: *Aurea Bulla*—the 1356 decree that fixed the constitutional structure of the Holy Roman Empire</term> and protected by clauses that prevent its repeal. See Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, *Book 7 on the Republic, chapter 19*; Kirchner, *disputation on the Republic 4, final corollary*; Heigius, *part 1, question 5, from the beginning*; and therefore it cannot be abolished by the Emperor. See Arumaeus, *On the Golden Bull, discourse 1, thesis 7.* Although it is not always perfectly observed. See Marquard Freher, *Treatise on Testamentary Guardianship, chapter 12.* And similarly, many things contained in the Imperial Recesses hold the place of fundamental laws, although many things regarding public law are found therein that are not fundamental, and some even...

A Political-Legal Dissertation

...now regarding things pertaining to private law. By these **Fundamental Laws**, personal Majesty is sometimes tempered, and the state is rendered "mixed" <note>a "mixed state" refers to a government combining elements of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy</note>. At other times, it is greatly amplified and preserved; thus, it would be a sign of weakness, not power, if it were within the prince’s right to diminish the Empire in any way. Similarly, it does not hinder the freedom of the will that I am not the Master of my own life and limbs <note>the author argues that just as a person’s "freedom" isn't limited by the fact they can't legally or morally destroy themselves, a king's "power" isn't limited by his inability to destroy the state</note>.

### CHAPTER II.

## On Personal Majesty. To what extent it seems to possess some Divinity, and that it is the supreme power.

We have thus far discussed **Real Majesty**. Now follows **Personal Majesty**, which is conferred upon a person and coincides with them. This is defined as the supreme and perpetual power, unbound by laws <note>original Latin: *legibus soluta*—a central concept in political theory suggesting the sovereign is above human-made statutes</note>, and applying to the things and persons within its jurisdiction. See **Jean Bodin**, *On the Republic, book 1, chapter 8, at the beginning*; Tobias Paurmeister, *On Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 3, numbers 1 and 22*; Clemens Timpler, *Politics, book 3, chapter 1, question 1*. It is the power of administering all means that exist as necessary for the Republic. It is the faculty of governing and disposing all cares of government for the safety of the Republic. This power is, as it were, the **head of the Republic**, belonging to the Emperor alone in the Roman Republic <note>here referring to the Holy Roman Empire</note>. Bulenger, *book 1, chapter 37, On the Roman Empire*. In this power consists the chief force of the entire State. This Sovereignty holds, as it were, the citadel of the Republic: moving all its members and forcing them into one body.

Therefore, **Hermann Kirchner** rightly warns (*On the Republic, disputation 2, thesis 2, letter a*) that **Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse** errs when he says (*On the Republic, book 8, chapter 3, § 2*) that Majesty is "something hidden" which, beyond its own nature, renders something admirable. Nor does **Justus Lipsius** reach the summit of Majesty (*Books on Politics, chapter 16*) when he calls Majesty a certain "venerable greatness" due to the merit of virtue or related things. Finally, even **Keckermann** defines Majesty poorly as a certain "force through which a Prince gains for himself a singular admiration and veneration in the minds of men, and fear joined with both." For although Majesty is sometimes used to mean the authority and gravity of the Person, and for the reverence of dignity—which **GOD** usually grants after the attainment of legitimate power (*Althusius, Politics, chapter 19, number 97*), and by which many have been deterred and called back from a proposal to kill a King (*Piccart, decade 6, chapter 1*)—nevertheless, in this context, it is taken in a much more specific sense...

<summary>This page defines "Personal Majesty" as the supreme, perpetual legal power of a ruler, distinguishing it from "Real Majesty" (state sovereignty). The author argues against scholars who define majesty merely as a psychological "aura" or "prestige," insisting instead on its definition as the governing "head" of the state's body.</summary>

<margin>...is defined by its meaning.</margin> Johann Camman, *Disputation on the Law of Majesty 1, thesis 16.* True Majesty, which is the subject of our current discussion, consists more in power <note>original: *potestate*</note> than in authority <note>original: *auctoritate*</note>; and it differs from the latter as a cause differs from an effect. When "Majesty" is used to mean reputation or authority, it is attributed to only one person. Hence, when addressing the Venetian Senate, we do not say, "Your Majesty," etc. Furthermore, although Jean Bodin <note>a prominent French political philosopher (1530–1596) known for his theory of sovereignty</note> recognizes another specific attribute of Majesty—namely, that it must be one's own, granted either by right of succession or election, and not belonging to another or held by favor <note>original: *precariò*, meaning something held temporarily at the will of another</note>—this does not seem necessary to me. This is because that point is sufficiently included in the first and second attributes: for if the Sovereignty is "perpetual" and "supreme," it can hardly be "by favor" or "subordinate."

II. Since he who holds such eminent power, even though he is a human being, has obtained a power that is a substitute for the Divine; he may establish honorable and Divine matters, though he uses human speech. This refers to the aphorism of Philip of Macedon recorded in Stobaeus, *Sermon 46.* It also suggests that he who wishes to exercise Kingship over others ought to be <term>as a god among men <note>original Greek: ὡς θεὸν ἐν ἀνθρώποις</note></term>; see Reiner Reineccius, *History of Julius, Book 1, Prolegomena Chapter 3*, or that he is closest to **God**. Juretus, notes on *Symmachus, Book 10, Epistle 27, folio 274.* For this reason, the ancients imagined Majesty had descended from heaven; and they worshiped her as a **Goddess**, the daughter of Honor and Reverence. Ovid, *Book 5 of the Fasti*:

> ---
> ->Honor and decent Reverence, with a calm face,<-
> ->laid themselves upon a lawful marriage-bed.<-
> ->From them was born Majesty, who governs the whole world,<-
> ->and on the day she was brought forth, she was great.<-

The same Majesty is believed to be closest to **God** by Gunther, who sings of her in *The Ligurinus, Book 5*:

> ->Always terrible, always to be feared, and full<-
> ->of her own vigor she remains; she is believed to be<-
> ->pressed by none with impunity, and is always feared by all and everywhere.<-

III. From this, it happened that we frequently see divine titles applied to Princes; they are described with the words "Divine Power" <note>original: *Numen*</note> and "Oracle." Clemens Timpler, *Politics, Book 2, Chapter 1, Question 6.* Likewise, in former times, they were surnamed "Divine" <note>original: *Divi*</note> and consecrated, or counted among the number of the Gods. Bulenger, *On the Roman Emperor, Book 1, Chapters 10 through 17.* Even the Hebrews call Princes and Judges <term>Gods <note>the author refers to the Hebrew term *Elohim*, which is used in the Bible for both the Almighty and for human judges or rulers</note></term>; just as they call anything else that excels in its own category "Divine." Drusius, *Notes on Genesis, Chapters 37 and 59, and Exodus 21, 32, and 35.* Hence, in our law, Majesty is called "sacred and holy," and the Emperor is hailed as "most sacred"; even his private affairs are called "sacred." Brisson, *Lexicon, Book 7, under the word "sacras"*; see also Sixtinus, *On Regalia, Chapter 1, number 31.* This is not because good Princes wish to impiously snatch away from **God** what is His own (as Bodin and Cujacius might conclude in their writings); rather, it reflects the height of their office. <unclear>v.</unclear>

IV. I cannot fail to mention here that our ancestors recognized a certain Divinity in their Prince, Eberhard, the first Duke of Württemberg. For he, by traveling around the cities of his jurisdiction and diligently inquiring among the citizens about the integrity of the magistrates and prefects, and among foreigners about the reliability of their hosts, acquired such love from everyone that his subjects, even while he was still living, referred to him among the gods with this kind of proclamation: **If he were not GOD, our Duke Eberhard could be a god.** This is the same man who, in the assemblies of Princes, when others were boasting of various goods of their domains, said: "But I glory in this alone: that there is none among my subjects in whose lap I would fear to rest alone in the vastest forest." <margin>Johann Agricola in *German Proverbs*.</margin> But I attribute these things to the ancient simplicity of that nation. Nevertheless, Pitfillius seems to wander too far in this argument when, in *Color 3, leaf 46*, he says: that a greater and surely prior care is taken by GOD the Savior for the Prince than for the subjects; and he asserts that a higher Angel is given to the Prince as a guardian than to any of the subjects. So too Moditius, who in *the section "The Pleasures of Princes," doubt 1, number 4, etc.*, assigns two guardian angels to Kings and Princes. Truly, GOD is no <term>respecter of persons <note>Original Greek: *προσωπολήπτος* (*prosopolēptos*). A biblical concept meaning God does not show favoritism based on worldly status or rank.</note></term>, as argued in *1 Corinthians 1, verse 26 and following*; and in the Kingdom of Heaven—that is, before GOD—he is greatest who is held in contempt by the world and exists like the little ones. *Matthew 18.* The eminence of Princes pertains only to this temporal life. Truly, the Most High GOD does not love creatures similar to Himself—that is, the high and sublime—but rather the humble and the poor. For thus He speaks through Isaiah: *To whom shall I look, if not to the poor man and the contrite in spirit, and him who trembles at my words?* And David says, *The Lord is high, yet He looks upon the humble.* Indeed, GOD loves high and sublime things, and through this, things like Himself: but those things which are truly sublime, not those which merely seem to be and are not. Therefore, GOD does not love the proud, who ought to be called elated and puffed up rather than high and sublime; but He loves the humble and those who tremble at His words, because those who cast themselves down more are exalted all the more by the Lord Himself. And those who are exalted by the Lord, they are truly high. Thus, the same people are both humble and sublime: humble in their own eyes, sublime in the eyes of GOD. Cardinal Bellarmine, in that *excellent treatise On the Ascent to God, step 10, leaf 244.* And that Kings, Princes, and other great men,

There, when the sun's rays first caught the fold of his silver robe, the brightness of the vibrating metal poured out a doubled light upon those watching, so that the terror of the sight struck the eyes of those looking on; and through this, the craftsman <note>Here referring to Herod himself, crafting his own divine image.</note> falsely claimed by his arrogance something more of himself than belongs to human nature.

Immediately, the voices of the flattering crowd rang out, sounding honors but bringing destruction, and with the theater seats shouting from every side, he was addressed as **God**: and that he might be favorable, he was humbly entreated, with the people saying that 'up until now we feared you as a man, but from now on we confess that you are above human nature.' But the King did not restrain this acclaim held against divine law, nor did he shudder at the impiety of such illicit flattery; until, looking up a little later, he saw an Angel <note>Original Latin: *Angelum*. He immediately felt that the one he had previously known as a provider of good things was now the minister of his destruction.

And behold, suddenly a torment seized him from an incredible pain and swelling of the belly. Looking at his friends, he said: 'Behold, I, your God, behold, I am immediately driven away and cast out from life, since indeed Divine power has just now proven your false words spoken of me. And I, who was just now called immortal by you, am even now being snatched headlong into death. But the sentence which **GOD** has established must be accepted. For we have lived in no contemptible way, and we have fulfilled a long life which is thought blessed.' And when he had said these things, driven more violently by the force of the pain, he was immediately carried back to the palace. And when it was spread abroad that he would die shortly, a huge multitude of every age and sex, convening in the customary manner..."

# A Politico-Legal Dissertation

even in his own century, Princes distinguished by the light of faith still dare and rejoice to be called "Divine" <note>original: "Divos"</note>; this persists as a vice of old custom and stands against Catholic practice. Certainly, the most illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit theologian and cardinal of the Counter-Reformation.</note>, *in the beginning of his book of revisions*, asserts that not even Saints should be called "Divines." And the Author of the *treatise against the Synod of Greece* (concerning the adoration of images, falsely attributed to Charlemagne), disapproves of what Constantine and Irene say: "through Him, the God who reigns with us" <note>original: "per eum, qui conregnat nobis Deus"</note>. *In book 1, chapter 2, and book 1, chapter 3 of the same work*, he does not approve that the same Emperors dare to call their deeds or Imperial decrees "Divine Matters" <note>original: "Divalia"</note>.

V. The essence of this Supreme Command, which we call **Majesty** in its *formal* sense, consists chiefly in this: that it is supreme and rules universally. It is called "Supreme" because nothing is higher than it, and he is "highest" whom no one follows. <note>These are references to the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*, the body of Roman Law: specifically *Law "proximus" 92, on the Signification of Words*.</note> He is the one who is before others, and before whom there is no one. <note>References to Roman laws on wills and status (*l. 34. de vulg. & pupill.*, etc.).</note> He is the one who stands alone. From this, the Imperial fortune is said to overtop all others. When I call Majesty the "supreme power," it follows that it is also the first power and, as it were, its own origin; for it depends upon or proceeds from no superior, except from **GOD** alone, who immediately precedes it and whose place it takes in this world. So say Alberico Gentilis <note>An Italian jurist and one of the founders of international law.</note> in *Royal Disputations 1, page 17*; Gewold in *On the Electors, chapter 1*; and Gerhard in the *section on the Magistracy, numbers 33 and 6*. Guntherus expresses this elegantly in the *Ligurinus, book 6*:

> ->This power sees no head above itself,<-
> ->*except for the King of the Heavens.*<-
> <note>original: "Nullum caput ista super se / Aspicit, excepto Cœlorum Rege, potestas."</note>

It matters not that Majesty is transferred from another. For Majesty is by no means from the people, even if the people transferred it to the Prince; rather, that very power which the people held from the beginning was from **GOD**, who transfers and establishes Kingdoms. Nor, because it was transferred by the people, does it have its origin in the one transferring it, as if it were merely delegated by them, according to Bornitius <note>Jacob Bornitius, a 17th-century political theorist.</note> *On Majesty, chapter 4, folio 16*; see also Arnisaeus <note>Henning Arnisaeus, a German physician and political philosopher.</note>, *On the Subjection of Clerics, chapter 1, number 2, folio 5*; and Börtius in Arumaeus’s *discourse 30, chapter 5, thesis 2, folio 901*. The Emperor receives Majesty from the Electors <note>The Prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire who chose the Emperor.</note> as an <term>instrumental cause <note>A philosophical term meaning the tool or means through which something happens, rather than the primary source.</note></term>. In turn, the Emperor bestows Royal power upon Princes and States as the <term>efficient cause <note>The actual agent or force that brings something into being.</note></term>. Similarly, the Pope is accustomed to being elected by the Cardinals; but the Papacy was not therefore instituted by the Cardinals. Concerning this matter, Bellarmine writes: *book 2 on the Pontiff, chapter 17*: The Electors are truly said to "create" the Pope and are the cause of such a person being Pope and having that power; however, they do not give him that power themselves, nor are they the cause of that power. Just as in the procreation of a human being: because the soul is infused by **GOD** alone, and yet the father who generates—by preparing the matter—is the cause of the union of the soul with the body: thus a man is said to be ge- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "generare" (to be generated/born), which is the catchword for the next page.</note>

<summary>This page defines the nature of Majesty as a supreme power derived directly from God, arguing that while humans (like Electors or Cardinals) may choose a leader, they act only as instruments for a power that originates divinely.</summary>

# Politico-Legal Dissertation

...even in his own century, Princes distinguished by the light of faith still dare and rejoice to be called **Divine** <note>original: "Divos." In Roman tradition, "Divus" was a title for a deified emperor; the author critiques its continued use by Christian rulers as a "faulty old custom."</note>: by an old custom, which is faulty and persists against the Catholic faith. Certainly, the most illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a central figure in the Counter-Reformation who wrote extensively on the relationship between church and state.</note>, in the beginning of his *Book of Revisions*, asserts that not even Saints should be called "Divine." And the Author of the *Treatise against the Synod of Greece, for the adoration of images*—which was falsely attributed to Charlemagne—disproves of what Constantine and Irene say: *through him, who is God reigning with us* <note>original: "per eum, qui conregnat nobis Deus."</note> (*book 1, chapters 2 and 3*). He does not approve that these same Emperors dare to call their own acts or decrees "Divine" <note>original: "Divalia."</note>.

V. The formal nature of this supreme Empire, which we call **Majesty**, consists chiefly in this: that it is supreme and rules universally. It is called "supreme" because there is nothing higher than it, and he is "supreme" whom no one follows (*law 'proximus' 92, on the Signification of Words*); he who is before others, and before whom is no one (*law 34, on Vulgar and Pupillary Substitutions; law 9, on Doubtful Matters; law 2, § 2, on Sui and Legitimate Heirs*); he who stands alone (*said law 9; law 1, § 6, whence cognates*). And for this reason, the Imperial fortune is said to surpass all others (*law 7, Code on property which is free*). When I call **Majesty** the "supreme power," it follows that it is also the first, and as it were, of its own origin: since it depends upon or proceeds from no superior, except from <term>GOD</term> alone; who immediately precedes it, and whose place it holds in this world. This is supported by Alberico Gentilis <note>An Italian jurist and one of the founders of the science of international law.</note> (*Royal Disputations 1, page 17*), Gewold (*On the Electors, chapter 1*), and Gerhard (*Commonplaces on the Magistrate, numbers 33 and 6*). Guntherus elegantly writes in the *Ligurinus*, book 6 <note>A 12th-century epic poem about the deeds of Frederick Barbarossa.</note>:

> ->This power sees no head above itself,<-
> ->*Except the King of the Heavens.*<-

It matters not if **Majesty** is transferred from another. For **Majesty** does not originate from the people who transferred it to the Prince; rather, that very power, which the people had from the beginning, was from <term>GOD</term>, who transfers and establishes Kingdoms. Nor does it follow that because it was transferred by the people, it has its origin from the one transferring it, as if it were merely delegated by them, as Bornitius notes (*On Majesty, chapter 4, folio 16*); see also Arnisaeus (*On the subjection of Clerics, chapter 1, number 2, folio 5*) and Börtius in Arumaeus (*said discourse 30, chapter 5, thesis 2, folio 901*). The Emperor receives **Majesty** from the <term>Electors</term> as an <term>instrumental cause</term> <note>The "instrumental cause" is the tool used to achieve an end; the Electors are the means by which God designates the ruler.</note>; in turn, the Emperor bestows Royal power upon Princes and States as the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary agent that brings something into being.</note>. In the same way, the Pope is usually elected by the Cardinals; but the Papacy was not for that reason instituted by the Cardinals. Regarding this matter, Bellarmine writes (*book 2 on the Pontiff, chapter 17*): "The Electors are truly said to create the Pope, and to be the cause that such a person is Pope, and that he has that power; yet they themselves do not give that power, nor are they the cause of that power." ### CHAPTER III.

### On the Temporal Power of the Supreme Pontiff.

Something must be said here regarding the temporal <note>Secular or political, as opposed to spiritual</note> power of the Supreme Pontiff <note>Latin: *Pontifex Maximus*, the Pope</note>, and whether all Christian Kings are his subjects and vassals. Indeed, on this matter, it is not only those who have exempted themselves from his spiritual power who dispute quite hostilely (see Johann Gerhard, *On the Place of the Magistrate, number 295 and following*), but also the defenders of the liberties of the Gallican Church <note>The French Catholic Church, which historically maintained a degree of independence from papal political interference</note>. See *The Researches of Estienne Pasquier, Book 3, throughout.*

But on the contrary, Doctor Marta, in *On Jurisdiction, part 1, chapter 18, and many following*, strove a few years ago to prove with many arguments that the <term>Supreme Pontiff</term> <note>original: *summum Pontificem*</note> holds the highest power in the world, even in temporal matters—not only by reason of sin <note>The doctrine of *ratione peccati*, which suggests the Pope can intervene in secular matters if a ruler's soul is at stake or if they commit a moral sin</note>, but directly and temporally, rather than just spiritually. Just as in the Church Triumphant <note>The Church in heaven</note> there is one Lord whom all things obey, so too in the Church Militant <note>The Church on earth</note> the Pontiff is the vicar of the one <term>God</term> <note>original: *Dei*</note>; and political reason also demands this. See Canonhiero, *On Introduction, chapter 10, section 2*; and add Reinaldus Corsum, *3rd Investigation, last chapter*. 

Plutarch, in his *Life of Numa*, thinks the word "Pontiff" is derived from "potency" <note>power</note>. The Canonists <note>Scholars of Church law</note> truly follow this etymology, confidently teaching that the Pope is the head of the heavenly and earthly kingdoms. Alexander Carerius of Padua, in *On the Power of the Pontiff, Book 2, chapter 3, number 5*, says that by divine and natural law, the priesthood stands above the Empire, and within the priesthood itself resides both jurisdictions by Divine and Natural Law. Augustinus de Ancona, in his *Summary on the Power of the Church, question 1, article 7*, states: The Pope possesses all power, even Royal and Imperial power, because he is not only consecrated as a Priest, but crowned as a King.

Antonius, Archbishop of Florence, in *part 3, summary, title 22, chapter 6, section 4*, writes: It is necessary for all Christian kings to be subject to the High Priest, the Vicar of Christ, the Roman Pontiff, just as they are to the Lord <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: *Iesu*</note> Christ himself. Giovanni Botero, the Italian cosmographer, says that the jurisdiction of the same Pope recognizes the horizon as well as all boundaries, whether of mountains or seas, and even the paths of the sun and the year. 

"Why do I speak of Princes or men?" asks Lipsius, the expander of *Our Lady of Halle* <note>Justus Lipsius, writing on the miracles of the Virgin Mary</note>. "The spirits of the air, the earth, and the underworld—the genii themselves—fear and tremble before that heavenly (Pontifical) power on earth; they acknowledge it even unwillingly and with reluctance." In recognition and testimony of this superiority and Majesty, all Kings kiss the feet of the Pontiff:

### III.
I do not make this dispute my own, and I gladly admit that if anyone wishes to discuss this matter precisely, and in accordance with the dignity and antiquity of the subject, it requires judgment, leisure, industry, and an exact knowledge of Church histories. Regarding the censures and excommunications of Kings, the same Bellarmine has examples in *Book 2 on the Pontiff, chapter 19.* And it would not be entirely absurd if these powers were applied properly: for what is more powerless than a King who fears neither God nor men? # On Majesty in General.

§. 14. and following, where he writes thus: The armed superiority of the Papacy is most useful to Christian Princes who are tempered in their rule: since it balances their disagreements; it is the arbiter of peace and of just war; and it exercises its arms for those who suffer injury, nor does it allow anyone to invade the Kingdom of another Christian; it joins them against the enemies of the Christian faith, and separates them from the treaties of enemies, and through crusades <note>original: "cruciatas"</note>, indulgences, and excommunications on behalf of good rulers and against evil ones, it builds and protects the Christian Republic. Without it, Christianity would have already been annihilated (speaking humanly and politically), if anyone were to consider history: smaller Princes would also have often been swallowed up by more powerful ones.

Nevertheless, no Prince living under a religion having a High Priest <note>original: "Summum Sacerdotem"</note> who is armed and possesses superiority over him can completely unbridle his own ambition. Hence, no Christian Prince has so far been able to preserve for himself a Monarchy over all Christian peoples. Because the Pope presides over them, and scatters or builds up their efforts as it is expedient for religion. For if that unique Prince were to fall into heresy, the religion itself would collapse; and his High Priesthood would be a mere lure for ruling, and the Pope would be reduced to a mere Chaplain. Just as once the Pythian Oracle <note>The oracle at Delphi</note>, as Cicero witnesses, "philippized" <note>To "philippize" meant to give oracles biased in favor of Philip of Macedon, usually due to bribery or intimidation.</note>.

But the Monarchy of the Hebrews under an unarmed priesthood suffered a single Prince: and when it was doubled, a heresy was formed under Jeroboam. Nonetheless, the Kings were for the most part impious, not fearing an unarmed priest. But Christian Princes are far better than those, being under an armed priesthood. Furthermore, so that they might maintain a universal Monarchy under this religion, some declared themselves the ministers, liberators, and primary defenders of the Supreme Pontiff, such as Charlemagne <note>original: "Carolus Magnus"</note> and Constantine. Their sons, opposing the Pontiff, were destroyed. 

Others wished to make the Pope without arms, such as Henry and Frederick, and other emperors from across the mountains <note>original: "ultramontani"; likely referring to the German Emperors of the Holy Roman Empire</note>; and they experienced loss rather than gain from this; and the ruinous factions of the Guelphs and Ghibellines <note>The rival Papal and Imperial factions in Italy during the Middle Ages</note>, the Papal and Imperial parties, arose. Others raised the heresy of Arius and others, such as the Emperors Constantine and Zeno <note>original: "Zezo"</note>, and those like them; and they were extinguished in themselves or in their sons. Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363)</note>, indeed, studied to recall Gentilism <note>Paganism</note> and Hebraism in rivalry: and in their corruption, he also perished. 

Furthermore, to what extent certain matters pertain to the Roman Pontiff when the Empire is vacant, Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit theologian and Cardinal</note> disputes excellently, *in the last book on the Pontiff, chapter 5, page 348.* The magnificent Herwart <note>Hans Georg Herwart von Hohenburg (1553–1622), a Bavarian statesman and scholar</note> also suggests a true judgment of the controversies of Emperor Louis IV against the Pontiff, *in his Louis IV against Bzovius <note>Abraham Bzovius (1567–1637), a Polish Dominican historian</note>, page 735, and c. 762, and c. 804, etc.*

# Political-Legal Dissertation

### CHAPTER IV.

### *On the Roman Emperor, and whether he has any power over other Kings?*

I have defined Majesty as supreme power <term>Imperium summum</term>; however, this does not mean that the EMPEROR is the LORD OF THE WHOLE WORLD <note>original: "IMPERATOR UNIVERSI MUNDI DOMINUS"</note>: in such a way that I would judge all other existing empires in the world to be subject to him by right, or to lack true Majesty. <margin>Cardinal Cusa, *On Catholic Concordance*, book 3, chapters 1, 5, and 6. Covarruvias on the chapter *Peccatum*, § 9. Ferdinand Vasquius, in *Illustrious Controversies*, chapter 20 and following. Cephallos, in *Mirror of Common Opinions*, question 576. Antonius Gabriël, book 5, final conclusion. Mr. Dr. Bocer, *On Regalia*, chapter 2, number 102. Andreas Knichen, in his *Synopsis*, number 23. Bornitius, *On Majesty*, chapter 7. Marcilius, *Commentary on the Institutes*, in the preface, folio 8. Etherius Mohr, *Dissertation on Jurisdiction*, thesis 11. And Bachov, on the *Disputations of Treutler*, 3, thesis 7, letter c, and on disputation 7, folio 19. I have written extensively on this in *On Appeals*, chapter 2, section 6 and following. Dissenting: Marta, *Treatise on Jurisdiction*, part 1, chapter 27. Lancellot. Conr. *Temple of All Judges*, book 1, chapter 1, § 1, folio 38. Paschal, *Treatise on the Crown*, book 9, chapter 21. Mr. Joachim Cluten, *Sylloge*, theses 1, 3, 9, and 10. Thomas Michaël, *Disputation on Jurisdiction*, theses 9, 10, 15, etc. Paurmeister, *On Jurisdiction*, book 1, chapter 1, and chapter 4, number 27, etc. Matthias Stephani, book 2, part 1, chapter 1, number 48, etc.</margin> Even Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), perhaps the most influential legal commentator of the Middle Ages.</note>, commenting on the law concerning "Enemies" <note>original: "l. hostes"</note>, regarding captives and the restoration of rights <term>postliminium</term>, declared that those who deny the Emperor is the Lord and Monarch of the whole world are heretics. Likewise, Hieronymus Balbus, the Bishop of Gurk, on account of asserting this same opinion, thinks that those who follow the views of Oldradus should be tortured with great torments; see Johann Dauth in his German writing for the City of Brunswick against Andreas Knichen, folio 28.

Certainly, (1) God, and after God, natural reason, established certain boundaries for Empires; and from the Law of Nations <term>Ius Gentium</term>—as the Jurist says in Law 5, "On Justice and Law"—distinct nations were established and kingdoms were founded. And since God, the Best and Greatest, has defined all things in the world by number, weight, and measure; it was therefore also necessary for several Empires to be established in the world. (2) This idea [of a single world ruler] also contradicts the laws of nature. Cranes and bees always choose one leader for themselves, not many; yet bees do not flock together from the entire world to choose one king. Individual kings are content with their own hives, just as among cranes, the entire flock has its own king. (3) It exceeds human grasp for one man to rule the entire world; this is contrary to the nature of an Empire: to restrain an infinite multitude of men and innumerable expanses of places, separated by nature and divided by customs. Indeed, Aristotle proves it is difficult, and even impossible, for a city crowded with an excessive multitude to be ruled by excellent laws (*Politics*, book 7, chapter 4).

<summary>This page argues against the legal theory that the Roman Emperor is the rightful ruler of the entire world, refuting older legal claims (like those of Bartolus) by citing natural law, the Law of Nations, and the practical impossibility of global governance.</summary>

# On Majesty in General.

The State: it is certainly much more difficult for the whole world to be ruled by one single presiding Prince; it is necessary that even Empires have their own limits. Politicians consider the advice of Augustus Caesar—to keep the Empire within its boundaries—to have been forged on the whetstone of prudence. <margin>Mr. Gruter in his *Discourse on Tacitus*, folio 149, etc.</margin> (4) It is absurd to say that something exists by nature if it has never been found in the nature of things. Moreover, there has never been a Monarchy that lacked boundaries or that encompassed the entire global orb, as Strigelius axiomatically states in his *Chronicle*, page 71. All kingdoms have fated limits beyond which they cannot successfully progress. Richter, in *Political Axioms*, chapter 37, page 113; which Bornitius brings up in this sense, *On Majesty*, chapter 7. 

Not even the Roman Empire itself, which extended widely. Albericus Gentilis, *On the Law of War*, folios 11 and 12. Under Trajan’s leadership <note>Trajan (reigned 98–117 AD) oversaw the Roman Empire at its greatest territorial extent.</note> it was most flourishing, and neither before nor after was it larger; yet it did not occupy the whole, indeed not even half, of the three known parts of the world. See Bodin, *Method of History*, 7, folio 300, who describes the limits of this Empire. 

Hadrian so little wished to be considered the "Lord of the World" that he yielded much to many kings, and indeed redeemed peace from most of them with secret gifts. Spartianus and Aurelius Victor. Finally, the founders of our laws never progressed to such madness as to boast that they were ever Lords of the whole earth. The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in Law 4 of the Code *On Commerce and Merchants*, confess that they are not universal Lords of the entire world. They do not deny that the King of the Persians is not subject to the Emperor, and that the Kingdom of Persia is foreign to them; they name limits for their Empire. 

Hence, those who are not subject to Roman rule are called "free." Law 5, 7, and 24 *On Captives and Postliminy* <term>Ius postliminii: the legal fiction that a person captured in war, upon returning, is restored to all their former rights as if they had never been captured.</term>. And unless there were thresholds and defined limits of the Empire, those who were captured would certainly not be considered to return by the right of postliminy. *Institutes*, section "But if by enemies," on how paternal power is dissolved, and the entire titles in the Digest and Code *On Captives and Postliminy*. 

This same point is confirmed by all laws that use phrases such as: "Those who are under our Empire," or "those whom our Empire rules"—Law *In omnibus* under the title *To the Trebellian Decree*; Law 1 of the Code *On the Supreme Trinity*; the final law, version *sancimus*, of the Code *On Private Buildings*, and similar laws. These operate with a relative restriction, and they hint that there are others who are not subject to the Roman Empire. The Doctors of Law on the law *Generaliter*, section "When however," of the Code *On Institutions and Substitutions made under condition*, etc. Hippolytus de Marsiliis, *Singularia* 308, beginning "The Doctors say..." 

Therefore, other places in the Civil Law where the Emperor is called "Lord of the World" <note>original: "Dominus mundi"</note> must be understood in a modified sense through synecdoche <term>synecdoche: a figure of speech where a part is used to represent the whole (e.g., calling the Roman Empire 'the world').</term>. Law *Deprecatio* on the Rhodian Law; the final law at the beginning of the Code *On those who flee to the Church*; Law 2, section "These therefore"; Law "We command," version "This edict," of the Code *On Testaments*. Petronius Arbiter, in the appendix to Virgil: "The Roman victor now held the whole world," etc., folio 125. Forster, in the aforementioned *History of Roman Law*, book 1, chapter 2, number 3—meaning, of course, the *Roman* world, and that part of the World...

It cites historical examples of Emperors like Hadrian and legal doctrines like postliminy to prove that the Emperor’s "world lordship" was a rhetorical synecdoche rather than a literal legal reality.</summary>
