### Political-Legal Dissertation

...which belonged to the Roman dominion. <note>original: "quæ ad Romanam pertinebat ditionem."</note> This is argued from the law *concerning the Roman world* in the Digest <term>Digest: A massive compendium of Roman legal opinions organized by Emperor Justinian in the 6th century</term> regarding the status of men, and the second law in the Code <term>Code: The *Codex Justinianus*, a collection of Roman imperial decrees</term> regarding the law of calumny. These laws do not refer to the entire world—insofar as it contained the Indians, Parthians, Persians, Tartars, and other nations and provinces then unknown to the West and the South—but only to that part of the world which was subject to their Empire. Both Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop</note> and Jacob Bornitius <note>Jacob Bornitz (c. 1560–1625), a German political theorist</note> correctly interpret our legal texts in this way.

From all of this, a just conclusion is drawn: those peoples who were never actually subject to the Roman Empire—whom the Roman Emperors were either never able to conquer or did not even know existed—are not bound by law to recognize their Empire. Rather, by reason of the Roman Empire, they are entirely free. In the very nature of things, jurisdiction or power over the entire world cannot be given to a single Prince unless the republics of the whole world consented to that Emperor, or if he had subjected them to himself by force in a just war. 

Furthermore, if the Roman Empire, as the "Fourth Monarchy" <note>The "Four Monarchies" was a historical theory based on the biblical Book of Daniel, identifying four successive world empires: Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome.</note> of the whole world, holds jurisdiction, then surely the preceding three Monarchies would also have held that right. But this is not true, because the Jews were free by divine law and were not required to obey any other King. Therefore, the previous claim must also be denied. Reineccius explains throughout his *Syntagma* that various kingdoms existed during the time of the first three Monarchies. 

Regarding the phrase **"Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's,"** <note>original: "Datæ Cæsari, quæ Cæsaris." A reference to Matthew 22:21.</note> Dauth concludes from this that the Fourth Monarchy was established and that Christ even subjected his own people to it. However, Christ's response is entirely ambiguous. For having seen the coin, he concluded from it that the Jews were subject, or had subjected themselves, and by that very act professed themselves subjects of Caesar. Therefore, he commands that things be given to Caesar—not by those who had never acknowledged Caesar, but he commands those who had subjected themselves to Caesar to give what they promised and to keep those pacts by which they came into Caesar’s power. 

Even the sons of **Charlemagne** and their successors divided the kingdoms absolutely, and no one held jurisdiction over the others. Indeed, at that time, the one who held Italy usually held the title of Emperor, but that title was merely a mark of honor, not because he held jurisdiction over the others, as Lehman notes. 

In truth, this division of empires among the descendants of Charlemagne was like the division among the sons of **Constantine the Great**. These two great Emperors sinned greatly in this: they divided the Empire and did not leave it to a single successor. The Romano-Frankish Empire was also divided under Emperor **Lothair**, and the Kingdom of Germany was separated from the title of Emperor. Nevertheless, there was still some respect shown to the Emperor; for instance, the King of France sought the "right of majority" <note>A legal declaration that a minor has reached full legal age.</note> from him.

<meta>This page continues the legal debate regarding the Roman Empire’s jurisdiction. Having established that the Empire did not naturally encompass the entire world, the author now addresses whether the Emperor can legally reclaim territories lost long ago to other nations.</meta>

### On Majesty in General

...as Juan de Mariana points out in *The History of Spain, book 9, chapter 5.* <note>Juan de Mariana (1536–1624) was a Spanish Jesuit and influential historian and political theorist.</note> Even in the time of Guicciardini, Italy recognized the name of the Empire more than its actual power. <note>Francesco Guicciardini (1483–1540), a famous Italian historian and statesman.</note> See Guicciardini, *page 48*; and Reinking provides many reasons for the decline of the Empire in *book 1, class 2, chapter 7.* 

It is pleasing, therefore, to ask here: does **prescription** <term>prescription: a legal principle where a right or title is acquired or lost through the passage of a long period of time (similar to "squatter's rights" or a statute of limitations)</term> hinder the Emperor from being able to recover provinces snatched from the Empire by force and injury? 

This is commonly denied, following Zoannetus in *On the Roman Empire, numbers 121, 127, etc.* and Dauth in the writing published by the Brunswicks in the year 1608, *page 29.* 

(1) Because against the obedience due to Caesar by **divine and positive law**, <note>original: "jure divino & positivo." Divine law refers to God's will, while positive law refers to human-made statutes.</note> no prescription can maintain its place. See Fortunatus Garzia, *On the Ultimate End of Law, both Canon and Civil, number 51.* 

(2) Nor can our laws admit any prescription against the "sinew" of the Roman Empire. For these laws were sought out and passed for the increase and breadth of the Roman Empire; therefore, they cannot be accepted or admit any interpretation by which they would cause the diminution of the Empire through the occasion of prescription. Things invented for growth cannot provide for detriment. <note>Zoannetus, as cited above, number 128.</note> 

Hence, our legal interpreters consider it a most firm axiom that no one can "prescribe" so as not to be subject to the Emperor. <note>original: "neminem, ut Imperatori non subsit, præscribere posse."</note> This is argued from the law *Competit* in the Code regarding the prescription of 30 or 40 years, and the chapter *Inter Corporalia* regarding the translation of Bishops. This is supported by many, including Thomas Michael in *On Jurisdiction, thesis 8.* 

Similarly, regarding the **Supreme Rights of Majesty**, <term>Majesty: Here referring to the sovereign power and rights held by a supreme ruler</term> whether they can be prescribed is considered such an uncertain matter that if anyone says their right is founded upon it, they are forced to confess they lean upon a completely unstable and uncertain foundation. <note>Balbus, *Treatise on Prescriptions, part 3, part 5, question 2.*</note> Nor are those of small authority who deny that those things which belong to Majesty as a sign of supreme jurisdiction can be prescribed. <note>See the legal scholars (Doctors of Law) cited: Borch, Friedrich Mindanus, Paurmeister, and Matthias Stephani.</note>

But truly, for me to cross over into their camp without conditions, there are many things that offend me on the way—at the very "threshold," as they say. For as it pertains to those peoples who were never subject to the Roman Empire, yet invaded Roman provinces with arms and have now possessed what they seized for a long time—through the space of many years or rather centuries—such as the **Franks, the English, etc.**, I surely cannot take away their right of prescription. 

For them, this right descends not from **Civil Law** (by which those not subject to Rome are not bound), but from the common **Law of Nations**. <term>Law of Nations: *Jus Gentium*, a set of universal legal principles believed to be shared by all civilized peoples, distinct from the specific laws of the Roman state.</term> Indeed, the Romans did not possess the world from the time of its creation; rather, they took it from others step-by-step and brought it under their power, not always by equal right—regardless of what Alberico Gentili disputes to the contrary in *On Roman Arms, book 2.* <note>Alberico Gentili (1552–1608), an Italian jurist and one of the founders of international law.</note> 

Here, therefore, the inference of **equity** <note>original: "æquitatis illatio."</note> militates: that whatever new law someone has introduced, they should eventually expect their adversary to use it as well.

### A Political-Legal Dissertation

...demanding that he be forced to use the same law, whether it be fair or unfair. *Law 1, Digest, on what legal right.* And by the same title by which the Romans deprived countless peoples of their liberty, by that same law those same peoples partly recovered their former liberty; partly other Barbarians, never subjected to the Romans, stripped them of the Empire, as I said in my *Treatise on Appeals, folio 40.* For what someone considers fair in another's case, he ought to admit the same in his own (*Law: if two, joined to the following section, on oaths*), unless he wishes to condemn his own law and his own reputation. 

And although the Romans might have been able to recover the taken provinces by right, and a war is considered "just" which is initiated to recover things which a foreign people holds by violence (*chapter: Our Lord, at the verse: thus a race & City 23. question 2; Bocer, book 1 on war, chapter 6, number 10*), nevertheless, overly ancient causes for making war are brought forward foolishly. If a dispute is handled civilly, so that legal actions are excluded by the **prescription** <term>prescription: original: "praescriptio," a legal principle where a right or title is acquired or lost through the passage of a long period of time.</term> of time, why should a warlike action not also be excluded by the **Law of Nations**? <term>Law of Nations: original: "Iure gentium," the body of customary rules and principles considered applicable to all mankind.</term> 

Surely if legal actions are barred by legitimate law in this way, why are the causes of war—which are effectively armed actions—not likewise barred? **Usucapion** <term>usucapion: original: "usucapio," the acquisition of ownership of property through long-term uninterrupted possession.</term> and prescription were introduced for the public good, so that there might be some end to litigation. Why not also an end to wars? 

Jephthah, the leader of the Israelites, recognized this equity when he responded to the King of the Ammonites regarding this right of prescription in *Judges, chapter 11*: <note>The author cites the biblical story of Jephthah's defense against Ammonite claims to land the Israelites had held for 300 years.</note> "While Israel dwelt in all those cities for three hundred years, why did you not recover them in that time?" This point is confirmed with many other reasons by Albericus Gentilis in *book 1 on war, chapter 22.* <note>Alberico Gentili (1552–1608) was an Italian jurist and one of the founders of the science of international law.</note> 

Regarding subjects, there seems to me to be a greater doubt: namely, whether they can be removed from the number of subjects and the **Majesty** <term>Majesty: original: "Maiestas," the supreme power or sovereignty of a ruler or state.</term> of the Prince through prescription, and thus become free. Certainly, the negative opinion has most serious and highly authoritative supporters, some of whom are listed—and to which he adds his own calculation—by the most learned Covarruvias in *part 2, re-reading of chapter: possessor in bad faith, section 2, number 10, joined to the last number at the end.* <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577) was a Spanish jurist and bishop.</note> 

Most significant reasons are not lacking here either. For things that cannot be possessed by common law cannot be prescribed (*chapter: that, distinction 93; chapter: against custom, distinction 10*). And just as in a donation it is necessary for the one to whom it is rightly made to be capable of receiving it, so it is much more required in prescription that the one who wishes to prescribe be able to possess the thing to be prescribed, as Chassanæus proves with the authority of many in *Customs of Burgundy, on Justice, section 2, verse: and the proof, numbers 12 & 13.* <note>Barthélemy de Chasseneuz (1480–1541), a French jurist.</note> From this it is said that things which cannot be granted cannot be prescribed (*Cravetta, on the antiquity of time, part 4, section: material, number 97*). 

Therefore, since a subject, insofar as he acknowledges himself as a subject, cannot become capable of Majesty—because by this reasoning he would cease to be a subject—it does not seem that a subject can prescribe Majesty against his Lord, nor free himself from subjection by this legal remedy. # On Majesty in General

...cite prescription <term>prescription: original: "praescriptio," a legal principle where a right or title is acquired or lost through the passage of a long period of time.</term> as their defense. Cravetta, *On the Antiquity of Time, part 4, section: for when it is finished, 45.* And thus Arnisaeus correctly understands the opinion of those who grant that prescription applies even against the duty of obedience, *On Majesty, chapter 2, folio 347.* This reasoning and the common tradition of the Doctors <note>The "Doctors" refers to the *Doctores Legum*, the established legal scholars of the medieval and early modern universities.</note> moves me to speak of those peoples who were once not defended by the Roman Emperors against enemies—as befits a good Prince—but were instead treated as if they had been abandoned. For this or other non-irrational causes, they believed they could legitimately withdraw themselves from the subjection and obedience of the Roman Empire. Having enjoyed this freedom and the possession of exemption in good faith for a time beyond memory, I would not hesitate at all to pronounce that these peoples hold their liberty by the highest and most perfect right.

However, no support for this claim arises for the cities of Italy and other Princes who withdrew themselves from the Roman Empire through trickery and open fraud, as Arnisaeus shows in the *referenced location, folio 248*, and as Paurmeister extensively deduces in *book 2, chapter 4, number 48, etc.* Furthermore, Albericus Gentilis <note>A famous Italian jurist and one of the founders of the science of international law.</note> says in *On War, book 1, chapter 22, folio 175*, that it is ridiculous for a certain theologian to try to teach that all things snatched from us can be "well-possessed" by the Turk <note>original: "Turcâ"; a reference to the Ottoman Empire, the primary external threat to Europe at the time.</note>.

Nonetheless, the response of Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a highly influential jurist in the field of civil law.</note> in *Counsel 248 and Counsel 267, beginning "it is asked,"* seems wise to me. He says it is dangerous to advise the Emperor to try to recover, or as he puts it, to "avenge" <note>original: "revangare," a medieval legal term for reclaiming territory through force.</note> the world by armed force. Many very bad and dangerous consequences could follow, and things that would generate a very great scandal must be avoided. Just as a more violent exercise or a heavy loss of blood is judged most harmful to the human body if it is not already in the best health, so too for the Roman Empire—or any other State affected internally by many dangerous diseases—an offensive war could only bring numerous disadvantages. It is better to protect well what we have and govern it rightly than to gape after other things and expose the remainder to danger.

Furthermore, it is not by chance, but because of sins and iniquities—and thus by the most just judgment of God—that kingdoms are transferred from nation to nation. The transfer of kingdoms is always legitimate in the eyes of God (Warenm. de Erenberg, *part 1, folio 34, On Covenants*). We ought to meet this divine ordinance and punishment first of all not with open war, but with serious repentance.

# On Majesty in General
### E 2

...a people or a King cannot be said to be superior to another people or Prince in terms of power, but rather in respect of courteous respect <note>original: "comis observantiæ." In legal terms, this is "comity," where nations show mutual respect for each other’s rank or laws without being legally subject to them.</note>. *Law 7, paragraph 1, on captives and the right of return.* This is a matter of precedence, not of command, as I have stated elsewhere in more than one place.

V. The modern Holy Roman Empire <term>Holy Roman Empire: original: "Romano-Germanicum Imperium," the political entity in Central Europe that began in the Middle Ages and claimed to be the successor to the ancient Roman Empire.</term> is rightly designated as "Roman." This is proven by Albericus Gentilis, *On the Law of War, book 1, chapter 23*; Arumæus, *Public Law, volume 1, discourse 2*; Mr. Daniel Otto, *Dissertation on Public Law, chapter 5, folio 107*; Reinking, *book 1, class 2, chapter 3*; and Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff, book 3, chapter 5.* Certainly, the Roman Monarchy endures to this day, because the prophet Daniel speaks of a certain Empire that will last until the end of time <note>This refers to the "Four Monarchies" interpretation of the Book of Daniel, where the Roman Empire is seen as the final earthly kingdom before the end of the world.</note>. For Constantine the Great <note>The first Christian Roman Emperor (reigned 306–337 AD), who moved the capital to Constantinople.</note> and his successors were Roman Emperors, even though they established their seat in the city of Constantinople; and Charlemagne <note>The King of the Franks who was crowned Emperor in 800 AD, reviving the title in the West.</note>, although he resided in Gaul and Francia, did not live in Rome. 

Frederick I <note>Frederick Barbarossa (reigned 1155–1190 AD), a powerful German Emperor who asserted imperial rights over Italy.</note>, the German Emperor, once asserted this same right. For according to Otto of Freising, *book 2, chapter 21*, the Envoys of the Romans spoke to him thus: "Listen with a serene mind and kind ears to what is brought to you by the bounteous Mistress of the world; the city of which, with God’s help, you are soon to be the Prince, Emperor, and Lord. You seek the Empire of the world; I, the City, rise up gratefully to offer the Crown, and I run to meet you joyfully. For why should he not arrive peacefully when he comes to visit his own people? You were a guest, I made you a Citizen: You were a newcomer from the transalpine regions, I established you as Prince. That which was mine by right, I gave to you."

To which the Emperor replied: "We have heard much of the wisdom or the bravery of the Romans until now, yet more of their wisdom. Therefore, we cannot wonder enough that we find your words more tasteless with the swelling of arrogance than seasoned with the salt of wisdom. It is clear how the strength of your nobility was first transferred from this city of ours to the Royal city of the East <note>Constantinople.</note>. Then came the Frank <note>Referring to Charlemagne.</note>, noble in both name and deed, and he bravely snatched away that nobility which still remained in you. Do you wish to recognize the ancient glory of your Rome? Look upon our Commonwealth: all these things are in our possession. All these things flowed to us together with the Empire. A naked Empire was not handed to us; it came clothed in its own virtue, and brought its ornaments with it. Your Consuls are with us, your Senate is with us, your soldier is with us. Let us review the deeds of modern Emperors. If our divine Princes, Charlemagne and Otto, did not receive the city as a gift from anyone, but snatched it from the Greeks or the Lombards by force of arms and added it to the borders of the Franks. I have made your Prince my soldier, and from then until the present, I have brought you into my jurisdiction. I am the legitimate possessor. Let anyone who can, snatch the club from the hand of Hercules <note>A classical proverb meaning to attempt an impossible task.</note>. The hand of the Franks or the Germans is not yet broken or weak."

# A Politico-Legal Dissertation
### ->page 36<-

By the term **Monarchy**, however, they do not mean a universal empire over the whole world, nor even precisely that species of government in which one person rules absolutely—from which the Greeks properly derived the word <term>monarchia: rule by one</term>—but in the present discussion, I speak of those Empires whose authority was distinguished among the other kingdoms of the world in their respective times, and to which the status of the People of God and the Church was subsequently more subject than to others. Just as the most brilliant light of the Sun seems to shine alone above all other stars, so the most powerful Empire that dominates others is thought to <term>monarchein: to rule as a monarch</term>, that is, to dominate alone and as the only one, <term>kat' exochen: by way of excellence or preeminence</term>, when considered in relation to other smaller kingdoms. See Conrad Grasser in *History of the Antichrist, exercise 1*; Kirchner, *Disputations on the Republic 3, thesis 6, a. & thesis 7, c.*; and myself, *On the Law of Territories, last chapter, number 4.*

That there were four such Empires—namely, the Assyrians, the Persians, the Greeks, and the Romans—is noted most clearly among Greek writers by Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric who lived in Rome during the reign of Augustus.</note>. In the beginning of his first book, he calls the Empire of the Assyrians the most ancient, and claims it can be traced back even to legendary times. To this, he joins the Median and Persian, then the Macedonian <note>The empire of Alexander the Great.</note>, and adds the Roman, which he says was the first and only one in human memory to bound the borders of its Empire by the rising and the setting of the sun. Annius of Viterbo, the commentator on Berosus, acknowledges these same four supreme Empires throughout his work, and a whole crowd of recent historians agrees. 

However, Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a famous French political philosopher who challenged the "Four Monarchies" theory as being historically inaccurate.</note> very contentiously disagrees with them in his *Method of History, chapter 7*, as does his defender Herpinus, and Tremellius in his commentary on *Daniel chapter 7*. These authors assert that those four Empires were neither the supreme nor the only great ones. Writing against Bodin are Matthew Dresser and Friedrich Tilemann—the former in a speech on this matter, the latter in a specific dissertation. They are joined by Conrad Grasser, Kirchner, Christian Matthias Dithmars, Joachim Cluten, Christoph Helvicus, Friedrich Braunborn, Johann Gerhard, Reinking (writing against Aben Ezra), and Oecolampadius. 

These men strive to prove that the **Fourth Monarchy** and its state were prefigured (though symbolically) by the Prophet Daniel. The arguments of both sides can be reduced to two classes. Some are taken from theological mysteries in the prophecy of Daniel (specifically chapters 2, 7, and 8), dealing with the Statue that appeared to Nebuchadnezzar in his dreams and the four great beasts rising from the sea. Others are drawn from historical records and the succession and transformation of Empires. Those visions of Daniel (truly a great prophet, and who...

# On Majesty in General
### ->page 37<-

[Daniel] was considered worthy to be adorned with a unique praise of virtue under both covenants <note>The Old and New Testaments</note>, (Ezekiel 14, verses 13 and 19, and chapter 28:3; Matthew 24, verse 15), which are to be referred to those supreme Empires. And it is indeed quite probable that the vision of the four beasts and the colossus—or statue—signifies exactly that many Empires, such that there will be no more in the future. Indeed, the Prophet himself interprets it this way in chapter 2: "You are a King of Kings," (he says to Nebuchadnezzar). "You, therefore, are the head of gold. And after you shall arise another kingdom, inferior to yours, of silver; and a third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over all the earth. And the fourth kingdom shall be as iron, by reason of its strength." In chapter 7, the four beasts are said to be four kingdoms that shall arise out of the earth. In chapter 8, mention is made by name of the King of the Medes and the King of the Persians, as well as the King of the Greeks.

Nor is it permissible, without a mark of rashness, to interpret this prophecy along with Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a famous French jurist and political philosopher who questioned traditional historical schemes.</note> as being about Babylon, which came under the power of the Medes, Persians, Greeks, and Parthians. For in chapter 2, verse 28, it is said that this vision contains things that are to come in the "latter days" <note>original: *in novissimis temporibus*</note>. In chapter 12, verses 4 and 9, we read that the book of Daniel is sealed and closed until the time of the end. Therefore, this prophecy contains a sequence of times leading up to the end of the world. Now, indeed, it has been many years since the location where Babylon once stood has even been known. Likewise, the Prophet speaks of separate Kingdoms, not of the city of Babylon. God revealed the prophecies not for the sake of Babylon, but for the sake of the Church.

We cannot agree with Franciscus Junius and Tremellius <note>Famous 16th-century Protestant biblical scholars whose Latin Bible was widely used by academics.</note>, who understand the fourth beast of Daniel as referring not to the Romans, but to the successors of Alexander. This is something that Conrad Grasser <note>A Swiss theologian and historian.</note> refutes explicitly and laboriously in the cited passage. Moreover, this opinion is also hindered by the fact that, as we said, the prophecy of Daniel is only to be understood in the "latter days." And because it is said in chapter 2, verse 41, that the fourth kingdom will be divided, this can be applied to the Empire of Constantinople and the Roman Empire; see also my treatise *On the Jurisdiction of the Roman Empire, question 2.*

But regarding this matter, I leave the judgment to the Church; for Daniel says in chapter 12, verse 10: "None of the wicked shall understand, but the wise shall understand." Nor are prophecies a matter of private interpretation, as Blessed Peter says. And furthermore, I add this, following the mind of certain men who consider themselves most skilled in the interpretation of the Prophets: namely, that the prophecies of Holy Scripture possess this character of divinity, such that not only one event corresponds to them, and that histories—though wonderfully diverse from one another—are nevertheless intertwined, united in a typical harmony <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as prefiguring something in the New Testament or the end times.</note>. Such is the case in Matthew chapter 24, where our Savior made mention, as if alternately, of the destruction of Jerusalem (which followed the first coming) and of the punishments which soon follow the second coming. Thus, this prediction of Daniel can perhaps be taken as referring to the kingdoms before and after Christ, and likewise to the Antichrist himself. # On Majesty in General.

F 2

The historians take the Empire of the Syrians and Assyrians <note>The author uses "Syrians" here likely referring to the Babylonian/Assyrian succession often grouped together in early modern chronologies.</note> as one and the same. For neither nation held distinct or separate kingdoms; rather, they possessed this power alternately, as Reineccius <note>Reiner Reineccius (1541–1595), a German historian and influential scholar of world history and genealogy.</note> teaches in the first volume of his *Syntagma*. This is much like how the second Monarchy is reckoned as the Kingdom of the Medes and Persians combined, because the Persians did not destroy the Medes but succeeded them, as noted in Reineccius, volumes 2 and 3. It should be known that Daniel, in said chapter 2, verse 41, etc., predicts that the final Empire—that is, the fourth Monarchy—will be divided toward its end, and that the Empire will be partly fragile and partly strong near its conclusion. Likewise, in chapter 7, verse 7, he says the last beast is unlike the others and has ten horns. By all these things, it is signified that the final stages of the last Monarchy will be weak; indeed, ten other kingdoms will arise from it. From this, it follows that the Majesty of the Roman Empire passed first to the Greeks, then to the Franks, and finally to the Germans. Consequently, though Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), the French jurist who argued that the Holy Roman Empire was not a true monarchy.</note> insists that the Germans today control only a tiny portion of the world with their Empire, it is, as a certain wise man among our people said, "at least the shadow of a great name" <note>original: "magni saltem nominis umbra est." A famous quote from Lucan’s *Pharsalia*, used here to describe the Holy Roman Empire’s decline from its ancient Roman peak.</note>. Speidelius <note>original: "Spegelius"; likely referring to the jurist Johann Jacob Speidel.</note>, in his *Lexicon* under the word *Law*, notes that by this very argument, Bodin—unwittingly and unwillingly—strengthens our position while destroying his own. From each of these points, it is not difficult to gather that Bodin is in error, and that Daniel is speaking of nothing other than those four most famous world Empires.

But one must not conclude the argument in this way: "Daniel foresaw those great future Empires. Therefore, they are resisted unjustly. Therefore, the dominion of the world is rightfully destined for the fourth Monarchy." Indeed, things have reached a point where certain people have fabricated specific "rights" for these supreme Empires. Hence Kirchner <note>Hermann Kirchner (1562–1620), a professor at Marburg who wrote on the rights of the Empire.</note>, in his second corollary of the third *Disputation on the Republic*, relates that the demand for "water and earth"—of which Herodotus speaks in Book 7 regarding the right of supreme empire—was a practice of the Persians. From there, he approves of what we read in Tacitus, *Annals* Book 13: "It thus pleased the gods that the power of decision should remain with the Romans, to give or take away as they saw fit, and they would tolerate no other judges but themselves." <note>original: "Ita Diis placitum, ut arbitrium penes Romanos maneret, quid darent, quid adimerent, neq; alios judices, quàm seipsos paterentur."</note> Kirchner adds that this right is granted to Monarchies by nature; for the lower must obey the higher, the weaker must be subject to the more powerful, and the more noble should rule over the lesser. In this same sense, the Athenians argued against the Melians in Thucydides, Book 5 <note>The original text says "lib. 15," likely a printer's error as Thucydides has only 8 books; the Melian Dialogue is in Book 5.</note>: that it is so arranged among men that while those of equal strength may dispute over what is right, the more powerful impose what they can, and the inferior do not refuse. (See other examples in Enenckel’s commentary on Thucydides, page 618). These, I say, are the outrages of tyrannical domination rather than things worthy of the name of "right." They have their beginning with Nimrod <note>A biblical figure traditionally described as the first king and an archetype of the tyrant who rules by force.</note>, that powerful ruler. If we were to use such arguments, all equality and justice among men would already be abolished. Truly, according to Augustine, because of this wickedness, "great kingdoms are but great robberies." <note>original: "magna Regna propter hanc vitiositatem, magna latrocinia esse." A famous critique of unjust government from St. Augustine’s *City of God*.</note>

VIII. From what has been said so far, it further follows that the crime of <term>Majesty</term> <note>original: "Majestatis"; here referring to "crimen laesae majestatis" or high treason, the ultimate crime against the sovereign power.</note> is committed...

### Political-Legal Dissertation

...the Crime of Treason <note>original: *Majestatis Crimen*</note>, not only against the Roman Emperor; but also against any Republic <note>In this context, *Respublica* refers to any organized independent state or commonwealth.</note> whatsoever that does not recognize a superior: whether it uses Justinian law <note>The *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the fundamental body of Roman law codified under Emperor Justinian I, which served as the basis for much of European legal theory.</note>, or not. This is supported by Master Bocer <note>Heinrich Bocer (1561–1630), a prominent German jurist and professor at Tübingen.</note> *On Regalian Rights, chapter 3, number 307; and volume 1 On the Crime of Treason, number 28.* Also Sixtin <note>Regner Sixtinus (1543–1617), a legal scholar known for his work on public and regalian rights.</note> *volume 1 On Regalian Rights, chapter 4, number 19.* Master Plebst, *Feudal Dispute 2, thesis 66.* Johann Camman, *Dispute 10, thesis 26.* Theodor Petrei, *in the Treasury of Criminal Conclusions, thesis 77.* On the contrary, Master Harpprecht <note>Johannes Harpprecht (1560–1639), a significant commentator on the Institutes of Justinian.</note> *at paragraph 3, number 19, etc. of the Institutes on Public Judgments.* see also Nicolaus Bethsum, *On Family Pacts, page 427, etc.* Nor does it hinder the argument that Master Reinking <note>Dietrich Reinkingk (1590–1664), a jurist who strongly defended the supreme authority of the Holy Roman Emperor over other European kings.</note> *book 1, class 3, chapter 11, page 81* says: That the Emperor alone possesses Majesty; because other Kings are addressed as "Your Royal Dignity" <note>original: *Ewer Königl. Würde*</note> and not "Your Majesty" <note>original: *Ew. Majest.*</note>, etc. For the essence is not in the name, but in the power; and this regards greatness, not superiority. And it is a most widely accepted rule, among both political theorists and legal experts, that Kings who do not recognize a superior are Monarchs within their own kingdom; and that the titles of Emperor are appropriate for them. Petra, *On the Power of Princes, chapter 3, question 4.* Piso Soacius, *Treatise on the Comparison of Roman and Venetian Magistrates, number 16.* Moditius, *in Decision section Law, doubt 4, from the beginning.* Arumaeus <note>Dominicus Arumaeus (1579–1637), a pioneer in the study of German public law.</note> *Feudal Dispute 3, thesis 12 and 13.* Myself, *On Appeals 2, number 2.* So also, it is a general and well-worn axiom among both political thinkers and our legal experts, that regarding a people or a city that knows no superior, the same judgment is held as for the Roman Prince <note>Referring to the Emperor as the "Princeps" or first citizen, following Roman tradition.</note>, and that they possess as much—and sometimes even greater—power within their own domain than the Emperor does throughout the Roman World, which I stated in my *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 2, page 23.* He who does not recognize a superior in his own territory has the same Sovereignty <note>original: *Imperium*</note> as the Prince has universally. There is no difference from the Supreme Prince except by reason of a smaller scope, just as a skiff differs from a ship. Pruckmann <note>Friedrich Pruckmann (1562–1630), a Brandenburg jurist and statesman.</note> *On the Law of Women, page 132.* For a King is a Monarch in his own kingdom. Said Afflictis, *chapter 1, number 8, On the New Form of Fidelity.* Chasseneuz <note>Barthélemy de Chasseneuz (1480–1541), a French jurist who analyzed local customs and sovereignty.</note> *in the preface to the Customs of Burgundy, on the word "Duke," number 3.* Schneidewin <note>Johannes Schneidewin (1519–1568), an influential commentator on the Institutes.</note> *part 5, On Fiefs, number 64.* The Princes of other nations who do not recognize a superior also have their own regalian rights <note>The specific rights, honors, and powers reserved for a sovereign.</note> and rights of Majesty, and indeed by their own right, as Gabriel says, *Roman 5, conclusion on the title of Acquiring Ownership, conclusion 3, number 3, etc.* Vultejus, *On Fiefs 1, chapter 5, number 7, in the section "to others also."* Rudinger, *Observations, page 268.* All those who are supreme, and above whom there is no other on this earth, and who know no superior Lord or external greater jurisdiction, can equally grant regalian rights. Sixtin, *volume 1 On Regalia, number 16.* Clarus, *section "Fief," 10, question 10.* Knichen, *On Saxon Non-Provincial Law, on the word "Dukes," chapter 1, number 6.* Plebst, *Feudal Dispute 2, thesis 33.* Conversely, such a King or people who has no superior, even if they should plot something with hostile intent and fraud against the Roman Emperor, they are not said to commit the Crime of Treason <note>original: *Crimen Majestatis*</note> or High Treason <note>original: *Perduellio* — specifically treason involving a hostile act against the state or sovereign to whom one owes allegiance.</note>. Bocer, *chapter 1, On the Crime of Treason, number 19 and following.* Just as likewise...

### On Sovereignty in General

Sovereignty <note>original: *Majestas*</note> is correctly attributed to any Commonwealth <note>original: *Respublica*; used here to mean any independent political entity.</note>; likewise, the rights of sovereignty are wrongly ascribed only to a Monarchical state, contrary to the common opinion of the learned Doctors of law. Johann Camman, *Dispute 1, thesis 104.* Since, therefore, both Aristocracy and Democracy possess sovereignty, if their dignity is harmed, it is rightly said that a <term>crime of Majesty</term> <note>Lese-majesty or high treason; an offense against the dignity or authority of a sovereign power.</note> has been committed. Who, indeed, unless they are a total stranger to political science, would deny that the Roman people, before the *Lex Regia* <note>The "Royal Law" by which the Roman people theoretically transferred their original power and sovereignty to the Emperor.</note>, possessed the most absolute and properly named sovereignty? I have argued this myself in my *Economy, title 3 and 4, question 9, at the end*, noting that they rightly punished the crime of high treason <note>original: *perduellionis*; an ancient Roman term for treason against the state.</note>.

Indeed, Theodorus Marcilius <note>A 16th-century humanist scholar and commentator on Roman law.</note> *in his preface to the Institutes, page 5*, seems to speak against the clear light of day when he denies that Romulus and the other Roman Kings possessed their own sovereignty. He argues this on the grounds that everything was governed by the Kings "by hand" <note>Meaning direct, personal rule rather than through institutional law.</note>; and yet, to govern all things by a Kingly hand is actually the greatest expression of absolute sovereignty. Furthermore, such a Crime is committed against a Kingdom or a free Republic regardless of whether it employs Justinian law or not; it even applies if the state is "infidel," or outside the Christian religion. For kingdoms exist by the <term>law of nations</term> <note>original: *jus gentium*; a concept of international law thought to be common to all human beings.</note>, and our Savior commanded that the things which are Caesar's must be rendered unto Caesar, even though Caesar was at that time a worshiper of idols. Sixtin, *book 1 on Regalian Rights, chapter 4, number 19.*

IX. What then shall we answer if a Prince professes to be a Client <note>A "client" state or ruler is one that seeks the protection of a more powerful patron while technically remaining distinct.</note> of another? Shall we still assign the rights of sovereignty to him? Truly, the jurist Proculus *in law 7, on captives*, says that a free people is one that is subject to the power of no other people, even if they are federated. This remains true whether they entered into friendship through an equal treaty, or if the treaty included a clause that this people or Prince should "courteously preserve" <note>original: *comiter conservaret*</note> the majesty of the other people. This phrase implies a mark of respect shown to a superior that is not unworthy of a free people; as Brissonius notes in *book 2 on Formulas*, this is added so that it is understood the other people is superior, not so it is understood that the first people is not free. For an alliance does not grant jurisdiction, nor does it bring about subjection to the party one is joined with. This is based on Baldus and Waremundus, *book 1 on Treaties, 3, number 45.*

There are, of course, two proper types of treaties: one is equal, made for the sake of friendship, where the allies stand in equal honor. This occurs when those equal in war settle on terms regarding the return of captives or the surrender of cities on fair conditions, as noted in *the law on petitions and the law on captives*. Or, it occurs when those who were never enemies join together in a social treaty to establish friendship. The other type of treaty is unequal, when an agreement is made that one people shall courteously uphold the power of the other people. In this treaty, some degree of subjection and surrender may be detected. And although in this regard I might easily agree with Machiavelli and Waremundus, *book 1, final chapter on Treaties, number 4*, that under the sweet appearance of friendship and most useful clientage, smaller powers are easily oppressed by the greater and can be reduced to servitude; nevertheless, I do not approve...

### A Political-Legal Dissertation

...I [cannot] agree <note>The text begins mid-sentence; the previous page likely ended with "non" (not), forming "non queo" (I am unable).</note>, with what has commonly pleased the commentators: namely, that an allied people commits the <term>Crime of Majesty</term> <note>original: *Majestatis Crimen*; high treason or an offense against the dignity of the state.</note> against the Emperor or the Roman people if they plot anything. On this matter, see Master Bocerus, *Treatise on Majesty, chapter 1, number 445.* Nor am I pleased by what jurists of great name believe: that the Crime of Majesty is committed if a foreign people, who are bound by a specific agreement to "courteously preserve" the majesty of the Roman Empire, stirs up any action against the Emperor or the Roman Empire.

This, I say, cannot be defended by legal or political reasons. For he who is not a subject by reason of his own person does not commit the Crime of Majesty. <note>original: *c. pastoralis... de sent. & re judic. in clem.*; referencing the Clementines, a collection of canon law.</note> Furthermore, such a people, who indeed observes the majesty of another people, is not a subject; rather, they remain a free people. <note>original: *d. l. 7. de captiv. & postlim.*; referencing the Digest of Roman law regarding captives and the right of return.</note> Therefore, the Crime of Majesty cannot apply to them. It is one thing to be obligated by treaty to preserve majesty, and another to be subject to that majesty; that people can act against treaties and conventions, but they do not truly commit the Crime of Majesty. In the same way, a **Vassal** acts against agreements when rising against his Lord, but he does not commit the Crime of Majesty.

And as for the fact that one people is sometimes said to be "superior" to another, this is not a matter of power—which is the same and equally supreme on both sides—but is a matter of the different respect or deference shown. Bornitius, *On Majesty, chapter 2, folio 8.* 

Among our Doctors of law, yet another species of treaty is posited, which Dionysius Gothofredus <note>A famous 16th-century jurist and editor of the Corpus Iuris Civilis.</note> recognizes <note>original: *ad d. l. 7. lit t.*; a citation to Gothofredus's commentary.</note>, which occurs when laws are given to those conquered in war, where everything is surrendered to the one who is more powerful in arms. But Waremundus <note>A pseudonym for the jurist Christoph Besold.</note> not undeservedly calls this type "miserable and lamentable." *ibid. chapter 4, number 6.* Livy records the formula for this in *Book 20*: "Are you the Legates and Orators sent by your people, so that you might surrender yourselves and your people?" "We are," etc. Such <term>surrendered people</term> <note>original: *dedititii*; individuals or nations that have unconditionally surrendered to Rome.</note> are not truly in an alliance, but are said to be under dominion; they are closer to captives than to allies, and they become almost tributary and tax-paying subjects. Cabotius rightly reckons that this kind of treaty should more correctly be called a law or the command of a superior. *Disputations, Book 2, chapter 10.*

To this species of treaty—where one is bound to "courteously preserve" the majesty of another—I believe the following are very closely related: **Protections**, **Clientages**, **Advocacies**, and the <term>Right of Protection and Defense</term> <note>original German: *Schutz und Schirms-gerechtigkeit*; a legal term in the Holy Roman Empire for the obligation of a lord to protect his clients or vassals.</note>. Master Dieter, *Basle Disputations 1, thesis 16.* In like manner, the one chosen as a protector does not obtain jurisdiction over the client, according to Gail, Bernhard Graeve, *Conclusion 54*, and Forster, *Part 2, Treatise on Jurisdiction, folio 473*, as proven in the title *on domestics and protectors, book 12 of the Code.* 

From this, Kirchner <note>Hermann Kirchner, a professor of history and rhetoric.</note> *Political Disputations, thesis 1, letter e.* affirms that the logic of Majesty does not diminish the right of the client, but rather preserves it for the client; and this applies regularly and universally to all Princes and Republics who commit themselves not to the power, but to the faith and protection of another, and that their majesty thereby...

...do not lose [their sovereignty], as Arnisaeus concludes and illustrates at length in chapter 4 of *On Majesty*. <note>original: *de Majestat.*; referencing Henning Arnisaeus (c. 1575–1636), a German political theorist.</note> But I have dealt with this matter myself in my *Treatise on Treaties*, and the Magnificent Lord Martin Magerus has surpassed everyone’s diligence in explaining the rights of <term>Clients</term> <note>original: *Clientum*; in this legal context, it refers to protected or subordinate states rather than individuals.</note> in his *Treatise on Armed Advocacy*.

I hold the same judgment regarding those who pay an annual pension to others so that they do not cause damage to the borders of their regions through raids. Such was the payment the Roman Emperor, in his capacity as King of Hungary, once provided to the King of the Turks <note>The Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.</note>. This Prince, mindful of his duty, takes on the role of a good <term>Head of the Household</term> <note>original: *patrisfamilias*; a Roman legal concept of a responsible leader who protects the family assets.</note>; sparing no expense, he averts damage that is otherwise inevitable. If Majesty were to suffer any loss here, then not even the Turkish Emperor himself—who is recorded to pay a great sum of money annually to the Tartars and those peoples who hold the mountains of Arabia—would possess it. See Soranzo’s *The Ottoman*, chapters 29 and 48, and I discussed this in my *Treatise on Appeals*, chapter 4, page 115. Thus the Romans once paid tribute to the Dacians (Soranzo, chapter 86). Hadrian also purchased peace from many kings, and he excused this by the example of Cato, who declared the Macedonians free because he could not hold them. (Aelianus Spartianus, in *Life of Hadrian*). Nor were those kings subjects who called themselves "servants of the Romans" (Montaigne, book 2, chapter 22) or others who called themselves "servants of Charlemagne" (Girard, volume 1, page 363).

### CHAPTER V.

## Since Majesty is the Supreme Command, what follows from it?

This supreme Right of the State is the most venerable source and fountainhead of all other powers within the State. Jean Bodin, *Method for the Easy Comprehension of History*, chapter 6, page 170. It is the basis and origin, both of jurisdiction and judgment, and of the magistracy and Command; and thus of whatever power exists in the same State. (Menochius, *On Presumptions*, book 2, 14, number 2; Mascardus, *Conclusion* 1054, number 2; Luis de Molina, *On Justice and Right*, volume 6, dispute 3; Gail, *On Public Peace*, book 1, chapter 11, numbers 4 and 5; Calvinus, *On Judicial Process*, page 227, numbers 14, 18, etc.; Wesenbeck, *Paratitla on Jurisdiction*, number 9). For absolute <term>Majesty</term> <note>original: *Majestas*; the highest legal authority or sovereignty.</note> represents the State itself, and all its dignity, strength, and power; and it is absolutely nothing else but the supreme power of all Law and Command, in any legitimate and separate State, according to the law of God, nature, and common policy. Just as the faculties of the soul, and all the senses and movements of the human body, proceed from the virtue of the soul and subsist within it, so from that sublime Command...

# On Majesty in General.

...they do not lose it, as Henning Arnisaeus <note>Henning Arnisaeus (c. 1575–1636) was an influential German physician and political philosopher known for his defense of absolute sovereignty.</note> concludes and illustrates at great length in *Chapter 4, On Majesty*. A Prince who is mindful of his duty here sustains the character of a **good head of the household** <note>original: *boni patrisfamiliâs*; a legal standard for responsible management.</note>; by sparing no expense, he turns away a damage that is otherwise inevitable. See Soranzo, *The Ottoman, chapters 29 and 48*, and I have discussed this in my *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 4, folio 115*. ### CHAPTER V.

## Since Majesty is the Supreme Power, what follows from it?

This Supreme Right of the State is the most venerable fountain and source of all other powers within the Republic. As Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist whose work *The Six Books of the Republic* is a foundational text on the theory of sovereignty.</note> writes in *Method of History, chapter 6, folio 170*, it is the basis and origin of both jurisdiction and judgment, as well as of the magistrate and the **Supreme Power** <term>Imperium</term> <note>Original: *Imperium*; refers to the formal power of command, particularly military or judicial.</note>; and thus of every power existing within the same Republic. See Menochius, *On Presumptions, Book 2, number 2*; Mascardus, *Conclusion 1054, number 2*; Ludovicus Molina, *On Justice and Law, volume 6, dispute 3*; Gail, *On Public Peace, Book 1, chapter 11, numbers 4 and 5*; Calvin, *On Judicial Process, folio 227, numbers 14, 18, etc.*; and Wesenbeck in the *Paratitla on Jurisdiction, number 9*. For absolute **Majesty** <term>Majestas</term> represents the Republic itself, and all its dignity, strength, and power; it is absolutely nothing else but the supreme power of all Law and Command in any legitimate and separate Republic, according to the law of God, nature, and common policy. It is not unlike how the faculties of the soul, and all the senses and movements of the human body, proceed from the virtue of the soul and reside within it. So too, from that sublime power—

<meta>This page continues the technical definition of "Majesty" (sovereignty). The previous page ended by stating that Majesty is the highest power, to which all other powers are inferior.</meta>

->### Political-Legal Dissertation<-

[...] sublime, and all other things are inferior to it, as Jacob Bornitius writes in *On Majesty, chapter 4, folio 16 & chapter 12, folio 105, etc.* See also my own treatise *On Appeals, chapter 2, under number 16, folio 60.* Just as all rivers originate from the Ocean and all flow back to that same source, in this same way—through various Investitures <note>The formal ceremony of transferring land or office.</note>, Commissions, and Grants—all jurisdiction proceeds from Majesty, and all returns to it through revocations, appeals, and so on. As William Onciacus notes in *Philosophical-Legal Questions, 29*: Truly, the duties, cares, and offices of majesty are so numerous that a Prince alone, or the people or the nobles together, are by no means able to perform them all by themselves. 

Therefore, Majesty (or the law representing majesty) can communicate its power and duties—and thus also its jurisdiction and Authority <term>Imperium: the supreme legal power to command and punish</term>—to magistrates and others in various parts, and distribute them both variously and most freely. However, it is also accustomed to take them away again, or to revoke them to itself either entirely or in part. Consequently, magistrates and prefects, judges and counselors arise in the Republic from Majesty as if from a primary spring, and they always depend upon it and cling to it with an inseparable bond. Moreover, whatever they are and whatever they rightly perform exists as something valid and firm only through the gaze and vigor of Majesty, which either commands or permits it. See Johannes Calvinus <note>original: "Calvinus"; referring here to the legal scholar Johannes Kahl (1550–1614), not the theologian John Calvin.</note> in *On Proceedings, folio 27 and following, and extensively on folio 404 throughout the entire chapter.* 

In this view, Etherius Mohr most aptly writes in his *Disputation on Jurisdiction, chapter 2, thesis 2*: Jurisdiction is viewed in a twofold way. First, insofar as it resides in the Supreme Prince, who acknowledges no superior; in this most general sense, it is called absolute and uncommunicated—the "lowest species" <note>In logic, a "lowest species" (infima species) is a category that cannot be divided further; here it means the core, indivisible essence of power.</note> which is not subdivided into other types. Second, insofar as it is communicated to inferior magistrates, and indeed from the Sovereign alone, either mediately or immediately. Hence it is also cautioned in Civil Law <note>The Roman law tradition.</note> that the jurisdiction or the power of judging cannot be granted to anyone by the mere consent of private individuals, nor can anyone become a Judge who is not already a Judge. *Law 3, Code on Jurisdiction;* Bronchorst, *1st Miscellany, Assertion 10.* 

By this same essential attribute of majesty, that common axiom is supported: however much someone may be invested in the most ample form, or however much jurisdiction is granted to someone, the one granting nevertheless always reserves the supreme jurisdiction to himself. See Petra, *On the Power of the Prince, chapter 9,* and as I said in my *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 2, section 16.* Thus, the Estates <note>The princes and cities that held seats in the Imperial Diet.</note> in the Roman Empire are said to have jurisdiction and autocratic command by their own right: not because they do not acknowledge their territories as being held from the Empire and the Emperor, but because jurisdiction adheres to those territories. They hold those territories from the Emperor irrevocably and exercise jurisdiction freely within them, yet they do so under the trust of the Empire and the Emperor.

II. To this belongs that famous question of Azo and Lotharius <note>Azo of Bologna and Lotharius were famous 12th-century legal scholars whose debate over whether the Emperor or the people held ultimate power became a cornerstone of Western political theory.</note>, ancient Legal Scholars, which they disputed before Emperor Henry VII.

<summary>This page explains that all legal authority and jurisdiction flow from the Sovereign (Majesty) like rivers from an ocean, and although this power is delegated to officials, the Sovereign always retains ultimate legal supremacy. It contextualizes this within the Holy Roman Empire, where local rulers hold power irrevocably but still technically under the Emperor's "trust."</summary>

->## On Majesty in General<-

...rules. <note>The text begins mid-sentence: "[he] rules."</note> Does the Emperor alone possess pure command <term>merum Imperium: the supreme power of the state, including the legal authority to execute capital punishment</term>, or do other magistrates have it as well? Indeed, when these two legal experts <note>Azo of Bologna and Lotharius, two famous 12th-century jurists who debated this point before Emperor Henry VI.</note> could not agree on this matter, they entered into a wager and left the judgment to the Emperor. Azo contended that pure command resides in the Emperor as if in a source, but that nonetheless other magistrates also possess this power. Lotharius, responding that only the Emperor has pure command and others have at most the exercise of it, won the wager. However, Azo's opinion was later accepted by the common consensus of the Doctors of law. Nonetheless, it is said from this that the Emperor ruled in favor of Lotharius, but did not judge fairly against Azo.

This much is true: Papinian <note>A celebrated Roman jurist from the 2nd century.</note> in *law 1, on the office of him to whom jurisdiction is mandated*, recognizes a difference between that jurisdiction which is specially granted by law, by a decree of the Senate, or by a decree of the Prince, and that which belongs to an official by right of his office. This latter is called "proper jurisdiction" in *law 4 of the same title; law 13 on the office of the proconsul; and law 5 where it says "by its own right" regarding jurisdiction*, because a magistrate can use that as if it were his own right. It is likewise certain that those who govern entire or whole provinces have the "right of the sword" <term>jus gladii: the authority to impose the death penalty</term>, according to *law 6, paragraph 8 on the office of the Governor*. Nor can that aforementioned *law 1 on the office of him to whom jurisdiction is mandated* serve as an argument for Lotharius. For while it is held there that magistrates have the exercise of "public judgment," this is expressly restricted in the same place to that jurisdiction which is granted by a specific law or individual decree; and this is contrasted with the jurisdiction that belongs to an official by right of his office.

Nevertheless, Lotharius’s decree is more consistent with political truth and the points established thus far: namely, that the Emperor alone has pure command, while the other magistrates of the Roman Republic have at most the exercise of it. See *law 4 on the office of the governor*; Jean Bodin in *Method for the Easy Comprehension of History, chapter 6*; Scipio Gentilis, *On Jurisdiction, book 3, chapter 3, page 348*, against Obrecht, *On Jurisdiction, chapter 4, number 77, etc.*; Doctor Bocer, *On Jurisdiction, 8, number 3*; Dominik Arumæus, *Discourse on the Principle Law 2, thesis 3 from the beginning*; Bronchorst, *1. Enantiophanon 15*; add Alciatus, *Parerga, book 2, chapter 6*; Bellonus, *Supputations, book 1, chapter 1*; Lyclama, *Membranarum, book 5, chapter 8*; and Tilemann, *volume 1, dispute 4, thesis 29*. 

For a magistrate has no right of his own, but his power is like a ray of light emerging from the brilliance of majesty. Jurisdiction and Command properly belong to the office of the magistrate; hence, some things are said to belong "by right of the magistrate." Yet, the office itself is usually given or taken away at the will of the Prince, or of the one in whom majesty resides, according to *law 1, at the beginning, on the Julian law regarding bribery*. Therefore, nothing but the exercise of power is transferred to the person. This is supported by the fact that the punishment of crimes and the power of the sword belong to the Prince alone; it is his alone to pass judgment on the life of a Roman Citizen, which previously was permitted to no one without the command of the people, according to *law 2, paragraph 16, on the origin of law*, who granted that command only precariously <note>original: "precariò"; meaning held by the favor of another and capable of being revoked at any time.</note>. From this, Joachim Stephan says in *On Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 2, number 6, 7, etc.*: "Just as the people," he says...

# A Politico-Legal Dissertation

...said, first that by its own right, the People <note>Referring to the Roman people during the Republic.</note> held **pure command** <term>merum Imperium: the supreme power of the state, including the authority to inflict capital punishment</term>, and this was granted to the Governors of Provinces through the Curiate Assemblies, and sometimes also the Centuriate Assemblies. Thus, when later all the right of the people was transferred to the Prince, the Prince by himself—or by right of his office—alone occupied this most full command. Although the Praetorian Prefect <note>The highest administrative and judicial official under the Roman Emperors.</note> also held the fullest power, or as Evagrius writes in *book 3*: <note>original Greek: κορυφαίαν τῶν ἀρχῶν</note> "the pinnacle of offices," it was nonetheless not given to him by the right of his magistracy, but by a special law. See Joachim Stephan, *On Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 3, number 25, etc.* Who says in the same place at *number 35*: Lotharius’s opinion seems not to be challenged if the state of the Roman Empire is considered as it was in the beginning, when all things were subject either to the people or to the majesty of the Prince, whether by right of **Patrimony** <term>patrimony: private inheritance or property</term> or the **Fisc** <term>fisc: the state treasury</term>; and those Provinces were administered by appointed governors and proconsuls, who held the exercise of power, but not the right of Command itself. For at that time, the Right always resided with the people or the Emperors.

But today, the form of the Commonwealth having changed, since Provinces have been converted into **Fiefs** <term>feuda: land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for service, becoming a form of private property</term>; these are no longer names of mere duty and administration as they once were, but of patrimony, nor can they be revoked, etc., as if granted by favor, but rather conferred by the right of contract. Add also Wesenbeck, *in the commentary on the office of him to whom jurisdiction is mandated, number 3 and following.*

### III.

Upon this same foundation is also built the following principle: That if Majesty should arrive in person, no magistrate may retain his jurisdiction unhindered, *based on law 58, On Trials; and law 5 of the Code, On the Office of the Governor of a Province.* Bodin, *On the Republic, book 3, chapter 6, number 313.* Hence, we find it sanctioned in **Saxon Law**, *Landrecht book 1, article 58: "In whatever land the Emperor comes, there the court is open to him, so that he may judge every complaint that comes before him, etc."* <note>original German: "In welch Landt der Keyser kompt/ daselbst ist ihme das Gericht ledig/ daß er alle Klag richten mag/ die vor ihne kompt/ &c."</note> For the supreme Prince always concurs with his inferiors and can precede them. Elbertus Leoninus, *Emendations, book 6, chapter 7.* In this sense, Pliny says most aptly in his *Panegyric, page 120 of Justus Lipsius's edition*: "The highest dignities of the Citizens are, as it were, depressed by the comparison of the Imperial height: and the closer they ascend to the greatness of the Prince, so much more do they seem to have descended from their own."

So it is that a Bishop, when a **Legate from the side** <term>Legato de latere: a cardinal sent by the Pope with the highest degree of authority</term> is present, cannot bless the people or carry his episcopal insignia. Giovanni Aloisio Riccius, *Ecclesiastical Practice, decision 570.* Likewise, a Patriarch cannot carry his cross in Rome. Nor do the Praetors of Cities carry the staff of justice when the Provincial Praetor is present. Rodolphus de Ducibus, *On the Leaders of Italy, number 342.* Thus, the Prince enters every Senate, but a superior Senator does not enter an inferior Senate. Langlaeus, *Semestria, book 7, chapter 15.* Not otherwise than by the light of the Sun, the other stars are obscured; and even when the Sun is below the horizon, they shine with no other light than that of the sun. So, when he who shines with Majesty is present, all other powers grow silent. Gunther, *in the Ligurinus, book 2.*

<note>original Latin: "Atque omnis Iudex, omnisq́; potestas, Atque magistratus, ipso præsente quiescant." This poetic legal maxim suggests that lower authorities lose their active power when the sovereign is physically present.</note>

See, however, Caspar Schifordegher, *book 3, treatise on the final question*, who teaches: that the Vicars <term>vicar: a deputy or official acting on behalf of a superior</term> of Princes nonetheless retain their ordinary **Jurisdiction** even when the Princes themselves are present. And add Dr. Bocer, *treatise on Jurisdiction, chapter 8, number 20*, who limits this same statement regarding those Estates of the Empire <term>Imperial Estates: the princes, prelates, and cities who held a seat in the Imperial Diet and were direct subjects of the Emperor</term> who have been irrevocably invested with their lands. From this, Klockh, in his *disputation on taxes, thesis 19*, relates that the Emperor cannot grant a toll or tax to someone that passes through another's territory. And in the *following thesis*, he says that the rule previously cited from **Saxon Law** <note>The *Sachsenspiegel*, the most influential legal code of the German Middle Ages.</note> now fails. For Princes and Counts, and other **Vassals** of the Empire, cannot be hindered by the Emperor in the exercise of their hereditary Jurisdiction, according to *title 7 on the nature of fiefs, book 1 of the Feudal Laws*.

So also the other Estates of the Empire hold their power even by an irrevocable privilege; they hold it not only from the Emperor, but simultaneously by the benefit of the Empire, and they are also considered to be members and parts of that Empire. And here it is doubted: Can the Emperor grant a pardon if someone commits a crime in the territory of another Estate? (And on this matter, I shall speak, God willing, *below in dissertation 3*, when I deal with the **Right of Majesty** regarding the granting of pardons for crimes.)

The people of Speyer <note>An important Free Imperial City where many diets and legal reforms took place.</note> have a singular Privilege, granted by Emperor Louis IV: *that no one who has been banished from their city because of their court's judgment shall be reinstated or brought back into it by the Imperial Majesty.* <note>original German: "daß keiner so ihres Gerichtes wegen verweiser ist vor ihrer Statt / von der Keys. Majest. u. wider darein gesetzt / oder darein geführt werden solle."</note> Christoph Lehmann, *book 7, chapter 21, folio 759*, and Charles IV confirmed this. See the same Lehmann, *in the same book, chapter 41, folio 787*. 

To this belongs what Ludovico Rodolphinus writes in *On the Dukes of Italy, number 81*: that in respect to the Duke of Milan, the Emperor is a **Private Person**, such that within that Duke's territory, he cannot speak the law or grant privileges. At *number 90* he says: the **Palatine Counts** <note>Officials of the Imperial court with the power to grant certain legal status, such as legitimizing children born out of wedlock.</note> of the Emperor cannot legitimize anyone in the lands of the Princes without their license; as he also relates at *number 92*: that some Princes of Italy made Decrees that no one may seek a privilege from the Emperor under the heaviest penalty. This same Rodolphinus, in the *following numbers*, treats this matter clearly; however, I do not think those points apply to the **Estates of the Empire**, who seem more strictly bound to the Emperor and the Empire. 

Likewise, it descends from the universal Jurisdiction of the Emperor that the **Imperial Chamber** <term>Imperial Chamber Court: the *Reichskammergericht*, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire, acting on the Emperor's behalf</term> and the Emperor himself, when they are present in the territories of the Estates, may summon persons by their own authority. Rodolphinus, *On the Dukes of Italy, number 101*; Ummius, *disputation 5, number 60, near the middle*. 

But whether today jurisdiction is presumed to be granted and transferred as "exclusive" or "shared" regarding the grantor or the ordinary official? Caspar Leipold teaches this in Arumæus, *discourse 13, question 1*; and Berlichius, *volume 1, chapter 2, conclusion*. And specifically, whether the Emperor runs concurrently in jurisdiction with the Estates of the Empire in their territories, consult the same Leipold, *question 3*, and Caspar Ziegler, *under the section "Territorial Resident," conclusion 1*.

# Political-Legal Dissertation

...conclusion 1, at the limit, in the beginning, page 190. Reinking, book 1, class 5, chapter 7. And furthermore, since as Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400) was a highly influential Italian jurist of medieval Roman law.</note> elegantly writes: "where the superior speaks, it is fitting for the inferior to be silent"; consequently, regarding crimes committed by the household members and attendants of the Prince within a city, it is not the city, but the superior Prince or his Councilors who ought to take legal notice. P. Heigius, question 25; and my own treatise *On the Law of Universities*, the final chapter, number 9, etc.

IV. Likewise, because **majesty** is considered the **highest power**, it is therefore far removed and different from the authority and power of other magistrates. This "height of power" must not be mixed with the commands of others. From this, more astute political theorists teach that a King or another supreme Prince is not correctly called a "supreme magistrate." <note>This distinction was crucial in early modern law: a magistrate is an official with delegated power, whereas a sovereign (Majesty) holds power inherently.</note> see law 3, *on Jurisdiction*. Arnold Clapmarius, *On the Secrets of State*, book 2, chapter 4. Vincent Cabot, *Disputations on Private and Jurisprudential Law*, book 1, chapter 7. Mr. Hilliger, in his commentary on Donellus, book 17, chapter 7, page 54 and following. Dissenting from this is Dr. Bocer, *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 8, numbers 53, 54, and 71. These same authors accurately distinguish between a King and even the highest magistrate. For to be a magistrate is either to perform ordinary **Jurisdiction** or to obtain **mere command** <term>mere command (merum imperium): the power of the sword, or the legal authority to inflict capital punishment</term>, law 13, *on Jurisdiction*, but not to possess majesty. 

And the word **magistrate**, according to Pomponius in law 2, *on the Origin of Law*, signifies anyone to whom the function of judging has been entrusted—not so that he might establish law (which is a perpetual right belonging to majesty alone), but so that he might state or administer that which has already been established. Thus, that command which a Governor held in a Province was the greatest of all others, according to law 4, *on the Office of the Governor*. But nevertheless, it leaves the majesty of the Prince far behind it. From this it appears that the rights of majesty differ entirely in kind from jurisdiction. Dr. Bocer, *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 1, number 43, and chapter 5, number 7. 

Cicero speaks distinctly and aptly in his speech *For Rabirius*: he assigns **command** to the magistrates, **authority** to the Senate, **power** to the common people, and **majesty** to the People as a whole. <note>original Latin: "Imperium cùm magis-tratibus, auctoritatem Senatui, plebi pote-statem maie-statem populo tribuit." Cicero was defining the balance of the Roman Republican constitution.</note> As for the fact that a certain "majesty" is attributed to the Roman Praetor as an official of the Republic (law 9, *on Jurisdiction*), that occurs through metonymy <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it.</note>, by which that which actually belonged to the people is applied (not unskillfully) to the magistrate who represented their majesty through his honorary legal function. Paul Busius, *Subtleties of Law*, chapter 2. Marcilius, at the preface of the *Institutes*, page 4. Dr. Bocer, *On the Crime of Majesty*, chapter 1, number 58 and following; and I have said as much in my notes on laws 8 and 9 of the *Digest* regarding justice and law, question 9. 

For almost the same reason, the power of certain magistrates was called "supreme." Tileman, *Disputation 2*, thesis 7, in the notes of volume 1. And majesty is said to be violated in the person of Councilors and others who are a "principal part of the body" <note>This refers to the legal fiction that the high-ranking advisors are limbs of the ruler's own body, meaning an attack on them is an attack on the sovereign.</note>, law *quisquis*, Code *on the Julian Law of Majesty*. Arnisaeus, *On Majesty*, book 1, final number. This is not because they have majesty in their own right, but because it tends toward the injury and contempt of the principal majesty if those who govern the people in the Prince's name are violated. Furthermore, majesty is above all ranks, from...

In the same way, the supreme Prince, since he is the source and foundation of honors, should not be considered a mere rank of honor himself. Just as it is said of a tree trunk, from which the branches spring; or of the number one, which is not a number itself, but the beginning of all numbers. <note>The author uses classical mathematical and natural metaphors: a source is fundamentally different from the things it produces. Just as "one" is the root of mathematics but not a "count" in the same way three or four are, a King is the root of the law but not a "rank" within it.</note> Piso Soacius, *On the Comparison of Roman and Venetian Magistrates, number 15.* Likewise, therefore, even the elites in an Aristocracy are not magistrates, as Philipp Hænon teaches in his *Political Disputations, 10, theses 12 and 38.* Frizius also teaches, in the works of Arumæus, *Discourse 16, thesis 18. b. page 440*, that the Emperor is not to be numbered among the ranks of honors, but is rather the summit of all honors.

### CHAPTER VI.

## That Majesty is Perpetual Power.

I added to the definition of Majesty that it is a **perpetual Power**. For truly, power cannot be "Supreme" unless it is also perpetual. Bornitius, *this work, chapter 8 from the beginning, and chapter 11.* By "perpetual," we understand that power which is not terminated or defined by any span of time, but as it is born with the Empire, so it dies with it. In democratic and aristocratic forms of government, this power lasts as long as the state itself, until it vanishes, is transformed, or the state itself is changed—even though the individual persons who hold that power may die and be replaced by others. <note>This refers to the legal concept of corporate continuity: the state or "office" remains the same even when the people occupying it change.</note> *Law "proponebatur" 76, on Trials.* In a Prince, that perpetuity is understood to last as long as he lives (as in the *Law of the Digest, on partnerships*), or even forever: either by reason of the status and form of the Empire, or in respect to a family to whom the Right of succession belongs. 

Therefore, he to whom supreme power is committed only for a time, or for the performance of certain tasks, is not a King; rather, he should be called a "supreme Magistrate." Those to whom supreme power is granted for some brief time do not properly possess **Majesty**. Instead, they should only be called "guardians of the supreme Power and Empire" and "Curators of the Commonwealth." Bodin, *On the Commonwealth, book 1, chapter 8, from the beginning.* Richard Dieter, *Disputation on Majesty, thesis 18, which is the first in the Basel Disputations, Camman 1, thesis 63.* Thus, someone can possess the highest legal right and yet still lack Majesty. *Law 2, section 16, on the Origin of Law.* Bornitius, *On Majesty, book 2, page 7.* For this reason, neither was a **Dictator** in the Roman Republic a King, even though supreme power was entrusted to him for a time. *Law 1, Digest, on the office of the Praetorian Prefect.* Nor among the Aedui <note>The Aedui were a powerful Celtic tribe in Roman Gaul.</note> was the **Vergobretus** (<gloss>Chief Official</gloss> <note>original: "Werckoberster"</note>: from which the term <term>Master Builder</term> <note>original: "Bawmeister," here used to mean a high civic magistrate</note> is still used in some places for a principal Magistrate) a King, though he was created there annually and held power over life and death. Vincent Cabot, *Disputations on Various Public and Private Law, book 1, chapter 7, from the beginning.* The same was true for the Consuls.

<summary>This page defines Majesty as a "perpetual" power that exists independently of the individuals holding it, distinguishing true sovereigns from temporary officials like Roman Dictators or Gallic Vergobrets.</summary>
