### Political-Legal Dissertation

...als for the Roman Consuls, before the Valerian law regarding the right of appeal <term>provocatio<note>The right of a Roman citizen to appeal a magistrate's decision to the people for a final judgment.</note></term> was passed; nothing of the royal power was taken away from them, except for the fact that their command was annual. *Digest on the Origin of Law, section 16.* Dieter, *Disputation on Majesty, thesis 19.* Coras, *On the Duties of the Consul, number 2.* And although later—so they would not possess royal power in all things—it was enacted that there should be a right of appeal from them, nevertheless, business was occasionally given to them by the Senate with the instruction <note>original Latin: "viderent ne quid Respublica caperet detrimenti"</note> that they "should see to it that the Republic suffered no harm"; and at those times they wielded the greatest power both at home and abroad. Coras, *in the cited place, number 4.* I also discuss this in my *Treatise on Appeals, book 2, chapter 5, from the beginning.*

II. And so Aristotle is in error when he claims that the <term>Aesymnetae<note>An elective office in ancient Greece where a ruler was granted absolute power to restore order or conduct a war, often described by modern scholars as a "constitutional dictatorship."</note></term> of the Greeks—who were chosen by vote to complete some business or a war, and were called "Rulers" or "Commanders"—were Kings, and reckons them among Monarchs. *Politics, book 3, chapters 10 and 11.* For indeed, one does not deserve to be called a Monarch or a participant in Majesty if the people or the nobles can abolish his command at their pleasure; or if, when the predefined time has elapsed, he himself is forced to abdicate. From this, our legal doctors equally slip when they say that the Roman people, if they wish, can take away or revoke the Prince's command. See Zasius *on the law "it is not doubted," 9, in the Digest on laws.* This is because when the People transferred majesty to the Prince, it became perpetual in itself and by its own nature: hence it is said in the *sole law on the office of the Praetorian Prefect* that the governance of the Republic was perpetually transferred to the Emperor. Likewise, I think they are true Monarchs who, by the vote of the People, become absolute rulers for life; contrary to Bornitius, *this work, chapter 11*; such as Caesar, who was made perpetual Dictator. However, nothing prevents a King from voluntarily abdicating his command and consigning it to the people, the estates, or a legitimate successor. The most illustrious Lord Lansius *in his consultative oration for Germany, page 83*, and Lord Hilliger *on Donellus, chapter 17, page 55.*

III. Therefore, those who have the administration of the Empire while the throne is vacant are not endowed with Majesty: such as, in the Roman Empire <note>Referring to the Holy Roman Empire</note>, the Elector Palatine (in the region of the Rhine, <gloss>and where one uses the Franconian Law</gloss>) and the Duke of Saxony (in lands living under Saxon Law). *Golden Bull of Charles IV, title 3.* Goldast, *Imperial Constitutions, Latin volume 2, on the articles of obligation of the Roman King, number 22, page 141.* I also discuss this *in my legal-political disputations on succession and election, book 3, last dissertation, number 3 and following.* Dieter, *Basel Disputations, 1, thesis 21.* Thomas Michael, *Disputation on Jurisdiction, thesis 29, from the beginning.* Likewise, Majesty does not belong to those who—either because the Prince is absent, a minor, or not in control of his mind—administer the Republic and are called Viceroys, Governors, or Regents of the kingdom. Vincent Lupanus, *Treatise on French Magistrates, book 1, title: Regent of France.* Dieter, *disputation on majesty, thesis 20.* Nor can the King of the Romans himself take this power...

### C H A P T E R VII.

-> *On Power Exempted from the Laws.* <-

It has been deduced above that Majesty is the supreme power of commanding, and that it recognizes no superior and possesses no equal. From this, it necessarily follows that the Prince, the Senate, or the people—to whom this supreme power belongs—are clearly bound by no laws, just as they are bound by no foreign rule. For one is not supreme who has either a law or a man above him. Hence Ulpian <note>A celebrated Roman jurist, c. 170–223 AD.</note> declares in *Law 31 of the Digest, on Laws*, that the Prince is released from the laws <note>original Latin: "legibus solutum"</note>. "Wherever the word of the King is, there is lordship, and who shall say to him: 'What are you doing?'" says the Wise Man. *Ecclesiastes, chapter 8, from the beginning.* Thus also speaks our Emperor <note>Referring to Justinian I, whose legal codes were the foundation of law in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, in *Novel 105, chapter 2, section 4, at the end*: "God has subjected the laws themselves to the Emperor, sending him to men as a living law." The Prince takes the place of the entire law. *Code, title on testaments, law 'of all'.* And majesty is worth more than the laws.

Therefore, supreme Command is also released from the laws: for a Prince cannot be bound by his own laws, since he is not inferior to himself, and laws are only issued by a superior to inferiors. Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, an influential Jesuit theologian.</note>, *On the Roman Pontiff, book 2, chapter 27, toward the end.* And also, as someone once wittily said, the "imperative" mood lacks a first person <note>A grammatical joke: one cannot command oneself; an imperative command is always directed at another.</note>. Mathesius, *on the 19th chapter of Sirach, folio 144.* On this matter our Doctors <term>Doctors of Law<note>The high-ranking legal scholars of the era.</note></term> disagree in various ways: Master Harpprecht *on the beginning of the Institutes, on the division of things, number 124, etc.*; Master Bocer, *Treatise on Investitures, chapter 3, number 78, etc.*; Master Thomas Lansius, a most distinguished man in every respect, *in his elegant discourse on the Royal Law, thesis 58, etc.*; Paurmeister, *On Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 6*; the most learned Bachovius, *on the Disputations of Treutler, 1, folio 24, etc.*; Henricus Scotanus, *Disputations on the 1st book of the Code, thesis 3 and following*; Master Johann Camman, *Disputation 1 on the Right of Majesty, thesis 28, etc.*; Valentin Forster, *Treatise on Roman Jurisdiction, on the second Law of Romulus, number 7 and following*; Martin Antonio Delrio, *Miscellanies on Law 31, on laws*; Hackelman, *Illustrious Questions 1, thesis 10*; Hilliger, *on Donellus, commentary 1, chapter 17, letter A*; Arumæus, *Public Law, volume 2, discourse 14*; Andreas Gerhardi, *Disputation on the Institutes 1, thesis 7*; Piccolomini, *Moral Philosophy, grade 10, chapter 9*; Ohemius, *Discourse on Consuls, chapter 1, number 14, etc.*; Keckerman, *Practical Disputations 29, problem 11*; Henricus Velsten, *Century of Political Questions, decade...*

# Politico-Legal Dissertation

8. *Thesis 6 of Lord Valentin Riemer, decade 1, thesis f. 7.* I myself, in my *Economy, titles 3 and 4, book 1, forensic questions, question 1,* have noted that there are almost as many opinions on this question as there are heads of those who have taken it up. From the decision on this matter depends the resolution of almost infinite controversies (which seem to many to be more difficult than the **Gordian Knot** <note>An ancient metaphor for an intricate problem solved by a bold action.</note>). The connections of these controversies remain hidden and entangled within themselves unless this difficulty is either untied or cut through. I am of the opinion—supported by political thinkers and jurists of the better sort—that a double power must be granted to those who possess **Majesty** <term>Majestas: the supreme, sovereign authority of a state.</term>: namely, an **Ordinary** power, which conforms to the laws, or *political* (that is, simply Civil); and another **Extraordinary** power, which is anomalous, or *architectonic* <note>Refers to a "master" power that organizes all others.</note>, or Civil *nomothetic* <term>Nomothetic: the power to establish or create laws.</term>, and released from the laws, which is commonly called the **fullness of power** <note>original Latin: "plenitudo potestatis"</note>. 

*Reverend Father Martin Becanus, in Scholastic Theology, on laws, chapter 6, question 12; Alberico Gentili, Royal Disputations, 1, folio 28; Author of the Antimachiavel, 1, theory 1, folio 60, etc.; Johann Dauth, in the explanation of law 3, Code on Testaments, number 2, folio 398; Henning Arnisaeus, on majesty 1, chapter 3, folio 50; Ludovico Rodolphini, treatise on the absolute power of the Prince, chapter 1, number 3, etc.; Petra, on the power of the Prince, chapter 2, against Covarruvias, Pinellus, and others cited by Pedro Agustin Morla, Emporium of Law, part 1, question 1.* 

See also what I have said in *On Appeals, chapter 1, near the end.* There are those who teach that the name of **absolute power** is contrary to the law and should be completely banished by jurists; but just as these authors do not wish to give absolute power to the Prince lest he fall into sin, so those who do grant absolute power give it to him only so that he may be able to do good, as I shall discuss below.

II. If we look at the **Ordinary** power of majesty, it is considered to be regularly subject to all laws. It is even bound by its own laws and those enacted by itself, according to *Law 6 on the Law of the Treasury; Law 6, section 1, on conditions and demonstrations; Law 7 of the Code, on those who can make testaments; the last law of the Digest, on the same; the second to last law on the institution of heirs; Law 4 of the Code on the Falcidian Law; Law 8, section 2, on inofficious testaments* <note>A legal term for a will that fails to provide for close family members.</note> and similar passages. *Bornitius, here in chapter 10.* For this power is the **executor**, not the **destroyer** of laws. And this power is what is meant by all those places in the **Justinian** legislation where it is said that the Prince is indeed bound by certain laws: such as the **Falcidian Law** <term>Lex Falcidia: A Roman law requiring that a testator leave at least one-fourth of their estate to the legal heir.</term>, the **Glycian Law**, and others. *Following Bartolus, Salicetus, and others. Alberico Gentili, Royal Disputations, 1, folio 28.* 

Indeed, I cannot see why any sane person should doubt or ask whether a Prince should regularly enjoy a legacy without the burden of the **Falcidian Law**, or enjoy an inheritance from an imperfect testament, by virtue of "released power." For there appears to be no reason at all why such an "exorbitant right" should take place there; moreover, since such a power is arbitrary, it does not admit a certain rule. Truly, it is characteristic of Empire to live according to the laws (*Law 2, Code on Testaments*), and it befits such great majesty to observe the very laws from which it might seem to be released. (*Law 23 on Laws, 3.*) Truly, Gothofredus, to *seem* and to *be* are different things.

The author argues that while a sovereign may technically be above the law, it is the mark of true majesty to live according to the laws they have established.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and philosophical inquiry into whether a sovereign (the Prince) is bound by the laws of the state. ### On Majesty in General

...Gothofredus <note>Denis Gothofredus (1549–1622) was a famous jurist who edited the *Corpus Juris Civilis*.</note> in his notes on Law 16, Code, on the military testament, states that the word "to seem" is sometimes a word of fiction and signifies an impropriety. See Calvinus, **Lexicon, under the word "videri" (to seem).** Therefore, the Prince **seems** to be released from all laws; but it is "shameful," as the jurist Paul says in the cited law, to claim legacies or trusts from an incomplete testament. For this would lean toward the Prince's private benefit and would not procure the welfare of the Commonwealth. And so, although the Prince may **seem** not to be bound by all laws and in all cases, in the truth of the matter he is constrained even by civil laws, unless the safety and necessity of the Commonwealth <term>Respublica: the state or public welfare.</term> should desire and demand otherwise. 

To this also contributes what is said: that it is a "voice worthy of the majesty of the one reigning" for the Prince to profess himself bound by the laws (*in Law 4, Code, on Laws*). This is the same as what the Divine Severus and Antoninus wrote in a rescript: "Although we are released from the laws, nevertheless we live by the laws" (*Section "fin." Institutes, on the ways testaments are invalidated*). Hence Apollonius of Tyana in *Philostratus, Book 8*: "When these things are said about the laws," he says, "if you do not think they command you, you yourself shall not command." *Pliny, in his Panegyric on Trajan* <note>Trajan (reigned 98–117 AD) was often held up as the model of a "constitutional" emperor who respected the law.</note>: "In the rostra, with similar devotion, you, Caesar, subjected yourself to the laws—laws which no one wrote for the Prince, but nevertheless you wish nothing more to be permitted to you than to us." 

Tiberius <note>Emperor Tiberius (reigned 14–37 AD) is often portrayed by historians like Tacitus as a master of political simulation and hypocrisy.</note>, who expressed the character of a good Prince in his words and by feigning virtue, when he had forbidden statues to be placed for himself by edict, added a prescription in these words: *Unless I permit it; and yet, I will not permit it.* Xiphilinus, in that passage, distinguishes between the apparent and the true interpretation of the Prince. From this it also happens that in many cases the Prince uses the same law as everyone else (*Novell 89, chapter 11; Law 31, Digest, on who can make a testament; Law "penultimate," on appointing heirs; Law 15, Digest, on the condition of an institution; Law 23, on legacies 3; Law 60, on conditions and demonstrations; Laws 6 and 22, section 2, on the law of the fisc; Laws 2 and 3, Code, lest the Fisc or the Commonwealth...*).

But here I cannot help but note the error of those who distinguish the supreme power and the Majesty of Empire from the will, humanity, and goodness of the Prince—those who separate the question of the Prince's will from the question of obligation. They say there is no obligation. They claim the "will" looks only to the modesty and goodness of the Prince, so that he might think "not everything that is permitted is honorable," etc. This opinion is erroneous and lays the foundations of tyranny. Humanity and goodness are an inseparable accident and a proper <note>original Greek: πάθος (pathos), meaning a fundamental attribute or property.</note> of power released from laws. Honorableness ought to be the indivisible companion of the will; the bond of obligation is most tight, by which the Prince is bound to modesty and goodness. 

And the Prince is released from the laws only conditionally for a certain cause—namely, for the sake of public safety. Therefore, if a release is given conditionally, and the condition does not occur—that is, if public safety does not require it—the release must be considered revoked. Raudensis, *book 1 on analogy, chapter 37, number 4.* For a "condition" is a quality by which something is "conditioned," that is, made into an act. Alciatus, *on the law "to a debtor," Code, on pacts*; and what is placed in a condition is not in the disposition (*Law "if anyone under a condition," Digest, if anyone having omitted the cause of a testament; Law "that damage which," penultimate section*).

<summary>This page argues that while a sovereign may be technically "above the law" (legibus solutus), they are morally and legally bound to follow it unless the public good necessitates a departure. The author warns that separating sovereign power from the obligation to be good and honorable leads directly to tyranny.</summary>

# Politico-Legal Dissertation

### [Section] 8. 
As noted in *thesis 6 by Lord Valentin Riemer, decade 1, thesis 57*; and by myself in my *Oeconomia, titles 3 and 4 of book 1, on the first question of the Pandects* <note>original: "ff. quaest. 1." The "ff" refers to the Digest or Pandects of Roman Law.</note>; there are nearly as many opinions on this question as there are heads of those who have taken it up. From the decision on this matter depends the resolution of almost infinite controversies—which seem to many to be more difficult than the famous Gordian Knot. The connections between these disputes remain hidden and entangled within themselves unless this difficulty is either untied or cut through. 

I am of the opinion, supported by political thinkers and jurists of the better sort, that those who possess Majesty <term>Majestas: the supreme authority or sovereignty of a state.</term> must be granted a twofold power: 

1.  **Ordinary power**, which conforms to the laws, or "political" <note>original Greek: "πολιτικὴν"</note> power—that is, simply civil authority. 
2.  **Extraordinary power**, which is anomalous, "architectonic" <note>In a philosophical sense, a "master-building" power that organizes all others.</note>, or "civil law-making" <note>original Latin: "nomotheticam"</note>, and is released from the laws. This is what is commonly called the **fullness of power** <term>plenitudo potestatis: the doctrine that a ruler has absolute authority over all legal matters.</term>. 

*See Father Martin Becanus, in Scholastic Theology, on laws, chapter 6, question 12; Alberico Gentili, Royal Disputations, 1, page 28; the author of Antimachiavellus, theory 1, page 60, etc.; Johann Dauth, in his explanation of Law 3, Code, on testaments, number 2, page 398; Henning Arnisaeus, on majesty, book 1, chapter 3, page 50; Ludovicus Rodolphinus, treatise on the absolute power of the Prince, chapter 1, number 3, etc.; Petra, on the power of the Prince, chapter 2, arguing against Covarruvias, Pinelus, and others cited by Pedro Agustin Morla, Emporium of Law, part 1, question 1.* 

See also what I said in my work *On Appeals, chapter 1, toward the end*. There are those who argue that the name "absolute power" is contrary to law and should be completely banished by legal experts. However, just as these critics do not want to give the Prince absolute power lest he fall into sin, so too those who *do* grant absolute power only give it to him so that he might be able to do good, as I shall discuss below.

## II. 
If we examine the **ordinary power** of majesty, it is considered to be regularly subject to all laws. It is even bound by its own laws and those passed by the ruler himself (*Law 6, On the rights of the treasury; Law 6, section 1, On conditions and demonstrations; Law 7, Code, On those who can make testaments; the final law of the Digest, on the same; the second to last law, On the institution of heirs; Law 4, Code, on the Falcidian Law; Law 8, section 2, on undutiful testaments, and similar citations; Bornitius, this chapter, 10*). 

For this power is the **executor**, not the **destroyer** of laws. All those passages in the legislation of Justinian <note>Justinian I (reigned 527–565 AD) was the Roman Emperor who codified the laws that form the basis of Western legal tradition.</note> should be understood as referring to this ordinary power—passages where it is said that the Prince is truly bound by certain laws, such as the **Falcidian Law** <term>Lex Falcidia: a Roman law requiring that a legal heir receive at least one-quarter of an estate, even if the will specified otherwise.</term> or the **Glycian Law** <note>original: "Glyciâ." Likely a reference to the Lex Glycia, a specific regulation regarding inheritance or public office.</note>, etc. 

Follow *Bartolus, Salicetus, and others; Alberico Gentili, Royal Disputations, 1, page 28.* Indeed, I cannot see how any sane person should doubt or even ask: should a Prince, by virtue of "released power" <note>original: "solutae potestatis," referring to being above the law.</note>, be able to take a legacy without the burden of the Falcidian portion, or regularly enjoy an inheritance from an imperfect testament? No reason appears there that would allow for this "out-of-the-bounds" law <note>original: "exorbitanti Juri"</note>; moreover, since such a thing would be arbitrary, it does not admit a certain rule. 

Truly, it is the characteristic of Empire to live by the laws (*Law 3, Code, on testaments*), and it befits such great majesty to observe the laws from which it itself might **seem** to be exempt (*Law 23, on laws, 3*). Certainly, the words "to seem" and "to be" are two different things, as Gothofredus notes.

<summary>The author argues that a sovereign possesses two types of power: ordinary power, which follows the law, and extraordinary power, which is above it. He maintains that while a Prince might technically be "released" from the law, he should still honor legal standards, especially regarding private matters like inheritance, to maintain the dignity of his office.</summary>

# On Majesty in General

Gothofredus, in his notes on the Code, book 6, title 16, *On the Military Testament*, <note>original: "thofr. in not. ad l. 16. C. de testam. milit." refers to the legal scholar Jacques Gothofredus.</note> observes that "to seem" is sometimes a word of fiction and signifies an impropriety. <note>original: "videri fictionis interdùm verbum est." In legal Latin, "videri" (to seem) often indicates a legal fiction where something is treated as true for the sake of the law even if it is not naturally so.</note> See also Calvin’s *Lexicon* under the word *videri*. Therefore, the Prince **seems** to be released from all laws; yet, as the jurist Paul says in the cited law, it is "shameful" to claim legacies or trusts from an imperfectly drafted will. For this would turn to the private advantage of the Prince rather than procuring the **welfare of the Republic**. And so, although the Prince may **seem** not to be bound by all laws in all cases, in the truth of the matter he is still bound even by civil laws, unless the safety and necessity of the Republic require otherwise.

To this also belongs what is said: that it is a "voice worthy of the majesty of one reigning" for the Prince to profess himself bound by the laws, as found in the Code, book 1, title 4, *On Laws*. This is the same thing that the Divine Severus and Antoninus wrote in a rescript: "Although we are released from the laws, nevertheless we live by the laws." <note>original: "licèt legibus soluti simus, attamen legibus vivimus." This is a famous Roman legal maxim expressing that a good ruler voluntarily submits to the law.</note> Hence Apollonius of Tyana says in Philostratus, book 8: "When these things are said concerning the laws, if you do not think they should command you, then you yourself shall not command." 

Pliny, in his *Panegyric* concerning Trajan, says: "In the rostra, with similar devotion, you, Caesar, subjected yourself to the laws—laws which no one wrote for the Prince, but nevertheless you wish nothing more to be permitted to yourself than to us." 

Tiberius, who expressed the character of a good Prince in words and by pretending, when he had forbidden by edict for statues to be placed in his honor, added a proviso in these words: "Unless I permit it—but I shall not permit it." Xiphilinus, in this passage, distinguishes between the **apparent** and the **true** interpretation of the Prince. Thus it also happens that in many cases the Prince uses the same law as everyone else. <note>The author here lists numerous citations from the *Novels* and the *Digest* (ff.) regarding inheritance, the treasury (Fiscus), and public law to show that sovereigns often operate under standard legal rules.</note> 

But here I cannot help but note the error of those who distinguish the supreme power and the Majesty of the Empire from the **will, humanity, and goodness** of the Prince; those who separate the question of the Prince's will from the question of legal obligation. They say, "There is no obligation. Let the will look to the modesty and goodness of the Prince; let him think that not everything which is permitted is honorable," etc. 

This opinion is erroneous and lays the **foundations of tyranny**. Humanity and goodness are an inseparable accident and a proper <term>essential quality</term> <gloss>original Greek: πάθος (pathos)</gloss> of a power released from the laws. Honor ought to be the individual companion of the will. The bond of obligation is most tight, by which the Prince is tied to modesty and goodness. 

The Prince is released from the laws only **conditionally**, for a certain cause—namely, for the sake of the public welfare. Therefore, since it was given conditionally, if the condition does not occur—that is, if the public welfare does not demand it—the exemption must be considered revoked. For a "condition" is a quality by which an act is established or performed. <note>Citing Alciatus and various sections of the Digest on the nature of legal conditions.</note> What is placed in a condition is not left to mere personal discretion.

### Political-Legal Dissertation

*...on the Rules of Law: a conditional disposition is not properly and simply such, but only in a certain respect.* <note>original: "det. de Reg. Iur. & conditionalis dispositio non est propriè & simpliciter talis; sed secundum quid." This refers to a specific rule of interpretation in Roman law.</note> *See also Book 1, § "if anyone simply," on Verbal Obligations; the law "this legacy" in Book 3 on Legacies; and whatever is granted for a specific cause ought to be regulated according to that cause.* I would never say that goodness, conscience, modesty, shame, and decency are foreign to the Majesty of the Prince. To me, it is one thing to ask what a Prince **can** do by his supreme power, and quite another to ask what a **good** Prince **should** do. A Prince who does something contrary to what befits a good Prince is not using his princely power—for no power has been granted to a Prince for the purpose of sinning—but is acting out of weakness and tyranny; for power must never be separated from decency. Finally, that opinion which claims the Prince subjects himself to the laws not by Right or by the precept of law, but merely by his own discretion, kindness, and humanity, can be refuted even by our own laws.

For in the Code, book 4, on the **Falcidian Law**, <term>lex Falcidia (the Falcidian Law) was a Roman law ensuring that a legal heir received at least one-quarter of an inheritance, preventing legacies to others from exhausting the estate.</term> the Emperor Alexander says: *Even in legacies given to the Prince, the Falcidian law rightly takes its place.* Here, the word **rightly** <note>original: "meritò"</note> is to be noted. For it is the same as saying "by Right," "by debt," or "as the law requires." This is supported by various legal precedents where "rightly" implies a legal necessity or a rational foundation. From this, it is said in the law regarding **undutiful wills**, <term>inofficiosum testamentum (undutiful will) was a legal challenge used when a testator unfairly excluded close family members from an inheritance.</term> that if the Emperor is appointed as an heir, the will can still be declared "undutiful"—that is, it can be challenged even if the Emperor is unwilling and resists. For a person is believed to be able to do what they can do even against an opposing party’s will. This is the view of Master Bocer on investments.

Nor can the opinion of Covarruvias stand, which he holds in his first re-reading of the chapter "Alma Mater." He releases Princes from the **coactive force** of human law <note>coactive force: the power of the law to compel or punish behavior.</note> and asserts that the Prince is only bound by a certain **directive force**. <note>directive force: the law as a moral guide that suggests the right path but lacks the power to punish the ruler.</note> This opinion is favored by Fachinæus and William Barclay in his work *Against the Monarchomachs*. <term>Monarchomachs (literally "those who fight kings") were 16th-century legal theorists who argued that the power of rulers is limited and that subjects have a right to resist tyranny.</term> This view is almost the same as the "error of the Greeks," who release the Prince from penal laws so that a Prince escapes all punishment for any crime he commits, as noted by Harmenopulus, Cujacius, and Vultejus.

III. But here I shall refute the opinion of those from whom I am forced to disagree for great reasons. For Cujacius, in his *Observations*, interprets Ulpian’s statement in the law "on laws" <note>original: "l. 31. de legibus"</note> as referring only to the **Lapsed Laws** of Julia and Papia. <term>leges caducariae (Lapsed Laws): Roman laws, specifically the Lex Julia and Lex Papia Poppaea, which penalized unmarried or childless individuals by diverting their inheritances to the state treasury (making them "caducous" or fallen).</term> He argues the Prince was released from these specific laws because Ulpian's statement was taken from a commentary on the Law of Julia and Papia, as the heading of the text indicates. However, this opinion is unworthy of being defended by a jurist of such great name. Indeed, the Emperor Justinian abolished the Lapsed Laws entirely, and yet, after this law was passed, he testifies in the **Novels** <note>Novellae (Novels): the "New Laws" issued by Justinian after the publication of the main Code.</note> that God subjected the laws themselves to the Emperor—surely not those laws which had already been abolished and from which all subjects were now already released. Furthermore, that method of arguing—the source from which the argument is drawn—

...then, according to his own opinion, Cujacius <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a towering figure in legal humanism who sought to reconstruct Roman law in its historical context.</note> takes an inscription from the Emperor himself; however, it was not approved, but rather utterly rejected. For indeed, solely out of reverence, the Emperor did not wish to commit the names of the legal experts to silence, but not so that anything could be inferred from it, or that some hidden meaning of a law could be extracted. *See § 10 of the Constitution on the Confirmation of the Digest.* Furthermore, they prove that the Prince is released not only from the laws of lapsed inheritances <term>caducaria (caducary laws) were Roman statutes that penalized those who remained unmarried or childless by making their inheritance "lapse" to the state.</term>, but from many other laws as well. *See Law 14, § 1 on Manumissions; Law 56 on Legacies, book 2; Law 3 of the Code on Testaments; and Law 23 on Legacies, book 3.*

Furthermore, there are those who believe Ulpian <note>Ulpian (c. 170–223 AD) was one of the most influential Roman jurists, whose writings form a large part of Justinian's Digest.</note> should be understood as speaking only of legal formalities, from whose observation they declare the Emperor to be free. *See Corasius, book 2 of Miscellanies, chapter 25; Donellus, book 1 of Commentaries, chapter 17; and Duarenus on the laws, chapter 5.* This opinion finds its foundation in the law *on the imperfect* <note>original: "l. ex imperfecto. C. de testam." referring to the Code of Justinian.</note> regarding testaments, where it is stated: "It has often been decreed that the Emperor cannot claim an inheritance from an imperfect testament." For although the **Royal Law** <term>lex Regia (the Royal Law) was the statute by which the Roman people supposedly transferred their legal authority and power to the Emperor.</term> released the Emperor from the formalities of the law, nevertheless, nothing is so characteristic of the Empire as to live by the laws.

From this, they argue by a "contrary sense": the Royal Law released the Emperor from legal formalities; therefore, he is not released from other laws. But this reasoning is perverse and not at all good. Indeed, an argument drawn from the contrary sense of a specific law existing in the Code is considered to carry very little weight. *See Vulteius on § "but also what to the Prince," number 7, on Natural Law; and Disputations, chapter 10; and Donellus on Pledges, chapter 16.* For Decrees are adapted to the specific cases proposed rather than being general edicts. Consequently, in this same law, when a dispute arose concerning a testament intended to follow formalities and was proposed to the Emperor, he could only respond regarding those formalities.

And although today those rescripts <term>rescripta (rescripts) were written answers from the Emperor to legal questions or petitions, which eventually took on the force of general law.</term> have the authority of a constitution, they differ greatly in the method of interpretation. Because they are adapted to the specific instance proposed, they do not contain general definitions of the law. *See Duarenus on the title of the Code: "If in a common and the same cause," etc.* Furthermore, this very law, from which they try to deduce that the Emperor is only released from formalities, actually proves the opposite. For in that law, the response is that the Prince is not so released from formalities that he can take something from a less-than-perfect testament.

And this rescript of the Emperor agrees perfectly with my opinion, by which I say that the Prince is released from the laws and their formalities; however, he cannot enjoy the benefits of a testament that does not conform to the laws. This is because this supreme power belongs to him not for the private utility of the Prince, but in view of public safety and necessity. Finally, therefore, this is our opinion, conforming to the authority of Politics and the law of Justinian: **The Prince is released from Civil laws.** <note>original: "Princeps legibus solutus est Civilibus," a famous legal maxim from the Digest of Justinian (1.3.31).</note> This law, speaking generally and placed under a general heading, must certainly be understood generally. Nevertheless, he cannot use that power unless necessity, or unwritten equity, or safety [demands] this...

Iur." referring to the Title 17, Book 50 of the Digest of Justinian.</note> and a conditional disposition is not properly and simply such, but only in a certain respect. *See Law 1, § "if anyone simply" on Verbal Obligations; Law "this legacy" on Legacies, book 3.* And whatever is granted for a specific cause ought to be regulated according to that cause. I would never say that goodness, conscience, modesty, shame, and decency are foreign to the Prince's Majesty. To me, it is one thing to ask what the Prince *can* do by his supreme power, and quite another to ask what a *good* Prince *actually does*. A Prince who does something contrary to what becomes a good Prince does not use his princely power—for no power was granted to the Prince for the purpose of sinning—but rather acts without restraint and tyrannically. Indeed, power must never be separated from decency.

Finally, that opinion which maintains that the Prince subjects himself to the laws not by right or by legal precept, but merely by his own choice, kindness, and humanity, can be refuted even by our own laws. For in *Law 4 of the Code on the Falcidian Law*, <term>The Falcidian Law (Lex Falcidia) was a Roman law ensuring that an heir received at least one-quarter of an estate, preventing it from being entirely depleted by individual legacies.</term> the Emperor Alexander says: "Even in legacies given to the Prince, the Falcidian Law *rightfully* has a place." Here, the word "rightfully" <note>original: "meritò"</note> should be noted: for it is the same as saying "by Law," "from duty," or "as the law requires." *See Law 51 at the beginning, On Partnerships; Law 17 on Proofs; Law 1 at the beginning, "By Command"; Law 1 at the end, On Public Places; Law 3, § 2 on Provisions; Law 4,* where it says: *it was rightfully established and has a reason.*

For this reason, it is said in *Law 8, § 2 on Undutiful Wills* <term>An "inofficious" or undutiful testament (testamentum inofficiosum) was a Roman legal challenge used when a will unfairly excluded close family members, treating the testator as if they were of unsound mind.</term> that if the Emperor is appointed as an heir, the will can be declared undutiful even against the Emperor's will and despite his resistance; for a person is believed to be able to do what they can do even if their adversary opposes them, etc. See Mr. Bocer, *on Investitures 3, numbers 81 and 83, and likewise 87.* 

Nor can the opinion of Covarruvias <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish jurist and bishop often called the "Spanish Bartolus."</note> stand, which he holds in *re-reading of chapter "Alma Mater," part 1, § 1, number 5,* who releases Princes from the coercive force of human law and asserts that the Prince is held only by a certain "directive force." This opinion is favored by Fachin, *book 1, chapter 2,* and William Barclay, *book 3, Against the Monarchomachs, chapter 15.* <note>The "Monarchomachs" were writers, originally Huguenots, who opposed absolute monarchy in the 16th century. Barclay coined the term while defending royal power.</note> This is almost the same as the error of the Greeks, who release the Prince from penal laws so that the Prince escapes all punishment for any crime he commits. See Harmenopulus, *book 1, title 1;* Cujacius, *Observations, book 15, chapter 30;* and Vultejus, *Institutes, § "but also what to the Prince," on natural law, etc.*

### A Politico-Legal Dissertation

...the demands of the people, *Law 15, on the condition of Institutions*, and I will treat this at length below. For this reason, **imperial rescripts** <note>original: "rescripta" - formal responses or decrees issued by the Emperor in response to specific legal questions</note> that are contrary to general law and public utility are declared void, as seen in *Law 6 of the Code, "If it contradicts law or public utility."* Consequently, it is never presumed that the Prince used this absolute power against reason, and in cases of doubt, his power is always brought back to the standard of justice. From this principle also descend the rulings of our legal interpreters: that the **"of his own accord" clause** <note>original: "Clausula motu proprio" - a phrase in a decree indicating the ruler acted on his own initiative, often used to bypass normal legal channels</note> does not take away a right already acquired by another person. 

Thus, when the **Treasury** <note>original: "Fiscus" - the private or state purse of the Emperor</note> or the Emperor's account succeeds to the right of a private individual, it exercises the rights of that private individual for the period prior to its succession. *Law 6, on the law of the treasury; Law 60, § 1, on conditions and demonstrations.* Nor can the Treasury, under the pretext of a debt, provide legal representation against private citizens. *See the entire title: "That the Treasury or the State...".* Furthermore, the Emperor by no means claims legacies or trusts from an **imperfect will**. <note>original: "imperfecto testamento" - a will that lacks certain legal formalities</note> *Law 23, on legacies 3; Law 3 in the Code, on testaments; Law 7 in the Code, on who can make a will; the final law in the Digest, on who can make a will.* The Emperor cannot be appointed as an heir simply for the purpose of a lawsuit. *The second-to-last law, on the appointment of heirs; Law 22, § 2, on the law of the treasury.* 

From this, it follows that the Prince is bound by the **Falcidian Law** <note>original: "lege Falcidiâ" - a Roman law ensuring that an heir receives at least one-quarter of an estate after all legacies are paid</note> if a legacy is left to him. *Law 4 in the Code, on the Falcidian Law.* And from this, if the Emperor is appointed as an heir, the will can still be declared **undutiful**. <note>original: "inofficiosum" - a legal claim that a will unfairly excludes close family members</note> *Law 8, § 2, on undutiful testaments.* Neither the Emperor nor the law can force a natural son into his father's legal power against his will. *Novell 89, chapter 11, from the beginning.* To this I also refer the conclusion of our interpreters: that **rescripts must be brought back to common law.** <note>original: "Rescripta ad jus commune reduci debere." This means special decrees should not override the general laws of the land.</note> *Guillaume, 1st observation, number 6.*

**IV.** However, although through those points which have been broadly deduced so far, the Prince regularly employs **ordinary law**: nevertheless, the Prince is released from legal formalities, as well as from the laws of **escheated property** <term>original: "caducariis" - refers to property that falls to the state when there are no valid heirs</term> and other similar matters, by both ordinary law and by a **singular privilege**. *Law 3, the section beginning "although," in the Code on testaments.* For it is fitting that the Prince has certain privileges, just as do the Clergy, Nobles, Scholars, Women, and Minors. Indeed, he who shines with **Majesty** <note>original: "Majestate" - the supreme authority or dignity of the sovereign</note> disdains to follow such trivialities of the law for the very best of reasons. 

For how would it not detract from such great authority if a Prince’s testament were declared invalid due to the lack of some formality received from civil law? *Mantica, On Conjectures of the Last Will, book 6, title 1, at the end; Menochius, counsel 351, number 8 and following; Sichardus on Law: "We sanction," in the beginning, number 18 and following, in the Code on donations; Rosenthal on Fiefs, chapter 12, conclusion 10, number 15; Pruckman on Regalia, the section on absolute power 4, chapter member 3, effect 1, page 645, and effect 2, page 661; Barry, treatise on successions, book 1, title 2; and my own work on succession and elections, book 1, dissertation 2.* Or if the presence of the Prince did not repair the lack of other formalities in the wills of private citizens? *Pruckman, same location, effect 3, page 677; Barry, same location.* Or if a legal recourse were granted against someone who buys from the Prince, or holds a case from the treasury? *Law: "Well from Zeno," in the Code on the four-year prescription.* Moditius *in decision § law doubts 83.* Or if a donation which the Prince bestows upon the **Empress**... <note>original: "Augustam"</note> *the second-to-last law in the Code on donations between husband and wife; Peck, on the testaments of spouses.*

*Book 3, chapter 26, or "toward the son."* Bernard Graeve, *Practical Conclusions, conclusion 38, number 25.* It would not be considered valid if **imperial donations**, or those made by private individuals to the Prince, were judged to require official records. *Law 34, section "excepted" and the following authorization in the Code on donations; Novel 52.* <note>The "Code" and "Novels" refer to the Body of Civil Law (Corpus Juris Civilis) compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note> However, the rule requiring donations to be recorded in official acts was introduced solely for this reason: so that otherwise, through secret frauds, anything might easily be fabricated to suit the convenience of a business deal, or what was truly done might be erased. *Law 27 of the Code on donations.*

Whether, however, one possessing **Regalian rights** <note>original: "jura Regalia" - the specific rights, such as coining money or taxing, that belong exclusively to a sovereign</note> can give a donation or establish a will without legal formalities, etc., is a subject of debate among Hartmann Pistor, *book 3, question 9;* Petra, *On the Power of the Prince, chapter 4, number 24;* Rosenthal, *chapter 12, conclusion 10, number 15, etc.;* Lord Bocer, *on donations, chapter 3, number 76, etc.;* Wehner, *Frankfurt Consultation 1; and myself, in a singular consultation inserted into my treatise on Subordinate Authority.*

Thus, minors are not admitted to honors. *Law 8 of the Digest on duties.* This does not concern the Prince due to a singular privilege; he is considered of age before others, and his guardianship ends at puberty in such a way that no curator or regent is given to him. Paul Montanus, *Treatise on Guardianships, chapter 37, number 68.* This is because, from an excellent natural character, the required number of years is unfairly demanded, and an education suited for one about to rule can easily supply the defect of age.

Hence, by the usage and law of the **Imperial Chamber** <note>original: "Camerali" - referring to the Reichskammergericht, the supreme court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, a minor reigning Prince is held to be an adult, and can be called into court on account of his advisors, by whose counsel he is deemed to act in all things. Therefore, what his age lacks, the fullness of counsel supplies. Rutger Ruland, *Decisions on Controverted Law, 5.*

Likewise, in marriages, those who possess majesty do not observe the **prohibited degrees** <note>Levels of kinship within which marriage is forbidden by the church or state</note> of relationship forbidden by positive law; the Emperor Isaac Angelus says this was approved by the Holy Synod. *Chapter 2 of his Constitutions.* And majesty has, moreover, other privileges based on nearly the same reasons. Gothofredus on *Novel 105* (which Ludovicus Bossius enumerates in his *Treatise on the Prince and his Privileges*, and Laelius Zecchus, *Politics, book 1, chapter 5, number 85*).

To this also pertains the entire title of the Code: *That the recovery of the Lord's property should not be barred by the prescription of time*, and likewise the title *On the privileges of the Lady Empress [Augusta], book 11.* There are others which Bornitius, *Treatise on Majesty, last chapter*, and Speckhan, *1, question 72*, recount.

Thus, it is also a privilege of the Prince that if he, or the **Treasury** <note>original: "Fiscus" - the public purse or the sovereign's financial office</note>, sells or gives away a thing, the possessor cannot afterwards be disturbed by the true owner of that thing. *The law "Well [enacted]" to Zeno, Code on the four-year prescription.* Tuschus, *letter E, conclusion 142 and following.*

These privileges, however, the Prince also grants to the **Empress** <note>original: "Augusta"</note>. *Law 31, § 1, on legacies; and myself, in my Economy, titles 3 and 4, book 1, question 7 at the end.* And therefore these differ from the **fullness of power** <note>original: "plenitudo potestatis" - the absolute sovereign authority to override laws</note>, which does not belong to her; nor should the regalian rights or the rights of the magistracy be granted to her, not even under the guise of a guardianship. Bodin, *On the Republic, book 1, last chapter, page 258 and following.*

Froissart states this elegantly in *book 1, chapter 119:*

> Sire, please do not hold any ill will toward me if I did not return immediately at the command of My Lady the Queen; for I hold my lands from you, and my oath of loyalty is to you, not to her. <note>original French: "Sire, ne me vueillez sçavoir nul mau'grè..." - Jean Froissart was a medieval chronicler; here he illustrates that feudal loyalty is owed to the sovereign, not his consort.</note>

The Empress <note>original: "Augusta"</note> possesses the same privileges as the Prince himself. For if something is bequeathed to the Prince, it is owed to his successor (should the Prince die before the person who made the will), because by a certain legal fiction, it is believed that the sovereignty <note>original: "principatus"</note> is never interrupted; however, this is not the case if something is bequeathed to the Empress. *Law 56 and following, on legacies, book 2.* And so the Empress has the same privileges as the Prince only insofar as they can apply to her and she is capable of holding them. An Empress does not succeed an Empress in the same way an Emperor <note>original: "Augustus"</note> succeeds an Emperor. The Empire can lack an Empress, but it cannot lack an Emperor, because the dignity of the Emperor does not die.

V. Truly indeed, just as the governance of God the Best and Greatest and the Empire of His Providence almost always follows the common course of nature—by which reasoning Scaliger defines Nature in *Exercise 188, section 1* as "the ordinary power of God"—yet meanwhile, as the author of Nature, He often spurns or neglects that same order. *Psalm 105, verse 37.* <note>The author likely refers to the Israelites leaving Egypt without any among them being feeble, or the halting of natural laws.</note> According to His wise and kindly omnipotence, He miraculously establishes and effects whatever He pleases; sometimes He even acts in a manner different from what He determined in His own promises, as Jehovah God. Alberico Gentili, *On Marriage, page 535.*

So likewise in the Republic, sometimes public favor and necessity reject the ordinary power that conforms to the laws. And for this reason, not without great justification, the supreme authority is equipped with that extraordinary and loftier "fullness of power" <note>original: "potestatis plenitudine"</note>. It is the image and pattern of God on earth—whence even Magistrates are called "gods" in Holy Scripture [Psalm 82:6], and Baldus called the Prince a kind of "bodily god" in his Republic (*Final section, on the prohibition of alienating a fief*), and Plautus, in the play *Casina*, calls him a "human Jove." This is so that whenever the safety of the people <note>original: "salus populi"</note>, public utility, necessity, the demands of justice, or a similar cause requires it, he can and should look out for everyone—as a "perpetual Consul of the Republic" (*Novel 105, chapter 2, near the end*)—and he can and must command for the common good at his own discretion, having set aside the "tips of the laws" <note>original: "Jurium apicibus," meaning legal technicalities or the strict letter of the law</note>. *Politics, chapter 7.* 

(Althusius disagrees in *chapter 9, page 123*, ascribing absolute power not to the personal Majesty of the ruler, but to the body of the "universal association"—though he will hardly win that argument.) It is necessary that somewhere in the Republic there be a power that is not only strong, but also free and released from the bonds of the laws <note>original: "legibus exsolutum," the root of the term "absolute"</note>. This power tempers or orders the Republic in every part; it can govern the state according to the whims of fortune, the storms of the times, and the movements of change. Otherwise, the state cannot be ruled. Many things must be left to the ruler's judgment, just as many things are left to a sea captain or even a father of a family, for whom fixed laws cannot always be prescribed. For if one is not released from the laws, how, I ask, can he handle the reasoning of the laws according to the variety of circum- <note>The text breaks here; the catchword indicates the next word is "circumstances."</note>

...of circumstances, and he will change and adapt them: <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing the idea that a ruler adapts to changing times.</note> Jean Bodin, *Book 1 of The Commonwealth, chapter 10.* Arnoldus Clapmarius, *On the Secrets of Commonwealths, book 1, chapters 11 and 12.* The Law speaks only in generalities; it is not tailored to specific events as they happen. Therefore, in any art, it is considered foolish to judge precisely according to written rules. Adam Contzen, *Book 7 of Politics, chapter 15, number 3.* This can be observed especially in the Faculty of Medicine. <note>Just as a doctor must treat the patient, not just follow a textbook, a ruler must treat the specific needs of the state.</note> And so in a Commonwealth, a command so strong and free is deemed necessary that it may sometimes prioritize individual interests over the common utility. <note>original: "singulorum commoda, communi præferat utilitati"</note> *Law 3, Code on the first-rank centurions, book 12.* Jacob Bornitius, *On Sovereignty, chapter 6, page 32.* Scipione Ammirato, *Discourse 4, section 7.* It is sufficient that this absolute power <note>original: "solutam hancce potestatem," referring to the concept of "legibus solutus," or being "released from the laws."</note> has one single law: namely, the safety of the people; which is why they rightly call it the supreme law. <note>original: "salutem populi... legem supremam"</note> To this pertains what is said in the *single Law, at the end of the preface, Digest on the office of the Praetorian Prefect:* A fuller license has been given for the correction of public discipline, and in *Law 3, on the office of the prefect of the watch:* He believed that protecting the safety of the Commonwealth belongs to no one more, nor is anyone else sufficient for that task, than Caesar. Laws were made for the sake of the Commonwealth, and so that it might be safe; the Commonwealth was not made for the sake of the laws. Therefore, the Prince must see to it that the Commonwealth suffers no harm, even if the strict technicalities of the laws are neglected. Laws ought to be established for what happens most often, not for things that might happen unexpectedly or by chance in a single case; legislators pass over what happens only once or twice. *Laws 2, 3, and 6, on laws.*

No laws can be written in such a way that they encompass all cases that might ever arise, whether regarding public or private law. *Laws 10 and 12, same title.* Therefore, it is plainly necessary that there be a power in the Commonwealth that can either decide cases not settled by law or, as the occasion demands, do, forbid, or permit something against the tenor of the laws for the sake of some common utility. *Argued from Laws 11 and 16, same title.* This is what Aristotle hinted at in *Book 3 of The Republic, chapter 7:* He says that beneficial laws ought to prevail, and that the person who presides—whether it be one person or many—should have the supreme power in those matters which the laws cannot possibly provide for, since it is not easy to explain everything and every detail. Other magistrates must always follow the laws; but the Prince, if he judges it to be in the interest of the Commonwealth, follows only the dictates of reason and the rules of virtue, disregarding the laws.

It is absurd to say that the law dominates sovereignty itself, since no laws can exist in a Commonwealth unless they are promulgated by the sovereign power. For no one can impose a law upon himself from which he is not allowed to withdraw, *Law "if anyone" in the beginning, on legacies, book 3;* and Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist (c. 170–223 AD).</note> and others deny that anyone can impose a law on themselves, *Law "that however," section "to the wife," on donations between husband and wife; Law 40, final section, on the freedom of trusts.* No one can command themselves, nor can anyone forbid themselves from doing something, *Law "if concerning his own property," on the undertaking of arbitrations,* and Bornitius, *chapter 8.* And although it is said in the Praetor's Edict that it is fair that whatever rule a person believes is fair for another, he should allow to be valid for himself as well, *Law "this edict," section 1, Digest, that which anyone [establishes as a law for another...]* But concerning the Praetor...

...this must be understood as referring to a magistrate who, after completing his term of office, can be called to court to answer for his actions. Sovereignty is by no means included in that category. <note>original: "majestas minimè continetur"</note> Henning Arnisaeus, *Book 3, number 7.* <note>Arnisaeus (1570–1636) was a German physician and political theorist who defended the idea of absolute monarchy.</note> A Praetor, upon laying down his magistracy, becomes a private citizen and is like any other private person; however, there can never be any comparison or proportion between the person who holds sovereignty and a subject. A private person is bound by the laws, but the Prince governs the laws themselves. And so, this **power released from the laws** <note>original: "legibus soluta potestas," the roots of the modern concept of "absolutism."</note> extends to the correction of laws and the enactment of new ones, as well as the disregarding of established laws in specific cases. Hence it is said that the primary goal of sovereignty is to animate the entire Commonwealth with that supreme command. Jacob Bornitius, *Chapter 5.* For what the Pilot is in a ship, or what the primary source of motion is in a clock, such indeed is the Prince, who is formed by sovereignty. The analogy of this power, which is free from any external bond (as I have already hinted above), is evident in the father of a household (from which "family" is derived—called a "tiny Commonwealth" by Apuleius, and the father its Prince). <note>Apuleius, *On the Doctrines of Plato*, or perhaps referencing the Digest law "familia."</note> He alone in his family commands the household members, nor does he receive the law from anyone else, whether wife or children; and he revokes or limits his own orders if it seems right to him. Therefore, that sovereignty is "released" is required not only by its very nature but also by its practical use and purpose. Jean Bodin, *On the Commonwealth, book 1, chapter 10.* Arnoldus Clapmarius, *Book 1, chapters 11 and 12.*

### VI.

From what has been said so far, it soon becomes apparent to what extent, where, and when a Prince, a senate, or a people should or can use that supreme power. For since this power was invented and granted for the sake of securing the safety of the Commonwealth with greater ease, it does not extend to harmful or unjust acts; nor should any privileged power be assigned to a Ruler for the purpose of doing wrong. This is because those things which **were introduced for a single purpose** <note>original: "ad unum introducta sunt finem"</note> ought not to produce the opposite result. *Law "Eleganter" 23, section "if anyone after" 3, at the end, Digest on the recovery of undue payments; Law "Legacies uselessly" 19, at the beginning, Digest on legacies 1; and Law "When such" 71, final section, Digest on conditions and demonstrations.* Hartwig Pistoris, *Book 1, question 48, number 8.* Furthermore, those things established for the growth of the Commonwealth ought not to provide an occasion for its diminishment. Cacherano, *Legal Counsel 40, beginning with the words "having seen." number 16.* Thus, the form of this extraordinary right is to decree for the public good, even against common law and private interest. **"He who wishes to do right on a large scale is forced to do wrong in the details."** <note>original French: "Il est forcé de faire tort en detail, qui veut faire droict en gros." From Michel de Montaigne’s *Essays*, Book 3, Chapter 13.</note> It is such that it sometimes seems to present a certain appearance of unfairness; yet this is repaid by the public utility. Bornitius, *Chapter 29.* Hence Ludovicus Rodolphinus <note>A 17th-century Italian jurist.</note> defines "fullness of power" as the derogation (or partial repeal) of common or ordinary law: a fullness of judgment subject to no necessity and limited by no rules of public law. *See also his Chapter 5,* where he teaches at length what that power effects. Finally, I take the words of the **Royal Law** <note>original: "legis Regiae." The *Lex Regia* was the Roman law by which the people supposedly transferred all their power and authority to the Emperor.</note> written for Vespasian to refer to this: that whatever [he deems] to be for the utility of the Commonwealth and the majesty of things divine, human, public, and private...

<summary>This page argues that sovereignty is an absolute power "released from the laws" (legibus soluta), comparing a Prince to a ship's pilot or a father. It asserts that while this power allows a ruler to override common law, it must always be used for the public good and the safety of the state.</summary>

## Concerning Majesty in General

[...and he] shall be considered the master of all things; to him shall belong the right and power to act and to do, just as it was for Augustus, etc. <note>original: "uti Augusto fuit." This refers to the *Lex de Imperio*, or the law that transferred the power of the Roman people to the Emperor.</note> as cited from *Antonio Agustín* and *Albericus Gentilis, Disputations on Royal Power, 1, folio 32.* The public speakers of the schools are accustomed to show us an elegant example of this right, when they introduce the Emperor Augustus speaking about the will of the poet Virgil:

> *Did he give these works only to perish? If it is even right to say so of the man himself.*
> *But the faith of the laws must be preserved: what a final will*
> *Mandates and orders to be done, it is necessary to obey!*
> *Yet let the venerable power of the laws be broken instead,*
> *Rather than having one single day consume the labors*
> *Gathered over so many nights and days.*
> <note>This famous anecdote recounts how Virgil, on his deathbed, ordered his unfinished epic, the *Aeneid*, to be burned. Augustus intervened, overriding the legal sanctity of a "last will and testament" to save the masterpiece for the sake of the public good.</note>

VII. This power, the **Right of Dominion** <note>original: "jus Dominationis"</note> (whence even the Emperors are addressed as "Lords," according to *Bulengerus, On the Roman Prince, book 1, chapter 36*), this force of power is called by the Italians the **Reason of State** <note>original: "Ragion vel Ragionamenti di Stato"</note>; as if you were to say the "right of the public good." Hence it is also named the **Political Right** <note>original: "δίκαιον πολιτικὸν" [dikaion politikon]</note> by Aristotle, as cited by *Clapmarius, book 4 on Secrets, chapter 2.* It is likewise called the **Royal Hand** <note>original: "Regia manus"</note> by the legal consultant Pomponius, *law 2 on the Origin of Law*; and by *Albertus Bolognetus, Treatise on Law and Equity, chapters 10 and 13*; and *Joachim Stephani, book 3 on Jurisdiction, chapter 2.* For the "hand" is taken to mean power, according to *law 4 on Justice and Law.* **State** <note>original: "Status"</note> is the proper suitability of any thing in its own condition: *the proper suitability of each one in his own state* <note>original: "conveniencia propria de cada uno en su estado"</note> as noted by *Perez in his Aphorisms, folio 171.* And the "Reasons of State" are the means by which this suitability is kept safe and sound, as argued by *Canonhiero in his Introduction, chapter 10, and as I have said in my Treatise on the Secrets of Republics.*

VIII. But by reason of this extraordinary power, Majesty is **released from the laws** <note>original: "legibus soluta"</note>—but only from **Civil laws** <note>man-made statutes of a specific city or nation</note>; not from Natural laws, nor from the original Law of Nations <note>original: "Gentiumve jure primævo"</note> as noted by *Camillus Borellus, Treatise on Magistrates, book 2, chapter 1.* Because these laws were established by Divine Providence, those who command and those who are subjects are equally bound to obey them. Whoever attempts to break or weaken these shall not escape the judgment of Divine Majesty. <note>Citing various legal authorities including Bodin and Vultejus.</note> In the view of divine law, natural law, and right reason, the one who commands is considered not as a Prince, but as a man, in which regard all men are equal among themselves. <note>This is a crucial limitation on absolutism: while the King is above human law, he is not above God or the moral laws of nature.</note> This is discussed by the illustrious *Enenckelnus, book 1 on Privileges, chapter 8, number 16.* Hence, natural law is said to be "indispensable" <note>meaning it cannot be set aside or granted an exemption</note>. For this reason, in ancient times, Dionysius replied to his mother when she made an unjust request: "The law of the City can indeed be changed, but the law of nature cannot," as recorded in *Plutarch's Sayings.* Considering these things, Canute, King of Norway, Denmark, and England, placed his throne on the shore...
<note>King Canute (Cnut the Great) famously set his throne by the tide to prove to his flattering courtiers that even a King's power is nothing compared to the laws of nature and God.</note>

# Political-Legal Dissertation

[...the King] ordered [his throne] to be placed or set up on the shore of the sea, and addressing the sea, he said: "You, sea, are under my dominion, and the land on which I sit is mine; I command and proclaim to you, do not rise onto the land, nor wet the clothes or limbs of your Lord, nor soak your Ruler with moisture." <note>This is the famous story of King Canute the Great (r. 1016–1035), a Viking king of England, Denmark, and Norway. He staged this scene to prove to his flattering courtiers that a king's power is nothing compared to God's.</note> The sea, not at all terrified by this voice, soaked both the land and the King's feet, whereupon the King cried out: "Let all inhabitants of the earth and the whole world know that my sovereignty is vain, my commands are vain, and the power of my kingdom is vain; and let them resolve that no one is truly worthy of the name of King except Him at whose nod the sea grows still and all elements obey." **Eberhard von Weihe**, *On the Vanity of Human Glory, folio 95.* And that the highest Princes are not released from the laws of nature is also apparent from this: because they are generally of shorter life. **Sánchez de Arévalo**, *The Mirror of Human Life, book 2, chapter 4.* For this reason, Emperor Frederick III used to say: that he loved those counselors who feared a Prince no more than they feared God. **Aeneas Sylvius** <note>Also known as Pope Pius II (1405–1464).</note>, *in the Parallels of Alfonso.*

IX. From this, furthermore, it immediately follows that if sovereignty proceeds from the people, the Prince is in no way released from the laws of the Empire—that is, the **Fundamental Laws** <note>Fundamental laws (leges fundamentales) were the constitutional rules that defined a state's structure, which the ruler was not allowed to change unilaterally.</note>—or the laws of the State; which I also stated above in *chapter 1.* Namely, the people are not considered to have transferred all power, as they either implicitly or explicitly withheld some from the beginning; just as terms added immediately to a contract shape it and give law to the agreement. **Schrader**, *Treatise on Feuds, part 2.* **Tiraqueau**, *On Both Forms of Withdrawal, part 1.* It is indeed very dangerous, as Jean Bodin says in *chapter 6 of his Method*, for a King to be created in such a way that he is bound by no laws at all, but conducts everything according to his own whim and judgment; since it could easily happen that such sovereignty degenerates into tyranny. Therefore, a statesman in the founding of a State should provide in a timely manner that every occasion for tyranny is prevented. This is achieved not so much by choosing a "good" Prince, as by arranging the system properly so that the government does not escape into tyranny; or if it turns that way, it may be countered in time. This can best be guarded against by Imperial laws and pacts, which are considered the law regarding the "form of majesty" that shapes the Prince. And therefore, if a Prince were to strive to overturn them, he would consequently throw himself, the Princedom, and the public safety into turmoil. **Bornitius**, *chapter 9.*

The Duchy of Württemberg, through the singular providence of God, possesses many such laws above others; the principal ones among them are the *Erection* (or the Imperial Diploma) by which the ducal dignity was conferred upon Eberhard I, as well as the <term>Treaty of Tübingen</term> <note>original: "Tübingische Vertrag." Signed in 1514, this treaty is often called the "Württemberg Magna Carta." It granted the people (the "Landschaft") significant rights and control over taxes in exchange for paying the Duke's debts.</note>, etc. So much so that Keckermann, in his *Politics*, reckons the state of that Duchy among the aristocracies. And furthermore, he who is elected Prince is not placed outside the limits of Nature, nor is he counted among the ranks of the Gods. Even Alexander the Great, regarded by his followers as a God, later laughed at the divinity and descent from Jupiter Ammon ascribed to him after he was wounded in a certain battle, [realizing his mortality] by the recognition... <note>original: "agnatio-" catchword for "agnitione sanguinis" (by the recognition of his blood).</note>

->### On Sovereignty in General<-

I 2
<meta>catchword: because</meta>

...[desi]gnation. Therefore, he who commands is bound to observe the law of nature, that is, right reason. I call that **natural law** <term>jus naturale: the universal rules of conduct believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason</term> which is contained in the Law and the Gospel (*Canon Law, Distinction 1, Canons 1 & 2*), by which everyone is commanded to do to another what they wish done to themselves, and is forbidden from inflicting on another what they would not wish for themselves. And divine law and the law of nature—or right reason—are the same, as argued by **Alberico Gentili** <note>An Italian jurist and one of the founders of international law (1552–1608).</note> in *On Marriages, folio 552, etc.* Let those words not be heard from a King which Pharaoh spoke in response to Moses: <note>original: "Quis est Dominus ut audiam vocem ejus?"</note> *Who is the Lord that I should obey his voice?* (Exodus 5:2). The law of Emperors is not above the law of God, but beneath it (*Canon Law, Distinction 10, Canons 1 & 2*). The Prince acknowledges himself subject to these laws (*Code of Justinian, On Legitimate Heirs; On Adoptions*); "there we agree with nature" (*On Bishops; On the Rules of Law*). Hence, he who refuses to obey laws passed against the will of God does not deserve punishment, but earns a great reward (*Distinction 9, Canon 1*). For one must obey God rather than men.

Whether **Sovereignty** <term>Majestas: the supreme authority of a state</term> is released from the **law of nations** <term>jus gentium: the customary law practiced by all civilized nations, often seen as a bridge between natural law and specific civil laws</term> is a question not without reason for doubt. Very often in our law, natural law and the law of nations are treated as the same (*On the Acquisition of Ownership; On the Rules of Law*). Likewise, civil law is sometimes substituted for the law of nations (*On the Rules of Law, law 32*). Under civil law, slaves are said to be treated as "nothings" <note>original: "pro nullis haberi"</note>, yet it is stated in more than one place that slavery was introduced by the law of nations. 

Therefore, whatever **Bronchorst** <note>Everard Bronchorst (1554–1627), a Dutch jurist.</note> and others may argue to the contrary, that which we call the Law of Nations must be divided into "Primary" and "Secondary" categories. For certain things ascribed to the Law of Nations proceed from simple natural reason, which Nature implanted in man at his first creation to serve as norms for distinguishing between the honorable and the shameful. Examples of this include religion toward God, **duty** <term>Pietas: a sense of obligation and devotion to God, country, and family</term> toward Country and Parents, the rule not to harm another, and the rule not to grow rich at another's loss (*On Justice; On the Recovery of Undue Payments*). 

This commonly called "primary" Law of Nations, I have indicated above, is Divine and Natural. Because these things were implanted in the human mind by natural law before any nation existed, they are more rightly called "Natural" than the "Law of Nations," for they stem from a more powerful and ancient cause. See the illustrious **Enenckel** <note>Georg Acacius Enenckel (1573–1620), an Austrian jurist and historian.</note>, *On Privileges, book 1, chapter 8, number 31, etc.* Distinct from this are wars, **slavery** <term>servitutes: here referring specifically to the condition of being enslaved as a result of war, a standard concept in Roman law</term>, and other things which men established by common consent through reasoning, usage, and the demands of human necessity. Who, unless deprived of reason, does not see that these are clearly different from the former and must therefore be separated from one another? 

Therefore, I assert that whatever the Law of Nations has prescribed by following nature binds the Prince as well, both by the compulsion of Natural Law and the persuasion of public consent. If, however, any sort of consent has introduced something against nature, the Prince ought to correct it (**Enenckel**, *chapter 8, number 50, etc.*). If something was found by the demanding usage of Nations, if the usage of his own particular Commonwealth demands it, he can disregard it...

<summary>This page argues that the Prince is legally and morally bound by Natural and Divine law, which are equated with "right reason." It distinguishes between "Primary" Law of Nations (inherent morality) and "Secondary" Law of Nations (man-made customs like war), asserting the Prince must uphold the former.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and political argument regarding the limits of a ruler's power. # A Political-Legal Dissertation

...because in law, the specific rule always takes precedence over the general rule, and in this consists the reason and necessity of **Civil Laws** <term>Leges Civiles: the specific laws established by a particular state for its own citizens</term>. Similarly, the "secondary" law of nations rightly recedes at times from natural equity; a most brilliant example of this is found in **prescriptions** <term>praescriptio: a legal rule where a right is gained or lost over time, similar to a statute of limitations</term>. It is not because it agrees with nature that someone should be enriched at another’s loss <note>original: "ne quis cum alterius damno locupletetur"; see Law 14, On the recovery of what is not owed; Law 6, at the end, On the law of dowries; Law 206, On the rules of law</note>, nor because it is equitable that what belongs to us should be transferred to another without our own action <note>Law 11, On the rules of law</note>. Rather, the **public utility**—specifically, the need to prevent property ownership from remaining uncertain and to ensure that lawsuits are shortened—must outweigh private interest. As **Vultejus** <note>Hermann Vultejus (1555–1634), a prominent German jurist.</note> notes on the *Institutes, section "but natural [things]" regarding usucaption*.

Therefore, it remains for us to say with **Dio** <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian (c. 155–235 AD).</note> in *Book 53*, that "those who rule are released from the laws" <note>original: "legibus soluti sunt Imperitantes"</note>. This means they are free from any necessity imposed by the laws: they are not constrained by any written constitutions, though they are certainly not exempt from laws innate to nature or introduced by the common consent of all nations. The **Prince** <term>Princeps: the sovereign or supreme ruler</term> is released from **positive law** <term>jus positivum: man-made laws enacted by a legislator</term>, because such law is established or set aside according to the will and judgment of the legislator, as stated by **Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French political philosopher who defined the concept of sovereignty.</note> in *On the Commonwealth, Book 1, Chapter 8*, and Vultejus in his *Institutes on natural law*. This is what is properly called "law" <note>Institutes, Book 1, Section 6; Digest, Law 1, On liberty; Code, final law, On the same</note>, and it differs entirely from **natural law** <note>Code, Law "We command" 37, On Bishops</note>. Indeed, the ruler is bound by natural law insofar as it rests upon reason or natural equity, or follows necessarily from it. This is argued by **Covarruvias** <note>Diego de Covarruvias (1512–1577), a Spanish canonist and jurist.</note> in *Various Resolutions, Book 3, Chapter 1, Number 8*, and **Antonius de Petra**, among others. For natural equity does not become "Civil Law" simply because it is reduced to writing, just as a custom remains a custom even if it is committed to paper.

**X.** From what has been deduced so far, it should be clear to everyone what answer we might expect to the following question: In the degrees of kinship prohibited by **divine law** regarding marriage, can a **dispensation** <term>dispensatio: an official exemption from a law or rule</term> granted by any man have a place? On this, see **Beust**, *Treatise on Marriage, Chapter 56*; **Beza**, *Treatise on Divorce and Repudiation, page 75*; **Covarruvias**, *Part 2 on Marriage, Chapter 6, Section 9, Number 10*; **Zepper**, *On the Mosaic Laws, Book 1, Chapter 10, Number 2*; and **Arithmaeus**. Regarding **Cambyses** marrying his sister, see **Gothofredus** on *Law 8 of the Code, On incestuous marriages* <note>Cambyses II of Persia famously married his sister, a case often used by jurists to discuss whether a king's decree can override natural taboos against incest.</note>. 

Meanwhile, however, the one enjoying supreme power "determines" natural law, and by applying it, effectively changes it <note>Law 6, On Justice and Law</note>. **Sarmiento** and **Bortius** (cited in **Arumaeus**) agree on this point. In this respect, some say that **Sovereignty** <term>Majestas</term> may even dispense against Divine law <note>Lancellotus in "The Temple of All Judges"; Vasquius in "Illustrious Questions," Number 18</note>. For a dispensation is a "rational tempering" of the law. However, as to whether the Prince is bound by the **secondary law of nations**, consult **Benedict Winckler** in *Treatise on the Principles of Law, Book 4, Chapter 13*. **Cravetta** also teaches that the Prince cannot contravene those things which belong to the law of nations.

<summary>This page discusses the legal maxim that rulers are "released from the laws," clarifying that this applies to man-made (positive) law but not to natural or divine law. It specifically explores whether a sovereign can grant dispensations for marriages prohibited by divine law, weighing the ruler's power to interpret natural equity against universal moral constraints.</summary>
