# On Majesty in General.

->I 3<-

XI. And since no human **Power** <term>Potestas: legal authority or force</term> is infinite, as **Tobias Paurmeister** <note>Tobias Paurmeister (1553–1608), a German jurist and statesman.</note> writes in *On Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 3, number 11 and following*, even this supreme right has two boundaries: internally, the **conscience**, and externally, **shame** <note>original: "pudorem"; refers to a sense of social decency or public honor</note>. The golden rule of the jurists <note>original: "JCtii l. 15. de condit. instit."; referring to the Digest of Roman Law, 28.7.15</note> imposes obedience to these laws—namely Natural and Divine Law, or the Primary Law of Nations, which is right reason—upon the Prince as much as upon the subjects. We must believe that we are incapable of doing those acts which offend **Piety**, our reputation, or our sense of modesty; and to speak generally, those things which are done against **good morals** <term>bonos mores: the established social and moral standards of a community</term>.

XII. Furthermore, that extraordinary **Power**—in view of which **Majesty** <term>Majestas: the supreme authority or sovereignty of a state</term> is considered "absolute" by all positive law <note>original: "l. 31. de legib."; a reference to the Roman law principle that the Prince is not bound by the laws</note>—is only to be used as a last resort. It should be employed only when, because of the strictness of legal mandates, the **public safety**, or truth, or justice would be endangered. <note>The author cites several legal authorities here, including Bacchovius, Treutler, and his own previous works on the "economy" of law.</note> If such a cause is absent, even those who hold majesty are bound by the **Civil Laws** which can be applied to them directly or at least by analogy, as **Bornitius** <note>Jacob Bornitius, a 17th-century political theorist.</note> notes in *On Majesty, chapter 10*. Supreme command is always fortified by "extraordinary right," but it ought not always to use it. 

The most wicked and ruinous **Counselors** are those who strive to wickedly transform this "power released from the laws" into a horrible storm of license to do anything, contrary to the laws of God, of Nations, and of the state's own Constitution. In doing so, they wrap the purple of majesty in the stained fleece of **tyranny**, and they clothe the dignity and liberty of the Citizens in the donkey-like and slavish garment of the most abject patience. They most confidently babble that the rights and reputation of Princes cannot otherwise be safe, as **Dr. Lansius** <note>Johannes Lansius, a legal scholar.</note> notes. Certainly, the Law is diminished if power grows too much; and one must not use Command where one can act through the Laws, as **Pierre Matthieu** <note>Pierre Matthieu (1563–1621), a French historian and playwright.</note> writes in his work on *Sejanus*. 

It is a perpetual rule that extraordinary means should cease where there is a place for the ordinary. Laws are only observed if the Prince observes them himself. As the saying goes: *I never saw laws poorly kept when the Prince keeps them.* <note>original Spanish: "No vi malguardadas leyes, quando el Principe las guarda."</note> **La Loya** <note>Likely referring to a Spanish moralist or writer.</note> writes in *Moral Concepts, number 436*: "Otherwise the State does not stand firm, unless the Prince himself observes the laws." **Piccart** <note>Michael Piccart (1574–1620), a German professor of logic and metaphysics.</note> also notes this. Therefore, royal power must not be extended so far that it can neglect the laws at its pleasure, or use the absolute power belonging to it based on personal whim. To this belongs what **Antonio Perez** <note>Antonio Pérez (1540–1611), the famous secretary to King Philip II of Spain.</note> says in his *Aphorisms*: *The road to the ruin of Monarchies is the abuse of absolute power.* <note>original Spanish: "Camino à la ruina de las Monarchias, el abuso del poder absoluto."</note> 

The abuse of "unbound power" accelerates the ruin of kingdoms. The Prince is said to be "not bound by the laws" only **politically** <note>original Greek: "Πολιτικῶς"</note>—that is, with respect to the proposing, abolishing, repealing, and substituting of civil laws. For the rest, he is bound to live by the laws, and not to dare anything against piety, the law of reason, and good morals...

<meta>catchword: ...is bound (tenetur)</meta>

<summary>This page argues that a sovereign's absolute power is limited by conscience, public decency, and the "law of reason." It warns that rulers who ignore these limits in favor of "extraordinary power" descend into tyranny and risk the ruin of their state.</summary>

### Political-Legal Dissertation

...is established. For this reason, God established **Sovereignty** <term>Imperium: supreme administrative power or command</term> from Heaven, so that He might impose those good things which are with Him upon difficult matters, and adapt the laws according to the variety of nature. *Novels of Justinian, 73, at the beginning.* The abuse of things arises from the justice of ownership, not from the justice of judgment; the latter belongs to the Prince, not the former, as I stated in my *Politics, book 1, chapter 1, number 36.* Indeed, the **Remonstrants** <note>A Dutch theological movement (also called Arminians) that broke away from strict Calvinism in the 17th century.</note> say, just as we do, that it is absurd for **Nicasius à Schure** to claim that God, out of a justice based on ownership, condemns more people than He saves. *Appendix to the declaration of the presbyters, in the preface.* A Prince is not "released from the laws" <note>original: "legibus solutus"; a Roman legal principle often misinterpreted as giving a king total license to break any law.</note> so that he may act out of lust or according to every impulse of his mind; rather, it is so that he may command freely for the sake of justice: by making laws, changing them, and varying all things as the **safety of the Republic** <term>Salus Reipublicæ: the public welfare or the preservation of the state</term> requires. *Jacob Bornitius, On Majesty, chapter 10.*

And although the Prince is called a **living law** <term>lex animata: the idea that the ruler is the embodiment of the law on earth</term> on earth, *Novels of Justinian, On Consuls, 105, at the end*, this is not said in the sense that he ought to prefer his own will to **positive laws** <note>Human-made laws currently in force.</note> which still have vigor and have not been legitimately abolished—unless it is done without injury to another. Rather, he is called a "living law" because he adds a soul to the mute law, and he protects and defends it. *Hegenitius, Treatise on Possession, book 1, chapter 6, number 25, etc.* And he should observe his own laws and those of his ancestors, *Guyon, book 4, volume 2, chapter 23, from "Various Lessons,"* since he is released from them only as far as punishment is concerned, not as far as fault is concerned. *Claude de Carmin, in The Tower of Babel, part 3, chapter 1, page 536.* A Prince has no power except that which is granted to him either by God or by the people. The presumption is that neither party gave the Prince **absolute power**, unless it is to be used in a case of necessity. A Prince doing what he ought not to do resists God; but he cannot truly do that (for true "power" is a matter of right), and therefore duty and power must coincide. **Marcus Antonius Pitfillius** states this beautifully in *Colors, 5, page 71:*

"Even if he is endowed with a double power," he says, "namely **absolute power** (which is power in itself, not as the order of business requires, but which decides questions more swiftly) and **ordinary power** (which proceeds rightly and by the order of law, in a civil and common manner), the wiser men have said that he must use the **ordinary power** in all things. He should never use the absolute power unless a greater cause compels him, if he wishes to avoid divine indignation."

Therefore, it seems he is not even able to use that power, since one is not said to be "able" to do what one does against the law and with sin. For he was established to do justice, etc. To this point pertains the *Code of Justinian, title "If against the law or public utility," law 3, "On offering petitions to the Emperor,"* where it is held that **rescripts** <note>Imperial decrees or formal answers to legal questions.</note> are invalid if they are contrary to the law and public utility, unless they benefit the petitioner while harming no one else. *Law 9 of the same title.*

XIII. In this, a good Prince differs from a **tyrant**: that the tyrant uses absolute power when he should not. See *Laelius Zecchius, Politics, book 1, chapter 5, at the end.* Therefore, the distinction (as I have already warned above) which some people use here between **power** and **will**, and between **being able** and **being obligated**, is vain. # On Majesty in General.

...and so on, Waremundus, *On Royal Subsidies, chapter 15, number 6, folio 178.* Keckermann, *Practical Disputations 34, question 13, at the beginning.* He cannot use the **fullness of power** <term>plenitudo potestatis: the doctrine that the ruler possesses absolute, unrestricted authority</term> when he ought not; unless we wish to say that a ruler can be a Tyrant and commit the crimes of an Empire, but simply ought not to. Nothing is forbidden to crime; yet crime is forbidden even to the highest power. That a **Prince** <term>Princeps: the sovereign ruler or head of state</term> ought not to use the fullness of power except rarely, and only for a great cause, is proven forcefully and by the authority of many by Ludovicus Rodolphinus in his *Treatise on the Absolute Power of the Prince, chapter 4.* The same author, in *chapter 6*, explains at great length when the fullness of power does not operate. Add to this Lancellotus Conradus, *Temple of All Judges, chapter 1, section 4, folio 443*, and the many following pages; Petra, *On the Power of the Prince, chapter 3, question 2, and chapter 21 and following*; and Camillus Borellus, *In the Summary of Decisions, title 12.* Especially when a matter can be handled through **ordinary law** <term>jus ordinarium: the standard, established legal procedures</term>, absolute power must not be used. (Amiralo, *book 17, discourse 2*).

Hence it is that when a Prince grants something, he is seen to have granted it according to **common law** <term>jus commune: the general body of law, largely based on Roman and Canon law, that applied across Europe</term>, unless the contrary is specifically clear. *Law 35, Code on Inofficious Testaments.* See also Rodolphinus, *chapter 3.* Furthermore, **rescripts** <term>rescripta: written responses from a ruler or the Pope to legal queries or petitions</term> must be reduced to common law, as noted by Gail, *Observation 1, number 33, 6*; they should not be extended to those things which a Prince cannot do except by his fullness of power. Thus, those things that depend on the Prince alone are considered so difficult to obtain that in law they are held to be impossible. *Law "when a slave," 39, final section, on legacies 1.* Hence also, the administration of justice according to the laws ought not to be delayed or hindered by any **pragmatic sanction** <term>pragmatica sanctio: a formal imperial or royal decree having the force of law</term>, even if issued twice; this is rightly sanctioned in the *Novels [of Justinian] 113*. We see this same principle inserted into the ordinances of the Great Council of Mechelen <note>The supreme court of the Burgundian Netherlands, established in 1473.</note>, *title 1, article 2.*

XIV. All things are left to the **discretion** <term>arbitrium: the power of making a decision, which the author argues must be guided by reason</term> of the Prince; but that discretion ought to be shaped by law and equity. Since **Sovereignty** <term>Imperium: the supreme power to command and enforce laws</term> is granted to the Prince as to a "good man," it is not conferred for his mere whim. *Law 75, Digest on the Rules of Law*; see also Johann Cammans, *Disputation 1, thesis 105.* Therefore, it is appropriate to measure this absolute power only by necessity and the **safety of the people** <term>salus populi: the welfare and preservation of the citizenry, often cited as the highest law</term>. For Princes are not masters of their subjects in the way that shepherds are masters of sheep, whom they can sell to butchers. (Boccalini, *Parnassus, part 2, chapter 6, folio 32*).

A King, like a **tutor** <term>tutor: a legal guardian for a minor child (the "pupil")</term> of his people, ought to observe the rules prescribed for guardians; he is only then considered a Master when he provides for his "pupils"—that is, when he protects the safety and security of the people. (Nicolaus Betfius, *On Family Pacts, chapter 6, folio 154*). What Girolamo Savonarola <note>A Dominican friar and influential reformer in Florence (1452–1498) who spoke against the corruption of power.</note> declares regarding the Great Pontiff [the Pope] in his *Oracles on the Renovation of the Church, at the end of book 1*, we can also apply to the Prince: "The Pope can do all things. That 'all' is understood to mean he can do all things that are consistent with Christ, and that agree with his intention. Therefore, explain that 'all' as meaning all good things. Because that which is evil, which is unjust, is nothing." <note>original: "Papa omnia potest: Quello (omnia) s' intende che può tutte le cose, che confanno con Christo, & che concordano con la sua intentione. Esponi adunque quello (omnia) civè tutte le cose buone. Perche, quello ch'e male, ch'e ingiusto, e nulla."</note> The Royal Hand, says Scipio Gentilis <note>A famous Italian legal scholar (1563–1616) who specialized in the limits of royal jurisdiction.</note>, *On Jurisdictions, book 1, chapter 1*, is defined no less by justice than by power...

<summary>This page argues that a Prince's absolute authority (plenitudo potestatis) should only be used in rare, necessary cases and must always be guided by common law, equity, and the welfare of the people. It compares the ruler's role to that of a legal guardian (tutor) rather than an owner or master.</summary>

# Political-Legal Dissertation

...to be followed: but especially by a certain simplicity and speed in executing what has been decided. See also Sixtinus, *On Regalia, book 2, chapter 3, number 41, etc.* If I were to show absolute Monarchs (as Boccalini instructs Princes in *Reports from Parnassus, report 6, folio 31*): **they should be absolute in their states when executing deliberations on their most important affairs; but in consulting upon them, they should be the heads of a well-ordered Aristocracy.** <term>Aristocratia: a form of government where power is shared among a council of the most qualified or noble citizens, rather than a single ruler</term> Indeed, a prudent Prince, although he might be able to usurp absolute power over his subjects, nevertheless does not do so unless it is pleasing to them; following the example of Henry the Great, King of France, **who was resolved to do no good by force.** <note>original French: "qui estoit resolu, de ne point faire de bien par force."</note> *French Mercury, volume 1, folio 45 b.* And a Prince who is forced to use such **absolute power** <term>potestas absoluta: power that is not bound by ordinary laws or statutes</term> against natural equity—even if for the public good or out of necessity—is the less happy for it; as Michel de Montaigne states excellently and almost divinely in *Essays, book 3, chapter 1, folio 810.* Meanwhile, in the case of a Prince doing something by absolute power, a just cause is presumed whenever there is doubt. Lancellotus Conradus, *Temple of All Judges, 1, chapter 1, section 4, folio 422.* Finally, lest I appear sacrilegious because I dispute so broadly about the power of Princes—due to *Law 2 of the Code on the Crime of Sacrilege* and the *Sicilian Constitutions, book 1, title 4*—I fortify myself with the authority and reasoning of Ludovicus Rodolphinus, *Practical Legal Conclusions, 9*; add Petra, *On the Power of the Prince, chapter 1*; and my own *Discourse on the Jurisdiction of the Roman Empire, question 1.*

### XV.

Whoever uses absolute rather than ordinary power without cause, although he has no man to judge his deeds, it is nevertheless certain that he sins before God, as Ifernia says in *Chapter 1, number 7, regarding what things are regalia in feudal use*; for God "will powerfully scrutinize the powerful." *Psalm 82; Wisdom, chapter 6.* <note>The author refers to Wisdom of Solomon 6:6: "For mercy will soon pardon the meanest: but mighty men shall be mightily tormented."</note> For the saying of Tauler is most true: **The higher the status, the heavier the fall, and the greater the guilt.** Seneca writes elegantly in *Thyestes*:

> Whatever a lesser man fears from you,
> A greater Lord threatens against you.
> Every king is under a weightier Kingdom.
> If you despise the human race and mortal weapons,
> Yet expect a God who remembers what is right and what is wrong.
<note>original Latin: "Quicquid à vobis minor expavescit, / Major hoc vobis Dominus minatur. / Omne sub Regno graviore Regum est. / Si genus humanum & mortalia temnitis arma; / At sperate Deum memorem fandi atq; nefandi."</note>

Indeed, a Prince is not punished by any human judge; but this is only a matter of fact and for the sake of public utility. Master Bachov, *on Treutler, dispute 5, thesis 6, letter c.* Johann Gerhard, *On the Magistracy, number 265, etc.* He lacks punishment, but not guilt. Carnin, *In the Opposition to the Tower of Babel, folio 542, etc.* There is no right against God; nor can that which is a sin be called "right." And thus a subject cannot punish a Prince, due to a lack of **jurisdiction** <term>jurisdictio: the legal authority or power to administer justice and interpret the law</term>; not because the Prince has acted rightfully. Dominicus Baudius says gravely in *Civil Wisdom, book 1, folio 37*:

> The King has right over his people,
> But the Divinity and immense Majesty of God [is over him]

### On Sovereignty in General

> *Over Kings themselves is a power, so that a tyrant*
> *Might not escape human turns of fate—he who*
> *Profanes every sacred thing, and the oaths of Jove:*
> *But punishment, though slow with its woolen foot,*
> <note>original Latin: "laneo pede." This is a classical metaphor suggesting that divine or legal retribution approaches silently and softly like wool, so the criminal does not hear it coming until it is too ever-present to escape.</note>

> *And never leaves behind the head that owes a debt to guilt.*

Furthermore, it has been more commonly agreed that even he who wickedly breaks through all the barriers of piety, law, and honesty can be called to judgment, and proceedings can be taken against him by public authority. For such tyranny is no longer power, but pure <term>latrocinium: banditry or organized robbery, implying the ruler has lost legal legitimacy</term>. ### Political-Legal Dissertation

...should arise; "My jurisdiction is [absolute]," let it not be said of a good Prince what Horace <note>Horace (65–8 BC) was a leading Roman lyric poet.</note> sings concerning Achilles:

-> — — — — *He denies that laws were made for him.* <-
<note>original: "Iura negat sibi data." From Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, describing the lawless character of the hero Achilles.</note>

So too the author of the *Saxon War* writes concerning Albert, Archbishop of Bremen, that he instilled the following precepts into the Emperor Henry IV <note>Henry IV (1050–1106) was Holy Roman Emperor; his reign was marked by the Investiture Controversy and internal conflicts.</note> while he was still a youth: "Do everything that pleases your soul, observing only this: that on the day of your death you are found in the right faith. Would that the ears of Christian Princes never heard these or similar voices; or if they do hear them, let them reject them with a severity similar to that of Antigonus, King of the Macedonians. When someone said to him that "all things are just and honorable for Kings," he replied, "By Jove, <note>A common classical oath referring to Jupiter/Zeus.</note> that is true only for barbarian Kings! But for us, only those things are honorable which are honorable (namely, by their very nature), and only those things are just which are just." See *Vasquius, in the preface to Book 1 of Illustrious Questions, number 103.*

Pious and prudent Princes should have their ears stopped with wax, like Homer's Ulysses, <note>In the *Odyssey*, Odysseus (Ulysses) has his sailors stop their ears with wax to avoid being lured to destruction by the Sirens' song.</note> against every song that is sweet only to the courtiers but exists as something mournful and fatal for the miserable subjects. Let them harden their ears against those flattering suggestions, just as an Asp blocks its ears to the voice of the snake-charmer; and let them fortify themselves with these sayings: *The mighty shall be mightily tormented,* <note>original: "Potentes potenter exequentur." A reference to the biblical Wisdom of Solomon 6:6, warning that those in power face stricter judgment.</note> and *the sin is not forgiven unless that which was taken is restored,* etc.

Certain <term>jurists</term> <note>original: "JCti" (Jurisconsulti). Legal scholars or experts in the law.</note> are inconsistent, for in their legal "Topics" <note>A "Topic" (Topica) was a method of categorizing legal arguments.</note> they mark a certain place for arguments where an argument is drawn from the **plenitude of power** <note>original: "potestas plenitudo." The doctrine that a sovereign has absolute, supreme authority to override ordinary law.</note> to the effect that whatever pleases the Prince must always be considered just. -> ### XVII. <-

Elsewhere, Aristotle says in *Politics, Book 4, Chapter 8*: "The highest end of Aristocracy is virtue; of Oligarchy, wealth; of Democracy, liberty." Likewise, we see that Kings and Princes hold nothing more anciently established than the stability of their Status, which is thought to consist in reputation, authority, and the prompt obedience of their subjects. We find through experience that in the organizing and preserving of every Republic, the primary consideration is the security of those who hold the <term>πολίτευμα</term>, <note>Greek: "politeuma," referring to the ruling body, the administration, or the political system itself.</term> that is, the supreme right of Command, and the preservation and strengthening of the current State of the Republic. From this arise the "Secrets of Empire," the "Secrets of Rule," and the "Images of Empire" about which Clapmarius <note>Arnold Clapmarius (1574–1604) was a political scientist famous for his work on the "Arcana Imperii" or "Secrets of State."</note> treats. Nevertheless, the tranquility of those who command, as well as the long duration of the current State of the Republic—which politicians call the common <term>Reason of State</term> <note>original: "rationem Status," the idea that the national interest justifies actions that might otherwise be considered immoral or illegal.</note>—is not the *principal* end of Empires, but a *subordinate* one. For while the current State is preserved and the stability of the Empire is provided for, by that very fact the principal end of Empires—namely, justice, honesty, and the public safety—is considered to be kept intact and well-maintained. Hence Clapmarius reveals in *Book 1, Chapter 5* that the end of the "Secrets of Empire" is the public good, and in *Chapter 6* he prescribes faith, honesty, and virtue as their limits, which Sepulveda <note>Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda (1494–1573), a Spanish humanist and philosopher.</note> proves by example in his commentary on *Aristotle’s Politics, Book 3, Chapter 9.*

Nothing is more frequent today, and indeed has been in almost every age, than that not only many from the ranks of the Politicians, but even certain Theologians, flatter Kings and other Great Men. Above all, they seek to establish for them an absolute and free power over their subjects. In the same vein, they abuse the authority of the sacred scriptures; they do this so that the conscience of Princes may be more secure, and the subjects—bound to an Empire comparable to Tyranny—will be more strictly compelled to endure it with a patient spirit.

I do not at all blame those who, otherwise being most zealous for legitimate liberty, defend even the harsh power of Kings, not out of the vice of flattery, but for this sole purpose: that they might cut down any seditious attempts "in the blade," <note>original: "in herbâ," a metaphor for stopping something at the very beginning before it takes root.</note> as they say, and not allow them to grow up in any way. However, I would not want that to be named a "Royal Right" <term>Ius Regium: a legal term often debated in the 17th century regarding whether 1 Samuel 8 describes a legal right granted by God or a warning about a tyrant's behavior.</term> or "Regalia"; for if such a right is used recklessly, it makes those ruling in this world the slaves of eternal destruction hereafter. Although it may not bind Kings to temporal punishment, it nonetheless binds them to guilt.

...concerning and indeed to be seen as an injury: by which even legitimate <term>power</term><note>Latin: *potestas*; here referring to the legal authority of a ruler</note>, if it be supreme and perpetual, is not infrequently accustomed to vex its subjects. He added that they had begun to plot this ever since they were first led out of Egypt by His help. "But," He says, "it will not be long before they regret this decision too late, when what is done cannot be undone, and they themselves will condemn their ingratitude toward Me as much as toward you. I do [not simply] command you to create a King for them whom I have designated; but before you do so, you shall forewarn them how much evil they are voluntarily taking upon themselves, and you shall protest that they are hastening toward a change of state for the worse against your will."

While the previous page focused on the biblical requirements for a king as laid out in Deuteronomy, this page details specific ceremonial and legal restrictions based on Rabbinic tradition and contrasts the "Duty of a King" (from Moses) with the "Right of the King" (from Samuel), addressing the arguments of major political theorists like Albericus Gentilis and William Barclay.</meta>

# Political-Legal Dissertation

A King is permitted to join himself in marriage to the wife of a king, provided she is the widow left behind by another King. He may join a funeral procession at his own discretion, and he shall recline at the funeral feast on a low bench (which some call the "Bed of Fortune"), while the entire multitude sits upon the ground. He conducts wars at his own discretion, though with the consent of the high senate. He may tear down walls (so that a path may be opened for him) and any other structures at his whim. From the booty taken by soldiers, he reserves a portion for himself first. He may not take more than eighteen wives, and his supply of horses shall be no greater than his equestrian order requires. Nor should he be anxious to amass a heap of silver and gold, except as the needs of the military and the State demand. He should write out for himself a copy of the <term>Pentateuch</term><note>The first five books of the Bible, containing the Law of Moses</note>, which he should keep with him when outdoors, and preserve it hanging around his neck when at home or in camp. It is not permitted for anyone else to ride the King’s horse, nor to sit upon his throne; it is also a divine offense to use the royal scepter. It is permitted neither to approach nor to look upon the King while he is cutting his hair, or when he is naked in the bath. 

This is truly the "Right of the King," issued by God the Best and Greatest with the intention of establishing law; it is clearly different and even contrary to that which Samuel, much later, indicated to the people as a warning and discouragement. <note>The author is contrasting the ideal laws for a king in Deuteronomy 17 with the warning of royal oppression in 1 Samuel 8.</note> But <term>Albericus Gentilis</term><note>An influential Italian jurist (1552–1608) who worked in England and helped found the field of international law</note> retorts, <margin>Disputation on Royal Power 1, page 18 and following.</margin> that Moses promulgated the law of commanding, while Samuel promulgated the law of obeying; he argues that through the latter, it is shown what subjects must endure, and through the former, what Kings ought to do. <term>William Barclay</term><note>A Scottish jurist (1546–1608) who defended the "Divine Right of Kings" against resistance theorists</note> argues in nearly the same sense, <margin>Against the Monarchomachs, book 2, page 255 and following; also book 3, chapter 6.</margin> <note>The "Monarchomachs" were writers, often Protestant, who argued that it was lawful for subjects to resist or depose a tyrannical king.</note> He says that doing such things as Samuel proposes regarding the King is tyranny and injury in actual fact; however, he claims this is called a "right" only in terms of the king's impunity for the crime. He argues that "power" here is understood not as that which is granted by a command, nor even that which is granted by permission (insofar as it frees one from sin), but only insofar as it exempts the actor from legal penalties, etc.

And thus, according to the view of Barclay and those who follow him, the Duty of the King proposed by Moses must be separated from the "lawful power" which they believe Samuel explains. For my part, I do not deny that it is by no means free for the people to disturb a legitimate and duly called King from his throne, even if he exceeds the limits of justice and charity, and does things even more severe than those predicted by Samuel. But I doubt whether this properly deserves the name of a "right" (*jus*); perhaps it does not stem from any prerogative of "permitted right," but—this is my opinion, saving the judgment of others—subjects are unable to hinder him only for the sake of avoiding a greater scandal and to prevent more serious uprisings. 

It seems to be deduced by an unjust logic that: "The people cannot punish a Prince who is unjust to his subjects. Therefore, it is permitted for a King or Prince to rage against his subjects contrary to what is right." For even when someone treats another with insult, he does not rightly avenge himself by his own authority, <margin>Law 25, paragraph 1, of the Digest on Agents.</margin> and yet no one can doubt that such an act is an injury (not a "right"). I do not see how something done against or beyond one's duty can deserve the name of a "right." Every transgression of duty is considered a sin; a sin [can] scarcely [be called...]

# On Majesty in General

...it seems it can hardly be called a "right" by any reasoning. I have already touched upon and extensively deduced this matter above.

VII. (5.) Subsequent usage, which is considered the queen of all interpretations, clearly teaches that those things enumerated by Samuel are not to be exercised as a right over subjects; nor was the people of Israel bound to endure them. *1 Samuel 11: verse 5.* Even after Saul was created King, he still plowed his own fields; nor did he maintain such a court as that putative <term>Royal Law</term><note>Latin: *lex Regia*. This refers to the list of powers Samuel warned the Israelites a king would seize, often used by absolutist theorists to justify total royal control over property and people.</note> would have granted him. Yet, as soon as necessity pressed, he commanded all the people to go to war. For ancient Kings were created primarily for that purpose: to go before their people into battle. This is also commonly done today among the Cannibals <note>A reference to the indigenous peoples of the Americas, as described in early modern travelogues.</note>. Montaigne, *Essays, book 1, chapter 30, page 181. 1 Samuel chapter 14, verse 45.* The people intervened and interceded so that the King's son would not be unjustly punished. *1 Samuel, final chapter, and 2 Chronicles chapter 21, verse 23.* Ornan said to David: "Take it, and let my Lord the King do whatever pleases him; but I also give the oxen for a burnt offering, etc." To which King David responded in the *following verse*: "By no means shall it be so; but I will give as much silver as it is worth, for I ought not to take what is yours from you." Yet David would have had the most just cause for exercising this "royal law" and seizing the threshing floor to consecrate it and erect an altar there. It is even more compelling that Rehoboam remained silent regarding that reasoning—whether we call it the right or the judgment of the King; and his advisors, both the elders and the younger men, all remained silent when Israel desired to be relieved of a heavy yoke, *1 Kings chapter 12.* This relief could not have been so persistently sought (if Samuel had prescribed a law of absolute obedience) without it being a crime. It would have been a most wicked conspiracy of the ten tribes of Israel to defect from Rehoboam and elect Jeroboam as king on that occasion; yet that deed is nowhere seen to be condemned. Rather, it is explicitly approved in *said chapter 12, verse 24.* Indeed, that act was from the Lord; but He does not commit sins, nor does He justify acts done against what is right. How was it that Ahab and Jezebel, in *1 Kings chapter 21*, desired Naboth’s vineyard through a great price, and even greater deceit and the highest infamy, when they could have had it through the words of the law: *He will take your vineyards*? It is condemned in *said chapter, verse 19* that Ahab took possession of that vineyard against the duty of a King. Queen Jezebel, in the *oft-cited chapter, verse 7*, says indeed to her husband: "You are of great authority, and you rule the kingdom of Israel well." This is identical to the words of another powerless <note>In this context, meaning "unrestrained" or "lacking self-control."</note> woman: "If it pleases you, it is permitted; do you not know that you are Emperor?" <note>A reference to the words supposedly spoken by Julia Domna to her son Caracalla, often cited to illustrate the corruption of absolute power.</note> as I have already mentioned above. He suffered the penalty for the abuse of the royal office. But Naboth is not blamed in any place for refusing and answering the King: "The Lord forbid me from giving the inheritance of my fathers to you," *verse 3.* If the Israelites had been obliged to give their vineyards by a law of obedience, Naboth’s action would have been wrong. See Pareus, *Theological Exercises, book 2, chapter 14.* And the Rabbinic commentary...

<meta>This page continues the legal and philological argument regarding 1 Samuel 8. The author is demonstrating that the Hebrew word "Mishpat" (translated in the OCR as "Mischat") does not necessarily mean a legal "right" or "law," but can refer to a "custom," "habit," or even a "corrupt practice." This supports the author's previous argument that Samuel's warning about the "Right of the King" was actually a warning about the "Ways of a Tyrant."</meta>

->### Political-Legal Dissertation<-

...it is stated: what the Jews say: that because at the very end of his life his soul departed with a burning desire for revenge, it happened that a lying spirit was put into the mouths of the prophets to satisfy his lust for vengeance. <note>The author is likely referring to the story of King Ahab and the lying spirit in 1 Kings 22, citing Paul Riccius's summary of Jewish Talmudic traditions.</note> *Riccius, in the Summary of Talmudic Doctrine, folio 277.*

VIII. (6) The genuine property of the holy language <note>Referring to Hebrew.</note> suggests nothing else. The Hebrew text says nothing at all regarding a legal right; instead, <term>Mishpat HaMelech</term><note>OCR: *Mischat hammelech*. This is the "Judgment of the King" from 1 Samuel 8:11.</note> means the same thing in this passage as it does earlier in this same book, *1 Samuel chapter 2, verse 13.* This was the "manner" of the priests (the sons of Eli), <term>Mishpat HaKohanim</term><note>OCR: *Mischat hacohanim*. Usually translated as the "priests' custom."</note>; that is, this was their wicked custom and daily injustice. The same meaning of the word <term>Mishpat</term><note>OCR: *Mischat*.</note>, by which it denotes habit and custom, is likewise found in *1 Samuel chapter 27, verse 11*: "And this was the judgment (that is, the manner, habit, and custom) of David all those days." *1 Samuel chapter 30, verse 25*: "He established this as a law, or a statute, and as a judgment (that is, a custom) for Israel." Nor is it only Samuel who uses this word *Mishpat* to mean "custom"; it is commonly done throughout the Holy Bible. 

Thus, in *Genesis chapter 40, verse 13*: "You shall give the cup to Pharaoh into his hand, according to the former judgment," that is, the old custom. *Joshua, chapter 6, verse 15*: "they circled the city according to this judgment (custom)." *Judges 13, verse 12*: "what was the judgment of the boy," that is, his manner and way of living; *ibid. chapter 18, verse 7*: "according to the custom of the Sidonians." *Psalm 81, verse 5*: "The rite of the God of Jacob." *Psalm 119, verse 132*: "Look upon me, and have mercy on me according to the judgment (custom) toward those who love your name." *Ecclesiastes chapter 8, verse 5*: "The heart of a wise man will know the time and the judgment (that is, the manner and custom)." *Book 1 of Kings, chapter 18, verse 28*: "They cut themselves according to the rite (that is, their custom)." *2 Kings 1, verse 7*: "what was the manner of the man." *2 Kings 11, verse 14*: "he stood by the pillar according to the custom." *2 Kings 17, verse 33*: "They served their own gods according to the judgment (custom) of the nations." *Ibid. soon after in verse 34*: "Unto this present day, they follow the ancient judgment (that is, custom)." *Nehemiah 8, final verse*: "they celebrated the solemnity according to the custom."

From these examples, it is crystal clear that the word *Mishpat* can be taken in both a good and a bad sense. In this instance, however, the arguments presented above seem to show it is taken in a bad sense. Regarding this same matter, Vatallus <note>François Vatable, a noted 16th-century Hebrew scholar.</note> writes as follows on the same passage: "Literally, 'this will be the Judgment'; which is to say: kings will use these manners and this custom toward you; they will exercise such tyranny, which it will be necessary to obey. Some of the Hebrews say these things are lawful for kings; others, however, say the Lord said these things to deter the people from seeking a king, etc." Likewise, Arias Montanus in his interlinear version, and also Tremellius, translate this passage as: "This will be the manner of the King." Even Homer, in the *Odyssey, Book 4*, uses the word <term>dikē</term><note>Greek: δίκη. Usually meaning 'justice,' but in Homeric Greek often referring to the 'way' or 'custom' of a person or thing.</note> to mean "custom."

> *“For this is the custom of divine kings: they hate one of mortals, and love another.”*
> <note>original Greek: Ἡ γ’ ἐστὶ δίκη θείων βασιλήων &c. This is a quote from Homer's Odyssey, Book 14, lines 58–59, describing the arbitrary nature of powerful rulers.</note>
> *Which is the habit of divine kings,*
> *To hate one of the mortals, and love another.*

It is pleasing to add what <term>Peter Martyr</term><note>Petrus Martyr Vermigli (1499–1562), a highly influential Italian-born Reformed theologian who wrote widely-read commentaries on the books of Samuel and Kings.</note> notes on this same passage. Samuel's speech is intended to dissuade: his goal is for the people to retain their liberty. On the contrary, the people absolutely want a king; one who might judge their cases, assert their liberty, and strike down their enemies. In response, Samuel enumerates the inconveniences that are bound to follow: as if he were saying, "if you wish to live comfortably and escape so many evils, do not create a king for yourselves." Samuel does not confirm this with historical examples, even though a wealth of examples was available. For the Jews had already had King <term>Abimelech</term><note>A figure in the Book of Judges who seized power by killing his brothers; he is often cited as a cautionary tale of early Israelite monarchy.</note>, a proud and powerless man; they could not have forgotten what disturbances he had caused in that Republic. They saw the neighboring nations being oppressed and plundered by their own kings. They remembered that Pharaoh had destroyed both himself and his kingdom: but Samuel does not recount these things. He only warns of what is going to happen. In the same way, when God deters men from sins, He sets forth the punishments. "On whatever day you eat of it," He said, "you shall die by death." <term>Rabbi Kimhi</term><note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), also known as Radak, a preeminent medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian.</note> says that the Jews disagree among themselves as to whether this is truly a <term>royal right</term><note>Latin: *jus regium*.</note>. Some say that the very name of "king" cannot exist without this right. Others deny it, saying that God is not establishing anything here, but is only threatening what will follow.

A simpler answer can be given: the true law of the King is described in <term>Deuteronomy</term><note>Referring to Deuteronomy 17:14–20, which outlines the duties of a king to be humble and stay faithful to God's law, contrasting with the "tyrannical" model Samuel warns about.</note>; here, however, a true right is not being proposed, but only a "usurped" one. For who may prescribe rules for a King? His heart is in the hand of God. He thinks he possesses as much right as he pleases. But you will ask, "How can he protect the Commonwealth and administer justice without attendants? How can he fight without arms and horses? How can he maintain his court without revenue?" This is indeed true: but a limit must be applied in the demanding of them. He ought to maintain a court and some degree of ceremony, but for the use of the Commonwealth, not for luxury. It is permissible to demand tributes with reason and in measure; but to take away the very soul of miserable subjects through force and oppression—as is done today—is intolerable tyranny. Such were the Kings of other Nations: such are those who terrify their subjects with splendor and pomp. Such are the men these people demand be given to them. The first King is recorded to have been <term>Nimrod</term><note>Latin: *Nimbroth*. Mentioned in Genesis 10:8–9.</note>. Therefore he is called a "mighty hunter before the Lord," because he was a great Tyrant and an oppressor of the people. The sins of the Jews had grown to such a magnitude that they had to be completely chastised by this servitude. They had possessed good and moderate judges. But just as the <term>Frogs</term> of old, not content with a log as their Prince, obtained a stork from Jove; so these men, not content with judges, demand a King from Samuel. They dreamed, perhaps, that their King would be such a one as is described in Deuteronomy: who would study the law of God and read His word perpetually. But it turned out far otherwise.

...fell. For in the whole Kingdom of Judah, scarcely four good Kings were found: David, Josiah, Jehoshaphat, and Hezekiah; although even they were stained by no small vices. The others, however, did not seem to be Kings, but rather plagues upon the Commonwealth. And yet, whoever they were, it was not permitted to shake off their yoke and desert them. Thus far, <term>Peter Martyr</term><note>Petrus Martyr Vermigli (1499–1562), an influential Reformed theologian whose commentaries often explored the limits of political obedience.</note>. Thus also <term>Paulus Tossanus</term><note>Paul Toussaint (1572–1634), a Huguenot minister and scholar.</note>, in his *marginal notes*, explains the little word <term>Recht</term><note>original German: "Recht", meaning "Right" or "Law".</note> used by <term>Luther</term> through the word *Weise* <note>original German: "Weise", meaning "Way", "Manner", or "Custom".</note>. And he says: <note>original German: "Allhie wird nicht gehandlet von dem/ das einem König von Rechts wegen gebürt: Sondern dessen sie sich pflegen anzumassen."</note> "Here, the discussion is not about what belongs to a king by right of law, but rather what they are accustomed to arrogate to themselves."

IX. Even if those things which Samuel mentions here had been legally permitted in the Israelite kingdom, they still could not be extended to other kingdoms. For the Prophet speaks of a King given by an angry God in place of a punishment, as I have just noted above. He speaks of a Dominion that carries with it ownership over both property and persons <note>Latin: *dominium rerum & personarum*. This refers to the legal concept where a ruler owns the very bodies and lands of his subjects, rather than just governing them.</note>. (See the argument in the said Chapter 8 of the first book of Samuel, verse 17, and as I said in my *Politics*, book 1, chapter 5, number 22). Behold, they themselves also say to Samuel: "Appoint for us a King, like all the nations" (verse 5). And yet, the kings of the neighboring nations were undoubtedly such as the Turks, Tartars, and Muscovites <note>The author uses these contemporary groups as examples of "Oriental Despotism," where the ruler's word was absolute law.</note>, etc., are today. For just as the peoples of Asia are of a more slavish disposition than Europeans, so they always obeyed the empires of tyrants more easily; the same can almost be said of Africans. For this reason, there are those who think that specific detail—"like all the nations"—displeased God. For among those nations, it was not God who ruled, but the King. This is the view of <term>Drusius</term><note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant divine and Hebraist.</note> on the difficult passages of Samuel. And likewise <term>Aristotle</term> acknowledges that God rules where the law rules, not the absolute power of a king (*Politics*, book 3, chapter 21). For the same reason, <term>Gideon</term> refused to have dominion over the Israelites: "I," he said, "will not rule over you; the Lord shall rule over you" (Judges 8, verse 23). Therefore, that "right" asserted by Samuel does not pertain to a royal Monarchy, and even less to that which is called "legitimate" and is classified among mixed states <note>The author is distinguishing between "absolute" monarchies and "mixed" or "limited" ones where power is shared with other estates or governed by law.</note>. And certainly, all the main points of that royal "right" are based on domination. For he says the people would be the king's slaves (1 Samuel 8, verse 17). The king would take the sons of his subjects—which is what the Turk does now, who in this manner gathers his <term>Janissaries</term><note>original: "Janitsaros". The elite infantry of the Ottoman Empire, famously recruited through a levy of young boys from subject populations.</note>.

This view also pleases <term>Henning Arnisaeus</term><note>A prominent German physician and political theorist (1575–1636) who defended the absolute power of monarchs.</note>, in *Book 1, On the Right of Majesty, chapter 3, number 3*. Thus <term>Blessed Ambrose</term><note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397), the Bishop of Milan and a highly influential doctor of the Church.</note>, in his *Apology for David, chapters 4 and 10*, says: "David sinned, as kings are wont to do; but he performed penance, he wept, and he groaned, which kings are not wont to do. What private individuals are ashamed to do, the king did not blush to confess. Those who are bound by laws dare to deny their sin; they disdain to ask for the forgiveness which he sought, who was bound by no human laws. He was certainly a King, and he himself was bound by no laws; for kings are free from the bonds of crimes. For they are called to punishment by no laws, being safe by the power of their command. Therefore he did not sin against man, to whom he was not held liable."

In the same sense, <term>Cyril</term> and <term>Didymus</term> are also cited in the <term>Golden Chain</term><note>The *Catena Aurea*, a collection of commentaries from the Church Fathers compiled by Thomas Aquinas.</note> on the 50th Davidic Psalm. <term>Antonio Agelli</term><note>An Italian scholar and Bishop of Acerra (1532–1608), known for his work on the Septuagint and the Psalms.</note>, from the congregation of the <term>Regular Clerks</term><note>Specifically the Theatines, a Catholic religious order founded in 1524.</note>, agrees in the book titled *Commentaries on the Psalms and the Canticles of the Divine Office*, printed at Rome at the Vatican Press, Year 1606, page 236, on Psalm 50: *To You alone have I sinned.* <note>Psalm 51:4 in modern numbering: "Against thee, thee only, have I sinned."</note> "Because since I excel all others in royal dignity and power, and I ought to give an account of my deeds to no one, I am subject to Your judgment alone, and I have You alone as judge. Therefore, if I have sinned in anything, I have sinned against You alone; I am Your defendant, to be condemned or absolved by You alone."

But truly, if anyone wishes to judge this matter from the foundations of the Christian faith, it will be found to be otherwise. A Christian Prince ought to love his neighbor just as much as any of the lowliest subjects, if he wishes to be a Christian: if he neglects this, he sins against his neighbor, to whom he owes charity. To <term>Natural Law</term><note>The concept of a universal law of right and wrong inherent in human nature, which exists regardless of the laws of a specific state.</note>, the Prince is bound as a human being; a point I have already taught above. This law established a certain kinship among us; and consequently, it is a crime for one human to harm another, according to *Law 3, On Justice and Law*.

If anyone does this, a reciprocal debt is certainly violated, and that law of nature is struck against. Nor is this a logical conclusion: "A Prince cannot be punished by his subjects. Therefore, in unjustly offending them, he does not sin against them." For to suffer an injury and to be able to avenge it are different things; nor is it necessary that, if the latter is removed, the former is taken away. In this way, a son cannot punish a father; and yet it cannot be wrongly said that the father has transgressed against the son. So too Saul sinned against the <term>Gibeonites</term><note>A group of people mentioned in the Bible (2 Samuel 21) who were wronged by King Saul; God sent a famine until Saul's descendants were punished for his crime.</note>, and they had to be atoned for by the blood of Saul's descendants, *2 Samuel 21, verse 3*. ## A Political-Legal Dissertation

...and to Aaron: *I have sinned against the Lord your God, and against you.* <note>Exodus 10:16</note>. And yet, those men were clearly absolute subjects of Pharaoh. Far be it from us to suggest that Pharaoh was more humane than the most pious David. Furthermore, the parable proposed by Nathan in *2 Samuel 12* proves that David had also sinned greatly against Uriah. Thus, when he says, *Against you alone have I sinned*, it means: "You alone knew the gravity of the sin while it was not yet public." See the notes of <term>Immanuel Tremellius</term><note>A 16th-century Italian Jewish convert and leading Hebraist (1510–1580) known for his Latin translation of the Bible.</note> on the aforementioned *Psalm 51*, and Mr. <term>Johann Arndt</term><note>A German Lutheran theologian (1555–1621) influential in the development of Pietism.</note> in *The Interpretation of the Psalter, Psalm 51, sermon 2, number 2.*

For this reason, Nathan also says to David in *2 Samuel 12, verse 12*, that God would repay David in public for what he had perpetrated in secret. To God alone was the <term>secret crime of the house</term><note>original: "caecum domus scelus"</note> revealed, as <term>Virgil</term><note>The Roman poet (70–19 BCE); the author is quoting Book 1 of the *Aeneid*.</note> speaks of it in the first book of the *Aeneid*. The Chaldean Paraphrast <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> understood this passage in the same way, stating: "Before you alone I sinned, and evil before you I have done."

Nor is it irrelevant what <term>Aretius Felinus</term><note>A pseudonym for the Protestant Reformer Martin Bucer (1491–1551).</note> says in his *Explanation of the Psalms*. David had sinned both against his most faithful soldier Uriah and against the entire army—whom he had ordered to be put in danger for the sake of killing Uriah—but while he was weighing how much he had despised and offended God by this crime, he was so tormented and torn in spirit that he felt this one thing, complained of this one thing, and said to the Lord: *Against you, against you alone, have I sinned.* He says, "The fact that I so despised your word, that I provoked you so greatly—this, I say, kills me, tears me apart, flays me," and so on. <term>Flaminio</term><note>Marcantonio Flaminio (1498–1550), an Italian humanist and poet who wrote paraphrases of the Psalms.</note> later inserted these words almost verbatim into his own explanations of the Psalms.

But I should not omit what <term>Savonarola</term><note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), the Dominican friar and reformer in Florence.</note> has to say about this passage:

> "I have sinned too much against you alone: because you commanded me to love you for your own sake, and to refer the love of all creatures back to you; but I loved the creature more than you, loving it for its own sake. For what is sinning, if not clinging to the love of a creature for its own sake? And what is this, if not acting against you? Certainly, he who loves a creature for its own sake makes that creature his God. I have therefore sinned against you alone, because I established a creature as my God. I have thus cast you aside and done injury to you alone. For I did not sin against any creature if I established my ultimate purpose in a created thing, because I was not commanded to love any creature for its own sake. For if you had commanded me to love an Angel alone for its own sake, and I had instead loved money for its own sake, I would certainly have sinned against the Angel. But since you alone are to be loved for your own sake, and the creature is to be loved in you and for you, I have indeed sinned against you alone, because I loved the creature for itself."

But what is worse, *I have done evil in your sight.* For I did not blush to sin before you. O God, how many sins have I committed before you which I would have by no means perpetrated before men—indeed, which I would have by no means wanted men to know? I feared men more than you, because I was blind, and I loved my blindness; therefore I neither saw, nor did I consider—

[I con]sideratred you; I had only eyes of flesh; therefore I saw only men, who are flesh, and I feared them. Who is so good? Who is so pious? Who is so merciful? You, who in your goodness, incomprehensibly surpass all creatures. For it is your nature to have mercy and to spare—you who manifest your omnipotence most especially by sparing and showing mercy. <note>This phrase "to spare and have mercy" is a staple of traditional Latin liturgy, emphasizing that God's power is best seen in his forgiveness rather than his punishment.</note>

I confess, Lord, against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you. Have mercy on me, and manifest your omnipotence in me, that you may be justified in your words. For you said: *I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* <note>Matthew 9:13.</note> Justify me, Lord, in your words; call me, receive me, grant that I may produce fruit worthy of repentance: for it was for this that you were crucified; for this you died and were buried. For many say: *There is no salvation for him in his God; God has forsaken him.* <note>Psalm 3:2 and Psalm 71:11.</note> Overcome those people, Lord, when you are so judged by them; do not forsake me completely. Thus are you judged by men; thus do men speak of you; these are their judgments. But you are pious, you are merciful; have mercy on me and overcome their judgments. Show your mercy in me, and let your goodness be praised in me. Make me one of the <term>vessels of your mercy</term><note>original: "vasis misericordiæ"; a reference to Romans 9:23, describing those whom God has prepared for glory.</note> that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. For men judge you as rigid and severe: overcome their judgment with your goodness and sweetness, so that men may learn to have mercy on sinners; and let those who do wrong be ignited to repentance, seeing your goodness and mercy in me.

Thus far <term>Savonarola</term><note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), a Dominican friar who briefly led Florence; he wrote this meditation on Psalm 51 while imprisoned and awaiting execution.</note>. The Reverend Father <term>Jean Lorin</term><note>original: "Johan Lorinus"; a Jesuit theologian (1559–1634) known for his massive, 16th-century commentaries on the Bible.</note> of the <term>Society of Jesus</term><note>The Jesuits.</note> provides various explanations from different authors in his learned and most laborious *Commentary on the Psalms*.

But let all these things, and all my own thoughts, be submitted to the judgment of those who perceive things more rightly and fairly.

### CHAPTER IX.

### Consequences of the things said so far: and various questions concerning absolute power.

From a correct judgment of this kind of absolute power, very many questions of the greatest importance find their resolution. For from this I deduce: that Majesty <note>The term "Majesty" here refers to the sovereign power or the person of the ruler.</note> cannot take away the property of citizens, nor their ownership, nor even a right descending from civil law, nor usurp the goods of subjects, without a cause—that is, unless public benefit suggests it. *Law 1, Digest on common estates; Del Castillo, Everyday Controversies, chapter 28; Pinel, part 1, rubric chapter 2, on the rescinding of sales; Cavallos, volume 4, question 906.* Explained at length by **Mr. Dr. Harpprecht**, *in the preface to the Institutes on the division of things, number 94, etc.*; **Mr. Dr. Bocer**, *on Investiture, chapter 3, number 74, and on taxes, chapter 6, number 25, etc.; Cravetta, counsels 172, 463, 615, 630, & 749;* Betsius, *on family pacts, page 515, etc.;* Bornitius, *on Majesty, chapter 10, page 76;* Bronchorst, *second explanation 63, and first Miscellany 1;* Pruckman, *in the section on "unbound power," page 292, etc.;* Freher, *on Peter de Andlo, book 2, chapter 8, page 187;* Hardevv, *on Dassel, counsel 1;* Camman, *1, thesis 59, and 2, thesis 33;* Arumaeus, *feudal dispute 3, thesis 11;* Brunning, *dispute on the universe, thesis 4, a;* Bornitius, *in the Treasury 7, final chapter;* Hunnius, *on transactions, chapter 4, exercises 1 and 2;* Keckerman, *practical disputes 34, question 7, at the end;* and to this belongs the entire treatise by Peter Antonio de Petra, on the right of the Prince. *Law 15, section 2, on the recovery of property, and law 11, on eviction, law 11, section 1, on tax collectors;* those laws which are brought forward to the contrary should be understood as referring to the lands of enemies. The Romans used to leave these lands to the surrendered not by the right of full ownership, but of possession; to expel these people and afterwards assign the estates to soldiers or to make them public was permitted by the right of war—a case in which we are not currently engaged. Gothofredus, *on the said law 11, Digest on eviction, and the same author at length on law 20, on captives and the right of return;* and as I have said *in my Economy, titles 5 and 6, book 1 of the Digest, question 3.* Add Ayrault, *on judged matters, book 4, title 7, chapter 3, and the following title, chapter 1;* and concerning the fairness of the Roman Senate in building aqueducts, see Frontinus, *on the aqueducts of Rome, page 126.*

No Majesty can take away either liberty or goods from me without cause, nor is it a sufficient cause if this is done for the sake of decoration or pleasure: as the destruction of the house of Ahab proves. <note>original: "1. Reg. 21." This refers to 1 Kings 21, the story of King Ahab and Naboth’s vineyard.</note> And the great piety of a certain Arab King also relates to this, of which Botero notably writes, *on the gods, page 107.* So also Cicero, *in defense of Caecina*, says: "If the people should order me to be your slave, do you think that order would be valid and firm?" And the same author, in the second book of *On Duties*: "He who administers the Republic must see to it that everyone keeps what is theirs, and that no reduction in the property of private individuals is made by the public." Furthermore, not even in the case of public utility...

->## On Majesty in general.<-

...utility, Majesty <note>Referring to the sovereign power or the person of the ruler.</note> can take my property away from me, unless the price is refunded: for the dangers of necessity ought to concern everyone, not just one individual, see **Gail**, *Observation 56*, and there in the very extensive conclusion of **Graevius**. And it is relevant here that all things are subject to the Prince’s <term>Command</term> <note>Latin: *Imperio*; referring to political authority</note>, not his <term>Ownership</term> <note>Latin: *Dominio*; referring to private property rights</note>, as I said in *Book 1 of Politics, chapter 1, number 36.*

II. Our learned Doctors deduce from this that a <term>fideicommissary substitution</term> <note>A legal arrangement where an heir is required to pass the inheritance to another person later, often used to keep estates within a family.</note> cannot be overturned by the Prince, even from his "fullness of power" <note>Latin: *plenitudo potestatis*; the concept of absolute sovereign authority</note>: **Cravetta**, *Counsel 736*, unless some cause concurs that concerns the public utility, and provided that the beneficiary is compensated at least at a fair valuation. **Petra**, *Chapter 32*; **Intriglioli**, *on substitutions, century 3, question 95*. They also hold that a Prince does not enter into an inheritance nor take a legacy from an imperfect will, **Pruckmann**, *section on unbound power, member 3, effect 10, page 801*. By the force of his "unbound power," he may confirm a will that was void due to a lack of legal formalities, **Pruckmann**, *effect 7, page 746*; or he may change a just and firm will, or alter clauses dictated by the testator. **Suetonius**, *in the Life of Tiberius, chapter 33*; **Covarruvias**, *Variations 3, chapter 6, number 5, etc.*; **Vasquius**, *Illustrations 52, number 26*; **Pruckmann**, *effect 8, page 770*. However, he cannot confirm the sale of a ward’s property by a mere decree, **Mr. Nebelkra**, *Decision 7*; nor can he take away the right of ancient possession, **Cravetta**, *Counsel 639*; or the right of <term>Majoratus</term> <note>The right of the eldest son to inherit the entire estate</note>, **Castillo**, *Book 1, Practical Questions 28*. Likewise, he cannot grant legal capacity to a daughter to the prejudice of the male relatives, **Pruckmann**, *page 332*. He cannot abolish a statute (against the husband's will) that prevents a wife from making a will without his consent, **Peck**, *on the Wills of Spouses, Book 3, chapter 25*; nor can he grant or waive a <term>peremptory exception</term> <note>A legal defense that completely defeats a claim</note>, **Cravetta**, *Counsel 555*; **Bronchorst**, *Miscellany 1, number 3*; nor can he compel someone to sell their own things, **Arithmaeus**, *Periculum 1, dispute 9, thesis 3*; or do similar things.

III. Here, likewise, a distinction seems necessary between cases where the rights of a third party are harmed, and those where no prejudice is brought against a third party. In the former case, only necessity and public utility have weight; in the latter, the Prince’s mere grace or favor can operate. But concerning absolute power in prejudicing a right acquired by a third party, see the extensive discussion by **Petrus Antonius de Petra**, *in his singular treatise on this matter, chapters 24 and 25, and throughout almost the whole book*. And our country’s experts say that even regarding those things which indirectly harm the right of a third party, that power can do nothing; hence the Prince cannot be appointed as an heir in a matter that is currently under litigation, **Petra**, *Chapter 14*. Regarding the <term>Clause of "Motu Proprio"</term> <note>Latin for "of his own accord," indicating a decree issued by the ruler's own initiative without a formal request</note>, *page 633*; the clause "from certain knowledge," *page 640*; "from the fullness of power," *page 651*; and "notwithstanding," *page 655 of the said treatise*, **Petra** deals with these at length, and let **Marta** be consulted, *Treatise on Clauses*.

IV. Thus the Prince is bound by contracts just like any other private person, not only by natural reason but also by civil reason, nor can he revoke a contract entered into even with his own subjects. *Law 26, Code on donations between husband and wife*; **Scheplitz**, *on the Customs of Brandenburg, part 1, title 8, section 3*. **Petrus**...

# Political-Legal Dissertation

Wesembec, *Counsel 2, number 65, etc.* (for indeed, in this matter it especially becomes a Prince to be sincere, Marnix, *section 7, resolution 2*) unless some just cause regarding the public good persuades him to revoke it. [See also] Cephallos, *Common Opinions against Common Opinions, volume 2, question 852*; Vincentius Cabotius, *2. Various Disputes, chapter 10*; Betius, *on family pacts, sheets 47 and 6*; Camman, *Dispute 5, thesis 57*; Brunning, *Dispute on Universities, thesis 4. b.*; Bronchorst, *1. Miscellany 2*; Keckerman, *Practical Disputes 29, problem 13*; Heinricus Velstenius, *Decade 8, thesis 7*. A Prince is not compelled to observe <term>Distributive Justice</term> <note>The fair distribution of benefits, such as offices or rewards, based on merit or status.</note> quite so precisely "to the fingernail" <note>An ancient idiom meaning "exactly" or "perfectly."</note>, as I have just now warned. However, with respect to <term>Commutative Justice</term> <note>Justice concerning private exchanges and contracts, where one thing is exchanged for another of equal value.</note>, since contracts cannot be "lame" <note>Legal slang for a contract that is only binding on one party and not the other.</note>, the Prince is no less bound than a private citizen, Henricus Scotanus, *Disputes from Book 1 of the Code, thesis 5*. Yet, for a [valid] cause, a Prince can free himself from an obligation arising from a contract; as the King of Spain did several years ago, Rodolphus Botereius, *History, book 3, page 302*, and as Meteranus records that he attempted even before then, *book 5, page 284*.

If a Prince has granted, promised, or sold the same thing to two or more people, [the jurists] consider the first person to have the stronger right, even if the second person physically holds the item; this is the opposite of what usually happens in dealings between private citizens. Scotanus, *in the aforementioned dispute, thesis 6*.

Finally, it may be asked here: should the Prince’s word be trusted if he is the only one testifying to a fact? It is better that I side with <term>Bodin</term> <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), an influential French jurist and political philosopher who defined the modern concept of sovereignty.</note>, who thinks the Prince’s testimony is insufficient when other supporting evidence is lacking. *On the Republic, book 1, chapter 10, and book 6, final chapter*. [See also] Fridericus Tilemannus, *Disputes on the Pandects, volume 2, dispute 3, thesis 37* (who cites many others, etc.); Bachovius, *volume 2, dispute 5, thesis 7, letter a*; Volcmar, *Treatise on Witnesses, century 1, part..., page 6*; Mynsing, *century 5, observation 34*.

But this dispute seems to me to have three parts. For either the Prince gives testimony for another person, or for the Empire (that is, in the interest of the Realm), or for his own personal benefit. When a Prince gives testimony for another as a private citizen, or as Prince by reason of his office, the response of a single witness is not to be heard at all, even if he shines with the highest honor of the Court. This was once decreed by the Emperor <term>Constantine</term> <note>Constantine the Great, Roman Emperor from 306–337 AD.</note>, *in law 9, section 1 of the Code regarding witnesses, and law 20 on inquiries*. <term>Cicero</term> writes in his speech *For Roscius* that this was established by the custom of our ancestors. This also seems to be consistent with divine law—or as we prefer to call it, natural law—according to the saying: *In the mouth of two or three witnesses every truth consists.* <note>original: "In ore duorum vel trium testium omnis consistit veritas." A reference to Deuteronomy 19:15 and Matthew 18:16.</note> It is sanctioned in the aforementioned law 9 that witnesses must be bound by the sanctity of an oath before they give testimony, and it is noted that the deposition of witnesses consists of two parts: the testimony itself and the oath, neither of which is valid without the other, *in the chapter "Fraternitatem" on witnesses in the Decretals* <note>Referring to Canon Law.</note>. This is so established that it is a common tradition among our people that witnesses can be strictly compelled to take a formal and solemn oath, Ruland, *on commissions, part 2, book 2, chapter 11*, to such an extent that custom does not prevent this even when dealing with <term>Illustrious persons</term> <note>Latin: "Illustribus"; a high-ranking legal status for the upper nobility and top officials.</note>, Ruland, *in the cited place and book 4, chapter 11, at the end of part 2*.

# Concerning Majesty in General.

...they bring together what Freher writes in his *Treatise on Reputation*, book 2, chapter 4, at the end. Indeed, Ruland signifies the same in *part... chapter... book 4, number 26, etc.*: that even for illustrious persons, a "hand-given pledge in place of an oath" <gloss>original German: Hand gegebne Treu an eines Eyds statt</gloss> is not sufficient. However, whether these rules have a place regarding the Prince, and whether a Prince should be believed at all when giving testimony for a private person who is his subject—or against a subject—if he does not have a co-witness, is doubted with good reason. Likewise, it is doubted whether faith should be given to a Prince who has not been sworn.

I know indeed that a Prince is presumed to be full of justice and to do all things deliberately as is fitting, and therefore it should not be doubted that he speaks the truth. This is the reasoning that has led our Doctors <note>The "Doctors of Law," or established legal scholars of the medieval and early modern periods.</note> to say simply that a Prince’s assertion must be fully believed—not only the assertion of a Pope, King, or Emperor, but even that of any other person holding Imperial or royal rights (Farinacius, *On Objections against Witnesses, question 63, chapter 3, number 84, etc.*). 

I know that so much was once attributed to the holiness and sincerity of Xenocrates <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and student of Plato, famous for his integrity.</note> among the Athenians that when he was once forced to give testimony and had approached the altar for the sake of swearing the oath, all the judges rose together and proclaimed that he should not give the oath. From this, it is argued that it is "uncivil" <note>Meaning it is an affront to the dignity of the office or person.</note> not to have faith in the word of unsworn Princes, since a physical oath is often waived by the consent and will of the parties themselves for those who are universally famous and esteemed (Freher, *On Reputation, book 2, chapter 6, number 18*).

But a case can nonetheless happen, and the weight of certain affairs may demand it, where it is necessary to discuss this controversy with precision. And then, certainly, if I were asked, I would respond that one should believe neither an unsworn Prince, nor a Prince as a sole witness. For it is in everyone's mouth: "the word of one is the word of none" <note>Latin: *dictum unius, dictum nullius*. This is a fundamental principle of Roman and Canon law requiring at least two witnesses for proof.</note> (Law *On Oaths*, Code *On Witnesses*; Chapter *Although to all*; Chapter *Coming*, and similar passages in the Decretals *On Witnesses*). 

And this proceeds not only from Canon and Civil Law, but also from Divine Law (*Deuteronomy 17 and 19; Matthew 18; 1 Corinthians 13*). For neither the Gospel, nor any divine or human law, condemns or justifies anyone on the testimony of one person, even an appropriate one (Chapter *To Admonish*, 33, question 5), so much so that it cannot be brought about by statute or custom—not even by the Prince or the Pope—that full faith be given to a single witness (Farinacius, *On Objections against Witnesses, question 63, number 8, etc.*). 

When Quintus Scævola <note>A famous Roman legal authority and statesman.</note>, a most excellent man, was produced as a witness against a defendant and had given his testimony, he added as he was leaving that he should only be believed if others had asserted the same; for to be believed on the testimony of one man was a matter of the worst example (Valerius Maximus, *Book 4, chapter 1*). A good Prince ought to do this same thing. And if a Prince is unwilling to imitate this example, any good Senate ought to follow the tracks of the Parlement of Paris <note>The supreme court of law in France during this period.</note>. For when King Henry II of France had ordered a certain man to be condemned because he had caught him in a capital crime, yet did not want the name and circumstances of the crime to be made public, the Parisian judges then responded to him that they were sworn not to condemn anyone unless he was convicted of a crime...
