# A Political-Juridical Dissertation

...against no one. Jean Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596) was a French jurist and political philosopher who developed the modern theory of sovereignty.</note> in *Six Books of the Commonwealth*, book 6, folio 757, is supported by Tilemann in part 2, dispute 3, thesis 37. Bodin reports in the same place that this same king <note>Likely referring to a French monarch such as Henry III.</note> gave testimony in a very serious case, albeit privately and while under oath before the judges. To this we add what is very commonly accepted: that a Prince should by no means be believed alone <note>Meaning his word cannot stand as the sole evidence without corroboration.</note> if he is testifying about the actions of someone else (Farinacci <note>Prospero Farinacci (1544–1618), a highly influential Italian jurist known for his works on criminal law.</note>, the aforementioned question 63, chapter 3, number 157 and following), or if harm to a third party is feared as a result; or if the Prince's assertion would cause detriment to another (Mascardi <note>Giuseppe Mascardi (d. 1588), a famous Italian jurist specializing in the law of evidence.</note>, conclusion 139, number 14; conclusion 141; and conclusion 1234, number 104; Farinacci, question 63, number 174 and following). 

Thus, in those matters that do not depend on the Prince's will and power, his assertion is not to be upheld, whether it concerns the act of someone else or his own (Farinacci, the above-mentioned question 63, number 151 and following). For example, if he testifies that a certain person was a traitor and that therefore a fief <note>A "feudum" or fief was land held under the feudal system; if a vassal committed treason, the land would revert to the lord or Prince.</note> has returned to him (Aurelius Corbulus, *On Emphyteutic Law*, chapter 12, question 5). 

The opposite must be concluded, and full faith must be given to the word of the Prince, if he testifies by word or by letter that something was done or conducted by him or in his presence by virtue of his office (Farinacci, the said question 63, chapter 3, numbers 80, 98, 139). Hence, the words of apostolic letters <note>Official documents issued by the Pope.</note> in which the Pope recounts his own action provide full proof, if the Pope's favor or intent is based upon them (*Clementines*, single chapter on proofs). 

For if one stands by the letters of a judge testifying to something regarding his official duties (the Law *si Publicanus*, section *on things*, in the Digest *on publicans*; Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a leading medieval jurist.</note> on the rubric for the Code *on the faith of instruments*), and if this holds even if the judge were someone like Ribaldus (as Jason <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), an influential Italian law professor.</note> says following Baldus, in the Law *pacta novissima*, number 7, *on pacts*), how much more should the word of the Prince be upheld, whose authority towers over all? (Mascardi, conclusion 1234, number 1 and many following). A Prince is to be believed more than a single notary, or even several (Antonio Gabriele, title *on proofs*, conclusion 2, number 11). 

Here, however, the limitation of Oldradus <note>Oldradus de Ponte (d. 1335), a canonist and civil lawyer.</note> also seems necessary (conclusion 258), where he distinguishes that the Prince’s words are either <term>narrative</term> <note>original: "narrativa"; words that simply recount a story or background.</note>, <term>assertive</term> <note>original: "assertiva"; words that declare a fact to be true.</note>, or <term>dispositive</term> <note>original: "dispositiva"; words that legally enact, grant, or settle something.</note>. In the first case [narrative], they do not constitute proof; assertive words regarding his own action do constitute proof. And dispositive words, whether uttered as the basis of a case or not, provide proof without distinction. Furthermore, for the Prince's words to sufficiently prove something even when testifying by virtue of his office, it is necessarily required that his legal intent be founded upon them (Mascardi, the said conclusion 1234, number 93, etc.). To such an extent that <term>enunciative</term> <note>original: "enunciativa"; words that state something incidentally or as a side-remark without legal force.</note> words, upon which the Prince’s intent does not rely, do not even create a presumption of truth; Mascardi treats this at great length (conclusion 622), as does Cephalus (counsel 465, number 47).

<summary>This page discusses the legal validity of a Prince's testimony, distinguishing between his private statements (which require corroboration) and his official assertions (which carry supreme authority). It categorizes royal speech into narrative, assertive, and dispositive types to determine their weight as evidence.</summary>

### CHAPTER I.

### *Vices of the first Table are also to be judged and punished by the Political Power.*

<note>The "First Table" refers to the first four of the Ten Commandments, which dictate duties toward God, such as the prohibition of idolatry and blasphemy. The author is arguing that the state has the right to punish religious offenses.</note>

If in any part of political discourse it is pleasing to begin, it is surely here that I wish to quote the Blessed Augustine, from *book 1 of On the Trinity, chapter 11*: <note>original: "Non pigebit me, sicubi hæsito, quærere; non pudebit, sicubi erro, discere."</note> *I will not be reluctant to inquire wherever I hesitate, nor will I be ashamed to learn wherever I am in error.* I place this principle before my simple and sincere mind. For I confess that I have adapted the reports and decrees of others to the confession of the Church in which I now live. If it should please anyone to insult these things, let him know that I do not care for envious slanders; but I most greatly desire the criticism of good men. But now, it is time to begin.

II. That supreme and perpetual power, exempt from the laws, which they call majesty, has certain specific connected attributes. That highest and absolute command exerts its force distinctly within the Republic. There are certain attributes which <term>accompany <note>original Greek: ἑπομένω (hepomenō)</note></term> superiority: without which a kingdom can neither remain safe and unharmed, nor can the royal force and dignity shine forth. In Monarchical Empires, these are designated by terms derived from the word for King: *Royalties, Royal and Sovereign rights, and the rights of royal power*; or in German: <note>original: "Keyserliche Hochheiten und Reservaten"</note> *Imperial Sovereignties and Reservations, etc.* See Johannes Cammann, *Disputation on the Rights of Majesty, 1, thesis 86 and following*; Paurmeister, *book 1 on Jurisdiction, chapter 4, throughout.* More correctly, they are called the rights of supreme command or of Majesty by a more general term. For not only Emperors and Kings, but also free peoples and those in other forms of government where the supreme power resides, possess such eminences. <note>The author argues that sovereignty exists in republics and democracies, not just in kingships.</note> This is based on the argument handed down by Deciano, response 18, number 315, volume 1; these rights I therefore ascribe more to the law of nations <note>Jus gentium: a legal concept of "natural law" or universal customs recognized by all civilized peoples.</note> than to civil law. This is against Master Bocer, *Treatise on Money, chapter 1, number 24.* Furthermore, this command

III. The **Right over sacred things**—which Virgil calls "sacred law" (and which brings about great reverence and majesty)—is also attributed to the supreme Sovereignty by Arnold Clapmarius in his book *On the Secrets of Republics, chapter 15*. And certainly, the ancients established that caring for and protecting sacred matters is so proper to the Prince that many held the offices of priesthood and kingship together, as noted by Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus and Henning Arnisaeus. > King Anius, both king of men and priest of Apollo.

Indeed, the knowledge of divine and human law was once joined; see Marcilius in his *dedicatory epistle to the commentary on the Institutes* and extensively in Cluverius, *On Germany, page 104 and following*. In this view, the knowledge of divine things is also ascribed to <term>jurisprudence <note>The theory and philosophy of law; the author suggests that legal expertise naturally includes religious law.</note></term>. And even today, Doctors are still inaugurated in **both laws** <note>This refers to the "Doctor of Both Laws" (Doctor Iuris Utriusque), meaning both Civil and Canon (Church) Law.</note>. Some who have departed from the Roman Pontiff <note>Referring to Protestant scholars who broke away from the Catholic Church.</note> say this right so pertains to majesty that they deny that those who recognize the Roman Pontiff as their superior in religious matters should be called supreme Princes. See Albericus Gentilis, Waremund ab Ehrenberg, and especially Friedrich Baldwin. In this respect, it would not be absolutely true what Sixtinus says: that the matter of <term>Regalia <note>The specific rights and privileges belonging to a monarch.</note></term> is purely secular. Yet, it could seem that Ecclesiastical law is in truth something separate from Sovereignty, because the Turk <note>A common reference in this period to the Ottoman Sultan.</note> does not possess this right over the Christians living in his territory.

IV. Since this matter is discussed in various ways by various people, I wish now to sample a few things from many, without prejudice to any sect, though gladly submitting myself to anyone suggesting better points. And first, indeed, it seems certain and clear: the **Civil Magistrate is the guardian of both Tables of the Decalogue.** <note>The "Tables" refer to the two halves of the Ten Commandments; the first deals with duties to God, the second with duties to fellow humans.</note> Specifically, he prohibits and punishes vices of character, even those committed against the first table—namely Blasphemy, Magic, Atheism, **Epicureanism** <note>In the 17th century, "Epicureanism" was often used as a derogatory term for godlessness or a focus on sensory pleasure rather than divine law.</note>, perjury, etc. And to this belong those things said to be of the **"mixed forum"** <note>Legal matters that involve both secular and religious authority.</note>; about which Lord Rutger Ruland wrote. Blasphemies, of whatever kind they may be, belong to the secular court...

V. Thus, in this view, the crime of Magic also concerns secular judges <note>original: "Laicos judices"</note>. If anyone was proved to have passed through a graveyard at evening as a sorcerer, collecting the horrors of the tombs and the mockeries of the wandering souls there, he would perish as one guilty of a capital crime, says Ammianus Marcellinus, *book 19*.

I call Magic here a **pact with the Devil** <note>original: "pactionem cum Diabolo"</note>, by which a human gives themselves entirely into the power of the Devil, and in turn binds the Devil to their service, for both benefit and harm. See Jeremias Nicolai, *Theology 3, chapter 16*. Nor indeed should anyone believe that a necessity is imposed on demons by arts of this kind (which even Theodoret seems to admit in *sermon 10 of the Cure of Greek Affections, page 139*), although sometimes, by the force of a pact entered into with a superior, the inferior spirits are truly compelled—and this is to cast out demons by Beelzebub. All such persons, by the prescription of the Imperial laws, are burned with flames <note>original: "flammis exuruntur"</note>, according to the law *3 and the last, of the Code regarding evildoers*. See the Most Serene King James of Great Britain, *in his Daemonology*; and Petrejus *in the criminal conclusions, thesis 64*. Sometimes, however, even those who have handed themselves and their salvation over to the enemy of the human race are converted...

### A Political-Legal Dissertation

...and the magic of hags <note>original: "laniarum," likely a variant of "lamiarum," referring to witches or mythical hags</note> is more foul than others, and is to be numbered among those magicians who, as Lactantius says in *Book 2, Chapter 15*, seek help from earthly demons and thus inflict diseases. VII. Likewise, other impious and forbidden arts must be condemned, through which some (often the imprudent) are accustomed to binding themselves to the enemy of the human race by an implicit pact (using images, symbols, or words, as mentioned by Hill in *Epicurean Philosophy, number 440*). In many things, the Devil is the ape of Christ; he is effective through certain words and ceremonies, acting as if they were sacraments. (See the excellent treatise entitled *The Mimicry of the Demon*, by Henri de Montaigu; as well as the French book titled *The Philosophy of Spirits*; and José de Acosta’s *History of the Western Indies, last book*). Concerning the Evil Eye <note>original: "Fascino," the power to harm or enchant through a glance</note>, see Alberico Gentili on *Eclogue, Chapter 18*.

There is, however, another kind of magic that is true and praiseworthy, proceeding from the harmony of the world and achieving wonders, about which Campanella writes in *Book 4 of the Sense of Things*, and Bulenger in his *System, volume 1*. Such was the magic of Balaam, the Queen of Sheba, and the Magi who worshipped the newborn Christ. Baronius notes this under the year 1 AD. These men came from the East, that is, from Persia. For the wise men of the Persians were called "Magi"; and no King was created unless he was chosen from their number and imbued with their disciplines, according to Strabo. Hence, in *1 Kings 5*, the wisdom of all the sons...

# On Majesty in General.

...of the East <note>original: "rum Orientis," completing "experientiarum" from the previous page</note>: but many impious things were mixed with their teachings. For they were Astronomers and skilled in the language of birds. *Isaiah 19, verse 10.* Master Eckhart <note>Johannes Eckhart, a medieval German mystic</note>, as cited in Tauler <note>Johannes Tauler, a disciple of Eckhart</note> on the 16th Sunday after Trinity, page 271, refers to true Magic when he says:

->It is a question among the Masters, which is better: the power of herbs, of words, or of stones? One should consider or realize that all words have power from the First Word. Although the uselessness of their variety (not considered by thoughtless people) debases the words—that is, they become despised and bring no benefit. Therefore, one should very diligently notice what one speaks and how the words are used; for it was not without great cause that the Eternal Word of the Heavenly Father, Christ, said: for every useless word that people have spoken, they will give an account on Judgment Day. But this is (alas) little regarded, and therefore such great evil and misery spring from it that it is pitiful. Herbs also have great power. I heard that a snake and a weasel were fighting with each other; then the weasel ran away and fetched a little herb, combined it with another herb, and threw the herb at the snake; then the snake broke apart and was dead. What gave the weasel the knowledge of the power in that herb? Therein also lies wisdom. Words also have great power; one could perform wonders (as has often happened and still happens) with words. Stones also have great power from their correspondence <note>original German: "gleichheit," referring to the Hermetic principle of 'like affects like'</note>, so that the stars work within them by the power of heaven. I will also add a wonderful example from the *Tripartite History*, Book 5, Chapter 45, of how James, the Bishop of that place <note>Jacob of Nisibis, a 4th-century Syriac saint</note>, defended Nisibis against Shapur, the King of the Persians; though this was miraculous, not magical. The venerable man, being moved, ascended a certain tower; and when he saw the thousands upon thousands of the army, he called down no other curse upon them than <term>Cyniphes</term> <note>stinging gnats</note> and <term>Culices</term> <note>mosquitoes</note>, so that through small creatures they might recognize the power from above. Indeed, following his prayer, a cloud of gnats and mosquitoes filled the trunks of the elephants (since they are hollow), as well as the ears and nostrils of the horses and other beasts of burden. But they, unable to bear the force of the tiny creatures, threw off their riders and drivers from their backs and threw the broken ranks into confusion; and abandoning the army, they fled with great haste. In this way, the most wretched Emperor, recognizing in himself a small and merciful correction made by God, who has providence over souls—

# A Politico-Legal Dissertation

VIII. Furthermore, it is in no way permitted for a Christian, while keeping his piety and conscience intact, to use the work of evildoers or sorcerers <note>original: "maleficorum, sive sortiariorum"</note> in times of illness or other misfortunes. Martin Del-Rio <note>A Jesuit theologian and famous demonologist</note> writes of this in *Book 6, chapter 2*. Indeed, the Law of God condemns wizards, magi, and such enchanters and imposters, and does not distinguish the intentions of those using their help in any way; rather, it curses those arts absolutely. Moreover, in Roman law, even those who consult such people are punished with death <note>original: "capite plectuntur," literally "struck by the head"</note>, as argued in the *Code on Evildoers*. See also Stephanus Forcatulus, Pareus, and others. Here, the words of Saint Cyprian <note>An early Christian bishop and martyr</note> in his treatise *On the Vanity of Idols* should be noted: 

> They distort limbs, break health, and provoke diseases, so that they may force people to worship them. Thus, fattened by the steam of altars and the pyres of cattle, they may seem to have performed a cure by merely releasing what they had previously bound. This is their only "remedy"—when their injury ceases. They have no other goal than to call men away from God and to turn them from the understanding of true religion toward the superstition of themselves. 

One may also add Lactantius <note>An early Christian author and advisor to Constantine</note> to this view; see, however, Paracelsus in his *Book 5 on the Origin of Invisible Diseases*. Even the pagans had certain sacrifices and remedies by which they thought they could turn away phantoms and magical arts, as noted by Natalis Comes. To this category belong those whom the Spanish call *Saludadores* <note>Spanish: "Healers," often claiming supernatural powers to cure rabies or pests</note>, about whom Antonio de Torquemada writes; and those on the island of Cyprus who "divide the winds" with a knife. This is described by Steffen de Lusignan in his *Description of Cyprus*, where he notes that although they strike the air in the shape of a cross and pronounce "good words," there is a superstition involved: the knife must have a black handle. But truly, can a witch <term>saga|A woman believed to practice magic or witchcraft</term> be forced—as is commonly done—to remove a disease that she herself inflicted, without violating one's conscience? See Remigius's third book, Prætorius's *Treatise on Witchcraft*, and my own *Treatise on the Consideration of Life and Death*.

IX. Atheists—that is, those who feel contempt for all religions—must be handed over directly to the punishment of the Magistrate. For just as there is no worse disease among all types of Republics than Anarchy (where no one commands and no one obeys), so too no plague more serious can befall the Church (and the Republic alike) than the lack of a Divinity, which the Greeks call *Atheism*. This is noted by Bodin, Campanella, and myself in my second book of politics. This state was even hateful to the Pagans themselves; hence the books of Protagoras of Abdera were once burned in the forum because they taught that nothing can be known for certain about the gods, whether they exist or not. Therefore, as Horus says in his *Hieroglyphics*, the Egyptians placed an image of an eye under a shoe <note>original: "oculum sub calceo"</note> to show that atheists are blind. For the fact that God exists, and is a certain primary cause which governs all things...

### On Majesty in General

...that God created all things <note>Completing the word "omnes" from the previous page's catchword</note> and preserves them, both our own eyes and natural law teach us, as Bulenger notes in his *Notes on Arnobius, chapter 2*. Therefore, it is a most wicked thing that in some places, "strong men" are considered spirited and obedient when, having cast aside all piety, they are hindered by no religion from daring anything they please, according to the *Anti-Machiavelli, book 2, theorem 1, at the beginning*. It is the supreme secret of the enemy of the human race to secretly propagate Atheism through authors who are recommended either for the subtlety of their intellect or for other reasons.

The greatest atheist was Lucian, who follows the Epicureans and mocks providence; he refutes the Stoics in this way: if all things happen by fate, then religion is of no use. See Lucian's *Zeus Confuted, volume 4, folio 250, etc.* The Cynics and Epicureans were also atheists, according to Lactantius <note>A 4th-century advisor to Constantine known as the "Christian Cicero"</note> in *book 2, chapter 1*. He refutes them in his work *On the Wrath of God, chapters 1 and 10*, where he fights for the existence of providence. Among the Latins, there was the poet Lucretius; for everything he raves <note>original: "delirat"</note> about belongs to Epicurus. See Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God, chapter 6*. Still more impure (for that sect has its degrees) was Martial; see *book 4, epigram 21*.

Among more recent figures, Pomponazzi <note>Pietro Pomponazzi, a Renaissance philosopher who questioned the immortality of the soul</note>, Pomponius Laetus, and Calderini were Atheists or Epicureans, as noted by Bucholtzer in his *Chronology, folio 434*. In more recent years, this impiety was fostered by Lucilio (Julius Caesar) Vanini <note>An Italian philosopher who was burned at the stake for atheism in 1619</note>, who wrote a sufficiently learned book on the *Admirable Secrets of Nature*, which was even approved by the theologians of Paris. However, he was immediately suspicious to me, as he attributes everything to nature, even calling her a "great Goddess," and refutes the Epicureans quite coldly. He had previously written a treatise adorned with a prestigious title, which he called the *Amphitheater of Eternal Providence*, in which he professedly attacks the Epicureans. Nevertheless, he was later convicted of Atheism and of a clever and hidden defense of it, and he was put to death by a cruel execution in France. See Rosset, *Tragic Histories, number 5*.

For the same reason, many of the doctrines of Girolamo Cardano <note>A famous Italian polymath and physician</note> should be avoided, as well as the Epicurean-Democritean philosophy of Nicholas Hill, an Englishman. Franciscus Junius, a famous theologian among the Protestants, was also once devoted to that more subtle form of Atheism, though he was later happily delivered from that error; see Melchior Adam’s *Lives of the Theologians, folio 195*.

Epicureanism, however, primarily strives for this: that all religion be held in contempt and the mind be freed from all divine fear. See Lucretius, *book 1*. Thus, Nature alone is held as God, as Lactantius says in *book 3, chapter 28*, which Lucian also confesses in *Alexander the False Prophet, volume 1, folio 570*, where he frequently pits Christians and Epicureans against one another. Today, we must certainly group with these people those who usurp religion for the "Reason of State" <note>original: "status ratione" – the political principle that the interests of the state justify any means</note>. See Boccalini <note>Trajano Boccalini, an Italian satirist</note>, *Reports from Parnassus, report 13*. These are people who know the errors of various religions and therefore worship none, as Lactantius notes in *book 2, chapter 3*. The truest principle of Atheism is to deny everything that cannot be seen: God, Angels, the soul, Demons, and even conscience itself; see Lactantius, *last book, chapters 9 and 13 toward the end*. Thus Lucretius, in *book 3*, busies himself with proving...

And therefore, the exemptions and immunities of the Clergy, and of the goods belonging to the Churches, are considered to have been introduced by <term>positive law</term> <note>Man-made law enacted by a ruler, as opposed to natural or divine law</note>; and they are in the power of the one who holds supreme authority. *By the argument of Novel 83, the decree "We establish," in the Code on Bishops and Clerics.* See <term>Cæphallus</term>, *Common Questions, contra common 550*; <term>Ventura Vincentius</term>, *Counsel on the Venetian controversies, chapter 8, throughout*; and <term>Thomas Michaël</term> *on Jurisdiction, thesis 10.*

But indeed, to the <term>Anti-Catholics</term> <note>Generally referring to Protestant writers of the era</note>, this is considered "Antichristian doctrine," which withdraws from Princes as many subjects as there are people who become Clerics. They say that this axiom can stand with no form of state without sending that state under the yoke of the Roman Pontiff. They do not think it safe if Clerics constitute a "peculiar homeland" or a "peculiar Republic" [State] of their own. And they think nothing more ruinous to a State can be imagined than this full exemption. They argue nothing is more unjust than if it is said that Clerics are not subjects, or that they are forced to fight for the Pope against the Republic, etc. And <term>Leidhresser</term> asserts *book 1, chapter 4* that this same doctrine immediately births the "murder of Kings." 

The exemption of Clerics fills the State with foreign men who do not benefit the State, but nonetheless snatch the fruits of labor away from the citizens. This exemption takes away from the Churches the right to elect their own pastors; it draws men and money to Rome, as <term>Arnisaeus</term> <note>Henning Arnisaeus (c. 1575–1636), a German physician and political theorist who supported absolutism</note> thinks *in his treatise on the subjection and exemption of Clerics, chapter 2.* He also busies himself in *chapter 3* to teach that: Clerics, as far as their Persons are concerned, are not exempt from secular jurisdiction by divine law or the practice of the early Church, but only in a qualified sense by the privilege of Princes; see <term>Pierre du Moulin</term> <note>A famous French Huguenot minister and author</note> at length, *treatise on Monarchy, chapters 15, 18, and following.* And likewise in *chapter 4*, <term>Arnisaeus</term> tries to prove, and <term>Cævallos</term> agrees *in question 899*, that the goods of the Churches and the Clergy do not pass outside the jurisdiction of the State. Also, in the time of Emperor Henry VI, the bishops wrote to him: "To you, whom God has exalted as Prince and Emperor of the Roman world, to whom we have done **homage** <term>Latin: *hominium*; a formal ceremony where a vassal acknowledged his bond to a lord</term>, and from whom we hold our temporal possessions, we are bound to assist in securing all your legal rights." If they gladly hear from the Roman Prelate the phrase, "What have you to do with the King?" then consequently they should not be annoyed to hear from the Emperor: "What have you to do with possessions?" 

In the year of Christ 1430, the clergy of Speyer obtained the **right of citizenship** <term>Latin: *jus civitatis*</term> and submitted themselves to the jurisdiction of the City Senate in temporal matters; see Lehman, *book 7, chapter 89, at the end.* The Protestants likewise judge as absurd the chapter *on constitutions* in the <term>Extraordinary Decretals</term> <note>A collection of Canon Law; the specific reference is *10. extr. de constitut.*</note>, where it is stated that "no power has been granted to the laity over churches or ecclesiastical persons," and that the laity are bound by the "necessity of obeying, not the authority of commanding." It further claims that if anything should be decreed by the laity on their own initiative regarding the benefit and favor of the churches, it is to have "no stability," etc. This is supported by *Distinction 96 and following.*

Let him who is well-versed in both political and ecclesiastical antiquities look into this matter. ->## Political-Legal Dissertation<-

...even one in the best possible state, should not be recognized as the head of the Church, or as the universal Bishop, even by human or positive law <note>Positive law refers to man-made laws established by a government or society, as opposed to "natural law" or divine decree</note>. Such recognition has served not so much to preserve unity in the Church or to prevent the freedom of thinking, speaking, and teaching differently about articles of religion, as it has served to strip away necessary liberty—which is consistent with the Word of God—and to introduce tyranny. Furthermore, it continues to serve this end by its very nature.

Nevertheless, others who are less argumentative have always asserted that it is a mark of religious wisdom to distinguish the Roman Court from the Church in which the **Pope** <note>original: *Pontifex*</note> sits, such as Jacob Arminius <note>Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609), a Dutch Reformed theologian who sought to moderate stricter Calvinist doctrines</note> in his *Public Theological Disputations, 21, page 203.* And Philip Melanchthon <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a key German Reformer and colleague of Martin Luther</note>, in the passages inserted into the *Formula of Concord* itself, considered that the Pope and the Bishops could be tolerated by Protestants in their own way. Conversely, many Catholics also subject the Supreme Pontiff to a **Universal Council** <note>original: *Concilio universali*; a general gathering of church leaders (Conciliarism)</note>; they concede that an appeal can be made from the Pope to such a council. See Herwart *against Bzovius, in defense of Louis IV, page 243 and following*, where he also discusses the reasons why such an appeal may be undertaken.

### III.
For this reason, those who deny total **exemption** <note>The "privilege of forum," which traditionally meant clergy could only be tried in church courts, not secular ones</note> to the clergy argue that whenever they attempt anything against public decency or the political state, they can be restrained by the **Civil Magistrate** <note>The secular government or legal authorities</note> without any privilege of court. This is supported by *Romans chapter 13* and the commentary there by Saint Chrysostom; *1 Peter chapter 2, verse 3*; and various legal authorities such as Cævallos and Cardinal Tuschus. By this same reasoning, the statutes of a secular Prince also regularly bind ecclesiastical property. Morla, in *The Emporium of Law, title 1, question 6.*

History also bears witness to this: for example, the **Vestals** <note>The Vestal Virgins, priestesses of ancient Rome</note> who prostituted their chastity were restrained by the Urban Praetors (secular judges), not by the high priests. In the primitive Church, the Popes did not claim even the slightest jurisdiction over priests for themselves, as witnessed by Justinian himself <note>Justinian I (r. 527–565), the Byzantine Emperor who codified Roman law</note> in *Novella 123, repeated in the Code regarding Bishops.* From this, they deduce that the **Crime of Lèse-Majesté** <term>Latin: *Læsæ Majestatis Crimen*; high treason or an offense against the dignity of the sovereign</term> can be committed by clergy just as by laypeople. See Lord Bocer, *On Regalia, number 102*; Alberico Gentili <note>An Italian jurist and one of the founders of international law (1552–1608)</note>, *On the Crime of Majesty, dispute 5*; and Johann Camman.

Indeed, even the Pope himself, if he rises against the Emperor, is considered to stain himself with the crime of treason by Lord Bocer and as I stated above in the first discourse on majesty in general, where I dealt with the Pope. For this reason, Solomon deposed the High Priest Abiathar (*1 Kings 2*). The same occurred in France to several Bishops, though after seeking the counsel of other Bishops, as noted by Jean Papon. Regarding the power of **Charlemagne** <note>King of the Franks and the first Holy Roman Emperor (r. 768–814)</note> over Bishops, consult Lehmann, *book 2, chapter 41.* However, Lehmann always extols the power of the **States** <note>The "Estates" or representative assemblies</note> which they held over the French Kings; yet he makes those same kings absolute when he discusses the authority of the King over ecclesiastics at the end of the cited chapter.

In this way, Emperors Valentinian, Valens, and Gordian forbade clergymen from acquiring anything for themselves, or through intermediaries, from the property of widows and orphans, unless by the right of a close relative; otherwise, the <term>Treasury <note>original: *Fiscus*</note></term> would seize it. *Theodosian Code, law 20, on Bishops and Clerics.* By a similar example elsewhere, it was prohibited for anything to be left to the Church or Clerics by will or <term>trust <note>original: *fideicommisso*</note></term> by deaconesses and widows who had surviving kin and offspring. *Theodosian Code, law 27, same title.* This was surely done lest the clergy, becoming insolent and corrupt with wealth, might be less pious and less upright.

It follows the example of **Aesop's Hen**; which, scrawny and in poor condition, laid an egg every single day, but once fattened, ceased to lay. This was also to prevent legitimate and blood-related heirs from being despoiled under the pretext of religion, and so that sordid <term>legacy-hunters <note>original: *heredipetae*; people who seek to be named in the wills of the wealthy</note></term> and seekers of wills could no longer play upon the minds of the simple and the credulous. For this reason, Saint Jerome praised these Constitutions in his *Book on the Life of Clerics,* and he grieved that they were being evaded by silent trickery. "I do not complain about the law," he says, "but I grieve that we deserved this law." <note>original: *Non de lege, ait, conqueror; sed doleo quòd meruimus hanc legem.*</note> A prudent and severe sanction of the law; and yet even so, greed is not reined in; we mock the laws through trusts, etc. See Guil. Forner, *Selections, book 1, chapter 28.*

But shortly afterward, that law was repealed. *Theodosian Code, law 48, same title.* Yet Charlemagne, having renewed the ancient law, again forbade property from being handed over to the Church to the fraud of the heirs, as is found in the *Capitularies, book 1, chapter 89.* Add Servin, *volume 1, plea 2, and volume 3, plea 4.* But truly, even in ancient times in England, it seems it was by no means lawful to assign inheritances to monasteries unless the King's grace had been obtained. John Selden in *The English Janus, book 2, folio 91.* Nor was this law uncommon in Germany at all times. ### CHAPTER III.

## Whether and to what extent Religion itself, and religious worship, are under the administration of the Prince and those who hold Majesty.

Everything discussed up to this point does not seem particularly complicated; thus, approaching the heart of the matter now, I wish to examine whether religion itself and religious worship fall under the administration of the Prince—always with due respect to the judgment of those who hold more correct views. <note>original: "salvo tamen semper rectiùs sentientium judicio." A standard scholarly disclaimer of the era.</note> The Ecclesiastical order is distinct from the Political and Economic <note>In this 17th-century context, "Economic" refers to the management of the household or private sphere, rather than modern finance.</note> orders, as noted by Heinrich Eckhard in *On the Ecclesiastical Order, part 1, section 1.* The internal power belonging to this order is rightly exercised by the clergy alone: in "loosing and binding" <note>original: "solvendo, ligando." This refers to the 'Power of the Keys,' the authority to forgive or retain sins and to excommunicate.</note> and in administering the sacraments. Minor excommunication, or the retention of sins (and even exclusion from the communion of the Holy Supper, according to Felix Bidembach in *Decade 10, final consultation*), also pertains to this internal jurisdiction. For this reason, a Minister of the Church is not subject to the secular Magistrate regarding confessions he has heard; therefore, he is not bound to reveal them to anyone. See Martin Del Rio, *book 6, chapter 1, section 2 of the treatise on magic.* <note>Del Rio was a Jesuit scholar; his work on magic also covered the laws regarding the secrecy of the confessional.</note> Likewise, King Saul lost his kingdom because he himself offered a sacrifice, attempting a task that belonged specifically to the Priest, as seen in *1 Samuel 13, verse 11, etc.*—though Drusius interprets this differently in his notes on that passage. <note>Johannes Drusius was a famous Protestant scholar of Hebrew and the Bible.</note> Therefore, the hinge of this entire controversy turns on this single point: whether, by virtue of his "architectonic power," <term>architectonica potestas (the supreme, master-building power of a sovereign to coordinate all aspects of the state for the common good)</term> a Prince can pass laws concerning *external* worship, and to what extent he can promote the business of the Faith.

This question is described by David Pareus, in his *Treatise on the Right of the Prince against the Pope, folio 72,* as being of great importance and as difficult to explain as it is worthy of study. Truly, however, even in the opinion of the saner Protestants, Religion and Piety are not the *direct* concern of political administration. For the state preserves only an external, visible morality; and thus it deals with matters other than those with which the Gospel is concerned, as Valentin Weigel writes in *The Place of the World, chapter 24, at the end.* <note>Weigel was a German mystic whose followers often argued for a sharp separation between inner spiritual life and outer political control.</note> From this, it seems that the regulation or governance of the Church and the Ecclesiastical Ministry does not strictly belong to Kings and other Rulers by the power of their command. This is supported by *John 7, verse 48, etc., and chapter 18, verse 36, and 1 Corinthians 1, verse 26.* See also Clemens Timpler, *Politics, book 4, chapter 2, question 1, at the end,* and Martin Luther, *in his booklet On Secular Authority.* Republics were instituted so that we might have the things necessary for leading this physical life well and happily; God willed these to flourish and be preserved even outside the Church for as long as He sees fit. For indeed...

For indeed Christ said: *Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. Matthew 22, verse 21.* And the Blessed Paul exhorts that petitions and prayers be made for Kings, and for all who are placed in high positions. *1 Timothy 2, verse 1.* Likewise, the Prophet Daniel says the same, *chapter 6, verse 22.* These rulers, however, were enemies of the Church at that time <note>Referring to the Roman Emperors and Babylonian/Persian kings who ruled while the biblical authors wrote.</note>. But Christ came from heaven, having taken the form of a servant, to establish the Church—that is, that philosophy and part of Statecraft <term>Polity: the organized structure of a government or society</term> which provides for the good of the soul and the spirit. He instituted certain officials, whom he nevertheless (as I have just said) preferred to be called ministers. The right of this ministry has nothing in common with the other part of statecraft, which concerns temporal matters; and vice-versa. *The Augsburg Confession <note>original: "Confess. August." – The primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church, presented in 1530.</note>, in the article listing abuses, under the title "On Ecclesiastical Power." Heinrich Scotanus, in his summary of book 1 of the Code, title 13, folio 91.*

II. Nevertheless, because (1) the Church ought to be governed aristocratically <note>An "aristocratic" church government refers to rule by a collective body of elders or leaders (a presbytery), rather than a single person.</note> (not democratically, as *Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621) was a Jesuit Cardinal and one of the most influential figures of the Catholic Counter-Reformation.</note> argues in Book 1 On the Pontiff, chapter 6*, nor even monarchically) as argued extensively by *Parker, in his treatise On Ecclesiastical Polity, book 3, chapter 13 and following; Theodore Beza, on Matthew chapter 18, verse 17; Balthasar Meisner on Church Government;* and myself in my *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 4, section 10.* (Bellarmine, however, laboriously attempts to prove the opposite and fights for Monarchy; see him in *Book 1 On the Pontiff, chapters 5 and 9 and following, as well as throughout Book 2.*) And because (2) those who possess majesty <note>In this context, "majesty" refers to supreme sovereign power held by a ruler.</note> are considered its principal members—for we are all one body in Christ, and individually we are members of Christ and of one another. *Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 26, on maintaining moderation in disputes.* And because (3) all things, especially in the church, ought to be done in an orderly fashion. Therefore, the civil magistrate, and especially the highest one (as the defender and protector of the church and church discipline), ought to carry out what he establishes together with the church, remove errors, ensure that pure religion flourishes in the church according to scripture, and institute proper order. *George Cassander, Consultation on the articles in controversy between Catholics and Protestants, article 16. Nicholas of Cusa, Book 3 On Catholic Concordance, chapters 7, 11, and 26.* And indeed, they hold this power solely for the sake of easier execution, not by their own inherent right. Nor do they attribute this right to just any Prince (for otherwise this would apply even to an infidel), but specifically to a *Christian Prince*. Here pertains the counsel of Philipp Melanchthon <note>A German reformer and collaborator with Martin Luther.</note>, which he wrote in the year 1537, and which was reprinted some years ago in Heidelberg and Amberg. There he proves that the care of establishing churches does not belong to the Bishops alone; nor should the authority of a superior Lord always be obeyed; but lower magistrates can also involve themselves here. And so, Melanchthon requires order, not absolute command <note>original: "Imperium"</note>. However, the most illustrious Bellarmine, *Book 1 On the Pontiff, chapter 6*, tries to prove that the government of the church does not rest with the Presbytery (or the elders), as Jan Hus <note>A Czech reformer who was burned at the stake for heresy in 1415.</note> wished—a view that has a plausible reason, especially regarding individual churches. But the heart of the matter seems to consist in this: who...

# On Sovereignty <note>original: "Majestate"</note> in General.
<sig>P 2</sig>

...should rule the whole catholic and universal church? The question is asked, therefore, whether one single church was established in the whole world by the Greatest and Best God <note>original: "Deo Opt. Max." – Deus Optimus Maximus, a standard title for God.</note>, or whether the churches of individual nations are separated from the others, just as Empires are diverse and have nothing in common with each other. The followers of the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> therefore claim that there is a catholic or universal church, which the Apostles’ Creed also mentions. And thus Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit Cardinal and a central figure in the Counter-Reformation.</note> says in *Book 2 on the Pontiff, chapter 18, folio 256*: Just as there is a Bishop in the church of a great city, an Archbishop in a Province, and a Metropolitan <term>Metropolitan: a high-ranking bishop who presides over an ecclesiastical province</term> in a kingdom, and after that a Patriarch; so the Pope is over all.

III. The Reformed <note>The "Reformati" refers to the Protestant tradition, particularly the Calvinist wing.</note> claim that it is a deadly form of servitude if Rulers—with all judgment regarding religion taken away from the Laity—are bound to believe at the whim of a Bishop or Pope, are held to force their subjects to believe, and are required to draw the sword against those who hesitate. Dr. Marta <note>Giacomo Antonio Marta, a legal scholar who defended papal jurisdiction.</note> defends this position. Indeed, from this tradition (which is attributed to the Jesuits), the Prince and secular magistrates are spoken of as nothing more than "spiritual executioners" for the Popes. As such, they would be compelled to punish those whom the tribunal <term>Synedrium: a council or court; here referring specifically to the Inquisition</term> of the Inquisition judges guilty, and they would be forced to carry out the decisions of the Clergy in spiritual and ecclesiastical business with blind obedience—not unlike how the Scribes and Priests once petitioned Pilate. *John 18, verse 30 and following. See* Bartholomew Keckerman <note>A German Reformed theologian and philosopher.</note>, *Practical Disputation 35, problem 14.* This view, however, is almost pleasing to certain of the Reformed, who take all judgment concerning religion away from political figures and strive to assign it to themselves alone. Hugo Grotius <note>A famous Dutch jurist and "father of international law" who argued for the state's right to govern the church.</note> argues against these people in *The Piety of the States of Holland*. Others say these views are contrary to the command of the Greatest and Best God, which hands the book of Deuteronomy to the elected King, so that he may read it all the days of his life: "that he may learn to fear the Lord his God, and to keep his words and ceremonies," *Deuteronomy 17, verse 18; and Joshua chapter 1, verse 8.* Furthermore, they say the name "Church" does not belong to the ministers of the church alone. Parker <note>Robert Parker, an English Puritan.</note>, *On Ecclesiastical Politics, Book 3, chapter 15*; Albicius, *Theological Exercise 4 on the Church, question 1, folio 52.* Therefore, the things that concern the church are not to be carried out by the clergy alone. Although the Emperor Constantine the Great <note>The first Christian Roman Emperor.</note> did not wish to judge theologians, *Tripartite History, Book 2, chapter 2*; just as it is held against Justinian that he was overly curious in deciding theological controversies, as noted by Alemanni in his *Notes on the Secret History of Procopius, folio 71 and following, and 86.* Likewise, the Emperor Valentinian did not wish to judge dogmas: "To me," he said, "since I am but one of the people, it is not lawful to investigate such things." *Tripartite History, Book 7, chapter 12.* So too Bellarmine, in *Book 3 on the Word of God, chapter 7*, says that by the custom of the church, the Laity have decreed nothing regarding religion, but rather the Clergy and the Pope. He says the same in chapter 8 and in his book *On the Laity, chapter 17.* Nothing pertai- <note>The text ends mid-word; the catchword "nere" on the original page indicates the next word is "pertinere," meaning "pertaining to."</note>

# Political-Legal Dissertation
<sig>P 2</sig>

...to belong to the magistrate <note>The "magistrate" refers to the secular governing official or sovereign.</note> the judgment concerning religion. In *chapter 18*, he says that the magistrate must defend religion, and that those who say all religions should be permitted are in error.

IV. Conversely, just as the Catholics endeavor to strip rulers of sacred right <note>original: "jus sacrum"</note>, so on the other hand, I believe those people stray from the "royal road" (indeed, perhaps even more so) who properly attribute the care of spiritual matters to the architectonic <term>architectonic: from the Greek 'architektonike,' referring to a supreme or master-building authority that organizes and governs all other sub-fields</term> or legislative power. These people believe that the Prince, by his Imperial and royal right, can reform Divine worship and that subjects ought to yield to such reformation. David Pareus <note>A prominent German Reformed (Calvinist) theologian, 1548–1622.</note> strives to prove this in many places, such as *in the dedicatory preface to his Commentaries on Hosea, addressed to Maurice, Landgrave of Hesse; in his treatise on the rights of kings against the Pope, last question; and in Zepper, book 2, On Mosaic Laws, chapter 2.* 

In this, he is largely in agreement with Heinrich Eckhard, *treatise on the magistrate, page 204, etc.*; Christian Matthias of Dithmarschen, *political college 2, dispute 6, thesis 4, etc., and his dispute on the norm and judge of theological controversies, thesis 61*; Jacobus Arminius <note>A Dutch theologian whose views led to the "Arminian" movement; he advocated for state oversight of the church to maintain peace.</note>, *in his articles, joined with his Letter to Hippolytus a Collibus, under the title "on the magistrate"*; Parker, *on ecclesiastical policy, book 1, chapter 34*; and the Decree of the States of Holland for the peace of the churches, from the year 1614, in the commentary right at the beginning. 

So that this opinion may be tempered, one should read the Advice of Johannes Brentz, *Whether the Anabaptists should be put to death* <note>original German: "Ob die Wiedertäuffer zu tödten"</note>, which appears in the *fourth decade of Theological Counsels* by Felix Bidembach, *in the 1st order.* Also, Minutius Celsus of Siena (which was the name Sebastian Castellio used to hide his identity, according to Simler, *in the epitome of Gesner’s Library*) in his *treatise on not killing heretics.* Various authors on whether heretics are to be persecuted are reviewed by Joachim Cluten (but these were compiled by Sebastian Castellio and published under the name Martinus Bellius; see Budovec <note>Václav Budovec z Budova, a Bohemian statesman and writer.</note>, *page 138, in the circle of the horologue*). 

Likewise, one must examine those points which Theodor Coornhert <note>A Dutch philosopher and theologian known for his advocacy of religious toleration.</note> disputes at length against Justus Lipsius, in his *Harmony of several points and articles of Christian doctrine, under the title "on the Church," throughout page 81, etc., page 150, etc., page 221, etc.* <note>original German: "Harmon. etlicher Puncten und Artickel Christlicher Lehr / tit. von der Kirchen"</note>. See also the anonymous author (whom I believe to be Theophilus Agricola, an associate of Caspar Schwenckfeld) *in the Concern regarding the outcry now being raised, that no one should be tolerated who is not, without any contradiction, either Papist or Lutheran* <note>original German: "in dem Bedencken von dem Geschrey so man itzt aufgibt / daß man niemands soll leiden / der nicht ohn alle Widerred Päpstisch oder Lutherisch seye"</note>, from the year 1558. Add to this *English Puritanism, published at Frankfurt, chapter 6, throughout page 40.* 

Furthermore, Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a Jesuit Cardinal and leading Counter-Reformation figure.</note> proves sufficiently enough against King Henry VIII of England that ecclesiastical government does not rest with Princes. Martin Chemnitz <note>A second-generation Lutheran theologian who helped solidify Lutheran orthodoxy.</note> argues excellently for this view in his *Theological Topics, title "on the church," chapter 4, page 324*: Just as the Roman Pontiff and his followers commit sacrilege by snatching the election and calling of ministers away from the church and transferring it only to himself and his own, so too is the magistrate guilty of the same crime when, having excluded the ministry and the rest of the church, he claims for himself alone the power of establishing the church. ### On Majesty in General.
<sig>P 3</sig>

...the magistrate is not the whole church, but only a member of it. Nor is he the Lord of the church; but its nurturer: indeed, only a minister, etc. Jacob Heerbrand, *disputation on Matters of Indifference <term>Adiaphora: matters that are neither commanded nor forbidden by Scripture, such as specific liturgical practices or the calendar</term> and the Gregorian Calendar, thesis 86, and many following.* Because the magistrate does not comprise the church alone, but if he is pious, he is a member of it: therefore, he should not decide alone concerning ceremonies and other ecclesiastical matters; but along with other members, the foremost of whom are the ministers of the church. And thus the church, which is the "mother of the household" <note>original: "mater familiâs"</note> and carries the keys <note>The "Power of the Keys" refers to the authority to admit or exclude members from the community, based on Matthew 16:19</note>, has the power of deciding on these causes, etc. Polycarp Leyser the Younger, *disputation on the Formula of Concord <note>A foundational Lutheran document from 1577</note>, decade 9, question 6.* 

Therefore, those who grant to the political magistrate the free power of imposing or abolishing ceremonies at his own whim are in error. For the church does not consist of the magistrate alone; but also of the pastors and the listeners, etc. It is scarcely the case, says Zacharias Fridenreich, *Politics, chapter 12*, that in ecclesiastical policy—whether in establishing it or governing it—we recognize any supreme and absolute power and judgment of the magistrate; rather, we join him with the clergy and the church: following the example of David, *2 Samuel 7, verse 2*, and Hezekiah, *2 Chronicles 30, verse 22*, while subjecting all things to the word of God. *Isaiah 8, verse 20.* Excepting that the patronage of a rightly established religion—namely, that he nourishes and defends the ministers of the church—seems clearly to be the proper and peculiar duty of the magistrate, etc. Whence Isaiah calls them the "nurturers" of the church <note>A reference to Isaiah 49:23, "Kings shall be your nursing fathers."</note>. 

I also understand Nicolaus Vigelius in this way, who I believe was misunderstood by Johannes Camman, *disputation on the rights of majesty 3, thesis 4*. For if the Prince had free power in ecclesiastical matters, he would be greater than the Pope: who, by all the best men <note>Likely referring to Conciliarists, who argued that Church Councils had authority over the Pope</note>, is subjected to a Council. And this would be to create a "political Antichrist," about which see what Martin Luther thought, as cited in Wolf’s *2nd volume of Memorable Events, folio 987*, and by me in my *Temple of Justice, number 64*. Paracelsus <note>The famous Swiss physician and occultist, 1493–1541</note> says this Antichrist is reigning now, *in his commentary on Daniel*. 

Therefore, what Rittershusius disputes against Fachinaeus, *on the Novells, part 1, chapter 3*, must be understood soberly: that Emperors can pass laws concerning ecclesiastical matters by their own right; since the King is more an executor, who promulgates, executes, and protects the holy laws [received] from the church. And even more so, a sound interpretation is needed for what Richard Harris writes in *The English Concord*: that the King is the supreme governor of the realm, as much in spiritual or ecclesiastical things and causes as in temporal ones. And from this primacy, he calls the king the primate and the supreme head of the church. And he contends that he holds this primacy by the very crown of his kingdom. Nor does he say it is absurd for even a pagan King to be the primate of the church, etc. (perhaps because the Romans also, after Pompey's victory, made arrangements concerning the Jewish priests, as noted by *Eusebius, Church History, book 1, chapter 12*). Just as Galfridus Bourdon, *in the Vision of the Christian Scipio, in the letter to Casaubon, folio 64*, asserts that the power of the king is spiritual. These things (I say) seem to me to require a sober interpretation:

Richter, *Ecclesiastical Axioms, 21.* <note>Philipp Melanchthon was a key German Reformer and collaborator of Luther; "political men" here refers to those who view religion purely as a tool for governance.</note> Much less should religion itself be accommodated to the "Reason of State" <term>Ratio statûs: the principle that the interests of the state should take precedence over all else, including religious or moral laws</term>; this was first done by Jeroboam, and among Christians by Theodoric, King of the Goths. *Boccalini, News from Parnassus, report 13.*

V. Now it is pleasing to subjoin several reasons for strengthening the presupposed opinion. (1) If the external worship of the Divine Power depended ordinarily upon the judgment or power of the Empire or royal law, then God and divine things would depend upon man; on which account Eusebius, following Tertullian, mocks the Romans in *History, book 2, chapter 2, at the end.* Subjects would be bound to obey a "reformation" just as they would any other political decree, and religion would be forever changeable. For an ethnic <note>In this context, "ethnic" means pagan or non-Christian.</note> or heretical King would enjoy the same Master-Building Power <term>Architectonica potestas: the supreme authority to structure and order a society</term>; and he would wish to use that power because no one believes themselves to be in error in this regard. Or religion would be used as a pretext for other endeavors. For the variety of religions, says Eberhard von Weihe, *On the Prerogatives of Succession, E. 5. b.*, has without controversy arisen from this: that political governors wanted to apply their dreams, traditions, and human "scabies" <note>Used metaphorically here to mean human flaws, corruptions, or irritations.</note> to the doctrine of Christ, only so that they might keep the state safe. (2) To disagree about true religion would no longer be heresy or schism, but would instead be the crime of High Treason <note>original: "læsæ Majestatis"</note>. And long ago in the primitive church, it was condemned to say: "I follow the religion of the Empe-"

### Of Majesty in General.
#### CHAPTER

<margin>Of the Emperor. *Tripartite History*, book 7, chapter 9, in the rescript of Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian.</margin>
( 3 ) Our Lord Jesus Christ himself willed to establish and strengthen his spiritual kingdom without the aid of a worldly Empire. Did any of the leaders or Pharisees believe in him? No, rather it was the crowd that did not know the law. <margin>John 7:48, etc.</margin> "Consider your calling, brothers," says Saint Paul <margin>1 Corinthians 1:26</margin>, "not many of you were wise according to the flesh, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth." See especially Hilary’s *Against Auxentius*. <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD) was a bishop and theologian who famously defended the church's independence against the Arian-leaning Emperor Constantius II.</note> It was not out of necessity that Christ and the Apostles propagated and protected their doctrine without the protection of a magistrate—as if no Christian magistrate were present who took religion to heart. For our Savior was omnipotent, and if it had been to the church's advantage, he certainly could have brought this about; nor would Christ, in his supreme goodness, have omitted it. But it was because the kingdom he was introducing was not a worldly one. <margin>John 18:36</margin> On this occasion, Brentius <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a prominent Lutheran reformer in the Duchy of Württemberg.</note> writes in the same place: "There is no reason for the Princes of this world to boast that they are the defenders of the Christian church. For the church cannot be defended by arms, because the kingdom of Christ is not of this world. If anyone wishes to be a Protector of the church, let him take up the sword of Peter, Paul, and the other Apostles and Martyrs—not the sword of Augustus or Nero. For Emperors defend towns and villages with their external sword; but Apostles defend the church with a spiritual sword, that is, by the word of the Gospel and by their own suffering." Melanchthon <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a key collaborator with Martin Luther and author of the Augsburg Confession.</note> notes something to nearly the same effect regarding that passage: "It is the nature of impious teachers that when they are judged by the Gospel, they strive to protect themselves by human force because they do not trust in God; this is why Judas summons the cohorts."

( 4 ) The first decrees of the Council <margin>Acts 15</margin> held the force of ecclesiastical law without the influence <note>original: "afflatu," literally "the breath" or "inspiration" of the imperial court.</note> of the Caesar’s Court. But you may say they did not have the power of coercive physical punishment, as the *English Concord* <note>Likely referring to the *Concordia Anglicana* (1612) by Richard Harris, which defended the King of England’s role in church governance.</note> argues on page 49. The response is: such power is not required; otherwise, the primitive church of our Savior God himself, lacking it, would not have been perfect (or would have been rebellious).

( 5 ) In Deuteronomy, the King is commanded to read the Divine Law, but it is said that he must receive this book from the Levites. <margin>Deuteronomy 17:18</margin> This relates to what the Greeks replied to the Latins (according to the Logothete in the *Chronicle of Constantinople*, page 18, etc.) after the expedition of Baldwin of Flanders <note>Baldwin I of Flanders (1172–1205) became the first Emperor of the Latin Empire of Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade.</note> when the Latins wished to introduce Papal jurisdiction. However, whether a political magistrate can enjoin the ministers of the church from publishing books on religious matters is debated in the *Theological Consultations* collected by Mr. Felix Bidembach <note>Felix Bidembach (1564–1612) was a Lutheran theologian who compiled official "Consilia" or expert opinions on church law.</note> (decade 8, consultation 7, and the three following). And Johannes Gerhard <note>Johannes Gerhard (1582–1637) was a towering figure in Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note> discusses in his *Commonplaces* <term>original: "loc. de ministerio," referring to the 'Loci Communes' or 'Common Places' of theology—a systematic way of organizing doctrine.</term> regarding the ministry (number 269): whether a magistrate can command ministers not to rebuke heretics.

# Political-Legal Dissertation

### CHAPTER IV.

### Whether and to what extent the calling of ministers pertains to the secular magistrate.

I. From what has been argued thus far, the followers of the **Augsburg Confession** <note>The primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church, presented in 1530.</note> believe they can conclude by a just consequence: the **right of calling ministers** <note>original: "Jus vocandi ministros"</note> does not belong to the magistrate alone, as political theorists today contend. (And long ago the **Henrician Heresy** <note>A term used by Catholic polemicists like Baronius to describe the position of Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV during the Investiture Controversy against the Pope.</note> held this, according to Baronius and Lehmann, *book 3, chapter 24, page 240, column 2.*) Neither does it belong to the people alone, as the **Anabaptists** <note>A radical reform movement that advocated for the total separation of church and state and congregational autonomy.</note> are said to teach; nor to the **Bishops** alone, as the **Catholics** claim; but to the **entire church**. (Thus, the right resides with the church, but the exercise of it resides with those who represent her.) See **Martin Chemnitz** <note>A preeminent second-generation Lutheran theologian.</note> *on the section on the church, chapter 4, page 324;* **Heinrich Eckhard**, *on the ecclesiastical order, page 90;* **Johann Forster**, *disputations on the decalogue, decade 1, problem 10;* **Gerhard**, *in the section on the ecclesiastical ministry, number 86, etc.;* **Christoph Matthias**, *Political College 2, disputation 6, theses 40 and 42;* **Cothmann**, *Academic Counsel 2, at the beginning;* **Antonio Albizzi**, *theological exercises, title on the Gospel ministry, question 13, page 217;* **Reinkingk**, *class 3, book 1, chapter 6.* See also **Hugo Grotius** <note>A famous Dutch jurist and philosopher.</note> in the notable treatise *The Piety of the States*, *from page 56 to the end;* and **Hadrian Saravia**, *treatise on the grades of ministers, chapter 13, number 27, page 363.* But compare this with **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine, a Cardinal and influential Jesuit defender of Catholic doctrine.</note> *book 1, on the Clergy, chapter 2 and following.* Indeed, **Vincent Cabot** admits that in the election of Priests, and even of the Supreme Pontiff, the roles of the people—not just the clergy—were once recognized. *1. disputation 4;* add **Isaac Pontanus**, *6. Origins of the Franks, chapter 5, page 437.* But he says the people held this right more from **custom** than from **law**. By law, they could request someone as their Bishop; by custom, they held the right of the vote. See **Joachim Stephani**, *book 4, on jurisdiction, chapter 11;* **Duaren**, *on ecclesiastical benefits, book 1, chapter 6; book 3, chapter 2; and book 5, chapter 1.* This also agrees with the chapters of **Charlemagne**; Lehmann, *book 2, chapter 33, page 125.* Compare Bellarmine, *book 2 on the clergy, chapter 7;* and the same author, in *book 1 on the Pontiff, chapter 6*, attempts to show that in the whole of Holy Scripture, not a single trace is found of the common people possessing the right to call ministers, but rather the **Apostles** alone. And since ministers hold the **right of the keys** <term>original: "jus clavium" — the spiritual authority to forgive or retain sins and to govern the spiritual life of the church</term>, Catholics contend that neither the common people nor a Prince can grant this to them.

II. Certainly, regarding the **right of Collation** <term>The act of bestowing a church office or "living" upon a candidate.</term> or **Investiture** <term>The formal ceremony of placing a high-ranking cleric in possession of his office and the lands associated with it.</term>, there was a most bitter struggle between the Popes and the Romano-German Emperors. **Gerhard**, *on the ministry, number 131;* see **Filesac**, *treatise on the authority of Bishops, 177, etc.* The core of the matter seems to consist in this: whether all priestly estates are under the patronage and protection of the Pope, such that the Bishops or Priests...

### Political-Legal Dissertation
<meta>catchword: sua,</meta>

The German-Roman Emperors once wrote about these matters. See Lehmann, *book 5, chapter 67, page 542, etc.* Likewise in England, the King holds the **Right of Patronage** <note>term: "Right of Patronage" (jus Patronatus) — the legal right of a layperson or sovereign to nominate a candidate for a church office.</note> and exists as the hereditary Patron. See Richard Harris, in the *English Accord*. And there, from ancient times, the power of election was in the hands of the clergy and monks, but they would request the chosen person from the King. No election of Prelates was pure, free, and canonical; rather, the King’s Court conferred all dignities, both of Bishops and Abbots, through the **ring and staff** <note>original: "per annulum & baculum" — symbols of spiritual and temporal power used in the Investiture Controversy to signify the appointment of a cleric.</note>, according to his own pleasure. See Selden in *The Janus of the English, book 1, number 39, page 55.* So also in Poland, the King has some power in appointing Abbots. See *Statutes of Poland, section on Abbots.* Similarly, the Kings claim such a Right of Patronage for themselves in Sicily; and when Baronius <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a Cardinal and historian who strongly defended papal authority.</note> denied this in his *Annals, book 11, in the Life of Urban II*, he was not only hindered by Spanish ministers from reaching the Papal dignity in the year 1605 (see *The French Mercury, part 1, page 3*), but King Philip III of Spain also specifically restrained those who denied him this right. See the *First Continuation of the French Mercury, page 11, etc.* In which places the granting of ecclesiastical benefits actually belongs to the Pope is reviewed in the *Political Treasury, part 1, report on Rome, my page 42 and following.* Regarding the Right of Patronage, see Gerhard, *section on the ministry, number 113 and following; also number 117;* and likewise Reinkingk, *book 3, class 1, chapter 9, numbers 25 and 53.*

V. Finally, I advise all who aspire to ecclesiastical dignities not to despise the warning of **Francis Lambert** <note>A French monk who became a Protestant theologian and advisor to Landgrave Philip of Hesse.</note> (a French theologian and monk who joined the Protestants in the time of Luther), who writes thus in his *Treatise on the Calling of the Faithful into the Kingdom of Christ, chapters 8 and 9*: The **External Calling** <note>term: "External Calling" (externa vocatio) — the formal, public invitation or appointment to a church office by a human authority.</note> to the ministries of the church has need of an **Internal Calling** <note>term: "Internal Calling" (interna vocatio) — the personal, spiritual conviction that one has been summoned by God to serve.</note>. When someone is externally called to the ministry of the holy word, and feels and experiences that he was first internally called and sent by the Lord, it is most certain that the external calling itself is from God. But if the internal calling has not preceded it at all, or at least does not soon follow, it is an indubitable fact that the external calling itself is the terrifying judgment of God, by which He punishes an ungrateful people by saturating them with prophets sent by nothing other than the spirit of Satan. Therefore, let every one of the faithful avoid every external calling—that is, let him not accept it—unless he is first moved to it by the Holy Spirit. He will know he is moved by the Lord through this: if he is affected toward accepting the external call in no other way than is fitting, according to the untainted words of the Lord, which are the surest testimonies of His will and His spirit. Therefore, whoever is externally called to the sacred ministries of the Kingdom of Christ, especially to that highest one which is to minister the word of God: before he accepts the calling, let him weigh whether he has received the spirit for it—which is to be internally sent or called. If he has not received it, let him ask of God, who gives gifts abundantly to all...

However, tithes in possessory cases <note>cases regarding current possession rather than ultimate ownership</note>, by virtue of the **Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance** <term>Imperial Chamber Court (Reichskammergericht): The highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire, dealing with disputes between the states of the Empire.</term>, belong to the Imperial Chamber Court if the dispute is between estates of the Empire. But even if a dispute regarding possession is pending in the Imperial Chamber Court, the "petitory" case <note>a legal action to determine the ultimate right of ownership, not just current possession</note> can be argued before the ordinary judge. I know this was done in the case of the **Steward of Waldburg** <term>Herr Truckfessen von Waldpurg: "Truchsess" was a title of high office (steward) held by the noble Waldburg family</term> against **Salem Abbey** <term>Salmansweiler: The Latin name for the Cistercian monastery of Salem near Lake Constance</term>. Finally, I warn those to beware of sinning who have valued the *fasces* <note>original: "fasces" — symbols of judicial power in ancient Rome; here used to mean the power of secular command</note> entrusted to them for pronouncing the law more than the priesthood which must be served through religious duties. See *Rufinus, History, book 10, chapter 23.*

# Political-Legal Dissertation

...he took care that the churches were restored to the Catholics. Ruffinus, *History*, book 10, chapter 19. In this regard, there is a very great difference between the majesty, or the right of Empire, which belongs to a Christian ruler, and that which belongs to an infidel Prince. The latter rules men as they are men; the former, however, rules them also as they are Christians, whom, by the reason of Christian charity, he strives to lead to the true knowledge of the true God.

II. The **Donatists** <term>Donatists: A schismatic Christian group in North Africa (4th–5th centuries) who argued that the church should be pure and separate from the state, often rejecting the authority of the Roman emperors in religious matters.</term> are to be cursed, for they contended that the church of Christ ought not to use the work and assistance of Princes, and that the state should have nothing to do with the church, nor the church with the state. Saint Augustine, *Book 3 against Cresconius* and *Epistles 48 and 50*. Gerhard, *On the Magistrate*, number 165. They seem very close to atheists who, along with **Muhammad** in the **Quran** <note>original: "Mahometo in Alcorano"</note> (*Sura 2*), contend that anyone who worships God and does good undoubtedly attains divine love. Bodin, *On the Republic*, book 4, chapter 7, number 484; see however Boccalini, *From Parnassus*, book 1, chapter 64, page 281.

There are those who—along with Francesco Pucci, in his *Treatise on the Efficacy of Christ the Savior in All Men as Men* (from whom Valentin Weigel does not much differ throughout his works, and especially in *On the Way to Learn All Things*, chapter 4, near the end)—attempt to bring a confusion of all religions into the church. Other writers have agreed with this opinion, as listed by Johann Gerhard in *Conclusion to the Century of Political Questions*, thesis 44 and following, and also by Isaac Casaubon in *Exercises against Baronius*, book 1, from the beginning. See my own work, *Politics*, book 2, chapter 1, number 36, and add Casaubon’s *Vindication*, book 2, chapters 3 and 4, and book 4, chapter 1.

There are also those who, with **Thomas More** in *Utopia*, book 2, page 265, consider it uncertain whether God, desiring a varied and manifold worship, inspires different people in different ways. Or those who, with the King of the Tartars (as cited in Lipsius, *Admonitions*, page 116, and Leunclavius, *Turkish Compendium*, chapter 190, page 397), say: "Let your Pope be yours, and my Pope mine; let your Luther be yours, and my Luther mine." To this belongs that saying of **Symmachus** <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 340–402 AD), a pagan Roman statesman who famously advocated for the preservation of traditional Roman religion in the face of rising Christianity.</note>, who in his *Report to Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius* <note>original: "Valent. Theod. Arcad. AAA." — The 'AAA' refers to the three reigning Augusti (Emperors).</note> said: "All nations aspire to the secrets of the divine power, but not by the same means; since not all are of the same temperament, they tend toward the same God by various paths." Thus also **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher and advisor to several Roman emperors, known for advocating religious tolerance.</note>, in *Oration 3*, page 57, says: "God has sown the veneration of Himself in the hearts of all men and made it common; but He has left the manner of worshipping Him to each person's own judgment. He, however, who thinks force should be used here, snatches away from mortals the freedom granted by God Himself."
