### On Majesty in General

...which Christ and the early Christians practiced, the **magistrate** <term>magistrate: The civil governor or state authority, as opposed to church leadership.</term> must take care of: namely, that he knows that **ministry**, not **Empire** <term>Empire: Here referring to *Imperium*, the legal power to command and use force.</term>, was established for the introduction and preservation of religion; for ministry, by its very nature, rejects **coercion**. In this regard, the Christian magistrate acts as a kind of servant or minister, not as a Prince. Therefore, heretics should be refuted with modesty, "delivered to Satan" <note>A biblical reference (1 Corinthians 5:5) to excommunication or removal from the church community, intended to lead the person to repentance rather than physical harm.</note>, seriously rebuked, avoided, guarded against, and no commerce should be held with them: they are to be shunned, treated as heathens and tax collectors, and kept under observation. This is so that they may all turn themselves toward repentance and turn away from the commands of men; that they may be put to shame, learn not to blaspheme, and, through the instruction of sound doctrine, be made sound in the faith, so that the spirit may be saved. See **Theodore Coornhert** <note>A Dutch politician and scholar (1522–1590) known for his early advocacy of religious tolerance.</note> *in his letter on the process of killing heretics against Lipsius, chapter 17.* See also **Timpler**, *dissenting in Politics, book 4, chapter 2, question 3.* The magistrate, by his own authority, must ensure these means are observed and not neglected; he should not employ other means under the pretext of any authority whatsoever. 

In this matter, there is an excellent maxim by **Emanuel Philibert**, Duke of Savoy, who used to say: *“That the Christian faith was never planted by the force of armies, nor by the violence of weapons, but rather by the word of God and by example; and with these same arts it must be replanted in the lands from which it has been uprooted.”* <note>original Italian: "Che la fede Christiana non fu mai piantata con la forza de gli esserciti..."</note>

Plausible are the words of the most distinguished Lord **Lansius**, *in his consultation on the Principality of the European provinces:* “A multitude of religions is better than a slaughterhouse of consciences: the former produces the superstitious, the latter produces atheists.” I add also the judgment of **Ximenius**, a Spanish theologian, *in the first century of Belgian Letters, number 33,* writing to **Cassander** about the Gallic <note>Refers to the French Wars of Religion.</note> disturbances: “We suffer, it seems to me, the punishment for our own folly in this regard, because we are so minded that we cannot tolerate those who differ from us in religion, unless we simultaneously wish them extinct and even strive to extinguish them. We then add oil to the fire for reasons that have no less power to nourish these contentions, even if they are covered by the cause of religion. Therefore, God must be entreated with the most earnest prayers that He might deign to somehow snatch the weapons—which He certainly did not stir up—from the hands of the unwise, not to say the madmen, etc.” 

**Acontius** agrees, *on the Stratagems of Satan, page 134, etc.* And it is pleasing here to add the judgment of **C. S.** in the *Great Book of Epistles against the Papists*, page 464, so that it may appear that even those who are otherwise said to reject all external means do not deny to Princes a certain right in this area. His words sound like this: *“All Christians should concern themselves with the Kingdom of Christ and His righteousness; therefore, no one can truthfully say that the authorities—so long as they wish to be called and be Christians—should not undertake Christian works or may not externally promote and maintain true godliness according to the Spirit of Christ. Yet no superior [magistrate] should...”* <note>original German: "Es sollen sich alle Christen vmb das Reich Christi vnd sein Gerechtigkeit annemen..."</note>

## A Politico-Legal Dissertation

**IV. But** <note original: "IV. Sed">This is the "catchword" at the bottom of the previous page, indicating the start of the next section.</note> he should neither force his subjects to his own form of worship nor to the Christian faith with violence; nor should he promote the same with the sword and bloodshed. Furthermore, he should not drive away or kill those who are not of his faith, as occurs under the **Papacy** <note>A common Protestant critique of the Roman Catholic Church's use of the Inquisition and state power to enforce religious uniformity.</note>: for such things are contrary and opposite to the gentle and voluntary Spirit of Christ.

Similarly, God will not have His kingdom in the **conscience** <term>conscience: The inner sense of right and wrong, which 17th-century thinkers increasingly argued was outside the jurisdiction of the state.</term> forced by any coercion; much utility may be achieved through dignified action and friendly requests. However, it does not follow from this that a Christian who is in a position of **authority** <term>authority: *Obrigkeit* refers to the governing body or magistrate.</term> should not, according to the recognized truth, desire and help to abolish false, idolatrous worship to the highest degree: for just as he is bound to abolish the offenses of life, so too is he bound to abolish the offenses of doctrine and idolatry.

But how and in what manner the **magistrate** should promote God's Word and abolish everything contrary to wholesome doctrine—this the **anointing** <note original: "Salbung">A biblical metaphor for the guidance of the Holy Spirit (1 John 2:27).</note> and the Spirit of Christ will surely teach him, provided he is a Christian and turns to God with his whole heart through fasting and alms in earnest prayer.

Here it will be highly necessary to have spiritual eyes, and to judge and undertake all things according to the right understanding of the Word of God, as well as according to the Spirit and knowledge of Christ, so that one does not sin through a carnal zeal. For to him who wishes to reform other people before himself, it might be said: **"Physician, heal thyself"** <note>A reference to Luke 4:23.</note>. Therefore, Christ also teaches: **"First cast the beam out of your own eye,"** etc. <note>A reference to Matthew 7:5.</note> It does not please God when we desire to make other people pious without any improvement and change in our own lives.

Nonetheless, even if such an abolition of vice cannot be achieved among the people or in the community, the authorities are still bound, by virtue of the command of their office, to abolish external **idolatry** and the public seduction of doctrine above all things: for every false worship has always been and still is a wellspring and root of all vice and unrighteousness, as all Scripture testifies.

This, however, should be done out of faith, and in this matter, one should look to no human being, but only to God and His honor. For if one acts out of faith, one becomes certain that the matter belongs to God, who will surely lead it to a conclusion, even if the whole world sets itself against it. One is indeed bound to obey God more than to please men <note>A reference to Acts 5:29: "We must obey God rather than men."</note>. Then, one can remain steadfast in temptation under the **Cross** <note>The "Cross" here refers to the trials and suffering a Christian must endure for their faith.</note>, provided one is assured in the heart that one seeks neither one's own welfare nor profit under the appearance of God's Word, but only the glory of His Divine Name—which lets no one who hopes and trusts in Him be put to shame.

<summary>This page argues that while a ruler must not use violence to force religious belief, they still have a duty to abolish public idolatry through spiritual guidance and personal piety. It emphasizes that true reform begins with the ruler's own life and that the state's role is to remove external obstacles to faith rather than coercing the heart.</summary>

## On Majesty in General.

**IV.** But nevertheless, rebels and disturbers of the peace can be restrained. Heretics are almost always seditious and cruel: concerning the cruelty of the **Arians** <note>A 4th-century Christian sect that denied the full divinity of Christ, often cited in the 17th century as a historical example of "heretical" violence.</note>, see the notes of **Barthius** on Phoebadius, page 60. And heretics almost always separate themselves; they are not separated by others. For this reason, they are called *Kätzer* <note original: "Kätzer">The German word for "heretic," traditionally derived from the "Cathars."</note> (Cathars) by the Germans, from the Hebrew word *Kozar*, meaning "he separated."

And so, it was not at all on account of the Catholic religion, but as a most just payment for the penalties of manifest **high treason** <term>high treason: The Latin *perduellio* refers to crimes against the state or the person of the sovereign.</term>, that so many "pseudo-martyrs" of England suffered. The **Jesuit Fathers** <note original: "Patres Soc. Jesu">The Society of Jesus, a Catholic religious order known for its defense of the Papacy during the Reformation.</note> have set forth their history in a massive volume. **Pareus**, in *On the Right of the Prince against the Pope, page 128*, attempts to prove this; see also the anonymous tract titled *British Justice* <note original: "Iustitia Britannica">Likely referring to William Cecil's 1583 defense of Queen Elizabeth I's treatment of Catholics, arguing they were executed for treason, not faith.</note>. But the Catholics hurl this same accusation back at our people; they call them seditious, disturbers, destroyers of monasteries, and so forth.

**V.** Not without reason, therefore, we loathe **war**, both in the process of reforming religion and in preserving it sound and protected from heretics. We reject that saying of **Lipsius**: *Burn, Cut* <note original: "Ure, Seca">A famous and controversial phrase from Justus Lipsius’s *Politicorum Libri Sex* (1589), where he argued that religious dissent should be "burned and cut out" like a gangrenous limb to save the state.</note> (found in his *Politics*, Book 4, Chapter 3), which forced him to leave the Low Countries. **Douza** complains about this matter in his *Elegies*, Book 1, page 79. Such a zeal is not according to knowledge, or is suggested at the wrong time, as noted by **Jacobus Arminius** in his *Oration on Concord*; **Joachim Cluten** in his collection of authors who wrote on the persecution of heretics; **Keckermann** in his *Introduction to Politics*, page 23; **Heinrich Eckhard** in his *Tract on Ecclesiastical and Political Order*, page 223; **Johann Forster** in his *Disputations on the Decalogue*, Decade 2, Thesis 6; **Timpler** in *Politics*, Book 4, Chapter 2, Questions 5 and 6; and **Cothman** on the title of the Code concerning heretics. Indeed, **Alberico Gentili** even believes that religion should not be taken away from those who have been conquered in war (*On the Law of War*, Book 3, Chapter 11).

**VI.** Truly **God**, to whom alone belongs the right of **reformation**, rouses men to this divine work—partly those powerful in prophetic authority, partly those in royal dignity, and partly men who are lowly in the eyes of the world. He does not always proceed in a uniform way. Therefore, an **ordinary calling** <term>ordinary calling: The standard process by which a minister is appointed by an established church hierarchy.</term> is not to be strictly insisted upon here (see **Christian Matthias Dithmarf**, *Political College 2*, Disputation 6, Thesis 16). For sometimes one or a few private individuals have renewed doctrine (**Richter**, *Ecclesiastical Axiom 29*). Sometimes God turns evil means into good; sometimes the ministry introduces perverted opinions, sometimes the Prince does, and sometimes both. Therefore, all should act fearfully and cautiously, and employ no means other than gentle ones (as I have already warned above), such as the **primitive Church** <note>The early Christian church of the first few centuries, often held up by Reformers as the ideal model of simplicity and non-violence.</note> employed.

**VII.** In the **Kingdom of Sweden**, the method used by **King Gustav** <note>Gustav Vasa (reigned 1523–1560), who established the Lutheran Reformation in Sweden.</note> is not unsuitable: for the reformation of religion was established by the consensus of the **Estates of the Realm**, and after a public disputation on the chief articles of the Christian faith was first held, over which he himself presided. **Chyträus** writes extensively on this in his *Saxon Chronicle*, page 292. **Queen Elizabeth** observed this same method in England, as noted by **Rodrigo Botero** in his *History*, Book 10, page 119, and by **Meteranus**.

# Political-Legal Dissertation

[The governing power] should not force its subjects to its own form of divine service or Christian faith through violence, nor promote the same with the sword and bloodshed. Neither should those who are not of the ruler's faith be driven away or killed, as happens within the **Papacy** <note>original: "Papstthumb"; a common Early Modern term for the Roman Catholic Church, often used polemically by Protestant writers.</note>; for such things are contrary and opposed to the gentle and voluntary Spirit of Christ. Thus, God does not wish to have His kingdom in the conscience compelled by any force; much benefit may instead be achieved through dignified action and friendly petition.

However, it does not follow from this that a Christian who is in a position of **authority** <term>authority: The German *Obrigkeit* refers to the governing body or the magistrate responsible for maintaining public order.</term> should not, according to the recognized truth, desire and help to abolish false and idolatrous worship to the highest degree. For just as he is bound to abolish offenses of life, so too must he abolish offenses of teaching and idolatry. But how and in what form the authorities should promote God's Word—and abolish everything that is contrary to wholesome teaching—the **Anointing** <note>A reference to 1 John 2:27, implying that the Holy Spirit provides inner guidance to the believer.</note> and the Spirit of Christ will surely teach them, provided they are truly Christians and turn to God with their whole hearts through fasting and almsgiving in earnest prayer. 

In this matter, it is highly necessary to have spiritual eyes and to judge and undertake all things according to the right understanding of the Word of God, as well as according to the Spirit and knowledge of Christ, so that one does not sin through a **fleshly zeal** <note>An impulsive or worldly passion for religious reform that lacks spiritual maturity or divine guidance.</note>. For to him who wishes to reform other people before himself, it might be said: "Physician, heal yourself." Therefore, Christ also teaches: "First cast the beam out of your own eye," <term>etc.</term> It does not please God when we desire to make other people pious without any improvement or change in our own lives.

Nevertheless, even if such an abolition of vice cannot be achieved among the people or in the community, the authorities are, by virtue of their office, bound above all things to abolish external idolatry and the public deception of false teaching. For every false worship has always been and still is a spring and root of all vice and unrighteousness, as all Scripture testifies. This, however, should be done out of faith, and in this, one should look to no human being but to God and His honor alone. For if one acts out of faith, one is assured that the matter is God's, and He will lead it to a successful conclusion, even if the whole world sets itself against it. Indeed, one is bound to obey God more than to please men. Only then can one remain steadfast in the face of temptation under the **Cross** <note>In this context, "the Cross" refers to the suffering, persecution, or hardships a Christian must endure for their faith.</note>, if one is assured in the heart that one seeks not one's own welfare or profit under the appearance of God's Word, but only the honor of His Divine Name—which lets no one who hopes and trusts in Him be put to shame.

VIII. Another question, though not out of place here and certainly of the greatest importance, is this: Should Christian Princes resist the asserted Papal tyranny, and block and break its path? IX. Stephen, King of Poland <note>Stefan Batory (reigned 1575–1586), known for his religious tolerance in a divided Poland.</note>, used to say that God had rightly reserved three things for Himself: to make something out of nothing, to know the future, and to rule over consciences. "Learn from me that piety is a duty of man toward God, over which the arm of the flesh <note>original: "le bras de la chair"</note> has no power." <note>original: "Apprenez de moy, que la pietè est un devoir de l' homme, envers Dieu: sur lequel le bras de la chair, n' a point de puissance."</note> This is the "Swan Song" <term>Swan Song: A final statement or gesture before death; here referring to the king's last official sentiments.</term> of King Henry III of France, as recorded by Pierre Matthieu in *The History of the Recent Troubles*, book 5. Furthermore, when Augustus, Elector of Saxony, once told Emperor Maximilian that he wanted his ministers to feel and believe the same things in religion that he himself held, so that they might all be of one mind and faith, the Emperor replied piously, wisely, and gravely: "I do not take that power upon myself. I neither wish to nor should I attempt it, for I have no empire over consciences, nor do I claim it; and I am not ignorant of what a slaughterhouse of consciences <note>original: "carnificina conscientiarum"</note> results if they are forced." This is recorded in Caspar Peucer’s *History of Prisons*, page 287, and repeated on pages 361 and 478. It is a matter of **natural law** <term>natural law: A philosophy asserting that certain rights are inherent by virtue of human nature and endowed by nature or a transcendent source.</term> to have a free conscience and to believe whatever you wish. Therefore, a Prince cannot take away this right, nor can he prohibit it even under the penalty of exile. As for whether it is permitted to require an oath of religion, see Johann Gerhard, *On the Magistrate*, number 210.

This even seemed fair to Socrates in a much lowlier cause. See Zacharias Fridenreich, *Politics*, chapter 26, page 141. Johann Mercerius disagrees in *Opinions*, chapter 26; he, like almost all Roman Catholics, thinks a Prince can compel his subjects to a religion. This is also supported by the Code, book 8, section 5, "On Heretics," and Frede...

# A Political-Legal Dissertation #

Today, many hold the view that a Prince or Count, etc., who comes over to our side <note>Meaning those who joined the Protestant Reformation.</note>, is able to apply the church property <note>original: *bona ecclesiastica* — lands, buildings, and wealth owned by the church.</note> within his territory to other more pious uses. However, the rulings and sentences of the Imperial Chamber Court <note>The *Reichskammergericht*, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> stand to the contrary; though a legal review <note>original: *revisio* — a formal appeal process in the Imperial courts.</note> was requested against them. On that occasion, all such reviews were left waiting for justice to take its course. See the tract titled *The Disturbed State of the Empire* <note>original: *Turbatus Imperii Status* — a famous 17th-century political pamphlet discussing the legal chaos of the period.</note>. On this matter, the author of the *Consilia* <note>A collection of legal advice or opinions.</note>, who participated in these decisions, argues in various ways. See **Christoph Schwannman**, *page 99, section "nothing hinders this,"* etc.; **Hermann Esaias Rosakorb**, *Forensic Practice, chapter 29, page 48, and chapter 30, page 55 and following*; the *Collection of Petitions* <note>original: *Symphorema supplicat* — a well-known legal reference work.</note>, *volume 1, title 3, page 219*; **Syring**, *Disputation on the Religious Peace, thesis 40*; **Cranius**, *On the Religious Peace, part 1, problem 4, in the connection*; **Treutler**, *part 2, disputation 13, thesis 2, letter D.*

III. At this point, I cannot help but warn those Great Lords who claim to profess a purer religion <note>A common self-description for Protestants (Reformed or Lutheran).</note>: they must not apply things dedicated to worship—which they consider superstitious—to their own secular <note>original: *profanis* — non-religious or worldly.</note> conveniences. By doing so, they make their own piety and religion suspect in the eyes of their adversaries, as if they were merely driven by a greed for profit. See the *Smalkaldic Articles* <note>A summary of Lutheran doctrine written by Martin Luther in 1537.</note>, article 3; **Schurff**, *century 1, counsel 48*; **Danæus**, *Politics, book 3, chapter 2*; **Henricus Scotanus**, *on the Code, book 1, title 2, page 26*; **Cranius**, *Treatise on the Religious Peace, part 1, problem 5*; **Latherus**, *On Wealth, book 3, chapter 18.* Rather, they should devote these resources to those hindered by old age or ill health, and to the ministry, which should not be second to the church office. <note>original: *argum. Novell. 3. §. quemadmodum* — a reference to the "Novels" or new laws of Emperor Justinian.</note> Some believe, and not without reason, that the neglect of this duty is the cause of many evils in many places. See **Paracelsus** <note>The famous Swiss physician and occultist, here cited for his commentary on the Book of Daniel.</note> *on Daniel, chapter 5.* **Henricus Petreius** discusses this matter gravely in a work that deserves to be read by all Protestant Princes, *Treatise on Monasteries, page 55b and many following.* **Eberhard von Weihe**, in his *Treatise on the Prerogative of Succession, letter H. 7*, dealing with ecclesiastical offices, says: "These were otherwise ordained with great and prudent counsel and singular skill. These institutions, as well as the monasteries, could have been preserved intact during the time of the cleansed religion <note>The Reformation.</note>, provided the abuses were corrected and removed." For the decree that the Emperors wrote back—"The goods which the error of the ancients assigned to sacred things, we command to be joined to our own treasury"—is, in our opinion, accepted far too broadly in this case, etc. **Barclay** <note>John Barclay (1582–1621), a Scottish satirist and poet who defended Catholicism.</note> sharply taunts our side on this account in his *Exhortation, book 1, chapter 4, page 36 and following*: "If, in your judgment, the monks were erring in morals or faith, why did you not eject them and substitute other mortals who could attend to these holy offices with purer morals and a restored faith, but with that same diligence of piety? Why, at the very least, were these goods not distributed to the poor, since they were given to the poor of old and handed over to divine worship by your own customs? It pleased you to seize God’s inheritance, to despoil Jerusalem, and by corrupting the wills, legacies, and benefits of the ancients who had consecrated these things to God, you bind your Provinces and your homes to the crime of dire sacrilege," etc. What **Blessed Bernard** <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a major leader in the reform of Benedictine monasticism.</note> says regarding Princes who abuse the goods of the Church, this he...

### On the Ecclesiastical Right of the Sovereign ###

Let the Princes who have the administration of ecclesiastical matters consider this as being equally said to them. The poverty of the poor cries out, the naked cry out, the hungry cry out; they complain and say: "It is ours, that which you squander; it is cruelly stolen from us, that which you spend vainly; it is taken from our necessities, whatever is added to your vanities," etc. <note>original: "Nostrum est, quod effunditis..." This famous passage is from St. Bernard of Clairvaux’s letter to Henry, Bishop of Sens, often cited to remind rulers that church wealth is "the patrimony of the poor."</note> *In the Letter to Henry, Bishop of Sens; Tauler in his Life, page 28, etc., in the Cologne edition.* Among the Heathens <note>Non-Christians or Pagans.</note> it was always an infamous vice to squander church property <term>bona ecclesiastica (church property)</term> under any pretext. *Scipione Ammirato, Discourse 15, chapter 5.* And [the author] sprinkles those who do the contrary today with the most biting wit, *Boccalini, volume 1, Parnassus 91*, as well as *Menippus Revived, Dialogue 75.* It is a most shameful thing for it to be said of Christians what the Lord of Accords <note>Etienne Tabourot (1549–1590), a French jurist and poet known for his wordplay and epigrams.</note> said of his fellow Catholics in his *Epigrams, leaf 18b*:

> Formerly, a hospital was built
> For the poor parishioners;
> But now, as everything goes ill,
> Nothing but dogs are housed there.
> Now the King wants by all means
> That we follow the original foundations:
> I think we would do it,
> If we were Turks or Pagans.

Indeed, even among those who are earnestly Catholic, many long for church property. Thus Scioppius <note>Kaspar Schoppe, a controversial scholar and convert to Catholicism known for his sharp polemics.</note> inveighs bitterly against King Philip III of Spain himself in his *Royal Council, page 25*, because he wished to take away several things from that famous Carthusian monastery <note>The Certosa di Pavia or a similar high-profile monastery in the Milanese territory.</note> located in the Duchy of Milan. Thus, in former times, under the Frankish Empire, Abbeys were given to soldiers <note>This refers to the practice of "commendam," where laypeople or soldiers were given control of monasteries to collect their revenues.</note>: *Pasquier, Researches, book 3, chapter 34; Hotman, Feudal Lexicon, under the word "Abbot"; Filefacus, special treatise under the title "Complaint of the Gallican Church"; Lehmann, book 5, chapter 67, page 540.* And Tithes were granted to these same people as fiefs, *Pasquier, in the cited book, chapter 35.* Emperor Henry IV also wished to take their goods away from churchmen. *Lehmann, book 4, chapter 3, page 278.* Julian the Apostate <note>The 4th-century Roman Emperor who attempted to revive Paganism and was accused of confiscating Christian church wealth.</note> did this as well, *Tripartite History, book 6, chapters 7, 10, and 32.* Certainly, even goods dedicated to a false religion should not be profaned, out of respect for religion. *Alain Chartier, cited in Pasquier, Researches, book 5, chapter 15, page 746.* And Justinian is spoken of poorly because he plundered the shrines of heretics, *Procopius, Secret History, page 51, where this is noted*; and for that reason Abraham Scultetus <note>A prominent German Reformed theologian.</note> criticizes Cardinal Wolsey, *at the end of the first decade.* Regarding the abuse of church property, such a poem exists in a Polish Dialogue *On Corrupt Morals, page 52*:

-> We bees knew a pleasing murmur once lived in these cells, <-
-> from which there was an abundance of honey for the pious. <-
<note>original: "Gratum murmur apes..." This Latin couplet uses the metaphor of bees and honey to represent the monks and the spiritual/material wealth they generated for the community, which has since been lost.</note>

It cites a wide range of historical and legal examples—from the Roman Emperor Julian the Apostate to King Philip III of Spain—to illustrate the spiritual and social dangers of "plundering" religious foundations.</summary>

...it is permitted, so that the offense might be turned aside, in consideration of the religion that was imposed upon us. III. Let the good and Christian reader consider whether what I have argued thus far from the Protestant perspective can be included in the following propositions: 

(1) The <term>Prince: Here used in the general sense of a sovereign ruler or head of state.</term> must entirely establish, promote, and reform divine worship. 

(2) But he does this not by <term>right of Empire: The supreme authority or sovereignty inherent in the state.</term>, but rather as the principal member of the Church, and with the Church’s consent. 

(3) Here, the Prince and the Church must employ those means which Christ and the Apostles prescribed. 

(4) Sometimes, for the sake of peace, many things are granted to Princes by agreement which they did not possess by right itself. Thus in Germany, the <term>reformation of the Church: Referring to the "Jus Reformandi," the legal right of a ruler to determine the official religion of their territory.</term> is attached to the ruler's superiority, not to the judgment of the Church. Or perhaps it can even be said: the Religious Peace <note>The Peace of Augsburg (1555) and later the Peace of Westphalia (1648) which established the legal framework for coexistence between Catholics and Protestants in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> grants this power to the States of the territory—who have rights only with respect to the Emperor and other states—but it does not exclude the Church of their own jurisdiction. See Reinking, *Book 3, class 1, chapter 6, number 6, etc.* 

(5) Likewise, once religion and the Church are established, the administration of certain matters pertaining to the Church can sometimes be entrusted to the Rulers (the magistrate encompassing the name of the people) by wise counsel and to avoid disturbances. And so in Germany, the States of our confession <note>The Lutheran or "Augsburg Confession."</note> hold the direction of the Ecclesiastical <term>Consistories: Administrative and judicial councils that managed church discipline and legal matters like marriage.</term>; they call ministers, judge matrimonial cases, etc. But nevertheless, they hold <term>Episcopal rights: Administrative powers traditionally held by bishops, which in Protestant territories were often transferred to the secular prince as "emergency bishop."</term> as a trust, not by right of Lordship. Joachim Stephani, *in Institutes of Canon Law and Book 3 on Jurisdiction.*

## On the Rights of Sovereignty.
<meta>catchword: only</meta>

...[duties] it is absolute, and animates the entire commonwealth with a universal power. From this, the <term>Regalia: These are the "royal rights" or prerogatives that belong exclusively to the sovereign power, such as coining money or declaring war.</term> or Rights of Sovereignty (which some, such as Petra in *Chapter 4 and many following*, list as almost infinite; and about which Sixtinus, Cammann, Carpzov in Arumæus, *Volume 3, Discourse 15*, and Einsidel treat excellently; and above others Choppin in his *Treatise on the Dominion of France*) can, in my opinion, be reduced to the following main points:

(1) To give laws and magistrates to others, but not to receive them oneself; and conversely, to be able to grant dispensations against the laws and the precepts of magistrates. 

(2) To judge everyone, but to be bound by the judgment of none; rather, to examine the judgments of all others. 

(3) To defend the commonwealth against internal and external force. 

(4) To provide the <term>sinews of affairs: A common historical metaphor (nervi rerum) for the financial resources, taxes, and treasury needed to run a state.</term>. 

(5) And that the sovereign alone is able to conduct those matters in the commonwealth which are more dignified and especially splendid.

II. The *Regalia*, or rights of the Empire, seem to differ from the right of Dominion and the eminence of the "fullness of power" not in kind, but as an effect differs from its cause; they appear to be its specific functions. Thus, being <term>released from the laws: original: "legibus solutum". This refers to the concept of "princeps legibus solutus est"—the ruler is not bound by the civil laws he himself creates.</term> is not a specific, separate right of sovereignty; rather, it is sovereignty itself and a certain universal right of sovereignty. See Arnisæus, *Book 2 On the Right of Sovereignty, 1, number 9*; see also Lord Doctor Bocer, *Book 1 On the Regalia, number 2*. Arnold Clapmarius disagrees in *Book 1 On the Secrets of Commonwealths, 11 and following*. 

And I myself once thought that only two essential marks should be attributed to sovereignty, and that the later one which some add (being "released from the laws") ought to be placed among the attributes that depend on the former ones. For by the very fact that sovereignty is called the highest and perpetual power of commanding, recognizing neither superior nor equal, I thought it necessarily followed that the same power is released from all foreign command. But nevertheless, since in the administration of any *regalia* whatsoever that eminence stands out, and since he who holds the decision-making power of the Empire uses all these royal rights with that free power, it cannot be a species distinct from the other *regalia*. I would think it more correctly said that the right of sovereignty regards universal dominion (which I treated above in <insert>section one</insert>) and the particular rights, the explanation of which I now approach.

III. Furthermore, the rights of sovereignty are distinguished and assigned in various ways; see Johann Cammann, *Disputation on the Rights of Sovereignty 2, thesis 45 and following to the end*; Clapmarius, *Book 1 On the Secrets, the said chapter 11*; Heinrich Velsten, *Century of Political Questions, decade 8, thesis 4*. Some say these rights flow from the three duties of sovereignty: **Ordaining**, **Judging**, and **Vindicating**. See Paurmeister, *Book 1 On Jurisdiction, chapter 3, numbers 13 and 6*, and Bortius in Arumæus, *Discourse 30, chapter 3, thesis 3 and following*. Thomas Michael, in *On Jurisdiction, thesis 24*, says that some *regalia* belong as a sign of superiority, and some by the force of a singular privilege; that is, some belong as a sign of supreme power, while some...

### Political-Legal Dissertation

...only by reason of preserved dignity. Fachinæus, *Controversies, Book 13, chapter 81.* It is common for these to be separated into "Major" and "Minor" rights. Vultejus and Bocerus call the Major rights those of dignity, Empire, or majesty; they call the Minor rights those of utility and the <term>fiscus: original: "fiscus". This refers to the public treasury or the financial interests of the state, as opposed to the private wealth of the ruler.</term>. They claim the former regard the person of the Emperor, while the latter regard the treasury. To this view, I believe what Joachim Stephani writes (*On Jurisdiction, Book 3, chapter 8, number 2, etc.*) is nearly identical: that the Royal Prerogatives consist of two things: (1) in <term>αὐτεξουσία: original: "autexousia". The self-determined power or liberty to act according to one's own will and pleasure.</term>, or the liberty of acting by one's own pleasure; and (2) in <term>δεσποτεία: original: "despoteia". Absolute lordship or universal dominion over property and things.</term>, or universal ownership of things. And in *number 28, etc.*, he teaches the same: that fiscal rights were later called "regalia" because the Emperors, after the government changed, granted them as royal <term>feuds: original: "feuda". Land or rights held by a subordinate from a superior in exchange for service and loyalty.</term>, etc. See Hotman in his *Lexicon* under the word **Regalia**. However, it seems to me that the Minor or fiscal regalia are nothing other than the effects of extraordinary collection and the management of the "sinews of the republic," or special methods of taxation. Properly speaking, there are no degrees within Majesty itself; it exists as an indivisible unit. Thus, by reason of their essence, some rights are not "major" and others "minor."

IV. Nor do I feel any hesitation here regarding what that most prudent of political thinkers, Arnoldus Clapmarius (*On Secrets, Book 1, chapter 21*), claims based on the opinions of legal interpreters when he says: "Those rights called 'regalia' by the Feudalists (*Book 2 of Feuds, title 56*) differ in many ways from the right of Empire. This is partly because regalia—whether major or minor—are granted to others as fiefs, just like immovable property. It is also because they do not carry such majesty within themselves," etc. For those who hold <term>territorial rights: original: "jura territorialia". The local jurisdiction or sovereignty held by princes within their own specific lands under the Emperor.</term> exercise other rights besides the fiscal regalia through the benefit of the Emperor, as will be shown in the proper place. Furthermore, the fiscal regalia belong to the Emperor by the right of majesty, not by private inheritance, and they are established by the force of <term>absolute power: original: "solutæ potestatis". Power that is "unbound" or released from the constraints of ordinary law.</term>. Granted, once these rights are established, the profit from them can be transferred to another; see Bortius in Arumæus (*Discourse 30, chapter 3, thesis 47, page 898*). In such a case, they are possessed not as a right of majesty, but like any other income—similarly to how the right of <term>tithes: original: "decimarum". A ten-percent tax or tribute, often originally for the church, but here used as a general example of a revenue stream.</term> is held by laymen. Truly, the faculty of establishing such regalia anew is granted as a fief just as rarely as the liberty to usurp the Major rights. Indeed, the power to impose these regalia proceeds from a more sublime power, namely from **lordship** <note>original: "δεσποτεία"</note>, which seems to be greater than **self-determined power** <note>original: "αὐτεξουσία"</note>.

V. Mr. Joachim Cluten, in his *Sylloge, theses 17 & 20*, distinguishes between "reserved rights" and the "administration of the rights of the realm," as does Jacob Bornitius in his *Treatise on Majesty, chapter 30 and following*. Bornitius separates "reserved rights" and "regalia" from the right of majesty. I see no harm if all these things are ascribed to Majesty and are said to belong to it essentially. For no one, unless they possess Majesty, can reserve anything for themselves individually. Nor do I quite understand how Bornitius attributes the right of coinage to Majesty, but separates from it the right of Markets, the <term>Staple: original: "Stapulæ". A right granted to a town to require passing merchants to display their goods for sale there for a certain period.</term>, the opening of Universities, or the granting of Asylums, etc. They are all called Regalia...

# On the Rights of Majesty.

...sometimes these rights are viewed as belonging to the King alone; for that reason, they are called the **rights of majesty**. Sometimes they are so named as being granted by the King alone; in this sense, they are merely the *use* of sovereign rights, lacking true ownership. They are called **Reserved** rights in respect to rights already granted, as if they were not conceded along with them. Within the concept of majesty, all these things are essentially one and the same.

### CHAPTER II.

## On the power of making laws.

Just as Majesty is freed from the bond of the laws, so it binds all subjects by the tie of its decrees, and either leads or pulls them toward the goal of civil society. <note>original: "can. quæ contra mores. distinct. 8." A reference to Canon Law regarding customs that contradict morality.</note> To establish laws, therefore (or to propose edicts—Petra, *chapter 10*—or to issue proclamations: Tuschus, *letter B, conclusion 2, etc.* <note>original: "Gebott und verbott". This is a German phrase meaning "commands and prohibitions."</note>), by which all subjects, both as a whole and as individuals, are bound, is the first and foremost attribute of civil majesty. See Vasquius, *Illustrious Controversies, 47.* Conrad Lancellot, *Temple of Justice, book 1, chapter 1, section 4, folio 311.* Bornitius, *On Majesty, chapter 16.* Johann Camman, *disputation 4, thesis 1,* and Lord Marta, *On Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 17.* For this reason, the Patriarch Jacob immediately joins the scepter with the lawgiver. <note>original: "Genef. 49. vers. 10." Referencing the biblical prophecy that "the scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet."</note> Without this right, political power cannot stand: for the strength of a Law is to command, to forbid, to permit, and to punish. <note>original: "l. 7. de legib." A reference to the Roman Digest, Book 1, Title 3, Law 7.</note> Every "perfect republic" <note>A technical term for a fully independent state that recognizes no higher earthly authority.</note> enjoys this royal prerogative, recognizing no superior. Likewise, the statutes of such states ought to be called the "common and civil law." Rol. à Valle, *On the Profit of Dowry, question 2, at the beginning.* 

To speak, decree, and render the law already established, or even to apply and execute it in fact, is the duty of other magistrates and judges; but in the present matter, establishing the laws must be a task worthy of the <term>Empire: original: "imperio". Here referring to the supreme sovereign authority of the state.</term> alone. *Final law, section 1, Code: On Liberty.* Hence, regarding the authority to establish law, the voice of the King is considered a "living law." <note>original: "vivâ lege". The concept of the ruler as "nomos empsychos" or law personified.</note> *Law 2, section 1, On the Origin of Law.* And what has pleased the Prince, with the intention of making a law, is thought to obtain the force of law. <note>original: "Quódque Principi placuit... legis vigorem obtinere putatur." A famous maxim of Roman Law from Ulpian.</note> *Law 1, Digest: On the Constitutions of Princes.* This is true whether his own spontaneous will introduced it, or whether a petition, a report, or a legal dispute provided the occasion for the law. *Law 3, Code: On Liberty.* 

In this view, God is said to have subjected the laws themselves to the Emperor, and to have sent him to men as a "living law," as stated in the *Novels, 105, chapter 2, toward the end*—namely, insofar as he can take away <term>positive law: original: "jus positivum". Laws created by human authority, as opposed to natural or divine law.</term>. Lancellot, *cited section 4, folio 315.* He may even decree something against natural law or the law of nations if there is cause. Lancellot, *cited section, folio 331.* He even limits divine law itself. Lancellot, *cited place, folio 332.* See what I said above in *Discourse 1.* Likewise, Law can invalidate contracts. Becanus, in *Scholastic Theology, title: On Liberty, chapter 6, question 9,* and it can grant legal capacity to persons, *question 10.* From these points, we can also conclude that the power of establishing law is not a matter of mere authority or jurisdiction, but belongs to the **Reserved Rights of the Prince**...

# A Political-Legal Dissertation

...to be the Prince's. <note>original: "principis esse"</note> Lord Bocer, *On Jurisdiction, number 18 and 43.* Fachinae, *Book 13, chapter 12, folio 204 and in the same book, chapter 22.* Camman, *4, thesis 12.* Sometimes, foreign peoples even adopt the laws of another, though they do not acknowledge its rule: thus the Poles use Saxon law. Falstin, *10, chapter 8.* And many cities use the law of Lübeck. Musculus, *On the Successive Assembly, member 2, class 1, conclusion 5, folio 85, and myself, On Appeals, chapter 2, section 7.* But this occurs by the approval of the supreme power, which, while introducing the laws of a foreign nation, is seen to establish them anew within its own territory.

II. Regarding the claim that a law cannot be given to subjects without the counsel of wise men, our interpreters of **both laws** <note>This refers to "Utrumque Ius," the study of both Civil (Roman) Law and Canon (Church) Law.</note> maintain: August Morla, *The Marketplace of Law, title 1, question 3.* Cornel Benincas, *on the external title concerning constitutions, question 7.* I understand this as the mere employment of counsel, which in no way diminishes the right of majesty but rather promotes its success and contributes to the happiness and glory of the empire. Camman, *disputation 4, thesis 9.* Cluten, *in Paradoxes, thesis 10.* Thus it is in France, Lehman, *book 2, chapter 39, folio 149,* as well as in Germany, according to the same author, *book 5, chapter 60.* Laws have always been approved in the assemblies of the leading men. Indeed, what is found in *the Code, book 8, regarding laws*, I refer to the drafting and the counsel for establishing the law. See generally Camman, *4, thesis 10.* For a law must be a common precept and the counsel of prudent men, *the Digest, book 1, concerning laws*, and what obtains the force of law should be determined by many, **not by one**. Velstenius, *decade 5, thesis 9.* 

Thus it is recorded in *the Digest, book 2, section 4, regarding the origin of law* that a certain Hermodorus of Ephesus, an exile in Italy, was the advisor to the **Decemviri** <note>The "Ten Men," a commission established in ancient Rome around 450 BCE to write the first formal law code, the Twelve Tables.</note> for the making of laws. Even the Decemviri themselves, who were forced to seek confirmation from the people for the laws they wrote (Livius, book 8), did not possess the rights of majesty. See, however, *the Digest, book 2, section 4, regarding the origin of law.* So too Justinian willed that a law would not be valid unless approved by the **Praetorian Prefect** <note>Originally the commander of the Emperor's guard, this office evolved into the highest administrative and legal official in the late Roman Empire.</note> (*New Constitutions 151 and 152*), yet he did not make that official a sharer in majesty. Likewise, in later times, the Senate was permitted by the Prince to create Proconsuls, to give deputies to the Consuls, and to grant judicial rights to governors; the Senate itself would sanctify the laws issued by the Princes with its own decrees, as Vopiscus testifies in his life of *Probus*. Similarly, among the French, the **Court of Paris** <note>The "Parlement de Paris," which was the supreme court of the French kingdom and had the power to register or protest royal edicts.</note> has the duty of approving laws and taking notice of the alienation of the royal **Domain** <note>The lands and estates belonging directly to the crown.</note>.

One might gather that the validity of Statutes is not at all required to be accepted by the customs and usage of the citizens, since their force depends absolutely on the will and command of the legislator, as the superior. For indeed, **what pleases the Prince has the force of law**, and the Prince's...

# On the Rights of Majesty

...is to command, and the citizens' duty is to obey. *Law 1, On the Constitutions of the Prince.* <note>original: "est jubere, civium obedire"</note> For this reason, laws are said to "bind the lives of men." *Law 9, Code on Laws.* Furthermore, anyone who treats the will of his Prince with contempt is denounced as being "swollen with the loathing of arrogance." *Law 12, under the same title in the Code.* Thus, it seems that citizens who fail to observe a statute are more deserving of punishment than they are of being allowed to legally exempt themselves or their court cases from that statute.

(2) It also seems argued that a statute not observed through use cannot be considered abolished by a contrary custom. After all, those who lack the power to create statutes without the confirmation of a superior cannot create a contrary custom without that superior's knowledge. *Argument from Law 2, Code on the nature of long-standing custom.* 

But there is another view that is most commonly accepted: namely, if a reform or a new statute is created that contradicts an old statute or an ancient custom, but both before and after that reform, the old statute or customs continued to be observed, then the ancient law and customs must be retained. The later reform is to be ignored because it was never accepted into actual practice. Paris de Puteo, *in the treatise on the Syndicate... and in this, a statute that is always practiced always prevails.* Alexander, *Counsel 6, number 2, book 1.* Legal experts provide this as a general rule: Statutes that have not been observed in the customs of the citizens have no force, nor do they bind anyone. Jason, *on Law 7, number 22, Digest on free men and posthumous children.* Rolandus à Valle, *treatise on dotal profit, question 99.* Schrader *on fiefs, part 10, section 20, number 151.* Schultes, *practical questions 1, volume 1.* 

Thus, the entire **Saxon Law**, <note>original: "Saxonicum Jus"; referring to the *Sachsenspiegel* or related legal codes used in German territories.</note> even though it has existed in writing for many centuries and has been confirmed by the Emperors (Musculus, *on the Successive Assembly...*), nevertheless only holds its authority insofar as it has been proven by use and accepted by the customs of the courts. Hartmann Pistor, *book 1, question 16, number 11.* Scheffer, *part 2, question 14.* 

The reasoning for this decision, however, does not seem to be based on the idea that a Prince (or anyone with the power to legislate) cannot exercise that power without the consent of his citizens or subjects. This is the opinion of the highly learned Becanus, who writes in his *Scholastic Theology* (see also Bellarmine, *On Councils, book 1, chapter 17*; Carnin, *In the Tower of Babel, chapter 3, page 75*): "The Prince does not have the power to establish a law if the community is opposed." 

While such a view might align with **natural equity**, <note>original: "æquitas naturalis"; the concept of justice based on innate human reason rather than written law.</note> one will hardly get court-oriented political thinkers to agree to it. Indeed, in our law, it is considered **sacrilege** <note>original: "sacrilegium"; in Roman law, questioning the Emperor's judgment was legally classified as a form of sacrilege or treason.</note> to dispute the judgment or power of the Prince. *Law 3, Code on the crime of sacrilege.* Therefore, I believe that statutes not approved by use are considered invalid only because a Prince who allows his statute to go unobserved is tacitly seen to have revoked his own will and law. By the same reasoning, a custom contrary to a law is valid, or a revoking...

### Political-Legal Dissertation

...history of the statute, made for the benefit of the people: so much so that our legal scholars say that the knowledge or consent of the superior Lord is not necessary in that case. Natta *Counsel 19, beginning "in the case of the Lord Treasurer," number 7; and Counsel 98, "in the case and question pending," number 6.* Rolando à Valle, *in the said treatise on the profit of dowries, question 99, number 12.* Schultes, *in the cited place, question 2, number 6, etc.* But it is sufficient, while a custom is being introduced, that the Prince does not contradict it; even if he is unaware that the custom is already in the process of being formed. Vultejus, *Marburg Counsels, 33, number 75, book 1.* 

Thus, custom has this unique, or rather remarkable, quality: that through its means, the people can silently abolish a law <note>original: "tacitè legem abrogare"</note>; something they are in no way permitted to do by an express act of will. Faber, *on the section regarding unwritten law, under number 11, Institutes on natural law and the law of nations, etc.* I believe, however, that this should be understood as follows: it is necessary either that the statute is not observed for such a length of time that it can be seen as abolished through disuse <term>desuetudo: the legal principle where a law loses its force because it hasn't been used or enforced for a very long time</term>, <note>based on the arguments handed down by Pedro Salazar, On Custom, chapter 8, number 12</note> or that certain acts contrary to the statute were performed by the people in the presence of the Prince or his officials, whereby the authority or binding force of the statute should be considered blocked. Pietro Ravenna, *Treatise on Custom, on the phrase: custom does not derogate from the law.* Pruckhmann, *Counsel 47, number 25, book 1.* Schultes, *question 2, number 34, etc.* 

It is also rarely the case that a law is repealed by mere lack of use; rather, contrary acts are required. Scheffer, *second part, question 4, number 2, etc.* Likewise, whoever claims that a law has not been accepted by usage must prove it. Schultes, *book 1, Practical Questions, question 50, number 8, etc.* Nor would I require here, as Scheffer does in *cited question 14, number 6*, that it be established that the law was actually observed at some point. Nevertheless, as I have already said above, it is just for the Prince to make laws with the consent of his subjects; and if this is not a matter of absolute necessity, it is nevertheless a matter of fairness and honor. And those laws are especially valid which the people request. Boccalini, *Reports from Parnassus, report 63, century 1, page 277.*

**IV.** The power to make laws itself is never delegated to another; nevertheless, authority and sanction depend solely on the Majesty. Thus, in the past, the Praetor <term>Praetor: a high-ranking Roman magistrate who had the authority to issue edicts explaining how he would interpret and apply the law during his term</term> used to issue edicts: that is, he would propose what the law would be during his year in office. Goveanus, *On Jurisdiction, 1, number 8.* Likewise, the edicts of the Aediles <term>Aediles: Roman officials in charge of public maintenance, markets, and festivals</term> were part of the "honorary law" <term>honorary law: jus honorarium; law created by magistrates to supplement or correct existing civil law</term>. And in a popular Republic, the law was rarely established by the whole people, but by a part, by a few, or by one person; and it was not thought to matter whether the people established it, or someone to whom the people gave the task. *Law 6, section 1, Digest: On what belongs to a Corporate Body.* Donellus, *Commentaries 1, chapter 8, near the end.* Tileman, *Disputations on the Pandects, 2, thesis 37, volume 2.*

**V.** From this it also follows that in a Monarchical or Aristocratic State, it belongs to the Majesty to approve the customs and practices of the people, either expressly or silently; and the people cannot introduce a custom there except by the (express or silent) consent of the Prince or the Senate. *Law 2, Code: Which [customs]...*

*...that it has existed for a long time. See Timæus; Faber’s Disputations on the Institutes, book 3, thesis 9; Mr. Harprecht on paragraph 12, Institutes on Natural Law; see also Nicolaus Betius on Illustrious Family Pacts, chapter 3.* It is not thought that a local statute, or a special law (which even subordinates are able to establish), can be contrary to universal laws. *See Mr. Bocer, book 2 on Regalian Rights, number 62 and following.* From this, it can also be made manifest how the right of establishing laws and statutes belongs to <term>Electors, Princes, Marquises, Counts, Barons, etc.</term> <note>These are the various ranks of nobility within the Holy Roman Empire who held varying degrees of legislative autonomy.</note> *Camman, book 4, thesis 8; add my own notes on law 9 regarding justice and law, question 3.* So too can <term>Colleges</term> <note>In this context, "Colleges" and "Universities" refer to any legally recognized corporate body or guild, not just educational institutions.</note> and other Corporations make statutes; but not concerning matters other than those over which they have been granted free administration. *As I have laid out in the treatise on Colleges and the Law of Corporations.* Here it can likewise be disputed: if a certain people is subjected to another, are they immediately compelled to acknowledge the laws of the victor? Regarding this, I have also written in *Politics, book 2, chapter 2.*

VI. Furthermore, he whose role it is to carry general laws also has the right to grant "singular law"—that is, **privileges**. *Law 16 on liberty; Lancellot. Conrad. 1. chapter 1. §. 4. page 339; Bornitius on Majesty, chapter 16, page 152; Camman 4. thesis 17; and Scotanus treats this matter beautifully and succinctly in the Paratitla of the Code, book 1, title 14, page 102, etc.* These privileges may pertain either to **Persons** or to **Things**. *Law on privileges, 196, on the rules of law.* And the **Law of the Twelve Tables** <note>The foundation of ancient Roman law, dating to c. 450 BCE.</note> hints at this when it says: *Let no privileges be proposed except at the Centuriate Assembly; <note>original: "Privilegia nisi Comitiis Centuriatis ne irroganto"</note> whoever shall do otherwise, let it be a capital offense.* Moreover, anyone receiving, seeking, or even boasting of a privilege admits by 그 (that very act) that he is a subject of the one granting it. *Reinking, page 251, book 2, class 2, chapter 8, number 20.* And although foreigners may also possess privileges, this happens in respect to the territory of the grantor in which they stay, or carry out trade, or converse; in which view foreigners are also, in some way, counted among the subjects, *as I said in Politics, book 1, chapter 11.* Whether it is actually beneficial to grant privileges is examined by *Carnin in The Assault on the Tower of Babylon, part 3, chapter 4, page 609.*

VII. By "carrying laws," we understand not only the making of new ones, but also the **confirming of old ones**; *Law 2, Code on Decurions; Constitution on the Conception of the Digests, §. 7.* It also includes the power to **interpret** them, so that the interpretation is held as the law itself. *Final law, §. 1, Code on Laws; Law 43 on vulgar and pupillary substitution; Law of Neratius 19, on the rules of law; Novel 143, in the beginning; Novel 161, in the beginning; Lancellot. Conrad. Temple of All Judges, 1. chapter 1. §. 3. page 289; Bornitius, chapter 17; Camman 4. thesis 105; Gæddæus on law 6, number 9, on the meaning of words.* Moditius, in *Decisions, §. the law is doubted, 15; Symmachus, book 10, epistle 40.* <note>Symmachus was a 4th-century Roman statesman known for his oratory.</note> *I await what the August deliberation may ordain; for it is permitted to him alone to judge concerning the divine decrees.* And the same author says elsewhere: *We are accustomed to venerate rather than to interpret the divine oracles.* And in this consists the difference between **civil law** and **princely rescripts**: <note>A rescript is a ruler's formal answer to a legal query or petition.</note> namely, that the latter may, through human interpretation, correct the "rigor of the law," which in many types of cases is more severe than <term>equitable kindness</term> <note>original: "benignitas suadeat æqua" — the principle that law should be applied with fairness and mercy rather than rigid literalism.</note> would suggest.

<margin>T 3</margin>

...as found in *Law 12, paragraph 1 of the Digest, regarding who and by whom manumissions are made.* <note>original: "l. 12 §. 1. ff. qui & a quibus manumiss." Manumission is the formal act of freeing a slave.</note> See also Paul Busius, *Subtleties of Law, book 1, chapter 7.* Formerly, this duty was even entrusted to the <term>Praetor</term> <note>A high-ranking Roman magistrate responsible for the administration of justice.</note>; and the interpretation that belongs to a judge or a legal expert differs greatly from it. See Busius in the *aforementioned book 1, chapter 3; book 2, chapter 2, article 19; as well as book 5, chapter 16.* For while anyone is permitted to interpret the law according to <term>equity</term> <note>Latin: "aequitas"—the principle of fairness and justice that looks beyond the strict letter of the law.</note>—see Becanus in his *Scholastic Theology, title on laws, chapter 6, question 4*—actually changing the law and establishing what is essentially a new law through interpretation belongs to the Sovereign alone. See Donellus, *Commentaries, 1.13*; Hunnius, *Treatise on Interpretation, book 1, chapter 1*; see also the Illustrious Enenckel, *Treatise on Privileges, book 2, chapter 2, number 14, etc.*; and Wilhelm Valentin Forster in his *The Interpreter, book 1, chapter 1.* There is one kind of justice for the Sovereign, and another kind of justice for the lawyers. Boccalini, *Reports from Parnassus, century 2, report 95, page 417.* However, as to whether and to what extent only the one granting a privilege may interpret it and judge it, see Moditius, *The Opinions of Princes, doubts 50, 60, 89, 229, and 233.*

VIII. Likewise, the power of changing a law belongs to the same person who has the power to establish it. *Code of Justinian, book 1, laws 1, the second-to-last, and the last; On the Rules of Law, law 35.* Donellus, *Commentaries, book 1, chapter 12*, with the notes of Hilliger; Winckler, *Principles of Law, book 5, chapter 7.* Indeed, even a law that is just can be justly changed over time; for human laws are not about the ultimate goal itself, but about the methods ordered toward reaching that goal. Bodin, *On the Republic, book 1, number 94*; Bartholomaeus Musculus, *On Successive Conventions, class 1, member 1, page 25 and following*; Bornitius, *chapter 18*; Camman, *thesis 4, number 107, etc.* And this is a characteristic effect of laws, not of a bound or restricted power: for if <term>Majesty</term> <note>The supreme power or sovereignty of a state or ruler.</note> were bound by its own laws, it could not establish new ones without first revoking the old ones. However, there ought to be an evident utility [benefit] for one to withdraw from that law which for a long time seemed equitable. *On the Constitutions of the Prince, law 2.* For the authority of laws becomes cheapened if the people see those things changed which ought instead to have been held and revered as if they were an Oracle. Aristotle, *Politics, book 2, chapter 6, near the end*; Dion, *book 5, page 501 in my edition*; Cabot, *book 2, chapter 1, page 179.* And political thinkers warn that in the changing of a law, there is a need for almost greater care and wisdom than was required in its first sanctioning. See my own *Politics, book 2, chapter 2.* But just as the Sovereign corrects Laws, so too does he revoke Privileges. Lancellotti, *aforementioned section 4, page 365; and I shall say more on this, God Best and Greatest permitting, in the discourse on the mixed state, toward the end.*

IX. Furthermore, because it is the role of sovereignty alone to command, and of subjects to obey—Lancellotti, *The Temple of Justice, book 1, chapter 1, section 4, page 433*—those who hold supreme power can therefore demand loyalty and observance of the laws from everyone equally. Hence Bornitius ascribes the right of Homage, loyalty, and obedience to the functions of majesty, *chapter 27*; nor can anyone usurp this right unless they possess majesty. See Comines, *book 3, chapter 1, page 189 in my edition*, although lower officials may also usurp this "regal" right <note>The author refers to "regalia," or rights traditionally reserved for kings but sometimes claimed by lesser lords.</note>.

### CHAPTER III.

## The Appointment of Magistrates.

I. For the sake of carrying out the execution of the laws, the <term>magistrate</term> <note>In this historical context, a "magistrate" refers to any high-ranking civil officer or judge empowered to administer the law.</note> is established; so that he may be a "living and speaking law," the servant and guardian of the "silent law." *Law 8, on justice and law.* <note>original: "l. 8. de justit. & jur."</note> For how little it matters that there is justice in the state, or that justice and law are established by the sovereign, unless there are those who may execute, speak, and decree it. *Law 2, paragraph 13, on the origin of law; New Constitution 161, at the beginning.* <note>original: "l. 2. §. 13. de origin. juris Novell. 161. in princip."</note> Therefore, so that laws may obtain their effect, magistrates, judges, and other powers are usually ordained in a republic. Although the law is called the soul and mistress of the state, it has no power of movement of its own. Since, however, a ruler cannot easily provide for everything himself, it is necessary that there be many magistrates appointed by him. In this way, as Aristotle prudently writes, Princes and Kings create many eyes, many ears, and likewise many hands and feet for themselves. *Politics, book 3, chapter 12; New Constitution 8, in the epilogue, where it says: "By the service of the Empire."* And for this reason, he creates them at his own risk and is held responsible for them. Lancellot. Conrad. *The Temple of Judges, book 1, chapter 1, paragraph 3, page 304.*

II. Since, therefore, the higher magistrates especially are, as it were, the limbs and hands of the <term>Body of Majesty</term> <note>Latin: "maiestatici corporis"—a metaphor for the state or the sovereign's authority as a physical body.</note>, their appointment—no differently than the laws themselves—is rightly said to belong to the supreme command. Regner Sixtin, *On Regalian Rights, book 2, chapter 15.* Doctor Marta, *Treatise on Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 42.* Bornitius, *chapter 21.* Canman, *6, thesis 57.* The Prince himself ought to confer the primary offices. Velstenius, *A Century of Political Questions, decade 10, thesis 3.* See also the serious remarks of Blaise de Montluc, *Commentaries, book 7, page 215, verso and following.* *Table Talk of Princes, book 3, chapter 16.* And this is called the greatest part of the imperial duty by Zonaras. Hence, in ancient Rome, the appointment of magistrates belonged to the favor of the people; and the Valerian law commanded that the person (and his goods) who held power without receiving it from the people be declared accursed. Livy, *book 2*; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *book 5.* Later, with the arrival of the <term>Principate</term> <note>The early period of the Roman Empire characterized by the reign of a single "Princeps" or first citizen.</note>, the creation of magistrates pertained to the care of the Prince. *Law 1, paragraph 1, regarding the Julian law on bribery.* <note>original: "l. 1. §. 1. ad L. Iul. ambit."</note> From this, to doubt whether the person whom the Prince has chosen is worthy is considered a sacrilege. *Law 2, Code on the crime of sacrilege.* For this reason, anyone who does not depart from a Province when a successor has been appointed to him commits the <term>crime of majesty</term> <note>Latin: "crimen maiestatis"—the legal term for high treason or an offense against the sovereign power.</note>. *Law 2, regarding the Julian law on treason; Pierre Ayrault, on adjudicated matters, page 556.* This also applies to a private citizen who, knowing it to be wrong, behaves with malicious intent as if he held a power or a magistracy. *Laws 1 and 3 of the same title.* Decianus, *Treatise on Crimes, book 7, chapter 9, numbers 2, 4, and 12.* Those rulers seem to have carelessly neglected (and almost abdicated from themselves) this greatest of <term>regalian rights</term> <note>Latin: "regale"—the specific rights and privileges belonging exclusively to a monarch.</note> who have made dignities and offices almost hereditary. See *Political Treasure, first report from France, page 183.* And because majesty, by the right of command, someone... <note>The sentence ends abruptly as it continues to the next page.</note>

III. I have said that the appointment of <term>major magistrates</term> <note>These were high-ranking officials who held significant delegated power directly from the sovereign, such as provincial governors or high judges.</note> pertains to the supreme power of the state. Even if magistrates are appointed indirectly through their jurisdiction, their creation is not usually counted among the <term>regalia</term>. <note>Regalia refers to the "royal rights" or specific powers and privileges that belong exclusively to a sovereign.</note> Molinæus, *on the Customs of Paris, title 1, glossary 5, number 57.* Nevertheless, this is still done through the mediated authority of the Prince: Master Hilliger, *on Donellus, chapter 17, section 7, page 48,* and so forth. I add here in passing that even before Pius V, Popes Paul IV and Pius IV had promised a higher degree of dignity to Cosimo de' Medici; however, fearing the offense of certain other Princes, they did not fulfill it. Natale Conti, *History of His Time, pages 454, 455, 551.*

We have a similar example in Charles the Bold (or the Warlike), the last Duke of Burgundy. He earnestly requested of Emperor Frederick III at Trier—by betrothing his daughter and sole heir to the Emperor's son Maximilian—that the Emperor create him King of Burgundy and a Legate and Vicar of the Empire. Fearing nothing less than a rejection, Charles ordered a scepter, a crown, and other insignia of royal dignity to be made; he also ordered the preparation of seats in the church, a throne, and everything required for the ritual of coronation and anointing. ### On grace and dispensation.

# On Sovereign Rights.
V 2

...and temples provided security to those seeking refuge. ### II.
The condition of magistrates <note>In this context, "magistrates" refers to appointed judges or lower officials</note> is different; they are by no means able to change matters once they have been judged: *Law 14, section "the judge after...", and Law 62, On Matters Judged; Law "The Governor", 42, On Minors; Law 33, On Matters Judged.* Paris de Puteo, in his *Treatise on Syndicates, section "Punishment," verse "According to,"* states they cannot change it even for a cause, such as by reason of innocence being discovered later. *The Code of Fabrianus, book 9, title 24, definition 8.* Freher, *Book 3, On Infamy, chapter 7, at the end.* Dr. Bocer, following Heigius and P. Dr. Bocer, *On Jurisdiction, number 65 and following.* And even if a sentence is of such a nature that it deserves to be changed, a lower judge nevertheless cannot do this.

### III.
Furthermore, the Prince is able to grant grace for a crime and for corporal punishment, even that which was imposed in place of a monetary fine; even if an opposing party should object. # Political-Legal Dissertation

It is also in the interest of the state, for the sake of the strength of public discipline, that crimes do not go unpunished. <note>original: "interest reipublicæ, ne delicta maneant impunita."</note> *Law 51, on the Aquilian Law; Law 6, paragraph "illicit," of the Code on Public Trials.* Just as punishing one person corrects a hundred others through the example set, so too by granting a pardon to one, a ruler ruins both that person and infinitely many others. Severity does not soften the wicked, nor does leniency bend the crooked. A Prince should therefore respond as Philip of Macedon once did to Harpalus, who was interceding for his friend: *It is better that he who committed the offense bears the shame himself, rather than I.* <note>original: "Meliùs est, ut ipse qui deliquit, ignominiam ferat, quàm ego."</note> Plutarch, *in his Apothegms; see also Simon Goulard in his Sacred Apothegms.* The saying of Louis, surnamed the Saint, King of France <note>King Louis IX, known for his personal piety and judicial reforms</note>, is also worth noting in the section on justice. Similar examples are found in Guillaume Paradin, *Book 2, chapter 97, of the Memoirs of the History of Lyon.* Otto Melander, *in his Serious Matters, book 1, number 233.* The saying of Bias <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> also deserves to be remembered: when he was about to condemn someone to death, he wept for the man's wretched and deplorable fate. But when someone asked, "Why do you weep, since it is in your power to condemn or free the man?" Bias replied: "It is necessary to feel compassion for Nature; but to depart from the law and the rule of justice seems even more dangerous." *Stobaeus, Sermon 44.*

### IV.
Lest a Prince strike against these rules, it seems worthwhile to imitate the statute of the Spaniards, where there is a Tribunal called the Council of the Chamber <note>original: "Consilium Cameræ"</note>; this consists of three or four chosen Doctors <note>learned legal experts</note> who deliberate with the King on granting pardons for crimes and other matters which they call "graces." Girolamo Conestaggio, *On the Union of Portugal and Castile, book 8, folio 401.* This is also worth noting: when an example is needed but mercy is also called for, it is better for the pardon to be introduced *after* the sentence has been passed. In this way, neither the demands of justice nor those of mercy are entirely excluded, but the matter proceeds with the best balance of both. Ayrault, *On Adjudicated Matters, page 566.* Heigius, *part 2, question 22, number 26.* Furthermore, the forgiveness of a punishment is considered nowhere more praiseworthy than if the Prince remits an injury done to his own person. Jean Bodin, *number 166.* On the granting of grace, Tuschus has much to say under *letter G, conclusion 51, etc.*; on the remission of punishment and infamy, see Tenninus, *Caution 208*; and on gracious restitution, consult Oddus, *Question 91, etc.* Farinacius discusses when grace is valid in *On Inquisitions, question 6.* However, when subreption <note>the concealment of truth to obtain a favor</note> or obreption <note>obtaining a favor by making false statements</note> vitiates the grace, even in criminal cases, consult Cravetta, *Consultations 2 and 729.* The same author records in *Consultation 68* that subreption voids gracious decrees by the law itself; it is considered subreption when a matter is described in general terms rather than specifically. Cravetta, *Consultations 79 and 591.* I add this as well: it appears that the Roman Emperor <note>Referring to the Holy Roman Emperor</note> cannot grant impunity to someone who has committed a crime in the territory of a State of the Empire (especially so that he may remain unpunished in his previous home), since the rulers are invested with jurisdiction exclusively rather than cumulatively in those granted lands; nor in the exercise of jurisdictio-

# On the Rights of Sovereignty

...lest rights be hindered. ### V.
To this point belongs the fact that it is the right of sovereignty alone to wipe away the staining marks of a faulty reputation. <note>This refers to the legal restoration of honor or "restitutio famae," which cleared a person’s record and restored their standing in society.</note> Radulph Fornerius, *Daily Matters, book 2, chapter 19.* Camman, *4, thesis 84.* See Moditius, *paragraph 'lex', doubt 6.* Symmachus says, in *book 10, epistle 3*: "One who has been marked by a judicial sentence implores the most proven remedy of Imperial pardon, so that by the remission of the judgment, he may close the wound to his Reputation." ->## A Politico-Legal Dissertation<-

Now it is understood that the observance of formalities <note>original: "solemnitatum"; these are the specific legal rituals or document requirements required for a contract or will to be valid</note> required by civil law is relaxed. This is supported by Albericus de Rosate, Baldus de Ubaldis, Jason de Mayno, Bartholomeus Salicetus, Fulgosius, Butigarius, and others, in their commentary on *the law regarding inofficious wills* <note>original: "l. si quando C. de inoffic. testament."</note>; for otherwise, that privilege of sovereignty would be superfluous. Thus, it is well established that Charles, Duke of Lorraine, when he was nominated as the Bishop of Metz, obtained a "mercy of age" <term>venia aetatis: a legal waiver allowing a person who has not yet reached the legal age of majority to act as an adult for specific purposes</term> in order to receive the investiture and administration of the Bishopric at the Emperor’s court in Prague in recent years. Thomas Michael, *On Jurisdiction, conclusion 32, letter c.* Reinking, *On Secular and Ecclesiastical Government, book 1, class 3, chapter 12, number 51.* The King of Denmark also obtained the same from Emperor Rudolph II on April 26, 1593. Schönberner, *Politics, chapter 18.*

### VII.
Generally, majesty alone grants a dispensation <note>a "dispensation" is a formal exemption from a law or rule</note> against the laws; that is, majesty frees one from the force of laws and judicial sentences, and, having weighed the necessity of the case, providently relaxes the law. Vasquius, *Illustrious Controversies, chapter 25.* Augustinus Morla, *In the Marketplace of Law, title 1, question 2.* Pruckmann, *Treatise on Regalian Rights, section on 'unbound power', pages 215 and 258.* Petra, *chapter 27.* excellently by Cammann, *4, thesis 60, etc.* This is what is called in the *Digest on the Constitutions of Princes* to provide aid "without precedent." From this perspective, the Prince is called the "Lord of the (civil) laws," just as Christ is called the "Lord of the Sabbath," which was instituted by God Himself. Regarding dispensations, see Becanus, *Scholastic Theology: On Laws, chapter 6, question 13.* Tuschus, *under the letter D, word 'dispensatio', and the word 'derogatio'.*

I also refer to this when a petition is made to the Prince so that the will of a mute or deaf person may be valid, according to *law 6, where Gothofredus notes law 7, on those who can make a will; see also law 10 under the same title in the Code.* Furthermore, a "singular restoration" <note>restitutio singularis</note>, which Princes claim for themselves, must be granted. Bodin, *On the Republic, book 1, chapter 10.* Ærodius, *On Adjudicated Matters, page 817.* Cravetta, *Counsel 266.* This applies against a final judgment <note>res judicata</note>, against a forfeited appeal, etc. Similar to this in the past was the "right of a third, fourth, or fifth referral," by which the greatness of the Emperors in exercising jurisdiction was displayed; for they were able not only to rescind matters that had been judged three times, but even those strengthened by a fourth or fifth sentence. However, this "restoration against a sentence," which is too common in France, breeds contempt for the Court of Paris. Lord Lansius, *Consultations against France, page 280.* The Prince also restores a lapsed legal proceeding <note>instantiam peremptam: a case that has expired or been dismissed due to a failure to meet a deadline</note>. Rodolphinus investigates this in *On the Dukes of Italy, number 190, etc.*, who says in the same work at *number 180, etc.* that the Princes of Italy also "breathe life" into lapsed proceedings.
