# Concerning the Rights of Majesty.

Nicodemus (in his dictionary, where he notes that an example of this matter exists in the Gospel) states that these rights can only be granted by a supreme Prince: namely, one who acknowledges no superior, or at least one who exercises the rights of empire. (Lancellotti, *Temple of Justice, book 1, chapter 1, section 4, folio 418*; The Fabian Code, *book 1, title 9, definition 17*; Trentacinquius, *final volume, title on payments, resolution 1 and following*; Papon, *book 5, title 9, decree 1*). For even Princes, Counts, Barons, etc., who are invested with all royal rights <term>regalia: the specific rights, lands, and privileges held directly by a monarch or sovereign</term>, are said by some to possess the right of grace <note>original: "jus gratiae"; the sovereign power to grant a pardon or commute a sentence</note> by virtue of dispensation. (Rolandus a Valle, *book 3, counsel 4, number 4*; Clarus, *final section, question 59, version "and indeed these"*; Hilliger’s commentary on Donellus, *22, chapter 9, letter g*). 

But in the Estates of the Empire <note>referring to the territories and political entities that made up the Holy Roman Empire</note>, the situation is different, because their sentences can be appealed, and the *Recesses* <note>Imperial Recesses were the official collections of resolutions passed by the Imperial Diet (Reichstag)</note> of the Empire prescribe a specific and unique manner for this matter. Because I have stated that the **right of asylum** <term>jus asylorum: a legal privilege allowing a city or church to protect a fugitive from immediate prosecution, particularly in cases of accidental crime</term> belongs to this right of majesty, I have decided to insert here, word for word, a clear privilege granted to the illustrious republic of **Reutlingen** <note>Reutlingen was a Free Imperial City, meaning it was subject only to the Emperor and not to any local prince</note>.

We, **Maximilian**, by the grace of God, Roman King <note>Maximilian I, though later Emperor, often used the title "Roman King" before his formal coronation</note>, at all times Increaser of the Realm, etc., publicly acknowledge with this letter and make known to everyone, that our and the Empire's dear faithful subjects, the Mayor and Council of the City of **Reutlingen**, have brought forward through their honorable embassy: how the same City of Reutlingen has been privileged until now, and how they and their ancestors have used and maintained the custom, that any person who—outside of the said city and its tithe-lands and outskirts—has committed an accidental killing <note>original: "ungefährlich Todtschlag"; a legal term for manslaughter or killing without premeditated malice, such as in self-defense or by accident</note>, has had sanctuary and safety in that city and its belonging territory. This meant that the person or persons could not be summoned to court in the said city for such a killing, nor could they be executed there, unless they had been denounced and accused as murderers. 

As this is well-known and public in those parts and regions, certain persons who committed *dangerous* <note>original: "gefährlich"; here meaning intentional, premeditated, or malicious</note> killings have dared to take advantage of and claim such freedom for themselves. From this, significant error and resentment have often arisen, which resulted in heavy disadvantage and damage to them and the common City of Reutlingen.

And they have humbly appealed to us and requested that we graciously provide for them in this matter.

Therefore, we—on account of their humble prayer, and also for the sake of the faithful and useful service they have often willingly performed for us and the Holy Empire, and may and should do in the future—with well-considered intent, good counsel, and certain knowledge, have graciously confirmed and ratified the above-stated freedom and custom. We have also decreed and ordained that henceforth any and every person who, out of the heat of anger or for the preservation and rescue of their own life, outside the City of Reutlingen...

->### Political-Legal Dissertation<-

[...within the city of] Reutlingen and the tithe-districts and boundaries <term>Ettern: a historical term for the enclosed jurisdictional boundary of a city or village</term> thereof, should commit or carry out a homicide, they shall have freedom <note>original: "Freyung"; here meaning a right of sanctuary or asylum</note> in the aforementioned city of Reutlingen and the tithes and boundaries belonging to it. For such homicides, they shall not be legally attacked, summoned, or complained against. Furthermore, as long as they reside within the city of Reutlingen and its said tithe-districts and boundaries and make use of this freedom, no judgment or legal proceeding shall be carried out against them, their bodies, or their property by our and the Empire’s High Court at Rottweil <note>The *Hofgericht* at Rottweil was one of the highest imperial courts in the Holy Roman Empire, known for its extensive jurisdiction</note>, nor by any provincial court or other courts. Should such a judgment or proceeding occur regardless, it shall have no force or power. However, where a **premeditated and dangerous homicide** <note>original: "vorbedächtlich gefährlich Todtschläg"; referring to intentional murder as opposed to accidental killing or manslaughter</note> has occurred, they [the city authorities] shall allow justice to proceed according to what is proper, upon the request of the plaintiffs against the perpetrators. The actions taken regarding such dangerous homicides shall in no way cause any derogation, injury, or loss to the aforementioned freedoms and customs.

And we therefore command all and every Elector, Prince (spiritual and temporal), Prelate, Count, Baron, Knight, Noble, Captain, Bishopric, Bailiff, Governor, Administrator, Official, Magistrate, Burgomaster, and Councilor—as well as our and the Empire's judges and jurors of our High Court at Rottweil, who are now or shall be there in the future, and all other provincial judges, magistrates, and jurors of any and every court, and all other subjects and faithful of ours and the Empire, of whatever dignity, status, or being they may be, earnestly and firmly: It is our will that you do not disturb or hinder the aforementioned Burgomaster and Council of Reutlingen and their successors in their aforementioned freedoms, customs, and traditions. Rather, you shall allow them, and the persons who have availed themselves of these rights, to enjoy them peacefully and remain completely undisturbed by them. You shall not pressure, trouble, or burden them, nor permit anyone else to do so. This is to be observed as dearly as one holds our and the Empire's favor, and to avoid our heavy displeasure and punishment, as well as a penalty <term>Poen: a legal fine or penalty</term>, namely **forty Marks of pure gold** <note>A "Mark" was a unit of weight for precious metals; "lötig" indicates the purity of the gold</note>. Anyone who insolently acts against this shall be liable to pay this fine as often as it occurs: half to us and the Imperial Chamber, and the other half to the honorable citizens of Reutlingen and their successors, without fail. In witness of this letter, sealed with our Royal hanging seal. Given at Mechelen on the 27th day of the month of January, after the birth of Christ 1495, in the ninth year of our Roman reign and the fifth of our Hungarian reign.

On the Rights of Majesty.

### CHAPTER V.

### The right to establish punishment, or the right of life and death; and absolute judicial power.

I have said that the essence of Majesty consists in this: that the sovereign judges all others, in both civil and criminal cases. From this, the right to establish punishment, or the **right of life and death** <term>jus vitae et necis: the ultimate sovereign authority over the lives of subjects</term>, pertains to Majesty (*Camman, Disputation 5, thesis 3*). Thus Polybius says of the Romans in Book 6: "The people alone may punish with death." And in the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The foundation of Roman law, dating back to c. 450 BCE</note>: "No decision regarding the life <note>original: *capite*, literally 'head' or legal status</note> of a citizen shall be made except by the Greatest Assembly." (*Theodore Marcile in his interpretation of the Twelve Tables, section 83*). Hence the common saying: **pure command** <term>merum imperium: the highest form of legal authority, including the power of the sword and capital punishment</term> is not granted except by a specific law. Thus among the Franks, Basanus, King of the Sicambri, ordered a sword and a rope to be carried before him wherever he went as a sign of justice; and before Charlemagne <note>Carolus Magnus</note>, a naked sword was carried perpetually in the imperial manner before his tribunal. (*M. Freher on Peter of Andlau, Book 1, Chapter 1; Philipp Camerarius, Century 1, Chapter 76*). In this view, pure command is also called "the power of the sword." Thus in England, the lives and limbs of subjects are said to belong solely to the King in this respect. (*Thomas Smith, The Commonwealth of England, Book 2, Chapter 4, page 67*).

II. Since indeed no law is valid without a punishment, it also belongs to the lawgiver to define the penalty—whether ordinary or extraordinary—or at least to commit it to the discretion of the judges within a fixed limit. (Indeed, Lancellotti notes in *The Temple of Justice*, Book 1, Chapter 1, that the Prince himself can kill offenders, but this is nevertheless considered cruel.) Hence the Prince can not only determine a penalty for every crime, but also, beyond the established penalty, take more severe vengeance on some as an example. (*Code of Justinian, On Marriage; On Punishments; Theodosian Code*). But this should not be done without the greatest cause. For instance, in the year 1055, Hanno, Archbishop of Cologne <note>A powerful medieval prelate and regent of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, when he discovered that judges had delivered a false verdict in the case of a poor woman, ordered all their eyes to be gouged out—except for one, who was his own godparent <note>original: *compater*</note>. He deprived this man of only one eye, so that, assisted by the other, he might lead the blinded men home. (*Dresser, Millenary, part 2, page 78 and following*).

III. All these things are therefore to be understood such that, in judging, the Prince is bound by laws and is not free from religious duty. This is illustrated with an elegant example by Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher who defined the modern concept of sovereignty</note> in the final chapter of *On the Republic*. The Prince’s power is not like that of the Japanese King <note>A reference to the practice of *seppuku* or ritual suicide, which was becoming known in Europe through Jesuit missionary reports</note>, who, when offended, could command someone to go away and cut open his own belly.

<summary>This page explores the sovereign "right of life and death," defining it as the core of Majesty and the source of all judicial authority. It uses historical examples from Rome, England, and the Holy Roman Empire to argue that while a ruler holds the "power of the sword," they should remain bound by law and morality rather than acting with arbitrary cruelty.</summary>

# On the Rights of Sovereignty

### X 2

He [the sovereign] can now proceed in those cases where, under other circumstances, formal legal procedures would be required. *Law: "apud quem," on manumissions;* <note>A reference to Roman law regarding the freeing of slaves.</note> Robertus Maranta, *On Judicial Process, distinction 9, numbers 3 and 8;* Rodolphinus, *On the Dukes of Italy, number 216,* (where he states that this is not permitted to those holding local office). He is able to deliver a sentence that does not conform to the legal petition regarding the order of the trial. Jason, *on law 1, numbers 21 and following, on producing documents;* and *on law 1, on the constitutions of princes;* and sentences that differ from the laws or are based on his own discretion; see Aerodius, *pages 762 and 764.*

Sometimes, he can condemn a criminal—one whose guilt is known to him with absolute certainty—without a summons or other similar formalities, and can even begin with the execution itself; see especially Augustinus Morla, *In the Marketplace, title 2, question 2;* Lather, *On the Census, page 815, etc.* It is by this reasoning that the French defend the death of the **Duke of Guise**, who was killed by the order of **Henry III, King of France**, before he even suspected he had lost the King's favor. *History of the Recent Troubles, page 160;* Jehan de Serres, *in the Inventory, book 3, page 1705;* Boccalini, *2nd Report, 44.* But see Rosset, *Tragic Histories, 2,* where it is recounted how the son of Guise avenged his father's death. This leads to the same question they ask: can the Majesty [the sovereign] take away the right to a defense? See Petra, *chapter 26.* However, no matter how persuasively this may be argued, it is never advisable for one enjoying sovereignty to use this violent remedy. Aerodius, *On Adjudicated Matters, page 547.* As **Tertullian** beautifully said in his *Apology, chapter 1*: "If they condemn a case unheard, besides the hatred of the injustice, they will also deserve suspicion of a bad conscience, being unwilling to hear what they could not condemn once heard." VI. Similarly, the judgment of controversies of great importance belongs solely to the **majesty** <term>majestas: the supreme authority or "majesty" of the sovereign</term>. Hence, if a curse is directed at the Emperor, he himself must be consulted, *law 1, Code: "If anyone speaks ill of the Emperor."* Master Bocer, *On Majesty, chapter 3, from the beginning.* And for this reason, some even say that presiding over the <term>crime of majesty: high treason or an offense against the dignity of the sovereign</term> must be numbered among the greatest **regalian rights** <term>regalia: the specific rights and privileges belonging exclusively to a monarch</term>; for otherwise, an inferior would be passing judgment on a superior. Gigas, *Treatise on the Crime of Majesty, title: "Who can preside over the crime of lese-majesty,"* Rodolphin. *On Dukes, number 141, etc.* Master Doctor Bocer disagrees, *Treatise on the Crime of Majesty, chapter 4, number 2, etc. and book 2, On Regalia, last number at the end.* Arumæus, *disputation F. 4, thesis 18.* Sixtin. *book 2, chapter 1, number 18.* A memorable example of this matter is provided by Bernard Girard, *volume 2, book 13, of the History of France, folio 14.* Regarding the murderer of **Emperor Albert**, the Pope <note>The High Pontiff</note> did not wish to decide anything concerning his punishment: <note>original French: "disant ledit Pape, qu' il appartenoit à un Empereur, & non à un autre, d' ordonner la punition d' un meurtre, commis en la Personne d' un Empereur."</note> *the said Pope saying that it belonged to an Emperor, and no other, to order the punishment for a murder committed against the person of an Emperor.* To this also pertains the trial of **Duke Biron**, who, by an ancient privilege, wished to be judged only by his peers (his colleagues); this was denied to him because the investigation concerned a crime of high treason. In other cases, a Senator is judged only by the Senate, Langlæus, *7th Semester, 18.* Based on nearly the same principle, the benefit of a certain privilege was recently denied to rebels; by the force of which the **Citizens of Frankfurt** cannot be summoned to court anywhere except before their own magistrates. See the *Counsel on this controversy* by Pius Felix, Emperor of Augsburg.

VII. Thus, today, only the Emperor can declare a person a **public enemy**, or **"Place them under the Imperial Ban"** <note>original German: "In die Acht erklären." The Imperial Ban was a form of outlawry in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>: Gail. *book 1, On Public Peace, chapters 6 and 12* (where he discusses the difference of the ban of lower officials) and *book 2, observation 130, number 13.* Heig. *book 1, question 9, numbers 42 and 52.* Sixtin. *On Regalia, book 1, chapter 4, number 8, folio 70.* See Modest. Pistor. *question 26, part 1.* To decide controversies regarding Duchies and Counties, according to the **Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber Court** <note>original German: "Cammergerichtsordnung," the procedural rules for the highest court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> *part 1, title 7.* See my own work in *Legal-Political Disputation on Successions, book 1, last dissertation, final number,* and in my *Treatise on the Jurisdiction of the Roman Empire.* Only the Emperor is able to do this; whether this also applies to minor fiefs and possessory rights is examined by Caspar Leipold, *On the Concurrence of Jurisdiction, question 5 and following,* in Arumæus, *discourse 13.* Likewise, the Prince alone judges regarding privileges and their interpretation, as well as other matters of greater importance. Gail. *1. observation 1.* Lehman. *last book, chapter 71.* I also gave warning of this above in *this discourse, chapter 2.* To this also belongs **adrogation** <term>arrogatio: the legal adoption of a person who is already legally independent (sui iuris)</term> of those who are under their own legal authority: *§. 1, Institutes on Adoption.* This can today be carried out before Princes and Marquises (whereas formerly it was only done before the people and the Prince). My colleague Harpprecht, *on the said §. 1, at the end.* Master Bocer, *On Jurisdiction, chapter 4, number 21, §. "Similarly."*

<meta>catchword: Bernard.</meta>

VIII. Conversely, just as no one prescribes laws to him who holds **majesty** <term>majestas: the supreme sovereign power</term>; so also no one else passes judgment on his decisions. Jean Bodin, *On the Republic, book 1, chapter 10, number 160.* Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, *On the Republic, book 9, chapter 1, number 18.* Clapmar, *book 1, chapter 19.* Johannes Camman, *disputation 6, theses 66 and 73.* And Ulpian says it is foolish to remind people that one cannot appeal against the **Prince** <term>Princeps: a general term for a sovereign ruler, such as an Emperor or King</term>. *law 1, §. 1. of the Digest: From whom an appeal is not permitted.* I have noted this myself in my *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 2, from the beginning*, unless perhaps the appeal is from a "poorly informed" ruler to the same ruler once he is "better informed." <note>This was a legal fiction used to allow a sovereign to correct an error or change their mind without admitting they were subject to a higher court's judgment.</note> Johannes Dauth Junior, *disputation inserted into book 2 of Public Law, published at Hanau, question 2*; and the Duke of Lüneburg, in a writing regarding the recent controversy that arose between His Highness and the people of Hamburg, *folio 7.* Otherwise, if a challenge is instituted—for instance, if an appeal is made from the King of France to the Pope or the Emperor—a **crime of majesty** <term>lese-majesty: high treason or an affront to the sovereign's dignity</term> is committed. Papon, *book 22, title 1, arrest 2*, as I also warned above.

IX. Not only is there no appeal from his judgment, but he can also appoint a judge in such a way that no appeal may be made from that judge; instead, once the possibility of appeal is removed, the sentence is to be executed. *law 1, §. 4. of the Digest: From whom an appeal is not permitted.* Lancellot, *book 1, chapter 1, §. 4, folio 429.* Master Anton Winter, *In the Assessor, part 1, chapter 4, number 54.* I have discussed this in my *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 2, section 18, folio 67.* Rodolphinus, *On Dukes, number 209.* Judges appointed in this manner are considered equal to the <term>exedria: the highest judicial chambers</term> and the consistories of final appeals. Berterius, *1. Pithan. 17.* I, in the aforementioned *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 2, section 21*; and also those States which are privileged regarding appeals. For if **majesty** is the administrator of the highest command and jurisdiction, it must also be its right to establish the supreme tribunal of justice and of final judgments. In this case, the one to whom the right of judging without appeal has been granted delivers the sentence in place of the people (in a democracy) or the Prince (in a monarchical state). Against such a sentence, even the Prince can grant **restitution in full** <term>restitutio in integrum: a legal remedy that restores a person to their original legal position, as if a judgment had not occurred</term>. *law 18, §. 2. on Minors; law 3, Code: If against a judged matter.* **Majesty** also always reserves for itself the **right of supplication** <term>ius supplicandi: the right of subjects to petition the sovereign for mercy or a review of a case based on equity</term>; since the sovereign is, as has been said, the supreme judge and must hear all complainants out of a regard for humanity and justice. *law 6, Digest; law "you lead," Code: on appeals.* I have noted this in the *said treatise, chapter 2, under number 8, folio 65.* See also Coler, *On the Roman Empire, thesis 21.* And thus I understand why some do not ascribe the right of final challenge and the right of restoring cases against sentences to **majesty** itself. Master Cluten, *paradox 12 and following*; but nevertheless, the right to appoint such a judge, and to not allow challenges by one's own right, belongs entirely to this category.

X. Likewise, the sovereign can judge in his own cause: (for to judge another is a jurisdictional act, which no one can exercise over one who excels in **majesty**). *law 3, on those things deleted in wills; law 41, on the institution of heirs, last section at the end; Institutes, on common substitution.* Lancellot Conrad, *book 1, chapter 1, §. 4, folio 375.* Trentacinque, *Various Resolutions, book 2, title: on judgments, resolution 5, from the beginning.*

It also highlights the sovereign's unique right to judge their own legal matters and the subjects' right to petition for mercy through supplication.</summary>

# Political-Legal Dissertation

### XI. Law

Bernard Grævus, *book 1, conclusion 21.* Rodolphinus, *on Dukes, number 207.* That which is not granted to an inferior. Schrader, *volume 2, counsel 26 and following.* And he who possesses **majesty** <term>majestas: the supreme, sovereign power of a state</term> cannot be alleged as a "suspect" or biased party. Menochius, *counsel 403, numbers 12, 13.* Grævus, *1, conclusion 33, number 5.* And so also Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential Jesuit theologian</note> believes that the **High Pontiff** <term>Pontifex Maximus: the Pope</term> can judge in his own cause, especially in councils. *1, on councils, last chapter.* To this I refer the fact that the **King in France** <note>original: "Rex in Galliis"</note> never litigates regarding possession. "The King must plead while in possession." <note>original: "Le Roy doibt plaider saisi." A French legal maxim meaning the King remains in possession of the disputed property or right throughout the legal proceedings.</note> Papon, *book 5, title 1, arrest 9.* 

But because it is indeed ruinous for anyone to do whatever they wish by their own decree, a sovereign—even if they are able to be their own judge—nonetheless usually commits their own cause to be heard by others who are outstanding in probity and gravity. They voluntarily subject themselves to the judgment of these men so that they do not seem to wish to rule tyrannically. The Illustrious Enenckelius, *1, on privileges, chapter 7, number 23.* Hilliger on Donellus, *17, chapter 2, letter b.* Michael Schiferer, in Arumæus, *volume 1, discourse 18, thesis 67 and following; and myself in the treatise on appeals, chapter 2, number 9.* Paul Busius attests that this is observed by general custom, *on law 10, at the end, on jurisdiction*; and Reinkingk also notes this regarding Spain, *folio m. 28, number 217.* 

This is also a matter of divine equity. *Job 31:* <note>Job 31:13</note> "If I have despised undergoing judgment with my servant." And the Illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine rightly notes: A Prince cannot subject himself to another as a judge, but only as an **arbitrator**. *book 2, on councils, chapter 18.* Thus, by the morals and customs of the Empire, it has been introduced that the Emperor or the King of the Romans, regarding causes for which he has been challenged, must answer not before the Roman Pontiff, but before the **Elector Palatine**. <note>The Elector Palatine served as the Imperial Vicar and had the right to judge the Emperor in certain legal disputes according to the Golden Bull of 1356.</note> Dominicus Arumæus treats this extensively and elegantly, *on the Golden Bull, thesis 77 and many following.* Marquard Freher, *on the origins of the Palatinate, part 1, chapter 13*; also in notes on Peter von Andlo, *folio 194. b. Defense of the Palatine Vicariate, folio 103, etc.* Arumæus, *on the Golden Bull, discourse 3, thesis 45.* Reinkingk, *book 1, class 4, chapter 5. Calvinist Wedel, folio 75.* 

So also in Silesia, certain judges are established before whom the King of Bohemia can be summoned. Here Henelius, in *Silesiographia folio 97*; see Schrader, *volume 2, counsel 23.* What is done in the **Electorate of Brandenburg**? <note>original: "Marchico Electoratu"</note> see Schepliz, *part 2, title 4.* Indeed, for this reason, so that the Prince does not seem to seek anything contrary to justice even in his own cause, our **Legal Consultants** <term>Jureconsulti: experts in the law whose opinions were often cited as authority</term> responded that if even the slightest scrap of doubt exists, it should be decided against the **treasury**. <note>original: "fiscum" — the state's financial interests</note> *law: I think. 10. of the Digest: on the law of the treasury.* And so Philip II, King of the Spains, as Botero recounts, *on the sayings, 2, folio 21. b.*, commanded the President of the Royal Council that in a doubtful cause, the ruling should be pronounced against himself: "knowing how much the respect for royal majesty weighs in litigation with private individuals." <note>original Italian: "sapendo quanto vaglia il respetto della maestà regia nelle liti co' particolari."</note> This is also what Louis V, King of France, commanded his son. Lord Lansius, *Oration for France, folio 191.* 

However, whether one may appeal from a judge who speaks the law between a Prince and his subjects, and to whom the appeal should be made, see Zasius, *singular responses 2, chapter 18.*

<summary>This page explores the legal paradox of the sovereign as both the source of law and a participant in it, detailing how monarchs voluntarily submit to independent arbitration or specific courts (like the Elector Palatine for the Emperor) to avoid tyranny and ensure "divine equity" in disputes with their subjects.</summary>

# On the Rights of Majesty.

§ I. The **Right of the Archive** <term>Jus Archivi: the sovereign's exclusive right to establish and maintain official repositories for public records, which grants these documents "public faith" or legal authenticity</term> can also be referred to here. On this, see Mr. Rutger Ruland, *on commissions, book 5, chapter 4, part 2*; Ummius, *disputations on procedure 17, number 9 and following.* For its reasoning rests on that most urgent presumption which exists in favor of the good faith and integrity of the one who holds **majesty** <term>majestas: the supreme, sovereign power of a state</term>.

---

### CHAPTER VI.

### On the right of waging war.

I have stated that it is the duty of majesty to defend subjects against all force. To this end belongs the power of waging war. *1 Samuel 11, verse 7; Novel 10; law 17 of the Code on military affairs, book 12;* Knichen, *on territorial rights, chapter 3, number 352;* D. Marta, *part 1, chapter 39;* Camman, *5, thesis 48, etc.;* Schönborner, *6, politics, chapter 12;* Ritter, *on homage, number 190 and following, also 195.* This power is now called the **Drafting, Military Following, Muster, and Selection** <note>original: "Raith/ Folg/ Musterung/ Ausswöhlung." These German terms refer to the various stages of raising and reviewing an army.</note>; see Thomas Maulius, *treatise on homage, chapter 5.* War is a just struggle carried out with public arms. Public arms are those belonging to any free people or to a Prince who is subject to the power of no other. Hence, a war is judged to be unjust if it is not initiated by the authority of the one in whom majesty resides. *Canon "quid culpatur" 23, question 1;* Mr. Bocer, *on war 1, chapter 5;* Alberico Gentili, *1, on the law of war, chapter 3.*

For this reason, the **private declarations of enmity** <note>original: "diffidationes"</note> or **feuds** <note>original: "Fehchoungen"</note> of private individuals are considered capital crimes. Heigius, *part 2, question 32, number 8;* Massa, *against the use of Duels, number 76.* And those forms of judgment called **self-justice** <note>original: "Selbstgericht." This refers to vigilantism or taking the law into one's own hands without a magistrate.</note> are barbaric, condemned by many recesses <note>A "recess" was an official decree or resolution of the Imperial Diet.</note> of the **Holy Roman Empire** <note>original: "Imperii Romano-Germanici"</note>, and also forbidden in Polish laws, such as the statutes of Poland under the word **war** <note>original: "guerra"</note>. Such also is the "remedy of plundering" <note>A legal recourse allowing a victim of theft to seize goods from the perpetrator’s community</note> mentioned in feudal law; Hotoman, *on title 22, book 2 of the Feuds.*

Rodolphinus reports that the Dukes of Italy can indeed wage war (*on Dukes, number 166*), though he denies this to the estates of France (*number 171*). Likewise, for the great nobles of the German-Roman Empire, the **Public Peace** <term>pax publica: the "Landfriede," a legal state established within the Empire to prohibit private feuds and ensure internal stability</term> greatly restricts ancient custom. See especially Gail, *on the public peace, chapter 4*, regarding **revocation mandates** <note>original: "avocatoriis mandatis"; orders issued by a higher court to stop proceedings in a lower court or to recall subjects to their duties</note> and whether they can coerce their own subjects with arms. Furthermore, the city of **Speyer** <note>An important Imperial City and seat of the high court</note> holds a unique privilege **to protect itself by its own power against anyone.** <note>original: "Von ihr selbst Gewalt/ gegen männiglich sich zuschirmen."</note>

Moreover, the carrying and the prohibition of arms belongs to the Princes; in our law, for instance, the use of arms is forbidden without the knowledge of the commander. *Law 1 and 2, on public violence, and the whole title on the use of arms, etc., book 11 of the Code;* Tuschus, *letter A, conclusion 515.* In former times among the Germans, only the **Knights** <note>original: "Equites"</note> carried arms, as noted by Goldast, *in notes on the ancient Exhortations, page 342.* Nor is it appropriate to carry arms in a time of peace; Borell, *on magistrates, book 3, chapter 17.* Thus, that force which is brought with arms is considered **public violence** <term>vis publica</term>, while that without arms is considered **private violence** <term>vis privata</term>, which is brough— <meta>catchword: infer- (brought against...)</meta>

It emphasizes that private feuding (Selbstgericht) is illegal under the Public Peace of the Holy Roman Empire, as military force is a strictly public prerogative of the sovereign.</summary>

# Political-Legal Dissertation

...is inferred. Duaren, *1. disputation, chapter 22.* And this **right of war** <term>ius belli: the legal authority to declare and conduct war</term> belongs so exclusively to the one with supreme power that it is considered the **crime of majesty** <term>majestas: treason against the sovereign or state</term> to hold a draft or organize an army without the Emperor’s command. *Law 3, section "by the same law" of the Digest on the Julian law of treason.* Johann von Elswich, *political disputation 13, thesis 9, "or to form an assembly."* Tuschus, *letter A, conclusion 229.* For this reason, Caesar acted wrongly (by acting prematurely) when he defended allies who were being harassed by Mithridates on his own private authority. Suetonius, *in the Life, chapter 4,* where Casaubon notes: Hence, to grant and entrust military command belongs to the supreme Prince; but once it has been granted, it exists as an ordinary right. Camman, *5, elective thesis 54 and 63.* And for this reason, the Philistines, as a sign of subjection, took away arms and the makers of arms from the Hebrews. *1 Samuel 13, verse 19.*

II. Just as the right of War belongs to the Prince, so too no subject is permitted to evade military duties. Zacharias Fridenreich, *Politics, chapter 28, page 167 and following.* Camman, *5, elective thesis 66.* Cunaeus, *On the Republic of the Hebrews, book 2, chapter 21.* See however Moditius, *section "plebiscite," doubt 87,* and Ritter, *at the cited place, number 193,* where he treats whether a subject must personally assist the Lord, especially outside the territory. By this same right, the Prince can compel subjects to keep watch. Rutger Ruland, *decisions on legal controversy 23.* 

Indeed, however, it is a hard thing to be forced into a war that the Prince moves out of personal passion, and to risk the safety of soul and body against one's conscience; for which reason Traiano Boccalini <note>A 16th-century Italian satirist known for his political commentary</note> prefers the condition of the French common people over the privileges that the Nobility there seem to possess in the highest degree. *2. From Parnassus, report 62.* From this, it seems subjects are not obligated except for the **defense of the land** <note>original German: "Zu einer Landrettung"</note>. Nor should war be moved without the knowledge of the **Estates** <note>original: "Ordinum," referring to the representative bodies of the realm</note>, as I said in the *axiom on Political constitution, final chapter.* On the **military service** <term>cavalcata: a feudal obligation to provide mounted military service</term> of subjects, and when **vassals** <term>vasalli: individuals holding land under a lord in exchange for service</term> are bound to serve, see Borrini, and also the treatise by Kohl, *on feudal services* <note>original Latin: "de servitijs feudalibus"</note>.

III. Outside the usual order, yet not inconveniently, it may be asked here (though it seems to belong to the *treatise on War*): Whether those soldiers have a vocation worthy of a Christian man who, content with their pay, voluntarily follow now these, now those sides of warring Princes (not being forced by the banners of their own Fatherland), caring little meanwhile which side has a just cause for undertaking the war? If this is examined by the scales of faith and charity, it seems it should rather be denied. See Luther's treatise, **Whether soldiers too can be in a state of salvation** <note>original German: "Ob Kriegsleut auch im Seeligen Standt sein können," Jena edition, volume 3, page 315</note>. Gail, *on the public peace, 4, number 33, etc.* Timpler, *4. politics, chapter 10, question 29.* Ummius, *disputation 14, number 79.* Add Lactantius, *Divine Institutes, book 1, chapter 18, from the beginning.* Moreover, whether Germans can offer their service in war to foreign Kings against the Emperor's will is investigated by Arumaeus, *title 4, discourse 20.*

### On the Rights of Majesty

...the right to maintain public workshops for the manufacture of arms <note>original: "morum," likely a typo for "armorum"</note>; and armories (**armories** <note>German: *Zeughäuser*</note>, which the feudal lawyers call *Armandiae* or *Armaniae*); these belong to the regalia <term>regalia: the specific rights, lands, and privileges belonging to a monarch</term>. *Chapter "What are the regalia," book 2 of the Feudal Law; Novel 85.* Camman, *elective thesis 64, etc.* For this reason, such workshops are called "sacred factories." To this should also be added the right of fortifying <term>jus muniendi: the legal right to build defensive walls or structures</term>, and of strengthening the walls of the city. *Law 9 on the division of things; Gail, book 2, observation 69, number 18; Knichen, in his overview, number 438, etc.; Camman, elective thesis 67; Moditius, section "plebiscite," doubt 77.*

Likewise, the right of building defensive works and fortresses. Tuschus, *letter F, conclusion 426; Justus Gebhard in Arumaeus, discourse 17, thesis 31, page 496; Killinger, in the 4th treatise on the law of joint inheritance.* Furthermore, all fortresses must be open to the sovereign—the right of **entry** <note>German: *die Öffnung*</note>; and he can place guards in a castle even against the will of the Vassal. Moditius, *cited section, doubt 33.* However, sometimes fortresses are opened to allies by treaty, and one or another person binds himself to this. Lehmann, *final chapter 27, near the end, and the following chapter.* And that subjects are bound to perform watch duty is also handed down by Borellus, *Treatise on Magistrates, book 4, chapter 11.* Or that the sovereign can grant cities the privilege that no fortifications or castles may be built in their vicinity. Anton Coler, *disputation on the Roman Empire, thesis 26.* Indeed, in Roman municipalities, walls could neither be repaired without the authority of the Prince or the Governor, nor could anything be placed upon or joined to them. *Law 9, section 4, of the Digest on the division of things.* And from this, Tacitus records that the Jews purchased the right of fortifying at a great price and by force. Cunaeus, *book 1, On the Hebrew Republic, chapter 7, page 58.*

It is fitting to add here a pragmatic sanction <term>pragmatic sanction: a formal decree issued by a ruler on a matter of great importance that has the force of law</term> of Emperor Rudolph I, which was recently produced at Speyer in a case of great importance: "We, Rudolph, by the grace of God King of the Romans, forever Augustus, make it known to all faithful subjects of the Roman Empire who will inspect the present letters, that in the year of our Lord 1279, in the seventh indiction, while we were sitting on the tribunal at Vienna, at the instance of the noble man, the Marquis of Hochberg, it was obtained by the common opinion of all present that no man, of whatever condition he may be, ought to construct a castle or any other fortification within the county of any Count, unless the Count's consent and pleasure have first been requested and obtained. Approving this opinion as having been delivered properly and reasonably, and confirming it by royal authority, we forbid all of you from violating or breaking this decree. Given on the day and place aforesaid." **Thus, one is not permitted to build a castle within a mile of Speyer.** From a privilege of Charles IV. Lehmann, *final chapter 43.* So also Charles IV grants Speyer a privilege **that they may fortify themselves.** Lehmann, *final chapter 57 and see chapter 58 at the beginning.*

### VI.
Indeed, just as only the Sovereign <note>original: "Princeps"</note> undertakes war—that is, declares who are enemies—so too only he declares who are friends. Thus, only Sovereignty <note>original: "majestas"</note> ends war through peace. See Marta, *On Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 39 at the end, and chapters 40 and 41.* Nor do military commanders have the power to establish peace without the consent of the people or the Sovereign. Cabotius, *disputation 2, number 15*; Bronchorst, *Miscellaneous, book 1, chapter 14.* At most, they may grant a temporary truce or ceasefire <note>original: "inducias, aut Treugas"</note>. Camman, *disputation 5, thesis 57.*

### VII.
To this I refer the power of granting security, the Right of Safe-Guard; <term>the escort authority to accompany someone on the open military highways <note>original German: "Gleidliche Oberkeit / auff freyer Heerstrassen zu begleiten"</note></term>: see Johann Camman, *elective thesis 21, 26, etc.*; see also the specific treatise by Maullius. Likewise, <term>to grant safe-conduct for legal proceedings <note>original German: "Gleid zum Rechten geben"</note></term>. See the excellent discussion by Ummius, *disputation 8, number 8*; see especially Georg Everhard, *volume 1, counsel 9*, concerning safe-conduct and who may grant it. See Arumaeus, *volume 2, discourse 5, page 52*, and also Papon, *book 5, title 7, arrest 1.* Furthermore, the power to sanction treaties is considered a right of majesty. See Waremund von Erenberg, *On Treaties, book 1, chapter 2, number 28, etc., page 135*, and *On Subsidies, page 81*; Bornitius, *chapter 25*; Camman, *elective thesis 69.* Sometimes the liberty of lower Princes or Republics is so great that they are able to arrange treaties either among themselves within the same Commonwealth, or even with others—provided they always respect the sovereignty of the superior Commonwealth. Thus, the Princes and Free Cities of the Roman Empire are permitted to contract treaties for the preservation of public peace and for their own legitimate defense. See Fridenreich, *Politics, chapter 24, page 643*, and see my own treatise, *On Treaties.*

...or to send, or to receive [ambassadors], is possible only for those who hold the supreme power of the state. Bornitius, *chapter 28*, and this right is considered to be granted to none of the subjects. On that account, in the year 1604, the envoy of the King of Spain requested that the King of Britain not deign to honor the speaker of the **Dutch** <note>original: "Batavorum"; referring to the people of the Netherlands</note> with the title of Ambassador. For it is the Prince's own prerogative to establish common deliberation concerning matters pertaining to the state. Camman, *6, thesis 82*; Bornitius, *chapter 26*; Börtius, in Arumæus, *discourse 30, chapter 3, number 21, folio 875*; and on the *Golden Bull, discourse 5, number 20*; Waremund, *treatise on burdens, chapter 1*. Bertram, in Arumæus, *discourse 9, thesis 17, etc., folio 109 and following*.

### CHAPTER VII.

## Royal Rights commonly called the Treasury.

Money is the **sinew of affairs** <note>original: "nervus rerum"; a classical metaphor suggesting that money provides the vital strength and movement for state actions</note>; and no state can stand without expenses: it has need of resources, without which nothing that is necessary will be done. Aristotle, *Politics, book 1, chapter 7, at the end*; Bodin, *On the Republic, book 6, chapter 2, number 638*; Simanca, *On the Republic, book 3, chapter 15*; Fridenreich, *Politics, chapter 17, at the beginning*; Henricus Klockh, *elegant disputation on the law of taxes, thesis 1*; and I myself, *in the treatise on the treasury, at the beginning*. Not only must resources and expenses be provided for the king so that the realm may be administered, but also a worthy reward and compensation for labor is owed to the highest magistrate; by whose vigilance the status of the state is kept safe, the wealth of all is **preserved in good repair** <note>original: "sartæ tectæ"; a Roman legal idiom meaning to keep a building or a state of affairs in sound condition</note>, and peace and tranquility are guarded inviolate. To such an extent that the tables of the Great in the state should not be looked upon with eyes full of envy, nor their banquets and other things, in which those occupied with public business demand that a pleasant recreation of the mind and an honorable relaxation be given to them. For this reason, in almost every polity, a certain part of the state's wealth is designated as the **patrimony of the state** <note>original: "patrimonium reipublicæ"</note>; which, leased to citizens for a certain time or in perpetuity for a fixed fee, might assist public necessities: as an ornament of peace and a support of war. *Le Guidon on the Finances of France, part 1, at the beginning*; and I, *on the treasury, chapter 1, number 5*. And such are the goods which, for the more convenient government of the state and the protection of its dignity, are granted to majesty...

Sometimes the liberty even of inferior Princes or republics is so great that they are able to arrange treaties either among themselves in the same republic, or even with others—provided they always make an exception for the majesty of the superior republic. Thus, for the Princes and Free Cities of the Roman Empire, it is permitted to contract treaties for the preservation of public peace and their own legitimate defense. Fridenreich, *Politics*, chapter 24, *folio* 643. See my own treatise, *On Treaties*.

...granted. Today they are called goods conjoined and incorporated into the kingdom, or united to the Crown; they are also called the **Dowry of the State** <note>original: "Dos reipublicæ"</note>, the **Chamber Property** <term>Cammergut</term>, or the **Domain** <term>Domaine</term>. The Prince is indeed the master of this dowry, but he cannot alienate <note>sell or transfer ownership of</note> it. To this category also belong payments and ordinary taxes: the **General ordinary tax** <term>Gemeine ordentliche Stewr</term>. From these funds, military forces are maintained; the remaining ranks of society also enjoy their assigned allotments or salaries; city walls and urban centers are repaired; and finally, all other things proceed from here that concern the common welfare of the subjects. Justinian, *New Constitutions 161, chapter 2.* Heigius, *part 1, question 17, numbers 3 and 1.* A tax <note>original: "Tributum"</note> is a burden placed on the fruits of the land, and it is contributed because of the possession of private soil. It is most commonly understood as the money commanded by Emperors and Governors from the inhabitants of a province for the wages of soldiers and the expenses of war. Wesembecius, *on the Digest, title on tax collectors, numbers 3 and 4.* Taxes were therefore weighed from individuals according to the measure of the census and their means. For this reason, citizens were held to declare all their means in good faith before the **Censor** (who was also called the Master of the Census, and later simply the Censor) so that they might be valued by him, and taxes might be commanded in proportion to those means, following a certain equitable ratio; for he is also called by this name, the **Equalizer** <note>original: "Peræquator"</note>. And if he did not observe a just measure, there was a right of appeal from him. *Law 5, Code on censuses and assessments.*

II. They properly gave the name **Tolls** <note>original: "Vectigalia"</note> to those things which were paid by the tax-farmers <note>original: "publicanis"; these were private contractors who collected taxes for the state</note> as lessees. These were gathered either from the cultivation of fields, which were mostly public land; or from public pastures, which was called the **Pasturage Tax** <term>Scriptura</term> <note>literally "the writing," because the number of cattle was written in the records</note>; or from the transit of goods, which was called a **Customs Duty** <term>portorium</term>. See by all means Valentinus Forsterus, *On Roman Jurisdiction, folio 489*, or even the **Riverbank Toll** <term>Ripaticum</term>. Rosenthal, *On Fiefs, chapter 5, conclusion 4*. Specifically, the toll <note>original: "vectigal"</note> is named from "transport" <note>original: "vecturâ"</note>; and it is that which is paid on those things which are imported or exported for the use of public life. *Law 21, On donations between husband and wife.* Henricus Klock, *in the said dispute, thesis 7.* Since the state, with great care and expense, must provide a level and safe path for those traveling through, it is hardly unfair that something be paid back by travelers as a reward and compensation for those expenses. See also on the difference between a tax and a toll, P. Perrenon, *Observations 2, final chapter.* However, if a mule-driver or a sailor does not pay the **excise** <term>gabella</term>, do the goods fall into **confiscation** <term>commissum</term>? This is disputed by Baldus, *on the Code, title on nautical interest*; Cumanus, *opinion 5*; and Thessaurus, *in Forensic Questions*, where he says that the judgment was pronounced in favor of the treasury against the merchants. But let what Elbertus Leoninus notes be added, *Emendations, book 2, chapter 11, number 12*: a distinction must be established between the carrier of the goods and the owner-merchant, such that by the fraud of the carrier, only the carrier’s own property should be confiscated—for example, his horses, vehicle, or pack-animal—but not the merchant’s goods. *Law "We command," Code on not excusing ships, book 11.* It is otherwise if the merchant himself employed deceit

# On the Rights of Majesty

...presented; for then the merchandise is also subject to seizure <note>original: "commissum"</note>. *Law: "cotem," section "Dominus navis" in the Digest on tax collectors.* Or if some custom or constitution subjects licit goods to seizure along with illicit ones, as René Choppin writes regarding the customs of the Angevins in *On the Jurisdiction of Anjou, book 1, chapter 53.*

### III.
Furthermore, the private possessions of individuals are subject to the republic and are considered part of public law, as it were. This is not because they have ceased to belong to individuals, but because they are comprised within the body of the republic like a limb, so that just as they enjoy the benefits of public protection, they are also compelled to be subject to public burdens. Thus, subjects pay tribute as if in recognition of the Universal Empire <note>The author distinguishes between private ownership and the ultimate "over-lordship" or sovereignty of the state.</note>. The illustrious Enenckelius, *On Privileges, chapter 5*; Cothman, *on the title of the Code "On the Supreme Trinity," question 3*; Scotanus, *in the paratitla on book 1 of the Code, title 33*; and myself, *Politics, book 1, chapter 4, number 36, and On the Treasury, book 1, number 6.* These authorities argue for and introduce this subjection. Tuschus, *letter C, conclusion 190.* This does not mean that the actual ownership, the <term>Grund und Boden</term> <note>German for "ground and soil"</note>, belongs to the Prince. Consequently, he does not enjoy the right of retraction <note>The right to step into a sale and buy property back</note> if one subject buys something from another. Rauchbar, *part 2, question 22.* In a free republic, taxes are imposed mostly on provincials, not on citizens. Thus, the Romans did not want immovable property <note>real estate</note> to be in the private patrimony of provincials, but rather in the ownership or property of the People. For this reason, their estates—both rural and urban—were called "non-manicipable things" <note>original: "res non mancipi," a Roman legal category of property transferred with less formality</note>, in which they held only the usufruct <note>The right to use and enjoy the fruits of property owned by another</note>. Later, these were for the most part made subject to tribute and stipends; see Joachim Stephan, *On Jurisdiction, book 3, chapter 6, numbers 16 and 17.*

### IV.
The ordinary revenues of the republic must be preserved as zealously as possible. For if taxes are not brought in, the republic cannot be preserved. *Justinian’s Novels 149, 161, 182, chapter 15; Novel 189, chapter 2; Law 1, section 20 in the Digest on investigations.* Guillaume Fornerius, *Selected Works, book 1, chapter 20*; Camman, *discourse 7, thesis 8.* Rightly, therefore, when Nero was wavering over whether he should order all taxes to be abolished, the Senators taught him that "the dissolution of the Empire would follow if the fruits by which the republic is sustained were diminished." Tacitus, *Annals, book 14.* For there is a just fear that if subsidies cease, necessary things will be abandoned. Symmachus, *Book 10, Epistle 50.* The revenue of the Roman Empire under Frederick Barbarossa <note>Holy Roman Emperor, reigned 1155–1190</note> was still sixty tons of gold, as revealed by Schneidewein, *Institutes, on intestate succession, under the rubric "On the succession of the treasury," number 5.* The Emperors were not cautious enough; they did not take precautions to prevent these revenues from passing to others. Consequently, the "sinews of affairs" <note>The financial resources necessary to take action</note> were cut off for their successors. Myself, *On the Treasury, chapter 2, number 4, version 2.*

### V.
To ensure that this patrimony is preserved and that subjects are not burdened by extraordinary collections <note>special, emergency taxes</note>, various benefits have been assigned to it—from the common practice of almost all nations—which increase the treasury of the Empire.

In the single chapter *where the regalia are listed* <note>original: "quæ sint regalia, enumerata"</note> (Lehman, Book 5, Chapter 67, page 539), it is said that to possess a treasury <note>original: "fiscus"</note> is a right of majesty. See Tuschus, *letter F, conclusion 381, etc.*, and Peregrinus in his *singular treatise*. This includes the proceeds from many fines and penalties (Wesembec, *on the title "on the method of fines"*; Camman, 9, h. 27). It also includes confiscations, according to Moditius (Section *plebiscitum*, questions 46 and 43), about which Carocius writes extensively in his *treatise on the seizure of goods, part 1*, and Tuschus (*letter C, conclusion 712*). These rights are therefore not thought to pass to a Vassal, even when he is invested with <term>mere and mixed empire</term> <note>The "power of the sword," or the highest level of criminal and civil jurisdiction.</note> (Lord Bocer, *on the law of jurisdiction 8, number 26 and following*). The oldest royal right <note>original: "Regale"</note> of the Frankish Kings was the **King’s Ban or Ban-penny** <note>original: "deß Königs Bann oder Bannpenning"</note>, also called the royal or lordly ban (Lehman, Book 2, Chapter 45, page 188, and Book 4, Chapter 22, page 363).

Whether a usufructuary <note>Someone who has the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property.</note> or a "good faith" possessor may keep fines and confiscations is discussed by Gilken (*on the law, "it is certain," chapter 4*). Paulus Busius (*on the republic, chapter 2, number 6*) argues that some people wrongly classify these regalia as rights of majesty, since they are nothing more than benefits for the treasury; Waremundus agrees (*on the subsidies of the kingdom, chapter 3, from the beginning*). However, I have stated above in *chapter 1 of this section* to what extent they are included in the rights of majesty, and I wish that to be repeated here. It is also necessary to warn that new "regalia" of this kind must not be established under the pretext of absolute power, as I shall also mention below.

I refer here also to goods that are taken away from the "unworthy" (Bornitius, *on the treasury, book 3, chapter 5*; Latherus, 2, chapter 8), or if someone is unable to inherit what was left to them by a deceased person. Camman reviews various such cases (*disputations 9 and 10*). The treasury also inherits from those born of an incestuous union (Mynsinger, 3, *observation 91*; Bornitius, *the said book 3, chapter 7*). As for whether a parricide <note>One who kills a parent or close relative.</note> is incapable or unworthy of a paternal inheritance, see Heigius (*part 2, question 33*).

In view of these revenues, the supreme magistrate is bound to administer justice for free and to carry out criminal sentences at his own expense (Heig, *part 2, question 23*; Wesembec, *legal opinion 150*). But if someone holds <term>mere empire</term>—**that is, if one is invested within a certain district with the blood-ban or criminal authority** <note>original: "so einer in einem gewissen Bezirk / mit dem Blutbann / oder der Malefizischen Oberkeit belehnet"</note>—is the lord himself or his subjects bound to supply and pay the expenses of the criminal trial and execution? Regularly, the magistrate is bound to pay those expenses and cannot burden the subjects on that account (Knichen, *on the pacts of investiture, part 2, chapter 1, number 170*). In this matter, the subjects have a well-founded case. Indeed, magistrates who hold "empire" and execute punishments are regularly compelled to bear the costs and burdens associated with punishment and the execution of justice themselves (Chassanæus, *on the customs of Burgundy, title "on confiscations," section 1, word "belonging," number 2*; Boerius, *on the customs of Bourges, title "on the jurisdiction of all judges"*; and Julius Clarus, *final section, question 99, number 5*). That the expenses for the execution of justice belong to the treasury...

# On the Rights of Majesty

The matter was decided also by the Court of Toulouse, *decision 41*, and Wesenbeck agrees in *Counsel 150*, as does Heig in *part 2, question 23*. For they receive fines and similar payments under that name specifically so that they may apply them toward investigating and punishing crimes, as well as for providing food for poor prisoners. Paris de Puteo writes extensively on this in his *Treatise on Syndics* <note>A "syndic" was a government official or representative; this legal text discusses their duties and expenses.</note>, *under the word "expenses," chapter 2, numbers 1 and 2*. For this reason, these expenses are said to be "necessary for the republic." *Law "with the shipmasters," 6, Code on shipmasters, book 11; Paris de Puteo, in the Treatise on Syndics, under the word "reward," number 3*. Peasants are so little bound to pay these costs that if they personally incurred any expenses while capturing a criminal, they ought to be reimbursed from the public funds. Paris de Puteo, *in the place cited above, following the teaching of Baldus in Law 1, Code on the services of freedmen; Boerius, decision 303, number 9, following the text in Law "Circensian," 20, Code on decurions, book 10*. Indeed, Paris de Puteo specifically writes that if magistrates attempt to extort these costs from subjects, the subjects may rightly complain of an injury. *Treatise on Syndics, at the beginning of the title on the excesses of kings and princes, chapter 1, number 67*.

And this seems to take place most especially if, in Imperial investitures—**when in investitures of capital jurisdiction** <note>original: "Wann in Belehnungen deß Blutbanns." The "Blood Ban" or *Blutbann* refers to the legal authority to preside over "high justice," involving crimes punishable by death or physical mutilation.</note>—nothing else has been provided for; in that case, one must rightly stand by the rules of common law. This is because the privileges and decrees of Princes are, in cases of doubt, to be interpreted according to common law, and they cannot be twisted to the prejudice of a third party who has the established law on their side. *Law 14 and the two following, Digest on laws; Law 141, at the beginning, on the rules of law; Chapter "those things from the law," 28, on the rules of law in the 6th book of Decretals, and the Doctors of Law in both places*. 

Nor does it hinder the argument if someone says that in neighboring villages, such expenses are imposed on the peasants and they are taxed in that name. For it is well established that a custom contrary to common law is not to be extended from case to case, nor from person to person, nor from place to place; rather, as much as possible, it must be interpreted most strictly. Baldus, *in the "Authentica" regarding the matter near the end, and there* Jason, *Code on the Holy Churches; Cravetta, on the antiquity of time, part 4, section "I pass now to the fourth," number 44 and following; Rolandus a Valle, counsel 55, number 13, book 1; Ludolph Schrader, on fiefs, part 10, section 20, number 165 and following*. Heig feels the same way regarding the terms of our specific case, *in said question 23, number 14*; and the traditions of Matthias Wehner also support this in his *On the Signification of Words*, under the term <term>Landbrauch</term> <note>original: "Landbrauch"; refers to local customary law or the "usage of the land."</note>. There he says: although a certain custom might seem well-known by the common usage of Germany, it must still be not only alleged but also proven specifically for the location in dispute.

Unclaimed property <note>original: "Bona vacantia"</note>; specifically the property of those who die without an heir. *Final law, Code on vacant goods; Guillaume Ranchin, treatise on intestate succession, section 23; Bornitius, on the treasury, 3, chapter 2; Camman, 8, thesis 4; Latherus, on the census, book 3, chapter 1; Barrius, treatise on successions, final book, title 5; Lord Adam Keller, on successions, title 28*. In these cases, however, the public treasury <note>original: "fiscus"</note> is not held liable beyond the value of the inherited assets. Cavallos, *volume 3, common opinions, question 822*. Closely related to this royal right is that which they call <term>le Droict d' Aubaine</term> <note>original: "le Droict d' Aubaine"; the Right of Albinatus, a French law where the king inherited the property of a foreigner who died in his territory without being naturalized.</note> in France. Ranchin, *in the place cited, number 4; Le Guidon, on Finances*.

Under Roman and Feudal law, "treasure trove" was often split between the landowner and the finder.</note> St. Paulinus provides a remarkable story of a shipwreck in *Letter 36*, where Daniel Rosweyde and Fronton du Duc also comment.

### VIII. Revenues from fishing
*Chapter 1, title 56, book 2 of the Feuds;* and from **saltworks:** *Marpurg Counsel 9, volume 1; Bornitius, On the Treasury, book 5, chapter 5; Hardevv. à Daffel, counsel 2;* as well as from **stone quarries.** *Rauchbar, question 22;* and **rivers.** *Rauchbar, question 23; Bulenger, On Taxes, chapter 31.* Also from **tolls:** <note>original: "vectigal"</note> and even from **mines of every kind of metal.** *Heigius, part 1, question 3; Farinacci, question 105; Bornitius, On the Treasury, book 5, chapter 4; Rauchbar, said question 22; Peregrinus, 4, On the Law of the Fisc, title 2, number 21, etc.; Master Dr. Bocer, On Investitures, 3, number 101, etc., and On the Law of Money, chapter 2, number 35, etc.; Buxtorff, thesis 89; Camman, 7, thesis 85, and many following; Bulenger, On Taxes, chapter 35; Klock, On Taxes, thesis 3, 6; Engelhard, On Taxes, folio 6.* Whether metal mines belong to the Nobles (*Wesembec, counsel 60*) or to the Lord or the Vassal is discussed by *Master Bocer, Treatise on the Law of the Lord and Vassal, folio 188, and others.* But should **coal** <note>original: "Steinkohlen"</note> be numbered among the royal rights? <note>original: "regalibus"</note> See *Wehner, Franconian counsels, 88.* Likewise, **Salt**, or salt-mines. *Bulenger, On Taxes, chapter 16.*

### IX. Variation of Rights
However, these **royal rights** <term>regalia: the specific powers and privileges belonging to a monarch or sovereign state</term> (which I also discuss here and there in my *Treatise on the Treasury*) vary according to the diversity of places and empires. Thus in England, as part of the Prince's private property, there is the **guardianship of male and female wards.** <note>The "Court of Wards and Liveries" allowed the King to manage the estates of orphaned heirs.</note> Nor do his vassals properly contract marriages without his command: *Thomas Smith, 2, On the English Republic, 4, folio 68 and book 3, chapter 5.* This might seem unfair elsewhere. They commonly call it *la noble garde* <note>original French: "the noble wardship."</note>; it is also used in certain parts of France. *Coteræus, On Military Law, folio 199; Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, 3, On the Republic, 2, near the end,* where he says that in some places the relatives <note>original: "agnatos"</note> receive the profits of the wards' estates. In many places, through long-term use and prescription, the **right of hunting** <note>original: "venatio"</note> has also been made a royal right. *Heigius, part 1, question 15; Friedrich Pruckman, under the section "hunting," chapter 1; Arumæus, Feudal Disputations, 4, thesis 15; but see Master Dr. Harpprecht, section 12, number 143, on the division of things; and Master Dr. Bocer, chapter 1, on royal rights, number 30, and On the Law of the Vassal, folio 197; Forster, Treatise on Ownership, chapter 9, number 12, etc.* They wish for this to be classified among the jurisdictional profits <note>Income derived from the exercise of legal authority over a territory.</note> by modern law. This custom was also introduced long ago into England by the Normans...

...introduced. *Selden, book 2, The English Janus, folio 78.* Thus, it is not hunting itself—as was the custom among the Romans—but rather the **prohibition of hunting** that is counted among the sovereign rights <note>original: "regalibus." These are "Regalia," specific powers or incomes reserved for a king or prince.</note>. *Borellus, On the Magistrate, book 4, chapter 3.* On the question of whether the right to hunt has been lawfully taken away from subjects, see *Felsten, Century of Political Questions, decade 8, final thesis; Anton Gerhard, Disputations on the Institutes, thesis 4; Arumæus, Disputations on the Principal Laws, 20, thesis 1; Konrad Pincier, Treatise on Jurisdiction, chapter 4, number 39 and many following; Timaeus Faber, Disputations on the Institutes, 12, corollary 2.* Add also *Petra, On the Power of the Prince, chapter 7; Lycklama, 3rd member, chapter 9; Speckhan, Century 1, question 97; Arithin, 1, disputation 3, thesis 5; Valentin Riemer, corollary 1, decade 4; Mohr de Nigromante, Treatise on Hunting, part 1, chapter 2; Mr. Anton Winther, my certain friend, Disputation on the Division of Things, thesis 11 and following; Fachinaeus, 1st Controversies, chapter 1; Gail, 2nd Observations, 68.*

It is not unjust that subjects are forbidden from hunting, because they long ago consented that wild animals should be left to the Princes as compensation for the troubles they endure in governing the Empire; so says Lucas Osiander, *on Job chapter 24.* There are those who believe that hunting rights arose from wartime domination and subjection, just like the right of serfdom <term>serfdom <note>original German: "die Leibeigenschaft"</note></term>, and that the victors reserved this right for themselves. That the prohibition of hunting was introduced by the Romans seems proven by the *Theodosian Code, on the hunting of wild beasts, book 15, title 11.*

However, Princes ought not to forbid hunting in those places where the power to hunt is still free to everyone, which they call **free hunting** <term>free hunting <note>original German: "freyer Bürsch." This refers to traditional communal hunting grounds not yet claimed by a lord.</note></term>. For a legitimate immunity cannot be taken away from anyone by right. Political thinkers also say it is least advisable to establish **new** sovereign rights <note>original: "Regalia nova."</note>.

->*The reservation of the ordinary sovereign rights suffers little injustice, unless they are used too insolently and tyrannically. Injustice occurs when new sovereign rights are formed.* <note>original Italian: "La riserva delle Regaglie ordinarie, patisce poca ingiustitia, se non fosse nel modo di servirsene troppo insolentemente, & tirannicamente. *Political Treasure, part 1, folio 26.* For example, if subjects are forced to use the Lord's mill (*Rutger Ruland, decision 24*) or are forced to buy wine only from the Lord. Let it not be said of a good Prince what Juvenal says in his 4th Satire:

> Whatever is conspicuous and beautiful in the whole sea,
> belongs to the treasury, wherever it swims.

Whether a Lord acquires the right of hunting through frequent prohibition and the patience of his subjects is explored by *Cravetta, counsel 657.* And on the effect of **prescription** <note>original: "præscriptionis." A legal principle where a right is gained or lost through the passage of time.</note> concerning hunting rights, see *Schwannmann in Feudal Counsels.*

Those "provident protectors of nature" <note>An early reference to wildlife conservationists.</note> are ridiculous, who take away the hunting of wild animals from the common people so that the species are not lost: for why, I ask, were they not wiped out long ago? Why did they not perish in the New World <note>original: "novis Insulis," literally "new islands," a common term for the Americas.</note>? There, formerly, the number of men was incredible, and the abundance of wild beasts was marvelous. Indeed, prohibition hinders the divine blessing; just as we find that things intended for common use vanish when they are hindered by a tax or some other means.

Indeed, when Princes abuse that right which they have enjoyed since antiquity, let them not be unwilling to hear Saint Augustine, who says: "Those who watch the hunter and are delighted shall see the Savior and be sorrowed." <note>original Latin: "qui vident venatorem & delectantur, videbunt Salvatorem & contristabuntur." This reflects a common theological critique that obsession with the blood sport of hunting distracts from spiritual life.</note> *Chapter "qui vident," distinction 86.* Add also what Mr. Lansius reports from the *Polycraticus* of John of Salisbury <note>A 12th-century English philosopher and bishop known for his political theory.</note>, *in his consultations, folio 536.* (On whether a Prince should study hunting, see Scipio Ammirato, *Discourse 2, chapter 1;* and Kirchner, *Orations 19 and following, volume 1;* Gerhard, *On the Magistrate, number 429, etc.*)

The Wills left by several Kings of France are entirely worthy of praise: <insert>"Compensation shall be made to the peasants who have holdings so near to the royal forests for the damage they have suffered from wild beasts."</insert> <note>original French: "Recompense estre faicte aux paisans..."</note> *The Grand Almoner of France, folio 242;* Jean du Tillet, *On the Titles, Grandeur, and Excellence of the Kings of France, title: Inventory of Wills, folio 347, etc.* 

Equally worthy of all praise is the famous saying of Louis, Count Palatine, Elector of the Holy Roman Empire. When serious complaints about wild animals were once brought to him, and his subjects complained that they were greatly burdened in this regard, the man who humbly set forth these complaints on behalf of the subjects added that His Highness would lose the prayers of his subjects unless he applied a remedy to this evil in time. He immediately replied: **that he would rather lack venison entirely than lose the prayers of his subjects.** For wild meat was never so pleasing to him, nor had it ever been, that his subjects were not far dearer; he preferred to look after the welfare of his subjects rather than the pleasures perceived from the consumption of venison. At the same time, he gave the order that the wild animals should be struck down in great numbers. Dr. Timothy Kirchner, *in the Oration he held on the death of this most excellent and praiseworthy Prince, folio 292, book 1.*

Regarding the use of hunting for health, see Mercurialis, *The Art of Gymnastics, book 3, chapter 15 and book 6, chapter 13.* Similarly, Rittershusius has some things to say on the use of hunting in his *dedicatory preface to Oppian.* There has always been great care for hunting among both "Barbarians" and Christians. Among the Turks, a thousand Janissaries <note>Elite infantry units that formed the Ottoman Sultan's household troops and bodyguards.</note> care for the hunting dogs. Tarduccius, *folio 245.* And Froissart writes of the King of France in *chapter 210:* <insert>"And with the King, there were easily thirty falconers on horseback for his service."</insert> <note>original French: "Et avec le Roy, avoit bien pour luy trente faulconiers à Cheval."</note> The Emperor Hadrian was so studious of hunting that it reached the point of being a fault. *Spartianus.* Odenatus <note>A ruler of Palmyra who fought against the Persians.</note> was hardened by a hunting life; he endured the sun and dust of the Persian wars. *Pollio in The Thirty Tyrants, number 14.* 

On hunting, see also Arumæus, *volume 4, discourse 37,* and the specialized treatises of Pruckmann, de Medices, and Mohr. One may also look at **the right to hunt** <term>the right to hunt <note>original German: "das Jagrecht"</note></term> by Noë Meurer. There are infinite legal questions on this subject. Mr. Rutger Ruland, *On Interrogatories, book 2, chapter 8, number 20.*

->**A Political-Legal Dissertation**<-

**X.** The most efficient method for increasing the Treasury or the Public Fund <note>original: "Fisci aut Ærarii." The Fiscus was originally the Emperor's private purse, while the Aerarium was the public treasury of the Roman state; here they are used to refer to the state budget generally.</note> is to reduce expenditures; to purge the city and the provinces of unnecessary men. For Alexander Severus <note>A Roman Emperor (reigned 222–235 AD) known for his attempts at administrative reform.</note> said it is a bad Emperor who feeds unnecessary men, not useful to the state, from the very vitals of the provincial subjects. *Lampridius.* Nothing is more shameful, or rather more cruel, than for those who have contributed nothing by their own labor to the republic to take from it; which the Emperor Antoninus Pius once said, according to Capitolinus. Nero, believing that the only fruit of riches and money was extravagance, and keeping no limit in giving or spending, finally assigned no duty to anyone without adding: *“You know what I need, and let us see to it that no one has anything.”* *Suetonius, chapters 30 and 32.* Therefore, in place of an oracle, let us take the words of the Poet:

> *If you enjoy your wealth rightly, there is no way a greater abundance*
> *Could be granted to you by Jove.*

Those who do otherwise perish amidst pomp and celebration; as Hira <note>likely Étienne de Vignolles, known as La Hire, a French military commander during the Hundred Years' War.</note> once said to King Charles VII of France when, even with the English waging war in France, he saw the King entirely occupied with the dancing of the women’s quarters, banquets, and other such costly delights. *Gaspar Ens, Epidorp. book 1, folio 13.* See also my own *Treatise on the Treasury.*

**XI.** But truly, sometimes the demands of necessity cannot be overcome in this way, and suggest other means; driving the Ruler to increase ordinary subsidies or to demand extraordinary ones. The French commonly call these collections *Aides* and *Tailles.* <note>The 'Aide' was an indirect tax on goods, while the 'Taille' was a direct land tax in pre-revolutionary France.</note> They differ from tributes in this: they do not involve a fixed payment, but an uncertain one arising from immediate necessity. Hence, legal scholars say that establishing customs duties and announcing extraordinary collections belongs to the Supreme Command, and must be referred to the royal rights <term>Regalia: the exclusive powers and privileges of a sovereign</term> of the high Prince. *Title: On new customs duties not being established.* *Lancellot, Temple of Justice, book 1, chapter 1, § 4, folio 377. Sixtinus, On Regalia, book 2, chapters 6 and 14. Master Bocerus, On Regalia, chapter 2, number 18, and chapter 3, number 213. Bornitius, chapter 23. The Most Honorable Rutger Ruland, Decision 11. Paul Busius, Disputation on the Republic, 11, thesis 10.* 

Customs duties are sometimes increased when necessity so demands. Just as among the Romans, an eighth part was eventually demanded, *Law 7, Code on Customs,* whereas formerly only a fiftieth or even a hundredth part used to be paid. *Cujacius, 6 Observations 28.* In the Holy Roman Empire, however, the imposition of customs duties is not within the power of the individual States; rather, the command of the Emperor is required. This is according to the Recess <note>An official decree or resolution of an Imperial Diet.</note> of Emperor Rudolph I. *Lehman, book 5, chapter 108, folio 629.* But the Princes of Italy do this by their own right. *Rodolphinus, On the Dukes of Italy, number 199, etc.* Whether they may be acquired through prescription <note>The legal process of acquiring a right through long-term, uninterrupted use.</note> is discussed by Modestinus Pistoris, *Counsel 6, book 2.* And their collection is so strict that goods fall into confiscation if they <term>so den Zoll überfahren: bypass the toll-gate or cross the border without paying the customs fee</term>. *Bornitius, On the Treasury, book 3, chapter 4.* Likewise, although the Lord of any territory, province, or community is not held liable for robbery committed there...
