### On the Rights of Majesty

...having been done, if he was unaware, or could not prevent it, as the Abbot <note>Referring to Panormitanus (Nicholaus de Tudeschis), a famous 15th-century canon lawyer.</note> asserts is the common opinion in *chapter 1, number 2, on the restoration of stolen goods*, and there also Antonius de Butrio, *number 19*. The text is quite clear in *the section "Since indeed,"* which Jacobus de Belloviso follows in *the authentic "That none shall judge."* However, if the Lord demands a toll <note>original: "pedagium," a fee paid by travelers for the use of a road or for protection.</note> from those passing through, he is bound to compensate them if any damage is caused to them on the public road; as Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a preeminent jurist of civil law.</note> holds in *chapter 1, the section on holding assemblies, regarding the keeping of peace and confirming of oaths.* Baldus says the same in the title *Who may grant a fief.* Taxes are also sometimes increased outside the regular order, or a poll tax <note>original: "capitatio."</note> is declared. This is a certain type of personal tax that was imposed on the head or the person, not on one’s resources; it was demanded even from those who have no recorded wealth and possess no estates. See the *Juridical Lexicon* of Calvinus, under the word *Capitatio*, and Scotanus in the *Commentary on Book 1 of the Code, title 52, on provisions and poll taxes.*

**XII.** These extraordinary collections can be demanded from all who enjoy the benefits of the commonwealth. Furthermore, in the highest and most extreme difficulty of the state, all immunities and privileges cease. Fridenreich, *chapter 28, folio 170.* Truly, those contributions ought to be converted only to public uses, following the example of the Emperor of the Turks, who supports his court from his gardens and other personal revenues. Indeed, they call extraordinary declarations *Haran agamenicani* <note>Likely a transliteration of an Ottoman Turkish or Arabic phrase; the author glosses it as "prohibited sweat of subjects."</note>, that is, the "forbidden sweat of the subjects," which is not spent except for the necessary uses of war. See Breüning in *The First Sea Voyage*; see also the *Council of Master Dr. Johannes Brentius, among the Theological Councils of Ibidem-bachius, decade 6, council 9*: **Whether and when a Christian authority may tax its subjects with a good conscience?** The Caliph Al-Ghabassi <note>A reference to an Abbasid Caliph, possibly Al-Raddi or another ruler known for his piety and handiwork.</note> once imposed this religious rule upon himself: that he would take no use of food, drink, or clothing except from the labor of his own hands. He was a maker of mats and most elegant floor coverings, which, marked with his own seal, he gave to his chief ministers to be sold in the marketplace. The great men of the land would buy them, and with the money from those gains, he prepared his own sustenance. From the *Travels of Benjamin*. If the Great Muslim King did these things, why should it not be unseemly for Christian Princes to abuse the labor and sweat of poor subjects for useless displays? See my *Treatise on Avarice, chapter 4, number 6, version 1.* As to whether a municipal city can declare a tax, and concerning the states of the German-Roman Empire, consult Busius, *disputation on the republic 11, theses 11 through 19*; I also treat this matter in the *Treatise on the Rights of Universities.*

**XIV.** However, quite different from these public requirements are the labors that subjects owe to their Noble Lords: <term>Service, socage, and daily forced labor.</term> <note>original: "Dienst / Frohn / alltägliche Frohndienst."</note> For these labors do not descend from the power of state jurisdiction, but from contract or long-standing custom. **XV.** Just as it is a right of majesty to demand taxes and other payments, so it is equally a right to grant immunity and exemption: *see the entire title of book 10 of the Code regarding those who have received exemptions from the Prince; and Novel 128, chapter 1*. Thus in Rome formerly the Senate, and later the Princes, administered this sovereign right. Bulenger, *on taxes, chapter 55, folio 180*. It should be known, however, that citizens hate those who are exempt, and a benefit given to a few is an injury to the common people: *see the entire title of the Code, that immunity shall be granted to no one*. Also Guillaume Forner, *selected works, book 1, chapter 20*. And finally, the unjust exaction of any extraordinary burdens...

### CHAPTER VIII.

## On those things which, due to their unique dignity, are distributed only by the Majesty.

Furthermore, there are many things in a commonwealth which, because of the highest necessity and greatest dignity, are considered reserved for the Sovereign alone. For instance, establishing **Postal Systems** <note>original: *Postas*</note> provides not only the greatest utility for those traveling or sending letters, but also contributes significantly to the security of the state. Through this medium, the Prince may have knowledge of what is happening in every corner of his Principality. Arnisaeus <note>Henning Arnisaeus, a prominent political theorist who wrote on sovereignty.</note> discusses this in *On the Right of Majesty, book 3, chapter 5, page 547.* For this reason, one of the Indian philosophers advised Alexander the Great to choose a seat for himself in the middle of his kingdom, so that he could more easily suppress growing uprisings and understand what was happening everywhere. This is cited in the same location from Plutarch’s *Life of Alexander.*

That these Postal Systems are among the <term>Imperial Reserved Rights</term> <note>original: *Reservatis Imperatoriis*; rights held exclusively by the Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> is proven by the **Imperial Recess of Speyer from the year 1542, in the section "and so that one also at any time," etc.** <note>original: *Reichs Abschied zu Speyr*; a formal decree or resolution from the Imperial Diet (Reichstag).</note> Furthermore, the Bohemian report promulgated by Emperor Matthias states: **"that the Imperial Post is a high <term>Regalian right</term> <note>A "regalian right" (regalia) refers to a royal or sovereign monopoly, such as the right to mint coins or control the post.</note> of His Majesty and the Holy Roman Empire, and concerns its faithful Electors and matters of the highest importance."** Reinkingk, *On Secular and Ecclesiastical Government, book 1, class 5, chapter 6, number 114.*

In the year 1579, the Emperor severely prohibited a certain Prince of Germany who was attempting to establish general posts through Belgium and Italy, in defense of this right reserved for his Majesty. Arnold Clapmar, *On the Secrets of State, book 1, chapter 21, near the end*; Thomas Michael, *On Jurisdiction, conclusion 12, letter B*; and Arnisaeus, *On the Right of Majesty, book 3, chapter 5, page 549.* Although other Princes may have posts and couriers in their own territories, they are considered private individuals in comparison to the Imperial post. Reinkingk, *in the same location cited above.*

Furthermore, the Majesty bestows public rewards and benefits, and confers honors, **Nobility**, and dignities. Bornitius, *On Majesty, chapter 20,* and also in his *Treatise on Rewards, chapter 3*; Camman, *Discourse 5, thesis 7.* This includes the condition that a person may be admitted to colleges where access is otherwise granted only to those born of noble blood.

# Political-Legal Dissertation

Peter Frizius, in Arumaeus <note>Dominicus Arumaeus (1579–1637) was a German jurist who helped establish "Public Law" as an academic discipline.</note>, *discourse 16, thesis 20, folio 453, volume 1,* notes that these rights are granted so that they might appear in tournaments. Vischer, in *On the Duel, folio 463,* adds: (or that they may dispense justice alongside knights, a privilege held by the citizens of Speyer <note>original: "Spitenfes" (Spiers/Speyer). This refers to the "Rechtsprechung," the right to sit in judgment.</note>. Lehman, *book 7, chapter 21, folio 759, and in the same book, chapter 41, folio 787.*) This **Royal Prerogative** <note>term: *Regale* (plural *Regalia*). These are the "Crown Rights" or specific powers and privileges that belong exclusively to a sovereign ruler.</note> was given by Emperor Charles V to his Vicar, King Ferdinand. Goldast, *in the Imperial Constitutions, folio 251.*

Just as it is a mark of majesty to decree legal punishments against offenders, so too is it considered a mark of the same majesty to bestow public rewards and benefits upon the good. Majesty, placed at the highest summit, is the fountain of all dignities: from which honors, titles, and every kind of preeminence are derived, and are communicated to the worthy like rays from the Sun. For **ennoblement** <note>original: *nobilitatio*</note> ought to rely on sound reason, unless we wish to expose this most eminent royal prerogative to contempt. Kirchner, *disputation on the republic 2, corollary 5.*

Hence, even if virtue itself may ennoble a person, and the preeminence of virtue descends from the Divine Will rather than human whim: nevertheless, unless a title is conferred upon someone by the vigor of this royal dignity, "natural nobility" is usually of little practical use. Obrecht, *disputation on the regal rights, thesis 124, etc.* In the same way, a Doctor requires not only learning but also the formal degree. Therefore, that opinion can hardly hold its ground which boasts only of those as "Nobles" who can count their waxen, smoke-stained ancestral images <note>A reference to the Roman *jus imaginum*, where noble families displayed wax masks of ancestors in their halls. "Smoke-stained" implies great antiquity.</note> and sixteen noble ancestors. Nature is not so exhausted that she cannot produce equals today to those who were once the heads of noble lineages. It has been a solemn custom for rulers at all times to substitute others in place of a failing or even a degenerating nobility. *Genesis 41, verse 39, etc.* And God Himself raises the poor from the dung-heap to place them among Princes. *Psalm 113, verse 7 and following.*

It is memorable what Aventinus <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a Bavarian Renaissance humanist and historian.</note> relates in *Annals of Bavaria, book 4,* as do Heinrich Mutius in *German Affairs, book 8,* and Lehman, *book 3, chapter 30.* They tell of **Charlemagne** <note>original: *Carolo M.* (Carolus Magnus)</note>. When he had entered the school he founded in Paris <note>original: *Lutetia*</note> and ordered the students to undergo a test of their studies, he discovered that the poorer and low-born students had progressed beyond all hope, while the Nobles had neglected the cultivation of their minds. Setting the former on his right hand, he said: "Well done in your virtue, my most pious sons, for you have diligently carried out our command. The greatest Bishoprics shall be yours; I shall receive you into my court; from among you I shall choose Senators; I shall enroll you in the register of Judges and Fathers of the Curia," etc. See Matthias Stephani, *treatise on Nobility, chapter 4.*

In ancient times, certainly, those born noble were held in less esteem than those who either increased their nobility or had just newly acquired it. The latter were called **Knights** <note>original: *Equites*</note>, while the former were called **Squires** <note>original: *Edelknecht* (German) / *Escuyers* (French) / *Scutarii* (Latin). These were "shield-bearers" who had the rank of nobility but had not yet attained knighthood.</note>; as if they were those who bore the coat of arms representing the fame of their lineage, and for that reason had no need of a formal girding or creation. Smith, *on the English Republic, chapter 19.* <note>Sir Thomas Smith (1513–1577), an English scholar and diplomat.</note>

II. To this belongs the right of granting the **Equestrian Order** of Nobles. Jehan Papon. <note>A 16th-century French jurist.</note>

### On the Rights of Majesty

Papon <note>Jean Papon (1505–1590) was a renowned French jurist known for his collections of legal decisions.</note>, *book 5 of the Judgments, title 4, on nobility, judgments 1 & 2.* Likewise, the **Right of the Golden Rings** <note>original: *Jus aureorum annulorum*. In Roman law, this was a privilege that granted the wearer the status of a knight.</note>: which only Princes used to bestow. *See the whole title of the Digest and Code on the Right of Golden Rings.* In its place today, they say, has succeeded the practice where the Prince is accustomed to grant **coats of arms** <note>original: *insignia*</note>, not only to individual families, but also those that become the property of Republics. Bartolus, *treatise on insignia and arms.* Others say that to grant the "right of rings" is effectively the same as what we call "dubbing a knight" <note>original: *Zu Ritter schlagen*</note>. Piso Soacius, *treatise comparing Venetian and Roman magistrates, number 39.* This is a dignity which all the great men of old, even Kings, aspired to. Lehman, *book 5, chapter 66.* Indeed, concerning the right of conferring nobility and similar dignities, just as all those who **recognize no superior** <note>original: *superiorem non recognoscentes*. This refers to sovereign rulers who are not vassals to anyone else.</note> undoubtedly enjoy this power, so too are their Nobles considered valid throughout the entire world. Vischer, *on the Duel, folio 462.* Thus, the **Estates of the Roman Empire** <note>The various territories and princes within the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, unless by a singular privilege, do not seem to be able to create nobles who would be regarded as such outside of their own territory. Peter Frizius, in Arumaeus, *discourse 16, thesis 4, and several following.* Anton Bullaeus, my friend, *Academic discourse 4.* Calefatus, *on knightly dignity, number 70, etc.*

III. It also pertains to the highest majesty to grant **Academic Authority** <note>original: *literariam majestatem*, literally "literary majesty."</note>. Hence follows the right of creating Doctors and Licentiates in all the higher faculties. Bachov, in Treutler, *disputation 1, folio 28.* Likewise, the naming of Masters of Arts must be ascribed to majesty. Indeed, even today the custom holds that it is not **Apollo** <note>original: *Phoebus*</note>, but the Emperor who creates **Poets** <note>original: *Vates*</note>, a fact which Justus Lipsius <note>A famous Flemish humanist scholar (1547–1606).</note> finds ridiculous. *In the Menippean Satire, on the Coronation of Poets*, see Piccart, *oration 11.* And that poets were already distinguished by the **Laurel** <note>original: *Lauro*</note> in ancient times is recorded by Paschal, *on crowns, book 5, chapters 12 & 14.* And so **Petrarch** <note>The famous Italian Renaissance poet.</note> was crowned with the Laurel, see Torsellino, *in the epitome of history, book 9, page 314.* And the first in Germany was **Celtes** <note>Conrad Celtes (1459–1508), the first German "Poet Laureate."</note>, by the hands of Emperor Frederick III. Adam, *in the Life, folio 30.* Furthermore, the **founding of Universities** <note>original: *erectio Academiarum*</note> is a right of majesty, Vultejus, *on fiefs, book 1, chapter 5, number 7,* and does not belong to an inferior. Moditius, *section "Plebeiscitum," question 78.* Lutheran writers note that the **Popes** <note>original: *Pontifices*</note> incorrectly claim this right for themselves: Kirchner, *disputation 2, corollary 4;* Christoph Matthias, *Political College 2, disputation 2, thesis 24.* Creating **Bachelors** <note>original: *Baccalaureos*</note> is not a royal prerogative, as I have said *in the treatise on Universities.* Hence, in our own University, the power of decorating candidates with that first "berry of the laurel" <note>A wordplay on the etymology of *Baccalaureus*: *bacca* (berry) and *laurus* (laurel).</note> is not sought from the Chancellor. I wish to add here the privileges and the founding of the **University of Tübingen**, as they existed in the Laubmaier library—a record that I hope will not be unpleasing to readers.

Just as it belongs to the sovereign power to decree legal punishments against wrongdoers, so too is it considered part of that same power to bestow rewards and public benefits upon the good. Majesty, situated at the highest pinnacle, is the source of all dignities. He discovered that the commoners and the poor had advanced beyond all expectation, while the Nobles had neglected the cultivation of their minds. See Matthias Stephani, *treatise on Nobility, chapter 4.* 

Indeed, in former times, those who were merely born Noble were held in lower esteem than those who had either increased their nobility or acquired it for the first time through merit. The latter were called **Knights** <note>original: *Equites*</note>, while the former were called **Noble Servants** <note>original German: *Edelknecht*; French: *Escuyers*; Latin: *Scutarii* or squires</note>. Smith, *on the Commonwealth of England, chapter 19.*

# THE ERECTION OF THE UNIVERSITY
### of the Tübingen Academy, 1476.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring floral and foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>IN the Name of the Lord, Amen. Heinrich, by divine permission Abbot of the Monastery in Blaubeuren; of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the Diocese of Constance, Executor and Commissioner for the matters written below, [appointed] by the Holy Apostolic See, together with certain colleagues of ours in this region: with the clause [stating]: "To the extent that you, or two or one of you, are specifically deputed in the subjoined Apostolic letters." Know that we have received, with the reverence that is due, the letters of the most Holy Father in Christ and our Lord, Lord Sixtus IV, by divine providence Pope; these were sealed with his **leaden seal** <note>original: "Bulla plumbea." A lead seal used to authenticate Papal documents, from which the term "Papal Bull" is derived.</note> hanging from hempen strings, after the custom of the Roman Curia; the letters were not erased, cancelled, or abolished, nor suspect in any part, but sound, whole, and unharmed, and entirely free from any flaw or suspicion. These were presented to us some time ago on behalf of the Illustrious and Noble Lord, Lord Eberhard: Count of Württemberg and Montbéliard, the Elder, who is the principal person named in the letters; they contain the following text, word for word:

SIXTUS, Bishop, Servant of the Servants of God, to our beloved sons, the Abbot in Blaubeuren and [the Provosts] of Saint Martin in Sindelfingen—monasteries usually governed by a Provost—and the Church in Herrenberg, Provosts of the Diocese of Constance: Greetings and Apostolic blessing. The Lord, abundant in mercy and glorious in all His works, from whom all gifts flow down to us—although He willed to commit the government of His spouse, the universal Church, to our insufficient merits and to impose the yoke of Apostolic service upon our weakness—so that, as if turning our gaze from the highest peak of the mountain to the lowest parts, we may look more attentively upon what contributes to the propagation of the orthodox faith for the enlightenment of this Church. We look to what suits the status of all the faithful, and we attend more skillfully to how the darkness of ignorance may be put to flight from those faithful; they ought to dwell by the gift of wisdom in the way of the commandments and the house of the Lord. We more readily stir them, by the help of our concern and Apostolic favors, to seek the **study of letters** <note>original: "literarum studia," referring to academic and university education.</note>, through which the Commonwealth of the **Church Militant** <note>original: "militantis Ecclesiæ." A theological term for the Christian Church on earth, which "struggles" against sin and ignorance, as opposed to the Church Triumphant in heaven.</note> is conducted, the worship of the Divine name and the faith is extended, and every condition of human prosperity is increased. ...indeed, a petition recently presented to us on behalf of our beloved son, the noble man Eberhard, Count in Württemberg and Montbéliard, contained the following: That in the cities, towns, and places subject to his temporal lordship, and also to that of our beloved son, the noble man Ulrich, also Count in Württemberg and Montbéliard—territories which are vast and wide, and abound in a multitude of inhabitants and a wealth of produce—there is no <term>University of General Study</term><note>original: "universitas studii generalis." The medieval technical term for a recognized university authorized to grant degrees.</note> to which the inhabitants of these cities, lands, towns, and places, and those of other neighboring areas, who wish to advance in the sciences, might conveniently go to study and learn.

Furthermore, [the petition stated] that if in the town of Tübingen, in the Diocese of Constance, in the Province of Mainz—a distinguished place full of suitable dwellings, where there is a very great abundance of all foodstuffs, and which is subject to his temporal lordship—there were to be established a University of General Study for every faculty and science, no such university presently exists within <note>original: "infra duas dietas vulgares." A "diet" was a standard measure of a day's travel, roughly 20-30 miles.</note>two common days' journey. For the easier support of the burdens and expenses of this same University once established, and especially for the salaries of those who will, for the time being, hold the <term>Chairs</term><note>original: "Cathedras." Formal professorships or teaching positions.</note> there, the following should be perpetually united, annexed, and incorporated: the parish churches of Saint John the Baptist in Brackenheim, and Saints Philip and James in Stetten, as well as those in Asch, Ringingen, and Eningen, in the Dioceses of Worms and the aforementioned Constance. These churches are known to be under the <term>Right of Patronage</term><note>original: "jure Patronatus." The legal right of a layman (in this case, the Count) to nominate a priest to a church office.</note> of the currently reigning Count of Württemberg. 

A suitable portion [of the income] would be reserved for the <term>perpetual vicars</term><note>The local priests who actually performed the ministry in the parishes, as opposed to the university professors who would receive the main income.</note> to be instituted at the presentation of the said University. Furthermore, in the Church of Saint Martin in Sindelfingen, in the said Diocese of Constance—which we recently ordered to be transformed into a Collegiate Church, transferring its primary dignity of the Provostship and eight <term>canonries and prebends</term><note>Income-generating offices within a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> to the parish church of Saint George in the said town of Tübingen, thereby making Saint George's a Collegiate Church, while the aforementioned Church of Saint Martin was ordered to be established as a monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine—two canonries and their prebends, after they have been established, should be suppressed and extinguished. Their fruits, rents, and revenues should be applied and assigned in equal portions as an endowment for four other canonries and prebends to be newly established there. 

It should also be established and ordained by us that for these ten canonries and prebends, which are under the said right of patronage, when they first happen to become vacant and successively in all future times, fit and learned ecclesiastical men shall be appointed to rule ten Chairs in the same University to be established; namely, four masters of arts, for whom the said four newly established [offices]...

Furthermore, we decree it now to be null and void if anyone, by any authority, knowingly or unknowingly, should attempt to act contrary to these provisions. 

Given at **Rome** at **St. Peter’s**, in the year of the Lord's Incarnation **1476**, on the **Ides of November** <note>November 13th</note>, in the sixth year of our Pontificate.

We were formally requested by Count Eberhard—who is primarily named in these documents as the petitioner—to deign to proceed with the proper execution of the instructions and the contents committed to us, following the specific procedure established for us in those same documents.

We, **Abbot Henry**, acting as the aforementioned executor and commissary, wish to reverently obey the mandates of our superiors (and most especially the **Apostolic mandates** <note>original: "Apostolicis mandatis," referring to the orders of the Pope</note>) as we are bound. Wishing to proceed cautiously and correctly in the execution of the business committed to us, and so that we might not seem to prejudice the rights of anyone who has—or claims to have—a legal interest in this matter, we issued a summons through these, our present letters. We cited and called all and singular persons of whatever dignity, rank, status, or preeminence, whether they might consider their interests affected collectively or individually, to appear before us at the place designated for this purpose. 

The purpose was for them to see and hear us become diligently informed regarding the facts exposed, narrated, and contained in the said **Apostolic letters** and every circumstance surrounding them. Once this information was received and the truth of the narrative was found to be sufficient, we intended to proceed properly to the execution of the Apostolic commission according to the form given to us. This was also an opportunity for any parties to speak or allege anything they might reasonably wish to propose or argue to the contrary in the places deemed appropriate. 

We set a specific, competent, and <term>peremptory deadline</term> <note>original: "terminum competentem peremptorium"; a final legal deadline after which no further arguments or delays are permitted</note>, with the formal notification that if they, or any other legitimate opponent or objector, did not appear—or if they appeared but offered no reasonable argument against the proceedings—we would nonetheless proceed without hesitation to the due execution of the business committed to us (observing all necessary legal forms), notwithstanding the absence or <term>contumacy</term> <note>original: "contumacia"; a legal term for a willful failure to appear in court or follow a summons</note> of those cited. 

At that deadline, the summons itself having been rightly and legitimately executed (with the record of that execution noted in order on the back of the document), and the summons being physically presented to us on behalf of the mentioned **Lord Count Eberhard**, and the failure of the cited parties to appear having been formally charged as contumacy, we deservedly—as was our duty—reputed them to be in contumacy, as no other legitimate objector or opponent appeared at all. 

Furthermore, we were requested with due urgency to proceed further with the execution of this commission according to its full force, form, and intent. Therefore, as the judge and commissary frequently mentioned, acting by virtue of the aforementioned clause regarding the truth of the facts stated in the inserted Apostolic letters, and having conducted our own diligent inquiry into these matters, and being sufficiently informed and taught by the testimony of trustworthy witnesses, we deemed it necessary to proceed to the execution and fulfillment of these duties committed to us. ...by our pronouncement, decree, and declaration, with the counsel and assent of legal experts, we have concluded in writing in the following manner:

**HAVING INVOKED THE NAME OF CHRIST.** Because we have seen and diligently weighed the matters brought before us in the present business regarding the facts narrated in the Apostolic commission inserted above, we have found the truth to be beyond doubt. Finally, for the easier support of the University's burdens and expenses—especially the salaries of those who hold the teaching chairs there—we unite, annex, and incorporate in the name of God the parish churches of St. John the Baptist in Brackenheim; Saints Philip and James in Stetten (in the Diocese of Worms); and those in Asch, Ringingen, and Eningen (in the Diocese of Constance), with all their rights and belongings, to the aforementioned University thus established in **Tübingen**. This is done with the consent of those concerned and by the authority of these present documents. 

We perpetually approve the fruits, rents, and revenues of each and all of these for the mentioned University and those governing and lecturing within it, decreeing by these presents: That upon the retirement or death of the Rectors of these parish churches, or their vacating of those churches in any other way, it shall be lawful from then on for the University itself—either by its own hand or through its agents—to freely take physical possession of the parish churches and their rights by its own authority. They may convert the revenues <note>original: "fructus, redditus & proventus," literally 'fruits, rents, and profits'</note> of these parish churches to the use and benefit of the University and retain them forever, without needing further permission from the local Bishop <note>original: "Diœcesani loci"</note> or anyone else.

By Apostolic authority, we assign to the perpetual Vicars <term>Perpetual Vicar: a priest appointed to perform the actual work of a parish when its primary income has been redirected (incorporated) to an institution like a university</term> of the said churches a sufficient portion from which they can support themselves, pay the Episcopal dues, and comfortably manage the other responsibilities required of them by that church...

...and it may continue. Regarding the eight canonries <term>canonries: administrative positions in a collegiate church held by a "canon"</term> and prebends <term>prebends: the portion of church revenues granted to a canon as a stipend</term> which we previously transferred by the stated authority from the Church of St. Martin in **Sindelfingen** to the parish church of **St. George** in the aforementioned town of **Tübingen**: two of these canonries and an equal number of prebends in the same parish church are to be suppressed and extinguished. We hereby suppress and extinguish them—both for the present and for any future time—whenever they happen to become vacant.

From these, we establish anew four other canonries and four prebends. For the endowment <note>original: "dote"</note> of these newly established positions, we apply and assign the fruits, rents, and revenues of the suppressed canonries and prebends in equal portions. This is so that whenever these canonries and prebends fall vacant in all future times—specifically the four newly established ones—four Masters of Arts <note>original: "Magistri in artibus," scholars who have completed the basic university curriculum</note> who are actively lecturing and presiding in those same arts shall be appointed. 

Regarding the other six aforementioned canonries and prebends, other learned and suitable clergymen—meant to preside over ten of these chairs <note>original: "cathedras," referring to the professor's seats of teaching</note> in the same university—are to be presented by the illustrious Lady **Mechthild, Archduchess of Austria**, etc., by virtue of her dowry <note>As a widow, Mechthild held significant lands and legal rights in the region which she used to fund the university</note> for as long as she lives, and thereafter forever by the said **Lord Count in Württemberg** and his successors through the aforementioned right of patronage <term>right of patronage: the legal right of a founder or donor to nominate a candidate for a church office</term>. Upon such presentation, they are to be installed as canons of the said church; once installed, they shall be bound and obligated to preside over the chairs themselves.

Furthermore, those holding these canonries and prebends and actively presiding over chairs in the university shall not be required—for as long as they preside over those chairs—to attend the divine services in the said Church of **St. George** (where twelve perpetual vicars have been appointed to celebrate and attend to the divine offices there). They are only required to attend to the extent that the canons of the Church of the **Holy Spirit** in **Heidelberg** (in the Diocese of **Worms**), who preside over chairs at the University of **Heidelberg**, are bound to attend. 

Without being required to be present or assisting in the divine services at the said Church of St. George, they may and should receive the fruits, rents, and revenues of their canonries and prebends. This includes even the first three years, during which—according to the sworn statutes of the church in **Sindelfingen**—new canons do not normally receive these funds (as they would instead go partly to the deceased canon’s estate and partly to the building fund <note>original: "Fabricae," the fund for the maintenance of the church building</note>). They shall receive these with full integrity, with the sole exception of the daily distributions <term>daily distributions: small additional payments given only to those church officials physically present at the daily prayer services</term>. They shall receive these just as they would if they were present for the divine services in the Church of St. George. Nor shall they be otherwise bound to attend the services in the said church, nor can they be forced to do so against their will, except as we grant by the same authority according to the practice of the Church of the Holy Spirit in **Heidelberg**. # ON THE RIGHTS OF MAJESTY.
### [The Imperial Privilege, continued]

...so that those striving in that wrestling-ground <note>original: "palaestra," a Greek term for a wrestling school, used here metaphorically for a place of rigorous study</note> of learning might be awarded worthy rewards for their labors, with the authorization of our Most Holy Lord, Pope Sixtus IV. We, therefore, considering the institution of the aforementioned Count [Eberhard] to be useful and fruitful not only for his own people but for all the faithful of the Holy Empire, and desiring to illuminate the aforementioned schools with various documents of learning, so that the multitude of students flocking there may rejoice in being more abundantly enriched: from the munificence of our liberality and the fullness of Imperial authority and power, out of certain knowledge, and with the sound counsel of the Princes, Barons, Nobles, and our faithful subjects, we more graciously grant anew to the said Count and his heirs and successors by the tenor of these presents, that from now and hereafter for all future times, they may cause all and singular Imperial laws, constitutions, and any other rights, wherever and by whomsoever enacted or promulgated, to which our predecessors of sacred memory, the Roman Emperors, gave right and authority, to be publicly read and practiced in their aforementioned schools by suitable persons; and they may cause the students of these laws to be elevated to worthy honors and degrees within the same. 

Decreeing and willing by this imperial edict that whoever they may be, of whatever status, rank, preeminence, nation, or language, provided that [no legal obstacle] stands in the way, who flock to the aforementioned place, they may be able to teach and hear the said Imperial laws, and be promoted and elevated to the usual and accustomed degrees in them. Furthermore, they shall be able to use, enjoy, and benefit from all and singular titles, dignities, preeminences, honors, prerogatives, and any other Rights and immunities, just as the rest of the doctors and scholars of Imperial laws throughout other schools located anywhere in the Holy Roman Empire enjoy and use by right or custom, notwithstanding any things to the contrary, which we expressly wish to be repealed by these presents. 

Therefore, let no man at all be permitted to infringe upon this page of our grant, decree, will, and repeal, or to go against it in any way with rash daring. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know he will incur our most grave indignation and a penalty of one hundred pounds of pure gold—one half of which we wish to be applied to our Imperial treasury, and the other half to the use of those who suffered the injury—without hope of pardon. [This is confirmed] by the testimony of these Letters with the hanging of our Imperial Majesty’s seal. Given in our town of Graz, the 20th day of the month of February, in the year 1484. In the forty-fourth year of our Roman reign, the thirty-second of our Empire, and the twenty-fifth of Hungary.

-> # A Politico-Legal Dissertation <-

...by a special <note>The word "li" completes "speciali" from the previous page.</note> Imperial Privilege, the Counts of the Sacred Palace <note>original: "Comites sacri Palatii"</note> now also possess this right. See Paurmeister, *On Jurisdiction*, Book 2, penultimate chapter, number 19. (And Otto IV gave this right to the Bishop of Speyer; see Lehman, Book 5, chapter 78.) From this, it is clear that even the creation of Counts Palatine belongs to the rights of majesty. See Lancellotti, *The Temple of Justice*, Book 1, chapter 1, section 4, page 364; on which also see Reinkingk, Class 1, chapter 4, chapter 13; Arumæus, volume 3, discourse 3. Princes and other Estates of the Empire also seem to enjoy the right of creating Notaries. Just as in the Duchy of Württemberg, the <term>town clerks</term> <note>original: "die Stattschreiber"</note> are equated to Notaries by Ducal constitution. However, there exists this difference between the former and the latter: the former [Imperial Notaries] may exercise their office everywhere, while the latter can only do so within the territory of the one who appointed them. See Gail, *Observations*, Book 2, observation 71, number 13; Matthias Stephani, *On Jurisdiction*, Book 2, part 2, chapter 5, number 7, etc. Nevertheless, the legal instruments they have drawn up within their own territory are also valid elsewhere. See Reiger, in the *Thesaurus of Law*, under the word "Notary." The Emperor directly explains what the office of the <term>Scribes</term> <note>original: "Tabellionum," a Roman term for public scriveners who drafted legal documents</note> was in former times in *Novel 44*. They were certainly like public servants, and they made stipulations on behalf of anyone. Finally, Pasquier notes how a Notary differs from a Scribe in *Researches*, Book 4, chapter 12. Tuschus advises that Bishops can also create Notaries in letter T, conclusion 290.

V. Furthermore, since the use of money (for the definition of which see Freher, *Parerga*, Book 1, chapter 14) or coinage is extremely necessary, a Republic cannot easily survive without it (Aristotle, *Politics*, Book 1, chapter 6). Rightly, therefore, the right of coinage is placed among the greater <term>Regalia</term> <note>Sovereign rights or prerogatives that belong exclusively to the ruler</note>. See Marcellus Donatus in his *Explanations*, page 1042; Bulenger, *On the Roman Princes*, Book 2, chapter 16; Bornitius, *Treatise on Coins*, throughout; Hoennon, *Political Disputations*, 5, thesis 78 and following; Arumæus, *On the Golden Bull*, 5, thesis 9. See especially Louis Servin, volume 3 of *Pleadings*, page 307; Camman, 6, thesis 12; Lehman, Book 2, chapter 39, page 158. This right applies whether the money is to be minted, changed, or entirely rejected, or whether a certain valuation and value must be established for it (Law 1, at the beginning, *On the contract of sale*). See Sixtin, *On the Regalia*, Book 2, chapter 7; Marquard Freher, *On Matters of Money*, Book 1, chapter 2; Covarruvias, *On the Comparison of Ancient Coins*, chapter 7; my colleague Master Bocerus, *On the Right of Money*, chapter 3; Busius, *Disputations on the Republic*, 11, thesis 1; Carpzov, *On the Capitulations*, chapter 8, number 13. Hence, there was a very ancient sanction in the Law of the Twelve Tables: "Let the Mint Masters <note>original: "Triumviri Monetales"</note> publicly stamp gold, silver, and bronze." See Freher in the cited place, chapter 3, number 1. And the Franks of old, when they first occupied the Gauls, seized this sign of supreme Majesty: to mint coins stamped with the image of their Kings. See Isaac Pontanus, *Frankish Origins*, Book 6, chapter 7, near the end. This was also done by the Macedonian Kings, whence their coins were named "Philippics" from the image of Philip impressed upon them. See Robbigius, Book 10, chapter 6. Numa is said to have been the first to strike money, according to Pliny, Book 33, chapter 3, and Canterus, *Various Readings*, Book 2, chapter 23. But it was already in use among the Hebrews before that; see the treatise by my dear Schickhard, *On the Coins of the Hebrews*. Roman— <note>The text cuts off here, continuing to discuss Roman coinage on the next page.</note>

-> # On the Rights of Majesty <-

...the Romans certainly managed their Coinage with the greatest diligence. <note>original: "Romani"</note> Adolph Occo, *in the preface to Roman Numismatics.* The Romans took such great care of it that ancient history can be reconstructed from their coins. See Melchior Adam, *in the Life of Hubert Goltzius.* <note>Goltzius was a famous 16th-century printer and student of ancient coins.</note>

VI. Furthermore, only the Emperor can determine the quality of Money—that is, establish how much gold, silver, iron, or other metal should be mixed in. (Hence, silver diluted in this manner is called "Royal." <note>original: "Regium"</note> François Baudouin, *on Constantine, book 2, page 123, etc.*). Similarly, the Emperor alone can give Laws concerning the proportion of Gold and Silver. *Single law, Code on the price of silver.* Baudouin, *in the stated place, page 117*; add Alemanus, *Palestra of Consultations, consultation 8, page 492.* From the fact that the right of Coinage belongs to Majesty, the learned Dr. Bocerus, *on Regalia, 2, number 224,* quite aptly deduces the meaning of the word "money" <note>The Latin "moneta" (money/mint) is here linked to the verb "monere" (to warn or remind).</note>: that the image or face of the Prince stamped upon the coin reminds the Subjects that they are subject to that Prince whose image the money bears. *Ref. Matthew, chapter 22, regarding the Tribute Money.* Coins are signs of the highest obedience; they are a summary of statues; or rather, they are "walking statues." Piscillius, *in Images of Princes, color 6, page 82, etc.* Therefore, it belongs to the same person who commands the Laws to prescribe the price, weight, and shape of Coins. For the Greek word *nomos* <note>original: νόμος, meaning law or custom</note> seems to have given the origin to the word *Nummus* <note>meaning a coin or piece of currency.</note>

VII. All the wisest men judge thus: that an unusual change and corruption of Coinage in the present age is a sign of great upheavals in the Republic; especially since Money ought to be the measure by which all things are measured. And truly, I know not which state of the Empire caused a coin to be struck with the inscription: *Money for the recent time* <note>original: "Moneta pro tempore nuper"; this refers to "emergency money" or debased currency issued during times of crisis.</note>. It noted that our age is so wicked that the coin lacked all honest material.

> *And since the ages are bad, the money is bad:*
> *If the times are bad, it is necessary that the money also be bad.*

And there is a very old German Proverb: **As the money, so also is the world.** <note>original: "Wie das Gelt / also ist auch die Welt."</note> Lucas Lossius says it best, *in Lüneburg, page 36:*

> *Seeing the sins of the falling world daily worsening,*
> *He offered this among many sayings:*
> **By the coin one shall learn /**
> **How the world turns itself upside down.** <note>original: "Bey der Münz soll man lehren / Wie sich die Welt thuet verkehren."</note>
> *One learns from coins how badly the times change:*
> *How all things rush into worse decay.*
> *Once the coins were golden, and the age was golden,*
> *Now the coins become bad, a mass of copper.*
> *Now the age of men is copper, now the offspring is copper,*
> *Daily it shall become more wicked hereafter.*

> As Naso <note>The Roman poet Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), specifically referencing *Metamorphoses* 1.127-131.</note> recounted in his truthful song, being well-taught, 
> The final age was made of cruel iron. 
> Immediately, every wickedness broke into this age 
> Of a worse vein; shame, truth, and faith fled; 
> In their place entered deceits, frauds, 
> Snares, violence, and the wicked love of gain.

It was already a common practice in the past to provide for the benefit of the State by increasing the price of money <note>original: "pretium monetæ augendo." This refers to "debasement" or "revaluation," where the nominal value of a coin is raised while its precious metal content stays the same or decreases.</note>; which Solon also did. Plutarch, *in the Life [of Solon].* So too Philip of Valois <note>King Philip VI of France (reigned 1328–1350).</note> subtracted something from the weight of the money. Girard, *book 2, folio 185 and 201.* Even the Turks sometimes use this caution. Soranzo, *at folio 68.* Nevertheless, this remedy should not be used except in cases of extreme necessity, as I said in my *Treatise on the Treasury*; see Conestagio, *folio 44.* Furthermore, Bellonus disputes whether pure gold or one type of coin is more excellent than another, *book 1, observation chapter 50, etc.* If currencies are changed, infinite lawsuits arise, regarding which I have prepared several Legal Opinions (*Consilia*), printed at *Augsburg and Tübingen* by Eberhard Wildius. The French once feared these same disputes and therefore provided against them with a special agreement: <note>original: "Et si dedans le temps du rechapt..." This 14th-century French legal clause translates as: "And if within the time of redemption of this pledge, the money was deteriorated in weight or in alloy, we shall return for every thirty sous, one silver mark."</note> Paradin, *chapter 39 of the History of Lyon.*

VIII. From what has been deduced thus far, it appears that those who, having no right, or acting without any authority or permission from the Prince, mint money, are considered guilty of high treason. <note>original: "crimen majestatis."</note> *Law 2, Code on false money;* Dr. Bocer, *on the crime of majesty, 2, number 62, etc.* This holds even if the money is legitimate and of fair weight and value. Menochius, *Arbitrary Cases, case 316, number 15;* Obrecht, *Disputation on Regalia, thesis 245, etc.;* Camman, *6, thesis 42.* However, lower republics <note>Independent city-states or smaller territories within an empire.</note> may enjoy this royal right. Tileman Friese, *in the Mirror of Minting, book 1, chapter 4, and book 4, chapter 36;* Sixtin, *2, on Regalia, chapter 7, number 91, etc.* <note>original: "Also ist die Münz bey den Geschlechtern vor zeiten in den Stätten gewest."</note> Thus, in former times, the right of coinage was held by the [patrician] families in the cities. Lehman, *4, chapter 14.* Thus, already under Dagobert <note>A 7th-century Merovingian King of the Franks.</note>, Speyer and the Monastery of Weissenburg held the right of minting. Lehman, *3, chapter 12.* Whence Dr. Bocer says most correctly, *chapter 3 on the law of money, number 5,* that not only does the right of minting belong to the Emperor, but also the right of granting the faculty to mint money. See Busius, *political disputation 11, thesis 2 through 11.* Their coins must nevertheless be regarded above all as the money of the Majesty itself; so that one who counterfeits them falls equally into the crime of diminished majesty. Peter Wesenbeck, *legal opinion 45.* This holds especially in our Germany: where the coins, by law, mostly bear the Emperor’s name inscribed in a circle, and the double-headed eagle with the Imperial orb <term>Imperial orb (globus imperii): A symbol of world-wide power, often held by the eagle or the ruler on coins.</term> placed on its breast. *Imperial Recess, Year [15]59, section 10.* But also in Germany, the Estates of the Empire [have] the money of the Emperor himself...

<summary>This page discusses the sovereign right of coinage (the 'regalia' of minting), noting that while rulers sometimes manipulate currency weight or value in emergencies, unauthorized minting is a capital crime (treason). It highlights that in the Holy Roman Empire, even when local cities or lords are granted the right to mint, the coins remain symbols of the Emperor's supreme authority.</summary>

# On the Rights of Sovereignty #

[...of the Em]peror, as some have presumed to tax in the past. Lehmann, *book 4, chapter 22, folio 367.* <note>Christoph Lehmann (1568–1638) was a famous German chronicler of the city of Speyer.</note> The Romans were more cautious in this regard; they did not wish that right to be granted to private individuals. *Last law, Code of Justinian, on counterfeit money.* Deciani, *Criminal Practice, book 7, chapter 24, number 3.* Gigas, *Treatise on the Crime of Majesty, rubric: how and by whom, question 62.* They also did not permit foreign nations to mint coins. Chifletius, *on Vesontio, folio 206, etc.* Likewise, on some coins, a stamped mark of a hand denotes authority. Rittershusius, *on Asylums, folio 49.* Nevertheless, Sovereignty, which gains no small amount of splendor for itself from minting coins, is seen to be diminished if the striking of one's own coinage is granted everywhere. John Selden, *book 2 of the English Janus, number 41, folio 88.* <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a celebrated English jurist and polymath.</note> Regarding coinage, see the individual treatises by Budé, Chokier, Tilemann Friesen, Marquard Freher, Jean Bodin, and Reiner Budel. Also, see the disputations on this matter by Hanfmann and Aur, *held at Basel*; and by Meurer, *held at Jena*. Camerarius also treats this matter in his *Treatise on Horsemanship, at the end.* Ayrault, *on Adjudicated Matters, folio 602.* The Statutes of Poland, *section "Money."* Balduinus, *on Constantine the Great, folio 117, etc.* And thus also <note>original: "einen Wechsel anstellen"</note> **establishing a money-exchange** pertains to the right of majesty. Papon, *book 5, title 1, arrest 8.*

**IX.** Closely related to the right of coinage is the right of measures, weights, and ulnas <note>An "ulna" (ell) was a traditional unit of length often based on the length of a man's arm.</note>. Knichen likewise counts this among the royal rights and asserts it is public property, *4, on the law of territories, number 232, etc., through law 9, Code of Justinian, on tax-collectors, book 10.* Borellus, *on Magistrates, book 3, chapter 15.* Scheplitz, *on the Brandenburg Constitutions, part 4, title 6.* Buchanan, *History, folio 338.* Hence the Hebrews call **Measure** *mesurah*, from the root *sur*, meaning "to hold a principality" or "rule"; because the measurement of things is the mistress of all, and the Prince of things to be divided. It is also called *Schaar*, a measure, because it was fixed to the gates. Avenarius, *Lexicon, on the word "Schaar."* Thus, a certain King in England punished the false ulnas of merchants by applying the measurement of his own arm and proposing it to everyone throughout England. Selden, *2, English Janus, folio 85, number 33.* Indeed, subjects are absolutely bound to take the form and weight of measures from the Sovereign’s Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the master standard kept by the ruler against which all other weights and measures were checked.</note>. Knichen, *stated chapter 4, number 237.* The Dutch, however—being more free than many others—resisted Charles V when he attempted to establish a single weight and measure for all trade of sellable goods throughout all the provinces of Lower Germany, as Meteren records somewhere. Thus, Christopher, Duke of Württemberg, used great prudence <note>original: "daß er das Meß vnd Gewicht/ in seinem ganzen Land gleich gemacht"</note> **when he made the measures and weights uniform throughout his entire land**; but the neighboring Imperial Cities did not want to consent to that ordinance—not only so that they might not seem like subjects, but also so that their markets might be more abundantly supplied with food.

**X.** In this same view, the right of establishing commerce belongs to sovereignty. Hence come formal and major Market-Fairs, called <note>original: "πανηγύρεις"</note> **panegyreis**, which are the more celebrated markets of a single Province or of the entire Empire (such as the Latin Festivals were in the Roman Republic; see Hospinian, *Treatise on Festivals, chapter 5, folio 45*)...

...today among us are the **Frankfurt Fairs**, etc., celebrated in a singular book by Henri Estienne <note>original: "ab Heinric. Stephano"; Henri Estienne (1528–1598) was a famous French printer and scholar who wrote a well-known praise of the Frankfurt book fair.</note>) are obtained only from the Emperor. *Single law, Code of Justinian, on Fairs; Law 1, Digest, on the same.* Camman, *6, thesis 4.* Börtius, in Arumæus, *discourse 30, chapter 5, thesis 26, folio 881.* And once granted, they cannot be transferred elsewhere without the consent of the Prince. Cravetta, *legal opinion 640.* Natta disagrees, however, in *legal opinions 511 and 512*, who is supported by Timannus à Kuyk in his *annotations to Cravetta's responses.* Relevant here is what the most distinguished and famous Lord Philipp Reinhard <note>Philipp Reinhard von Hanau-Münzenberg was a legal and political official.</note> writes in the *Counter-report of the County of Wertheim, chapter 13, at the end*, as follows: <note>The following passage was originally in German.</note> **In the same way, it belongs among the Royal Prerogatives—granted by the Roman Emperor through a special privilege—to establish annual fairs. Just as then, the late Emperor Maximilian II most graciously granted to the well-born Lord, Count Ludwig of Stolberg and Königstein, and also his descendants the Counts of Wertheim, in the year 1566, that they may hold, conduct, and use three markets annually in the city of Freudenberg.** 

Nevertheless, the Emperor has never been accustomed to give the privilege of fairs to anyone without first hearing from the adjacent and neighboring cities whose interests might be affected. Gail, *2, observation 69, numbers 24 and 25.* Georg Schönborner, *5, politics, chapter 12.* The Emperor can also take away the **Right of Fairs** <note>original: "Jus Nundinarum"</note> when the cause is clear. Thus, Charles IV took it away from the people of Frankfurt and transferred it to Mainz; however, after the death of Günther, he restored it to them through the intercession of Rudolf of the Palatinate and the Margrave of Brandenburg. Peucer, *book 5 of the Chronicles, page 805.* Arnisæus, *book 2, on the rights of majesty, chapter 3, number 18.* I believe the **staple right** <term>staple right: a medieval right where a city could require merchant travelers to offer their goods for sale for a set period before moving on</term> or the right of the marketplace, also belongs here. Mynsing, *legal opinion 19.* Sixtin, *2, on regalia, chapter 3, number 39, etc.* Klock, *on taxes, thesis 56.* Lehmann, *book 4, chapter 22, folio 363 and folio 366.* And certain fairs have this magnificent privilege: that no one can be arrested there. Berlich, *volume 1, conclusion 53.* And as to why they are called *Messen* <note>The German word for trade fairs, originally meaning "Masses," as fairs often coincided with religious festivals.</note>, Lord Gryphiander examines this in his *disputation on Democracy, thesis 76, etc.* Regarding annual fairs and their privileges, see also Marchantius, *on Flanders, book 1, folio 32, etc.* Regarding the fairs established at Lyon, see Paradin, *History of Lyon, book 1, chapter 9 and following*; regarding those at St. Denis, see Girard, *volume 1, folio 450.* The **proclamation of legal holidays** <note>original: "indictio Feriarum"; the scheduling of court recesses or public festivals</note> also pertains to this. *Law 26, section 7, Digest, on those causes...* Wesenbeck, *on the Digest title regarding holidays, number 4.* Ummius, *disputation on procedure 7, number 36.*

**XI.** The **right of giving the language** <note>original: "Jus etiam dandæ linguæ"</note> is also a right of majesty, and it seems to be part of the legislative power. Brunning, *disputation on Corporations, thesis 7.* And so the Romans, even in the provinces, did not deliver judgments except in Latin; later they also used Greek after the Empire was transferred there. Thus, the Latin language, which was used everywhere in the Chancelleries, was abolished by Emperor Rudolph I. <note>Rudolph I (reigned 1273–1291) was the first Habsburg king of Germany; he promoted the use of the German language in official legal documents over Latin.</note> Tschudi, *on Raetia, chapter 36.* Lehmann, *in the Speyer Chronicle, book 5, chapter 107.*

# On the Rights of Majesty.

...is granted to someone by either expressed or presumed will. As for the reasoning by which the ownership of **pure authority** <note>original: "merum imperium." In Roman law, this refers to the high power of the sword, including the right to inflict capital punishment.</note> or **mixed authority** <note>original: "mixtum imperium." This refers to lower judicial powers and the administration of civil justice.</note> is distinguished from power that is absolute from the laws, consult Joachim Stephan, *On Jurisdiction, chapter 4, number 32.* And finally, reader, observe that my explanation of the rights of the Empire is undertaken here only insofar as they belong to the majesty of the Ruler, and thus are required for the constitution of the head of the commonwealth. The treatment of those rights used in social interaction and other duties of the state is a different matter and does not belong here; see Busius, *On the Republic, book 3, chapter 2, from the beginning.* Although occasionally in this section, I have mixed in things that relate more to the preservation of the commonwealth than its initial constitution.

### CHAPTER IX.

## Concerning the granting and transfer of the rights of majesty.

**F**urthermore, the highest rights of the state, both ecclesiastical and political, are considered to be so properly characteristic of majesty that they are indivisible and can never be shared with anyone without a change in the state's status. Regnerus Sixtinus, *On Regalia, book 1, chapter 5, from the beginning;* and myself in *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 2, number 16.* If any subject should wish to claim these rights for themselves, they commit the **crime of high treason** <note>original: "crimen majestatis." This is a violation of the sovereign's dignity or power.</note> because they violate the public state. *Law 3, Digest on the Julian Law of Majesty; Law "Sacri Affatus," Code on Various Rescripts.* 

Likewise, they do not allow for **prescription** <note>The legal principle where a right is gained or lost by the passage of time. Here, the author argues you cannot "earn" sovereign rights just by using them for a long time without permission.</note> as long as the republic stands; see at length Gilkenius *on the Authentic "Quas Actiones," Code on Holy Churches, chapter 9.* For mortals do not prescribe against God, nor do private individuals against the commonwealth. Peter Heigius, *part 2, question 40, number 79;* Thomas Michael, *On Jurisdiction, thesis 24, at the end;* see also my work, *On Appeals, chapter 2, number 8, folio 42.* 

Nothing, however, prevents these rights—with the permission and consent of a superior—from being exercised by others in a granted portion of governance, or even being received as a **fief** <note>original: "Feudum." A grant of land or rights held in exchange for service and loyalty.</note>; this occurs with a lessening of majesty, according to Lord Doctor Bocerus, *Treatise on Investitures, chapter 3, number 97, etc.;* and Bornitius *On Majesty, chapter 14.* In this respect, **sovereign rights** <note>original: "regalia." These are the specific rights, such as coining money or collecting tolls, that belong to a monarch.</note> are seen to belong to someone either by their own right or by another's right. Only the Emperor and other "perfect" <note>Meaning fully independent and self-governing.</note> republics hold sovereign rights by their own right. Henning Arnisaeus, *Politics, chapter 11, folio 153.* Those who use them by the favor of another—whether by fief, by right of privilege, or some other title—are considered to hold them by another’s right; or they defend themselves by "immemorial" prescription. Cravetta, *Counsel 338.* 

Someone can even have the financial benefit of a sovereign right without holding any of the dignity of the office. Thus, in the old Roman Empire, the **tax farmers** <note>original: "Publicani." Private individuals who bid for the right to collect taxes.</note> did this, and today in Poland, the Jews purchase the rights to collect tolls. Just as it is permitted for me not only to appoint a manager for my property, but I can also establish a **long-term lease** <note>original: "ius emphyteuticum." A type of Roman law contract where someone uses land for a long duration, behaving like an owner but paying rent to the true owner.</note> for another person over that same property; while meanwhile keeping...

<summary>This page defines the "Rights of Majesty" as indivisible and eternal powers that cannot be usurped by private citizens without committing treason. It explains that while these rights strictly belong to the sovereign, they can be leased, granted as fiefs, or managed by others (like tax collectors) without the sovereign losing ultimate ownership.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the transferability of sovereign rights. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing the crime of treason (lèse-majesté) for those who usurp these rights. This page explores how these rights can be legally held by subjects without the Ruler losing ultimate sovereignty.</meta>

->**Political-Legal Dissertation**<-

...meanwhile <note>original: "interim." This continues the sentence from the previous page regarding the legal status of granted rights.</note>, the ownership remains with me, even though I may not be able to revoke that right. In this way, I would think that all **regalia** <note>original: "regalia." These are specific royal rights or privileges, such as the right to mint money, collect tolls, or exploit mines.</note>, both the "greater" and the "lesser" kinds, can be granted to others. See *above, section 3.* This is contrary to what Clapmar (in *The Secrets of Empires, book 1, chapter 21*) and Jehan Papon (in *Legal Decisions, book 5, title 1, number 1, page 238*) believe. I agree instead with Thomas Michael (*Disputation on Jurisdiction, thesis 24*) and Camman (*Disputation 1, thesis 93*). From this, a common saying has arisen among legal interpreters: **Dukes who possess regalia have the fullness of power <note>original: "plenitudinem potestatis." This refers to a high degree of autonomous authority.</note>, even if they acknowledge a superior.** (Ludovicus Rodolphinus, *On the Fullness of Power, chapter 2*).

And indeed, regalia granted to others still deserve to be called regalia, insofar as they proceed from the King alone; yet they cannot be called **rights of majesty** <note>original: "jura majestatis." This refers to the core essence of sovereignty that defines a supreme ruler.</note> unless they belong to someone by their own inherent right. Some even argue that rights of majesty can hardly be granted at all (Papon, *book 5, title 1, decision 1*). If regalia are shared by the **law of partnership** <note>original: "jure societatis."</note>, then the form of the republic is changed, and the state becomes "mixed." The **abdication of majesty** is another matter entirely; this is where a Prince loses all power in a specific territory or part of it. 

This point is also worthy of note: a Prince of Germany who claims regalia through **prescription** <note>original: "præscribens." In law, prescription is the acquisition of a right through long-continued use or custom rather than a formal written grant.</note> does not possess them as "majesty," but as perpetual privileges. Therefore, this hardly differs from an **investiture** <note>original: "investitura." The formal ceremony or legal act of handing over a fief or right from a lord to a vassal.</note>, except that the rights cannot return to the Emperor upon the holder's death. Thus, cities have "prescribed" regalia, but in essence and substance, they are no different from those held by investiture; they differ only in the manner of how they are acquired and how they might end. So, those in the **Roman Empire** <note>Referring here to the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation.</note> who claim regalia by prescription are not "free" (independent sovereigns) because of it; rather, they acquire only the **exercise** of those regalia rights through long usage. For them, prescription takes the place of a royal grant, and the **supreme superiority** <note>original: "summa superioritas." This is the ultimate legal authority of the Empire.</note> of the commonwealth remains intact. 

Therefore, to hold majesty by grace (that is, through privilege, investiture, or prescription) is not to hold majesty itself, but rather to have a certain **participation** in it—much as Bellarmine speaks in other terms (in *On Christ, book 3, chapter 15*). Prescription itself does not change this, because majesty is not something the "Estates" <note>original: "statibus." The princes, prelates, and imperial cities that held seats in the Imperial Diet.</note> can take for themselves absolutely; they only acquire the exercise of specific rights that others might hold through a formal gift or investiture.

### II.
Here we must note that common theory of the learned: in whatever manner the grant of regalia is made, that higher and majestic **Authority** <note>original: "Imperium."</note> is never considered to be included in that gift. Instead, it is always assumed that a greater power than what was granted has been reserved and retained by the sovereign. (See the chapter *Dudum*, section *Hoc igitur*, on prebends in the *Sext*; and the law *Inquisitio* in the Code on payments). Also see Peregrinus (*On the Law of the Treasury, book 1, last title, number 33*) and Knichen (*On the Law of Territory, chapter 1, number 315*). The Emperor grants regalia to the Estates "privatively" and through a contract, by which he promises he will not take them away from them; but he also bestows them "cumulatively," meaning he retains his rights of ownership and oversight. Various questions of great importance can be raised here, the study of which is both necessary and fruitful.

# On the Mixed State of the Republic
<page-num>209</page-num>

(1) If a territory is granted, should it be understood that the **regalia** <note>original: "regalia." These are specific royal rights or privileges, such as the right to mint money, collect tolls, or exploit mines.</note> are also granted? Wesenbec addresses this in *Legal Counsel 109*. Likewise, does a general grant of regalia include the "greater" rights <note>original: "majora." These are the most significant powers of a ruler, such as the power of life and death or declaring war, as opposed to "lesser" rights like fishing or forest rights.</note>? Borcholten defines this based on the status of the persons to whom they are granted in his commentary *on the one chapter of what constitutes Regalia, number 7*; see also Rosenthal, *On Feuds, chapter 5, conclusion 9*; Zal, *Epitome of Feuds, part 5, number 13*; and Reinking, *book 1, class 4, chapter 16, number 31, etc.* (2) Furthermore, if someone is invested with a Duchy or County along with a general grant of all regalia, they also obtain the greater ones. Arumaeus, *Feudal Disputation 4, thesis 22*. (3) However, I believe this should not be stated quite so simply: just because some specific regalia are granted, it does not follow that things similar to those expressed are also included. Peregrinus, *On the Law of the Treasury, book 6, regarding those who have treasury rights, number 100*; Rosenthal, *the said chapter 5, conclusion 13*. This holds true unless a general clause is added at the end. Zalius, *the said part 5, number 11*; Borcholten, *the said chapter, number 11, etc.* Valascus discusses whether a newly created Duke automatically obtains these regalia by that fact alone in *On Emphyteusis, question 8, number 22, etc.*

III. Thus, the Dukes, Cities, and other **Estates** <note>original: "status." These are the representative groups or territories that had a seat in the Imperial Diet, such as princes, counts, and imperial cities.</note> in the **Holy Roman Empire** <note>original: "Imperio Romano-Germanico."</note>—and in others as well—are subject to the Emperor and the Empire, not only regarding feudal jurisdiction but also in their own persons. They are bound not just by the name of the **fief** <note>original: "Feudi." A land holding granted by a lord in exchange for service.</note>, but by their personal obligation: Rosenthal, *On Feuds, chapter 5, conclusion 13*; Musculus, *On Succession, member 1, folio 14*; and myself in *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 2, number 20*. Indeed, they are considered **liege vassals** <note>original: "vassalli ligii." These are vassals who owe primary and supreme allegiance to their lord, in this case, the Emperor.</note> of the Empire. Knichen, *On Territorial Law, last chapter, from the beginning*. Even if they are invested with the most extensive legal clauses, and their power elsewhere is found to be very great—commonly referred to as **territorial sovereignty** <note>original: "**Lands Obrigkeit**." This German term refers to the high degree of legal and administrative control a prince had over his specific territory, though still theoretically under the Emperor.</note>—the explanation of this belongs to the treatment of subordinate states. I have already discussed this in a separate dissertation. Although Bernhard Zeritz (*Treatise on the Prerogatives of Princes, H, etc.*) says that the Princes of Germany possess **Majesty** <note>original: "majestatem." The supreme authority of a state.</note>, in practice they seem to enjoy the *use* and *effect* of majesty rather than majesty itself. The following axiom should be understood "with a grain of salt" <note>original: "cum mica salis." # A SINGULAR DISSERTATION
### ON THE
# MIXED STATE OF THE REPUBLIC.
### CHAPTER I.
### *Whether a Mixed Republic Exists.*

I rightly preface this treatise—where I simultaneously discuss the state of the Roman Empire and attach the weightiest questions—with that saying of Tiberius Decianus: <margin>*Compare book 8, number 169.*</margin> In grave matters, one who relies on the authority of some learned man is excused, even if he errs. It is an ancient (and in my judgment, true or probable) opinion that not every State of a Republic is "simple"; but that there exist certain tempered or mixed ones, composed of two or three types of government. For since supreme power—and the forms of Republics born from it—regularly descends from the full and free exercise of the rights of sovereignty: therefore, if the rights of supreme command and the marks of the greatest power (its insignias and functions, so to speak) are not all held by one alone; and if the King, or the People, or the Senate does not possess the power that is "released from the laws" <note>original: "legibus solutam." This refers to absolute power where the ruler is not legally bound by civil statutes.</note> in all respects, then a Mixed (and not uniform) state of the republic exists. This is supported by Niccolò Machiavelli, *Discourses, book 1, chapter 2*; Clapmarius, *On the Secrets of Republics, book 5, last chapter*; Vincent Cabotius, *Disputations, book 2, chapter 4*; Paul Busius, *On the Republic, book 2, chapter 6*; Bartholomaeus Keckerman, *Practical Disputations 36, problem 8*; Arnisaeus, *Political Doctrine, chapter 8*; Thomas Smith, *On the Republic of the English, book 1, chapter 6*; Clemens Timpler, *Politics, book 5, chapter 2, question 7*; Lord Joachim Cluten, *Paradox 14*; Velstenius, *A Century of Political Questions, decade 7, thesis 5*; and extensively and excellently by Pietro Andrea Canonhiero, *Introduction, book 6, chapter 3*. Neither Monarchy, nor Aristocracy, nor...

<header>Concerning the Rights of Sovereignty.</header>

...Kirchner maintains that no pure and unadulterated Democracy has ever existed anywhere without some tempering, nor can one be shown to exist today (*Disputation on the Republic 3, final corollary*). Paul Busius writes that this mixed form is preserved today in most kingdoms of Europe (*On the Republic, book 2, chapter 6*), since no Kings or Princes—whose power over the "heads of sovereignty" <note>original: "capitibus majestatis." This refers to the specific legal prerogatives that constitute sovereign power, such as the right to wage war or coin money.</note> is shared with the estates or a Senate—can be said to maintain a "pure" status. The Reverend Father Contzen feels the same (*Politics, book 1, chapter 14, section 3*). Likewise, in a popular State, the Senate almost always shares the highest power of the republic with the common people, etc. Waremund von Erenberg testifies that few or no Kings or Princes are found whose power is not greatly curtailed by specific capitulations <note>original: "capitulationibus certis." These were legal contracts, common in the Holy Roman Empire, where a ruler agreed to limits on their power in exchange for being elected.</note> (*On the Likelihood of Royal Subsidies, chapter 11, number 40*). For my part, I hardly dare to assert that any purely simple state exists. Indeed, in a Mixed State, the form of the republic will be said to have deflected from the rule of its own nature, yet it has not entirely cast it off; hence it generally follows the class and name of the part which is dominant. Lipsius (*Politics, book 2, chapter 2*). And not infrequently, one is called a Monarch and King who is nothing but the Prince of a mixed state. And so here likewise, as in a simple Polyarchic <note>A state ruled by many, such as an aristocracy or democracy.</note> state, sovereignty properly and in its entirety resides with that collective body which shares in the majesty. In the Prince, however, power is not absolute, but determined.

II. But just as many have fiercely denied that any state is mixed, so the few who affirm it seem to have touched upon the reality of the matter; but they have, in my opinion, wrongly confused the **right of government** with the **method of governing**. Therefore, two things must be avoided here. (1) The opinion of Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist who was a famous opponent of the idea of "mixed" sovereignty, arguing it must be indivisible.</note> is to be rejected, who denies that any state is mixed (*On the Republic, book 2, chapter 1*); he is supported by Zacharias Fridenreich (*Politics, chapters 18 & 29, folio 201*), Jacob Bornitius (*Treatise on Majesty, chapters 11 & 13*), and see Franzius in Arumæus (*volume 3, discourse 27*). (2) Here especially (as I also warned in my *Treatise on Monarchy, chapter 2*), care must be taken lest we confuse the **method of governing** with the **state itself**; and lest we take a Monarchy governed Aristocratically, for example, to be a Mixed State. Yet Lipsius (*Politics 2.2*), Kirchner (*Disputation on the Republic 3, thesis 7, letter e*), Keckermann (*Politics 2.4*), and others seem to do this, against whom Daniel Otto of Oehringen rises up in dispute in Arumæus (*volume 2, disputation 22, thesis 13 and following, up to 34*). And truly, if a republic were defined not by its legal right but by its method of government, then a Master embracing a slave with fatherly love would become a father—not merely in affection, but by law—which no one would easily suggest.

III. Many things seem to stand in the way of a mixture of republics. They say that two contraries cannot exist simultaneously in the highest degree; like water and fire, so are true monarchy and democracy. But nevertheless, nature permits this if something is yielded on both sides. Here we have a hateful and perennial enemy...
