# Political-Legal Dissertation

...we have Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist whose work "The Six Books of the Republic" defined sovereignty as absolute and indivisible.</note>, whose primary reasoning seems to be that sovereignty cannot be divided or pulled apart. I deny this presupposition. Indeed, while the form of a republic is preserved, sovereignty is not shared; but immediately a mixture of forms is created. Someone might object: once a republic is established, it is illegal to change it. I say that a republic can be established from the beginning in such a way that sovereignty is not absolutely entrusted to one person or a few. For power can pass from the people to a Prince either fully or conditionally, as Vasquius notes (*Illustrious Questions, chapter 47, number 9 and following*). Or even in the transformation of a republic, just as power is sometimes taken away entirely, nothing seems to prevent absolute power from being limited at times. Nor is it rare for a "balance" <note>original: "temperamentum"; in a political sense, a moderation or balancing of power.</note> to creep in, which is hardly ever perceived until after a transformation has occurred, as Bodin himself warns (*On the Republic, book 2, chapter 6*); and physicians observe the same thing in the human body. And elsewhere, Bodin recognizes the "Principate" <note>A system where a leader has primary status but shares power with other institutions, like a constitutional monarchy.</note> as a certain middle state between Aristocracy and Monarchy—namely, a certain mixed form. Daniel Ottho, in his aforementioned disputation (thesis 34 and many following), has set out to attack two people from the many who have broken away from Bodin: specifically Keckermann <note>Bartholomäus Keckermann (1572–1609), a leading German intellectual who argued that sovereignty could be shared.</note> and myself. I will now briefly examine his attacks. 

(1) He says it can never happen by nature, nor can it even be conceived in the imagination, that supreme power or sovereignty can be mixed with an inferior and yet remain supreme. I respond: it remains supreme, but not in one individual; rather, it resides in the entire body or college of **rulers** <term>ἀρχόντων (archontōn); Greek for "those who rule" or "magistrates."</term>. However, it is not distributed equally among them; a great eminence is granted to the Prince (even greater than what the Duke <note>Referring to the Doge of Venice, who held the highest rank but had strictly limited power compared to the Venetian Senate.</note> has in the Republic of Venice), for otherwise it would simply become an Aristocracy. 

(2) He thinks it involves a contradiction: for supreme and absolute power to be held by one, and for that same power to be held by many. But no sane person would ever think this. It is truly a Monarchy if supreme power resides with one. In a mixed state (which is classified as a "polyarchic" <note>original: "Polyarchico"; a system where power is held by many people.</note> state), the same power is entrusted to several people. 

(3) He infers that nothing is more contrary to sovereignty than for it to be divided and shared. I grant this if this statement is applied to *monarchic* sovereignty absolutely; otherwise, in every polyarchic state, it is certainly shared. 

(4) He says it is repugnant to sovereignty to depend on a superior. But it is clear that in a mixed state, sovereignty belongs **to the whole** <note>original: "in solidum"; a legal term meaning the authority is held by the group as a single entity rather than by its members individually.</note> to the college, even though the head in that college usually excels the other members in many ways. However, the head does not enjoy every right of power individually. And thus this sovereignty, which such a college possesses, is subject immediately only to God. 

(5) He also brings this up: in a monarchy that is mixed with an aristocracy, everyone is inferior to the Prince and held to offer him obedience. I would deny this, except regarding the rights that belong to him alone. 

(6) He thinks it matters a great deal whether the rights of supreme sovereignty are contracted or detracted...

...[continued] etc., I do not deny: namely, if the rights are contracted, a mixture occurs; if they are withdrawn, it becomes a pure Aristocracy. (7) He says: once the rights of sovereignty <term>Majestas: the supreme authority or "majesty" of a state</term> are established, a supreme magistrate must be appointed. This is exactly what I mean; namely, that sometimes not everything is in the hands of one person, nor are the rights of sovereignty absolutely surrendered; therefore, such a ruler differs from a true monarch. Mr. Otto <note>Daniel Otto (1585–1643), a German jurist and political theorist who wrote extensively on sovereignty.</note> responds to these exceptions of mine in his *Special Treatise on Sovereignty, chapter 2, number 15, etc.* But I gladly and rightfully submit these and all my views to the judgment of anyone who thinks candidly. And I only add this: that Mr. Otto himself, in his *Treatise on Public Law*, concedes the existence of a mixed form.

IV. For if a King frequently uses the counsel of the estates of his Empire and the leading men of the people, that is indeed an aristocratic mode of ruling; however, the form of the commonwealth does not become "mixed" simply because sovereign power is found to be communicated with them to some extent. But that happens only when the estates <term>Ordines: the social ranks or representative bodies of the realm, such as the nobility, clergy, and cities</term> possess the power not simply to give advice, but also to prohibit or impede at the same time—and the Prince is bound to follow their counsel or their dissent.

### CHAPTER II.

## On the Roman and Polish Empire.

The mixed state admits many variations. Sometimes the rights of the Empire are divided, so that the King has some and the Senate has others; or the nobles have some and the common people have others. Sometimes they are shared: so that neither the King can obtain them without the Senate, nor the Senate without the King; or the common people and the higher nobility enjoy them together. Sometimes the supreme power is tempered in other ways (besides a mixture). In the first kind of mixed state, the rights of sovereignty are separated, and different rights are assigned to different orders. In this mixture, a very harmonious balance seems to exist: for some rights are best exercised by one person—for instance, the power of judging and punishing—while there are others in which the orders or "estates" of the Empire can hardly be denied participation without injustice. For example, the right of declaring war, and other similar matters.

II. I would think—always deferring to the judgment of those more skilled—that the *Holy Roman Empire* <note>original: "Imperium Romano-Germanicum"; the complex political union of territories in Central Europe presided over by an Emperor.</note> can provide an example of a state where sovereignty is, as it were, divided. For in that state, political critics have discovered that the Emperor <note>original: "Cæsarem"</note> is not an absolute monarch, but that there exists today a state mixed from Aristocracy and Royal Rule, where the rights of the Empire are separated. See Velstenius, *decade 7, thesis 6*; Keckermann <note>Bartholomäus Keckermann (1572–1609), a German Reformed philosopher who wrote on systematic politics.</note>, *Practical Disputations, last problem 12*; Joachim Cluten, *In the Bundle of Daily Affairs, thesis 16*; Cruger, *Political Disputations 4, thesis 112, and many following*; Heigius, *part 1, question 2, number 14, and many following*; and Paurmeister <note>Tobias Paurmeister (1553–1616), an influential German jurist and statesman.</note>.

# On the Sovereign Rights

...for the *Corpus Juris* <note>The body of Roman civil law compiled under Emperor Justinian in the 6th century.</note> was never received as a law itself, but rather in the place of the "art of law." Furthermore, we had an Empire and laws in Germany before the Roman laws were known there even by name. Lehman, *in the Speyer Chronicle, book 5, chapter 4.*

IV. Likewise, this opinion gains strength from the fact that today in the Roman Empire, certain things are said to be common to the Emperor and the Estates; some are considered the Emperor's own, reserved for his judgment alone; and some are deemed outside the Emperor's authority. Denaisius illustrates this with many examples in *On Chamber Law, section: The Emperor’s Eminence in the Empire and those following.* There, he says that the following are common to both the Emperor and the Estates: Waging war (especially if he wishes the <term>Estates: The princes, bishops, and imperial cities that held a vote in the Imperial Diet</term> to provide aid for it); entering into a treaty; and making laws. *On the form of a Council Resolution <note>original: "de form. eines Rathschlusses"</note>; see* Franciscus Burckhardus, *in The Religious Exemption <note>original: "in der Freystellung"</note>, book 3, chapter 14.* Lehman, *book 7, chapter 124.* Paurmeister, *book 2, chapter 2, number 50, etc., and also number 63, and many following.* Add the Author of the *Political Treasury*, *1. Waremund, *in Likelihood of Subsidies, chapter 5, number 41, page 82.* The concurrence of the Emperor and the Imperial Chamber is also seen in the "mandates of revocation," in establishing punishments for peace-breakers, and in the absolution of the same from the <term>Imperial Ban: A legal status where a person was declared an outlaw, losing their property and legal protection</term>.

The following are the Emperor's own: To settle fiscal cases, as well as those concerning territories, towns, or fortresses. To grant foreign princes the license to recruit soldiers within the Empire; and to decree legal proceedings against those who are not subjects of the Empire. The following are considered reserved for his judgment alone: matters concerning the "greater fiefs" <note>Major land holdings held directly from the Emperor by high-ranking nobles</note> and disputes over seating and precedence among the Estates. The following are considered outside the Emperor's authority: to issue any edict against the Chamber or to detract from its ordinance; to summon cases from the Imperial Chamber to the Imperial Court, and so forth. Denaisius recounts these specifically (on whose authority let them be stated). There is also the very great liberty, especially of German nobles, in the fact that they can participate in foreign wars at their pleasure. Paurmeister, *book 1, chapter 3, number 22 and 6. On the Diets and what the Estates can do there, see* Reinkingk, *book 1, class 5, chapter 8.*

# Political-Legal Dissertation

...refutes this; because certain things belong to the Emperor himself, and others belong to others. And throughout the **Imperial Recesses** <note>The "Recesses" (Abschiede) were the official collection of laws and decrees passed at the conclusion of an Imperial Diet or parliament.</note>, mention is made of **the Imperial Highness and Reserved Rights** <note>original German: "der Kayserlichen Hoheit und Reservaten"</note>. Those who, on the contrary, insist that it is a monarchy—among whom is Mr. Johann Ulrich Wolff in his *political disputation 5, thesis 11, etc.* and Reinkingk in *book 1, class 2, chapter 2*—almost all of them nevertheless profess that this monarchy is tempered by aristocratic principles, through the councils and assemblies of the Electors, Princes, and Estates.

The highly learned Kirchner writes of this throughout his work, especially in *disputation 5, thesis 1, letter C, also orations 15 and 16, volume 1*; as does Christ. Matthias in *political college 2, disputation 1, thesis 6*; Philipp-Johann Treutler in his *disputation on the forms of republics, final thesis in the Basel disputations*; Anton Coler in *section 1, thesis 30 and following*; and Cothman in his commentary *on the title of the Code regarding the Supreme Trinity, questions 1 and 2*.

These authors seem to me to be mistaken because they claim the Emperor cannot change that order, and because some things which belong to the essence of absolute majesty are held to be outside his power. Thus, the patrons of the previously mentioned opinion define the state by the order of its administration and by mere appearances; as was said above, this ought not to be done. Furthermore, the arguments of those who fight for a **Monarchy** only offend the concept of a pure **Aristocracy**, not that of a **Mixed State**. 

In a Monarchy or a "full kingdom," the method of ruling is entirely within the power and will of the Ruler, who is bound by no positive laws. But in the Roman Empire, everyone everywhere admits that the power of the Emperor cannot prevail against the Recesses and Laws of the Empire; this is proven by the words found in almost all Recesses: **"So have we therefore reached an agreement with the Estates, and they in turn with us."** <note>original German: "So haben wir uns demnach mit den Ständen / und sie hinwiederumb sich mit uns verglichen."</note> 

Truly, Germany has always been impatient with absolute rule. One may look to Lazarus Schwendi in his *Counsel on the Government of the Roman Empire, especially number 12, and on the ancient state of Germany*; and likewise Comines in *book 4, chapter 1, page 275, and also chapter 3, page 291.* 

On whether the **Election Capitulation** <term>Election Capitulation: A mandatory contract signed by the Emperor before his coronation, outlining the conditions of his rule and protecting the privileges of the princes.</term> diminishes Majesty, see Arumæus in *volume 4, discourse 3.* On the time it was introduced, see Arumæus in the same place, *discourse 4*, and Carpzov in his *treatise on the Capitulation found in volume 4 of Arumæus.* Lehman also investigates the beginnings of the Capitulation in *book 2, chapter 4, and book 4, chapter 10, page 300*, where he reveals that it was already customary under the Franks. 

If indeed the **Council of Regency** <note>The "Reichsregiment" was a short-lived executive body intended to share power between the Emperor and the Estates.</note>, instituted by Maximilian I at the Diet of Augsburg in the year 1500, had not fallen into disuse through the efforts of Charles V (see Sleidan, *book 7 at the end*), I would refer the German state to an **Ephoristic Kingdom** <term>Ephoristic Kingdom: A government modeled after ancient Sparta, where the monarch's power is legally checked by "Ephors" or overseers representing the people or the nobility.</term>, where Monarchy is mixed with Aristocracy (rather than where the rights of supreme sovereignty are divided). 

Regarding this question—namely, whether the Roman Empire is monarchic—see the conflicting arguments in Goldastus’s *Imperial Politics, page 623 to the end, and page 645.* Today, Catholics especially defend the Roman Empire as being a full Kingdom.

It highlights the role of the Election Capitulation and historical attempts like the Council of Regency in limiting imperial power.</summary>

# On the Mixed State of the Republic.

...they believe. For by this reasoning, they trust that their religion can be more easily restored. Some of our own people agree with them, for they see that the power of the Emperor is being restricted so that the license of the many may be expanded. The Calvinists retort that the Catholics are striving for the advancement of Papal rather than Imperial majesty. Indeed, they claim none hold the reputation of the Empire in greater contempt than those who extend the **Austrian Privileges** <note>Refers to documents like the *Privilegium Maius*, used by the Habsburgs to claim exceptional autonomy from the Empire.</note> too broadly against the Emperor's sublimity and the unity of the Empire. But it is also argued on the other side, and it is established that those privileges are most ancient, known already under the **Swabian Emperors** <note>The Hohenstaufen dynasty, such as Frederick Barbarossa.</note>, and are thus rightly and diligently defended. I acknowledge my own infancy and lack of experience: Julius Pflug, in his *Oration on Germany* (which Goldast also included in his *Imperial Politics*), reviews the subtle reasons by which the Roman Empire might reach its pristine dignity—that is, a truly Monarchical State. Which now, things standing as they are, would be impossible and perhaps destructive, since it could not be done without the most ruinous upheavals; see also Clapmarius, *Book 5 on Secrets, Chapter 12*. Add Barclay's *Mirror of Minds, page 142 and many following.*

VI. From this consideration, the resolution of many questions of the greatest importance depends; however, I am not the one to establish anything certain about them, but only those who have acquired skill through long use of such matters. Just as a gold coin is rarely found that is melted from pure gold, and the quantity of the mixed foreign metal is only exactly investigated with the help of a **touchstone** <note>The "Lydian stone" used to test the purity of precious metals.</note>; so likewise, although it is clear that the Roman-German Republic is not an **absolute monarchy** <term>παμβασιλείαν: Greek for total or absolute kingship</term>, it is not for everyone to estimate to what extent it recedes from that state. This is reserved for one whom constant experience has unlocked the secrets of the Empire and the public state. The things I shall debate in the following, I propose not with the mind of judging, but of discussing.

VII. From these things, therefore, it first seems possible to be derived: that the Princes, Counts, and other Estates of the Empire are not properly called subjects of the Emperor (alone), but rather subjects and members of the Empire. Thus, the Emperor alone, on account of some crime, cannot deprive them of benefits and privileges, or subject them to the **Imperial Ban** <note>The *Reichsacht*, a form of outlawry where a person was deprived of all rights and their lands could be seized.</note>, unless the matter has been publicly deliberated in the Imperial Diet; especially if from that condemnation, dangerous movements in the Empire are to be feared. Nicolaus Betsius, *On Family Pacts, page 448*. *The Donauwörth Information, page 142*. Bernhard Zieritz, *Treatise on the Prerogatives of Princes, H 7*. For the execution of such a ban cannot be done without war, which they say neither the Chamber <note>The *Reichskammergericht* or Imperial Chamber Court.</note> nor the Emperor himself can declare; see, however, Georg Everhard, *volume 2, counsel 17*. This question was once debated at the time of the **Schmalkaldic War** <note>A 16th-century conflict between the Emperor and the Lutheran princes.</note>, and also by Elector Maurice after it ended; and now the Palatines <note>The representatives of the Elector Palatine.</note> are bringing this dispute back onto the stage. But certainly Frederick...

Meibom, in *History of Bardowick, page 15, etc.*

VIII. This is supported by Rosenthal, *chapter 10, conclusion 11, number 11*; Hortleder, *volume 1, on the German War, book 3, page 612*; Buxtorff, *on the Golden Bull, thesis 87*; and Arumaeus, *on the Golden Bull, discourse 4, thesis 16 and 17*. Dr. Bocer partly disagrees in his *Treatise on Investitures, chapter 3, numbers 66, 71, etc., and number 96*; see also his *Treatise on Royal Rights, 4, number 17, etc.*, whom Daniel Otto sufficiently refutes in *On Public Law, chapter 11, page 70, etc.*; add *chapter 2, extracts on fiefs*. That this was not permitted to the Emperor even in ancient times is apparent from this: that long ago the Estates alleged a primary cause for depriving **King Wenceslaus** <note>Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia, who was deposed as King of the Romans in 1400.</note> of the Imperial dignity—namely, that he had elevated the Lords of Milan and Pavia to a higher rank of dignity, creating the former a Duke and the latter a Count within the fiefs of the Empire. See Besius, *in the cited place, page 552*. However, see the *disputation on the Judge* by Johann Stoll of Ravenspurg, held at Jena in the year 1617, thesis 81, where he says: that **Emperor Charles V** invested Duke John of Cleves with the **Duchy of Jülich and Berg** <note>original: *Ducatu Juliacensi & Montium*</note>, as well as the County of Ravensberg, without the vote and consent of the States of the Empire. See the *Saxon Deduction regarding the succession of Jülich, Cleves, and Berg, etc., produced 5.* This was also manifest in the example of **Elector Maurice** <note>Maurice, Elector of Saxony, who famously switched sides during the Schmalkaldic War.</note>, who in the year 1548 was solemnly invested with the Electorate of Saxony at the **Diet of Augsburg** <note>The general assembly of the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, with the Electors sitting beside Charles, as Johann Sleidan narrates in *book 20, on the state of religion*. But Emperor Charles alone, in the camp at Wittenberg, had already granted the electoral office and the majority of the provinces of **John Frederick** <note>The "Magnanimous," whom Charles V had defeated and captured.</note> to him before that. Sleidan, *in the same book*. For there, none of the Electors were present with him except for the Elector of Brandenburg, who nonetheless had not come for that reason, but to intercede for the captive Elector. Sleidan, *in the cited place, book 19*. And as far as the **capitulation** <note>The *Wahlkapitulation*, a written agreement a candidate for Emperor had to sign before election to limit his powers.</note> is concerned, he responded that it does not speak of the feudal goods of the Empire, but of those that are otherwise vacant.

IX. From this it also becomes clear that it is sometimes permitted to appeal to the **Imperial Estates**. Specifically, a petition or rather a plea is made from an "ill-informed" Emperor to the Estates of the Empire and simultaneously to the Emperor himself, so that he may be "better informed." See the **proclamation of the Possessing Princes of Jülich from the year 1610, folio 1, face 2** <note>Referring to the legal dispute over the succession of the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg.</note>. Justus Springer, *on religious peace, page 9, etc.* Conversely, it is not permitted to appeal from the revisers of the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>The *Reichskammergericht*, one of the two highest courts in the Empire.</note> to the Imperial Majesty. Vultejus, *on law 1, number 96, Code on the jurisdiction of all judges*; Graevaeus, *practical conclusions, part 1, final chapter, consideration 1*.

He did not grant this power to the Chamber cumulatively <note>That is, he did not share the power with the court while keeping a copy of it for himself.</note>, because it was done by agreement; nor did he deprive himself of a power which it seems he never truly possessed.

# Political-Legal Dissertation

[Signature: Ee 2]

...we are able to understand that such absolute power has not been left to the Emperor that he could, as they say, **change square things into round** <note>original Latin: *mutare possit quadrata rotundis*; a legal proverb meaning to turn things upside down or claim the power to change the fundamental nature of truth and law.</note>, according to Lord Bocer, *On Jurisdiction, chapter 8, number 86*, and Schönborner, *Politics, book 5, chapter 33*; nor does he possess whatever **Royal Law** <note>The *Lex Regia*, which in classical Roman law transferred all power from the people to the Emperor.</note> the Roman Emperor of old used to have. It is, however, more consistent with the truth that the Emperor can be summoned before the **Count Palatine** <note>One of the high-ranking Electors who traditionally held the right to judge the Emperor in certain civil disputes.</note> in civil matters only, and not in criminal ones. See Wehner, *in Practical Observations, under the word "Austräg"* <term>Austräg: a traditional system of arbitration where disputes between Imperial Estates were settled by their peers rather than by the Emperor’s personal court.</term>; see also Freher, *On the Origins of the Palatinate*; my own *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 2, number 9 at the end*; and Goldast, *On the Rationale of the Constitutions, volume 1, in the notes on the Golden Bull, chapter 5.* Lehmann also records that Frankish Emperors were deposed, *book 2, chapter 19, page 151, column 2.*

But regarding these questions and other related ones, one may look at the opposing writings published in the case of **Donauwörth** <note>A Free Imperial City whose religious and political conflicts in 1606–1607 were a major catalyst for the tensions leading to the Thirty Years' War.</note>, titled *Information* and *Reminder*. Other questions of even greater importance also coincide here: namely, can the Emperor, for a specific cause, grant a dispensation by virtue of his absolute power against laws passed by the common consent of the **Imperial Estates** <note>The princes, prelates, and cities that held a vote in the Imperial Diet.</note>? Can he, in a case of necessity, neglect the order of the law? Likewise, is the Emperor **authorized to make a final resolution** <note>original German: *einen Schluß zumachen befugt*</note> when the Estates disagree with one another? Certainly, this was done in the constitution of the **Religious Peace** <note>The Peace of Augsburg (1555), which established the principle of "whose realm, his religion."</note> regarding the **Ecclesiastical Reservation** <note>original German: *Geistlichen Vorbehalt*; a controversial provision intended to prevent Catholic church lands from becoming Protestant if a high-ranking cleric converted.</note>. It is also seen in the Imperial Recess of the year [15]44, in the section beginning **"But when we..."** <note>original German: *Als wir aber*</note>. Reinkingk provides another example, *page 245, number 35.*

Truly, if the Emperor did not have this power, there would be **anarchy** in the Roman Empire, and no majesty would be sufficiently complete. See the writings exchanged during the time of **Rudolf II** <note>Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1576–1612) known for his patronage of the arts but also for the political instability and religious conflict of his reign.</note> and printed at Munich, in a letter to the Prince of Anhalt. If this power is not granted to the Emperor, then factions, leagues, and eventually civil wars arise. Reinkingk discusses dissensions and unions at length in *book 1, class 2, last chapter.* It also seems safest that these questions not be confined to general rules, nor decided by academic discourses, theses, and disputations (all of which cause disturbance), but rather by custom and the vote of the Estates, adapted to the circumstances and occasions. Often, under the **shadow of defense**, liberty is hidden, which tends toward the impunity of crime; Lehmann provides an example of this in *book 5, chapter 27.*

I am pleased to add some noteworthy points here from Cusanus and Pflug: **Nicholas of Cusa** <note>A 15th-century German philosopher, theologian, and cardinal who wrote extensively on the reform of the Church and the Empire.</note>, a Cardinal and most skilled in the greatest and most hidden affairs of the Roman Empire, and counselor to Emperor Sigismund, committed the following to writing regarding the state before and after the **Interregnum** <note>A period between the mid-13th century when the Empire lacked a strong, recognized central ruler.</note> in *The Catholic Concordance, book 3, chapter 26*: "Formerly the Empire was ruled imperatively, because the Imperial voice was armed with power and vigor. There was no law that even the greatest man could violate with impunity; for unless a law retains its power of censorship and its stinging sharpness, it is blunted and falls into disuse. For it is necessary that harmful appetite be held by the bridle of the law and limited within its own boundaries. A law without correction, having no power of censure, loses its life, nor does it deserve to be called a law, just as..."

# On the Mixed State of the Commonwealth

[Signature: Ee 3]

...just as a dead man is not truly a man. In those days, the laws flourished, and the imperial statutes were feared. To ensure that the severity of the laws was strengthened through constant use, the greatest annual assemblies of the Princes were summoned. In these meetings, no lawbreaker, regardless of how much power they possessed, escaped unpunished. Indeed, it was necessary to accept with equanimity not only the imperial sentence, but the judgment of all the Princes—and even that of one’s parents and dearest friends. Because of the oath sworn to the Empire, no one, when questioned, could fail to approve and praise a settled law; nor could they fail to judge according to that law, even in a case involving their own son. It was necessary for a single judgment, representing everyone, to be brought forth and executed according to the law. Thus, without partiality and by common agreement, legal sanction maintained its authority, and no one could break it with impunity. From this came common peace and a happy fatherland. (The same author, chapter 28).

Furthermore, it was the custom of the Emperors to readily admit accusations of broken faith and perjury, so that fidelity—the sole foundation upon which the empire stands—might never be cheapened through neglect. The punishment for one failing to keep faith was the loss of status. In those days, the Emperor was the public figurehead for the defense of peace; moreover, he maintained a paid army from the public treasury. He was feared on all sides by the Princes and governors, and adored, venerated, and honored everywhere by the people as the defender of the fatherland, the preserver of liberty, the reliever of the oppressed, and the most rigid punisher of those who disturbed the commonwealth. In those times, one who committed an offense against him truly offended the **Supreme Majesty** <term>Supreme Majesty: referring to *crimen laesae maiestatis*, or treason, which was viewed as a crime not just against the ruler, but against the sacred order of the state.</term>; and this was the greatest crime: to sin against the father of the fatherland and of all. If I were to record all those things most worthy of report, I would become more long-winded than intended. (Ibid., chapter 29).

From these things, however, consider how far the state of modern government has fallen, where none of these practices are fully observed. All care for the commonwealth has perished; with the reins loosened, everyone bypasses the laws with impunity. Where there was once veneration with trembling and fear, there is now disregard or contempt. All laws are woven like **spiderwebs** <note>original Latin: *aranearum telis*; a reference to the classical proverb that laws are like cobwebs, catching small flies but letting large wasps break through.</note>; even the tiniest locusts can hardly be held in them. It is not like it once was, when the strongest nets were continually stretched at the boundaries of greed to entangle troublesome transgressors. Now, all stay awake only for their private gain; there is no care for the neighbor or for the future because of the negligence of the Emperors, who think they can restore and reform errors through **piety** <note>In this context, "piety" likely refers to a misplaced leniency or a preference for religious devotion over the "stern" administration of justice.</note> alone. All judicial authority has ceased, and rebels are not punished. Many powerful Princes have arisen out of tyrannical domination, while the Empire decreases, etc. (The same author, chapter 30).

There is, moreover, another destruction of the empire: since the Emperor exists only as an administrator for the utility of the commonwealth, he often enters his reign through pacts with **Electors** <term>Electors: the high-ranking German princes who held the right to choose the Holy Roman Emperor, often extracting "capitulations" or concessions in exchange for their vote.</term> who seek their own interests. Because of his oath, he does not dare to reclaim imperial rights that have been occupied against the law, nor to abolish burdensome tolls that weigh down the commonwealth, or other useful...

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the decline of the Holy Roman Empire, specifically citing Nicholas of Cusa’s "De Concordantia Catholica." It explores how the greed of regional Princes and the Emperor's inability to revoke poorly-conceived land grants have led to a breakdown of central authority.</meta>

# Political-Legal Dissertation

[Page 222]

...is inhibited from making new ordinances or revoking those grants which were unwisely given or pledged by his ancestors without a general assembly—often motivated by inordinate love, personal affection, or blood ties—to the <term>detriment of the empire<note>original: "præjudicium imperii"; refers to actions that weaken the legal or financial standing of the central state</note></term>. Emperors should not be permitted to make such <term>prejudicial alienations<note>original: "alienationes præjudiciales"; the legal transfer of property or rights that harms the state's interests</note></term>. The Princes ought to assist the Emperor so that he might always be "Augustus" <note>A traditional title for the Holy Roman Emperor, meaning "Increaser" or "Majestic," implying he should expand rather than diminish the empire.</note>; however, because they are bound by their own interests, they remain silent. They fear that if they speak up, the things once granted or pledged to them by former relatives or parents who ruled the empire might be taken away. Thus, while they watch the Emperor do the same, they say nothing, lest they condemn themselves. When everyone cares only for increasing their own wealth while the empire itself wastes away to nothing, what can follow but the destruction of all? Since there is no longer a greater power to preserve and pacify the realm, envy and ever-growing greed will produce wars, schisms, and divisions. Then, like any kingdom divided against itself, that which was collected through iniquity will be brought to desolation. 

The Princes living under the Empire are thus deceived when they seize and collect imperial assets from every side to make themselves more powerful and stronger. Once they have torn apart and swallowed the power of the "head" and the "members" of the empire, the <term>hierarchical order<note>original: "hierarchicus ordo"; the structured system of authority where everyone has a specific rank and duty</note></term> will cease to exist. For there will be no "first person" to whom one may appeal. And where there is no order, there is confusion; and where there is confusion, no one is safe. Thus, with the nobles bickering among themselves, men will rise up seeking "justice" only through their own arms. Just as the Princes devour the empire, so the common people will devour the Princes. (The same author, *On Catholic Concordance*, book 3, chapter 39).

Consequently, the greatest effort must be made to ensure that the power of the empire is revived; otherwise, no effect will follow from any laws already established or yet to be ordained. The strength of the law lies in <term>coercion<note>original: "coërcitio"; the legal power to compel obedience through punishment</note></term>. Coercion guards and executes power. If it is removed—since we strive for the forbidden and are prone to evil from our youth—legal censure, and consequently peace and justice, will not long endure.

Since this is the case, a method for this must be provided through reformation. In former times, the Bishops, Abbots, Princes, and Counts were accustomed to perform annual and daily services, both personal and material, for the empire according to the province and land subject to them. From these resources, certain <note>original: "Stipendiarii"; paid soldiers or those funded by a specific revenue stream</note> were maintained for a daily imperial army for the defense of the <term>Commonwealth<note>original: "Respublica"; referring here to the public welfare and the collective state of the Empire</note></term>. Even the Emperor himself used to maintain a most honorable Imperial state. When this army for the defense of the Empire and the Commonwealth failed, the Commonwealth suffered greatly. 

It would therefore be beneficial to apply the most diligent labor to this ordinance: that through moderate annual contributions, based on various domains and locations, such an army might be established so that justice and peace may be preserved through it. It would be easy to reserve a competent portion for the state of the Empire annually from the <term>tolls<note>original: "telonia"; duties paid on the movement of goods</note></term> and <term>taxes<note>original: "gabella"; specifically consumption taxes or salt taxes, though here used generally for imperial levies</note></term> granted to the Princes for the sake of the Commonwealth. This portion could be drawn from all tolls at a moderate rate. Julius Pflug <note>A 16th-century Catholic Bishop of Naumburg known for his attempts to find common ground during the Reformation.</note>, the Bishop, holds very similar views.

# On the Mixed State of the Republic.

->...Bishop of Naumburg.<-

A man of exquisite prudence and great virtue, and for these and other ornaments of his soul very dear to the Emperor Charles V <note>Charles V (1500–1558) was the Holy Roman Emperor who oversaw the early years of the Reformation and attempted to maintain the unity of his vast European empire.</note>, writing *in his booklet on the Republic of Germany*. And these things (he says) so far concern the best state of our Republic, in which neither profitable benefit, nor equal right, nor concord, nor liberty, nor true dignity, nor the just Rule of one, nor finally that Most Sacred religion of the immortal <term>GOD<note>original: "DEI"</note></term> could be found lacking. But now I wish either that the same Republic had contracted no stains thereafter, or that it were within my power to pass over those very same things. For with how much greater pleasure of mind I dwell upon the thought of those best things, by so much more bitter a pain am I affected whenever the evils of this age and time come to my mind. 

But because I have decided not only to recount the good things of superior ages, but also to open and treat the wounds which we have received in later centuries—to see if in any way both these might be healed and those might be recovered—I must indeed do what this place and the public safety demand. And first indeed, although Republics are less likely to be shaken the better they are constituted, yet since it is so arranged that they are no less changeable than other human things, and these have (as Plato says) <note>Pflug refers to Plato's theory of political cycles (*kyklos*), where regimes naturally decay and transform into other forms over time.</note> "natural conversions"; certainly when our German Empire had flourished for a long time and for several centuries, at length a chance, hostile to our affairs, brought it about that after the death of Frederick the Second <note>Frederick II (1194–1250) was a powerful Hohenstaufen emperor whose death led to a period of chaos and a lack of centralized authority.</note> it lacked an Emperor for eighteen years. 

Meanwhile, since our Ancestors did not have one person whom they might obey, they seem almost to have lost that best form of their Republic of which we have spoken. Although the Republic later recovered this through Rudolph of Habsburg <note>Rudolf I (1218–1291), the first Habsburg king, who ended the "Great Interregnum" and attempted to restore order.</note>, it did not flourish after the interregnum as it had before. For at the time when the Magistrates and Princes of our nation were stripped of the protection of their Prince, and did not have one by whom they might be defended, they themselves strengthened their own resources by whatever means they could. And many of those things which before were the property of the Emperors, they transferred to themselves, so that while each one in his own City and jurisdiction performed the duty of the Emperor in both ruling and protecting, he himself relied upon the Empire's own <term>sinews<note>original: "nervis"; in early modern political thought, "sinews" refers to the financial and legal resources—like taxes and land rights—that give a state its power.</note></term> and, as it were, its strengths. 

And when our Magistrates and Princes had usurped those things for some time, and could not be moved from their possession without force, Rudolph preferred to yield from his own right rather than offend the wills of those whose labor he could usefully employ both at home and in military service. Nor did he ever suspect that it would happen that those who had grown powerful out of the very patrimony of the Empire would not obey him and his successors of their own accord, nor would they help the Republic with grateful minds. And although this Prince decided that he could hold the Empire much more easily by benefits than by force and arms, nevertheless no small part of the public resources and profits of that same Empire was lost. Indeed, from that time, the rights and taxes were weakened more and more every day...

### A Politico-Legal Dissertation

...he is inhibited from making ordinances, and from revoking those things that were given or pledged by his predecessors unwisely—without a general assembly—out of inordinate love, personal affection, or blood-ties, to the prejudice of the empire. Emperors should not be permitted to make such prejudicial <term>alienations<note>The legal transfer of property or rights from the central Empire to local lords.</note></term>; rather, the Princes ought to assist the Emperor so that he might always be *Augustus* <note>original: "semper Augustus". In the context of the Holy Roman Empire, this title was interpreted not just as "Majestic," but etymologically as "the Increaser" of the realm's territory and rights.</note>. 

However, because the Princes bind him—lest the things once granted or pledged to them (sometimes through legal fictions, or by the relatives and parents who previously headed the empire) be taken away—they remain silent when they see the Emperor doing the same, so as not to condemn themselves. For when everyone cares only for increasing their own holdings while the empire tends toward nothing, what follows but the destruction of everyone? Since there is no longer a greater power to conserve and pacify the empire, envy and ever-growing greed will produce wars, schisms, and divisions. Then, just as every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, that which was unjustly gathered will be scattered. 

Thus, the Princes under the empire are deceived when they attract and collect imperial rights from all sides for the purpose of becoming more powerful and stronger; for once they have torn asunder and swallowed the whole power of the "head" and the empire, as well as its members, the **hierarchical order** shall cease. For there will be no "first" among them to whom one may turn. And where there is no order, there is confusion; and where there is confusion, no one is safe. And so, with the nobles quarreling among themselves, they will rise up seeking all "right" through their own weapons; for just as the Princes devour the empire, so the common people will devour the Princes. 

->The same author, *in chapter 39 of "On Catholic Concordance"*<- <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464) wrote *De Concordantia Catholica*, a major work of political theory arguing for a balance between the power of the Emperor and the consent of the governed.</note>

Consequently, the greatest effort must be made to ensure that the power of the empire is revived; otherwise, no effect would follow from all things currently ordained or to be ordained. The vigor of the law lies in <term>coercion<note>original: "coërcitione". The legal principle that a law is only meaningful if the state has the power to force compliance.</note></term>. Power guards and executes this coercion. When power is taken away—for we "strive for the forbidden" <note>A reference to Ovid: *Nitimur in vetitum semper, cupimusque negata* (We always strive for the forbidden and desire what is denied).</note> and are prone to evil from our youth—legal censure, and by extension peace and justice, will not persist for long.

Since this is the case, a method for this must be provided through a **reformation**. Formerly, Bishops, Abbots, Princes, and Counts were accustomed to perform annual and daily services—both personal and material—to the empire, according to the province and land subject to them. From these resources, certain soldiers were maintained for a daily imperial army for the defense of the Republic; and the Emperor himself used to maintain a most honorable Imperial state. Since this army for the defense of the Empire and the Republic has failed, the Republic has suffered greatly. 

It would therefore be beneficial to apply the most diligent effort to this ordinance: that through moderate annual contributions, adjusted by domain and location, such an army might be raised so that peace and justice might be maintained through it. A competent portion could easily be reserved annually for the state of the Empire from the <term>tolls<note>original: "teloniis". Fees collected for the transport of goods.</note></term> and <term>duties<note>original: "gabellis". Specifically salt taxes or other indirect taxes.</note></term> currently granted to the Princes for the Republic, and abstracted from all such tolls in a moderate proportion.

It appears to be most true, as the wisest men have on their lips, that there is no <unclear>reason</unclear> why anyone should not measure the good state of a Republic by virtue and piety rather than by money, riches, and power; since the end goal of a Republic is the very method of living well and blessedly. Therefore, our grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and ancestors had surely and diligently taken care lest those good morals of our people, by which our Republic seemed to be sustained, should be corrupted. They entered into a plan so that the severity of the laws might tighten whatever reins of duty and discipline the thinning of Imperial power might have loosened. Indeed, there is a great connection between the Magistrate and the Law. Therefore, it was forbidden by public law for anyone to harm the Majesty of the Emperor, or to take up public force <note>i.e., private warfare or rebellion</note> in our Republic; and whoever did contrary to this would be afflicted with the heaviest punishment. ### On the Mixed State of the Republic

...[stu]pid <note>Completing the word "stupidi" from the previous page's catchword.</note> they were, they could not easily undermine its state. Furthermore, to prevent the nobles—in whose virtue the Republic had always found its great defense—from becoming corrupt or falling into some kind of lawlessness, our ancestors did not allow the **Censorious laws** <note>Laws regarding the supervision of public morals, modeled on the Roman office of Censor.</note> to be removed from our Republic. Instead, any of the nobility who entangled himself in serious crimes or harmed the Republic and its leaders was marked with severe infamy during the tournaments. These contests were established like the **Greek Olympiads** <note>The author uses the "Greek Olympiads" as a metaphor for the great knightly tournaments of the Holy Roman Empire, where a noble's reputation and lineage were publicly vetted.</note> and were watched publicly by nearly all of Germany. This was done so that those whom a love of the Fatherland or the authority of the Emperor could not keep in their duty might be deterred from wickedness by the fear of punishment and disgrace. Thus, this social order would be less likely to tear apart the Republic with the very weapons it had so often used to protect it.

Prudence also dictated that **military discipline**, which had produced not only great utility but also distinguished honors for our Republic, should not be easily corrupted—and rightly so. For if the lives and conduct of any men require a stricter and more severe discipline, it is surely those of soldiers. If this discipline is loosened, they set no limit to their desires in the lawlessness of their swords. They become a plague not only to enemies, but even to allies, friends, and the people of the provinces, nor do they spare or keep their hands off those with whom they share their quarters.

And a little later: In the first place, it is established that our Emperor does not possess enough from the public funds of our Republic to allow himself and his family to live comfortably. However, the Princes and Magistrates of our individual regions abound in wealth; such property and fortune flow to them that they are able to live not only comfortably, but luxuriously and with a certain splendor. I cannot easily say what effect this has, or how much it detracts from the Emperor’s reputation and authority. Certainly, one of two things must happen: either our Emperor is despised by those who ought to be under his power (as is the case with current times and morals), or he must repair these losses to the Empire’s patrimony through his own private inheritance, if he has any. The former cannot fail to harm the Republic, while the latter is even less beneficial, for we tend to care more diligently for those things that return a great profit to us than for the meager things we might own. 

Therefore, so that our Emperor might receive as much utility and profit from our public funds as is proper, if I were to persuade the Princes and Magistrates of this same Republic to restore the <term>public taxes</term> <note>original: "vectigalia publica," referring to tolls, customs, and tax revenues.</note> of the Empire which their ancestors transferred to themselves—and thus increase the <term>Prince’s revenue</term> <note>original: "censum Principis." In this context, "Princeps" refers to the Emperor as the first of the Princes.</note> for the common good of all—there would surely be no reason for anyone to criticize my advice. For if the **Lombard Princes** <note>The Lombards were a Germanic people who ruled a kingdom in Italy; their legal codes were often studied as precedents for feudal law.</note>, when they first established their kingdom, gave from their own private property that which belonged to the public law...

He chooses the counselors, names the bishops, and is the absolute executor of the decrees made in the conventions. He is the supreme judge of the Nobles in criminal cases. He holds in his hand all means of rewarding and bestowing favors upon those who please him. This is noted by Boterus in his *Report on the Empire of the World*, by Stanislaw Krzistanovvic in *On the State of Poland*, and by Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian and statesman.</note> in book 56, folio 1134 (where he reports that the King of Poland can pass no law without the counsel of the state and the consent of the Nobility). ### CHAPTER III.
## On Other Types and Examples of the Mixed Republic.

I. A **Monarchy** is considered mixed with an **Aristocracy**, a **Democracy**, or with both, when the primary care of governing is entrusted to one individual, but not the sole care. In such a system, others—who represent either the common people, the Nobility alone, or both at once—possess some portion of that government. Johannes Althusius <note>A 17th-century political philosopher known for his theories on federalism and popular sovereignty.</note> and several other political thinkers have adapted all their principal teachings to this state; indeed, they approve of no other form of government and recognize none as legitimate except a republic of this kind. This is the view of the author of *Vindication against Tyrants* <note>original: *Vindiciae contra Tyrannos*; a highly influential 1579 treatise arguing that it is lawful to resist a king who violates divine or civil law.</note>; George Buchanan in *The Rights of the Kingdom among the Scots*; François Hotman in *On the Ancient Kingdom of Gaul*; and Philipp Hoenon in his *9th Political Dispute*. To these thinkers, a Monarchy exists where the kingship is tempered and altered by Aristocratic or Democratic elements (or both). An Aristocracy exists where, in addition to the Senate, there are **Ephors** <note>original: *Ephori*; originally high-ranking Spartan magistrates, here used to mean representatives who check the power of the ruler.</note> representing the people. A Democracy exists where certain men, in the name of the Nobles, restrain the license of the common people. Henning Arnisaeus, in *Political Doctrine, chapter 8, page 164*, as well as Velstenius in *Seventh Decade of Political Questions, thesis 5*, admit only that single mode of mixing which was discussed in the preceding chapter (see Keckermann, *Practical Dispute 36, problem 11*). And truly, this matter does not seem to be without doubt: for a city of this kind—where all three species of Republic are mixed together but the rights of majesty are not clearly distributed—might seem to be a Democracy instead. However, in a Democracy, the majority of the people decides; here, the King, the nobles, and the common people constitute **three orders** and cast three votes. Nor can the majority of the people prejudice the rights of the others.

II. Among those who rule alongside the people, the Prince, or the senate, their title and power must be investigated. Regarding the first point: they are usually referred to by various names, such as the **Estates**, the **Orders**, the Counselors, or the Senators of the Kingdom—or in French, *Les trois estats* <note>The Three Estates: the Clergy, the Nobility, and the Commoners.</note>. Political writers more commonly call them **Ephors** (following the custom of the Spartans), from the Greek word *ephoran* <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐφορᾶν</note>, meaning "to overlook," because they keep their eyes fixed on the safety of the state (see Drusius on *Genesis, chapter 92*). The Jews called such a body the **Sanhedrin** <note>original: *sanhedrim*; the supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish nation.</note>. But where a Republic admits only an Aristocratic tempering, it is almost always the Dukes, Barons, and other high-ranking nobles who perform...

Regarding that serious dispute among political thinkers: **Are the Ephors in this state more "principal" than the Prince?**—on which Keckerman discourses after Hotman and Junius Brutus, *in the cited chapter, page 565, and in the final practical dispute, problem 10*—I decide it thus: by his very nature, the Prince is the head even of the Ephors (provided, however, that if he acts against his office, he is then regarded as a private person and an inferior). But where, by a special pact, the Ephors are deemed superior in all things, that Republic should not be estimated as a mixed state, but as a pure **Aristocracy**. Aristotle, *Politics, book 3, chapter 10.* Polybius, *book 6, number 4.* Cragius, *On the Lacedaemonian Republic, book 1, chapter 4.* Indeed, it was mixed from all three even earlier, if we believe Justin, *book 3,* where he says Lycurgus gave the power of wars to the kings, judgments to the magistrates, the guardianship of the laws to the senate, and the power of creating magistrates to the people. The oath of the kings and subjects is found in Xenophon, *On the Lacedaemonian Republic, page 44.* And Paruta, *book 1, discourse 1, page 13,* wonderfully commends this state even before the Ephors were established, and judges it to have been mixed from the three; but he maintains that after the Ephors it declined toward popularity <note>meaning a "popular" or democratic state.</note>. For any Ephor could cast a king into chains, as seen in Aemilius Probus’s life of *Pausanias*.

*The first kings of the Egyptians did not lead their lives according to the custom of other monarchs, namely, managing all things according to their own whim without being subject to any censures. Instead, everything—not only public affairs but even the regulation of daily life and their very diet—was shaped according to the standard of the laws. For no servant, neither bought nor born in the house, was employed for their personal service; only the sons of the noblest Priests, over twenty years of age and the best educated of their nation, were chosen. This was so that if the King had the finest caretakers and companions with him day and night, he would commit nothing base or worthy of blame. For no Prince proceeds to excessive wickedness unless there are those at hand who serve his desires. Specific hours of both night and day were defined, during which the king was required to act not according to his own pleasures, but as established by the laws. Upon waking at dawn, letters written from everywhere were first to be received, so that he could manage all things more correctly if he had exact knowledge of every business of the kingdom. Then, adorned with the symbols of royalty and a magnificent robe* <note>original: *trabea*; a ceremonial Roman robe, here used to describe Egyptian royal attire</note>, *he went to sacrifice to the gods. When the victims were brought to the altar, it was the custom for the High Priest, standing by the king, to announce prayers in a loud voice before the crowded circle of Egyptians: that the gods might grant health and all other good things to the king, as he maintains justice and equity toward his inferiors.* And what follows there is most worthy of reading.

Such was also the state of affairs in former times among all the northern nations. And it remains so today in the Danish kingdom: see Lauterbeck, *book 1, last chapter, in the <term>Book of Rulers</term>* <note>original: *Regentenbuch*</note>; although Mr. Cluten disagrees in *Collection of Everyday Matters, thesis 10, letter e.* It is the same in the Swedish kingdom: this is proven by the formulas of the oaths to be sworn by both the new king and by the lawmakers and councilors; see *book 2 of the Swedish Laws, chapters 4, 5, and 8.* Add also the account of the deposition of Sigismund, King of Poland, *page 79 and following*, where the oath the king is bound to swear is recorded. There are also several laws limiting the power of the king, *ibid. page 342 and following*, such as that he must be a Catholic, that he may not marry a non-Catholic, and that he may not accept another kingdom. Join to this the speech of Skytte, the Swedish ambassador, to the King of England. They decreed by common vote of the people that this official was greater and more powerful than the king. Finally, once the king was created under certain laws and conditions, they addressed him with these words: "We, who are as worthy as you, and have more power than you, etc., elect you King, etc., with these and those conditions." <note>original Spanish: *Nos qui valemos tanto come vos, y podemos mas que vos &c. vos eligimos Rey &c. con estas yestas conditiones*</note> François Hotman in *Franco-Gallia, chapter 12, page 98.* But most of these things, gradually diminished by the ambition of the Castilians (or perhaps placed in jeopardy by the excessive license of the Aragonese), were completely abolished not long ago, along with all the immunities of that kingdom, by Philip II, King of Spain. Pierre Matthieu, *1, page 114*; Thuanus, *book 104*; Antonio Pérez, *in his reports.* See also my *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 1 at the end.* The Kingdom of Navarre was almost identical. See the *History of Gaul regarding the Kingdom of Navarre, from the beginning of the title 'double acknowledgment'; also, my own page 361, etc.* where the coronation of Charles in the year of Christ 1387 is discussed.

VI. A tempered and mixed state of the republic is one composed of Aristocracy and Democracy, in which the nobles rule in such a way that the people also share in the government. Today, most cities are governed by this form; accordingly, Keckermann calls it a "City Government" <note>original German: *Statt Regiment*; a system where urban administration is shared between elite families and trade guilds</note> in his *Politics, book 2, chapter 5.* In the free German cities of old, there seems to have been an oligarchy; for almost everywhere, a few men from the nobility administered the state. But when their republics were brought to ruin by the overbearing rule of these few, the nobles were in some places expelled, in others they stepped down voluntarily, and in others they made a certain number of commoners <note>original: *plebeiis*</note> sharers in the conduct of affairs in equal number. See Lehman in *The Speyer Chronicle, book 6, chapter 8 and following*; add also *The Alsace Chronicle.*

### CHAPTER IV.
## On the Lawful Kingdom.

I. I also recognize a mixed state where the freer power and personal majesty of a ruler is trimmed back and limited by <term>fundamental laws</term> <note>These are the core constitutional rules that define how a state is governed</note>; or where certain prescribed laws for governing are established. This is what political writers, following Aristotle, call a *Lawful Kingdom* <note>original: *Regnum Legitimum*</note> (because the power of administering the republic is restricted by laws there); others call it a princedom. There is little difference between this and an <term>Ephoristic kingdom</term> <note>named after the "Ephors" of Sparta, who were overseers intended to balance the power of the kings</note> (which was discussed in the preceding sections), and they often overlap; namely, so that the Ephors are merely the guardians of the fundamental laws and privileges that enclose absolute power within certain boundaries. However, between a "lawful" kingdom and a "full" <note>or absolute</note> kingdom, although the Prince ought to have laws and obey them in both, this distinction exists: in the lawful kingdom, the King holds an authority prescribed and defined by laws in specific matters, and the judgment to modify those laws does not rest with him, but with the whole republic. In contrast, a "full" King holds that judgment himself and acts in the place of the whole republic; when something occurs contrary to the reason of the law, he mitigates the law through a decree and interpretation, which is commonly called a <term>dispensation</term>. As Ginés de Sepúlveda notes on Aristotle's *Politics, book 4, chapter 4, number 49*: just as in a Democracy, it is proper for laws to exist, yet those laws are in the power of the people; just as in Rome, the people could release whomever they wished from the laws, etc.

II. Thus, an infinite power was never permitted to the princes over the **Belgians** <note>Referring here to the people of the Low Countries or Netherlands</note>; for they were bound by certain formulas of privileges and rituals. If they departed from these and did not follow better counsel when warned, it was then the duty of the <term>Orders</term> <note>The representative estates or assembly of the provinces</note> to ensure the republic was well-administered. See Hugo Grotius, *On the Antiquity of the Batavian Republic, throughout*; the anonymous Belgian noble, *Oration on the Law of the Belgian War*; and throughout the work of Meteren (especially *book 14, folio 574*, where an entire treatise on this matter is inserted); as well as Jean Le Petit, *In the History of the Belgian Troubles*; and Isaac Pontanus, *In the History of the City of Amsterdam.*

III. Those laws which constitute a lawful kingdom vary among different nations. Thus, in the fundamental laws of many kingdoms and cities, it is found inserted—and most diligently guarded against in the marriages and elections of foreign Princes—that magistracies and honors should not be entrusted to foreigners. Examples are found in Sweden, Poland, Hunga- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "Hungary"</note>

There is another even more beneficial law: that wars should not be undertaken without the consent of the citizens, nor should they be forced to serve militarily outside the territory (unless for the defense of the fatherland), etc. For what is more grievous than to follow a Prince's ambition at the cost of one's soul, alongside the loss of body and fortune?

IV. These laws and privileges are protected by a manifold fence. And a few years ago, under the leadership of Bocskai <note>Stephen Bocskai, who led a 1604 uprising against the Habsburgs</note>, the Hungarians intended to do the same to their king. Whether this was done justly or unjustly is not for someone to decide without a deeper knowledge of that state's condition. Under a similar condition, Kings were formerly elected by the Swedes; who, among other things, pledged as follows: *If we (which God forbid) or another should dare to act contrary to these things, or permit them to be done; then the Senators of the three kingdoms, Bishops, Prelates, Knights, Nobles, Citizens, and common inhabitants shall be bound to resist us; and he who, out of honor and the oath he has taken, refuses to preserve the aforementioned things, shall in no way be considered a delinquent against our royal authority, the republic, or others.* — *Retaliation against Peter Parvus, Chapter 13, page 85.*

### CHAPTER V.
->*On the Oaths of Princes.*<-

However, not all empires exist as "mixed" forms simply because they are under some condition or a specific given law; nor do all oaths that bind Princes to the laws of the republic immediately diminish the rights of <term>majesty</term> <note>sovereignty or supreme power</note> and, as Tacitus speaks, "dissolve the force of the Principate." For by some oaths, they are bound only to honor, or to the observance of the laws of God and Nature; such a mutual and general obligation, consistent with natural and divine law, detracts nothing from the right of superiority. See *Bodin, On the Republic, Book 1, Chapter 8, Number 83; Arnisaeus, Politics, Chapter 11, page 263.* Since (as the common axiom among legal experts holds) an oath does not introduce a new obligation, but merely confirms an old one. Indeed, because the hearts of Kings and Princes are in the hand of God, human weakness—always needing divine help—sometimes knows not how to seek any other remedy, nor recognize it when found, except to demand a truthful oath from those about to govern regarding the preservation of justice. Olaus Magnus <note>original: *Olaus Magnus, septentr. histor. 14. cap. 20.*; a 16th-century Swedish historian and cartographer</note> and Cluten <note>original: *Cluten. paradox. 11.*</note> express this beautifully. A horrendous example of the punishment for those who fail to uphold the pacts and privileges sworn by their ancestors—even to those who have surrendered—is shown by the descendants of Saul. This was due to a pact broken by Saul out of misplaced zeal, as recorded in *2 Samuel 21* <note>Saul’s family was punished with famine and death because Saul had violated a long-standing peace treaty with the Gibeonites.</note>. Generally, however, that a Lord ought to swear an oath to his subjects is noted in the *Policraticus* <note>original: *Polycratia*; a famous medieval work on political ethics by John of Salisbury, lib. 5. cap. 11.</note>; and King James of England agrees <note>original: *Jacobus Angliæ Rex, in tractat. de Monarch. fol. 11.*</note>, as does Ritter in his *Treatise on Homage* <note>original: *tractat. de Homag. num. 117.*</note>. Ritter, in section 121, discusses at length the formulas by which Kings in various realms bind themselves, many of which Mr. Brunning has also collected. Indeed, no <term>republic</term> <note>original: *Respublica*; used here in the classical sense of any organized state or commonwealth, not necessarily a non-monarchy</note> was ever instituted or founded without a contract first being entered into by both sides, and pacts agreed upon between the subjects and the magistrate <note>original: *Danæ. 1. polit. Christ. cap. 4.*</note>. Yet these laws and conditions are partly general—concerning the inherent duties of the magistrate and subjects, whether tacitly or expressly prescribed—and partly specific, proposed in clear words regarding the certain form and manner of administration and subjection for each individual state. These are called the **rights of the realm**, as well as the **fundamental laws of the realm**. The former have a place in every kingdom; the latter are unique to specific peoples and usually constitute a **mixed republic** <note>original: *Rempublicam mixtam*; a government that combines elements of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy to ensure balance</note>. Regarding such empires, I understand the principle that <term>homage</term> <note>original: *homagium*; the formal acknowledgment of allegiance by a subject to a lord</note> is called a "covenant" <note>original: *fœdus*</note>; just as subjects are bound to submission, so Kings in turn are bound by an equal bond to remain faithful <note>original: *fidelitatem*</note>.

II. That the oath, by which a Prince binds himself simply to good and correct administration, can hold its place even in an "absolute monarchy" is apparent from this: the Emperor Trajan swore an oath to the people <note>original: *apud Dionem. lib. 68.*; referring to the Roman historian Cassius Dio</note>, as noted by Pliny in his *Panegyric* <note>original: *Plinius, in Panegyr. in edit. Levinei.*</note>; see also Bodin <note>Jean Bodin, a foundational theorist of absolute sovereignty</note>. Thus, that fundamental law in France—stating that the King cannot separate or sell off any lands unified with the Crown—detracts nothing from the monarchical principle. I discussed this in my *Treatise on Appeals* <note>original: *tractat. de appellat. cap. 16.*</note>. Just as the judgment of a person who promises to conform to equity remains free, so too does a ruler possess "power unbound by laws" <note>original: *legibus solutâ potestate*; a Roman law concept meaning the sovereign is above the civil law but still bound by natural/divine law</note> even when he pledges under oath that he will rule justly and attempt nothing to the detriment of the Empire.

III. Here the question is asked: in a case where both the subjects and the Prince are required to swear an oath, which of them should swear first? Certainly, if there are specific articles and conditions, it is better that the Prince swears first <note>original: *Althus. polit. cap. 19. num. 7.*; referring to Johannes Althusius, a theorist of federalism</note>. Because where subjects are bound conditionally, it is necessary that the condition be satisfied first...

# A Politico-Legal Dissertation

...the Prince does. For example, as witnessed by Meteren <note>original: *Meterano*; Emanuel van Meteren (1535–1612), a Flemish historian known for his history of the Netherlands</note>, Albert and Isabella, the Sovereigns of the Netherlands <note>original: *Belgii Principes*; referring to the Archdukes Albert VII and Isabella Clara Eugenia</note>, swore their oaths to the cities before the cities swore to them. I would offer a different answer if the oath were general and *unrestricted*. See the response from the University of Freiburg, recorded among the *Brunswick Consultations*. Nevertheless, Trajan swore his oath first, followed by the consuls <note>original: *Plin. Panegyr. dict. fol. 71.*; referring to Pliny the Younger’s speech praising the Roman Emperor Trajan for submitting himself to the law</note>. This leads to a specific question:

Whether a high <term>Cathedral Chapter</term> <note>original: *Thumbcapittul*; the body of clergy that advises a bishop and elects his successor</note> has the power, during the election of an Archbishop or Bishop, to revise the old <term>capitulations</term> <note>original: *Capitulationes*; written agreements or contracts where a candidate for high office agrees to certain conditions before being elected</note> and prescribe new ones—even if they are contrary to the prestige of a Prince—such as requiring that he shall not hire any servants, even for his private service, or dismiss them without their permission, along with other similar conditions that are arguably contrary to divine law and established custom? And whether a Bishop, after he has been in power for several years and reached old age, might take proper legal measures against the members of the Chapter to rescind such capitulations and return to the old rules?

I argue that: 
(1) I assume first that a Bishopric has the nature of an **elective kingdom**, and must be judged by the same rules that govern elective realms. 
(2) Thus, a Bishop does not inherit any right from his predecessor, just as he cannot be burdened by his predecessor’s debts, and so forth. 
(3) A Bishop receives all his rights solely through the **election**. 
(4) In an elective kingdom, it is entirely within the power of the estates or the electors to prescribe whatever capitulations they please, which they judge to be for the common good and public utility, as I have stated elsewhere in my treatise *On Succession and Election*. 
(5) History is full of examples of empires where harsh capitulations eventually turned absolute rule into a **mixed** or **aristocratic** form of government. 
(6) The **Holy Roman Empire** provides a primary example of such a change; through these capitulations, it has remarkably limited the absolute power of its Emperors, and a newly elected Emperor cannot appeal to the older, more lenient capitulations of his predecessors. 
(7) It does not matter that these capitulations are considered "contrary to reason." This is certainly the view of court-politicians, who are enemies of all liberty; it is not the view of those who know that similar restrictions are placed on other Kings. Even the Roman Dictator was not allowed to ride a horse <note>An ancient Roman religious and legal restriction meant to ensure the Dictator remained on foot with the people and did not act like a foreign cavalry-king.</note>. 
(8) The reason for a capitulation is to ensure that a Prince does not employ ministers of a foreign religion, flatterers, traitors, or agents of tyranny. All authors who have written on the authority of the Chapter when a see is vacant, or on the power of Parliaments and Senators of a Realm, agree on this; see also Arnisaeus <note>original: *Arnifæus*; Henning Arnisaeus (c. 1575–1636), a German physician and political theorist who supported a limited form of absolutism</note>, in his *Politics, book 2, chapter 3*.

However, I hear that an excellent jurist is preparing a unique and laborious treatise on this very question: Whether the Estates of the Empire assembled in 1522 at the **Diet of Nuremberg** had legitimate reasons for complaining about the frequently renewed, overly strict, and binding sworn capitulations which the Canons of the Cathedral Chapter present to their superiors...

<summary>The author argues that elective offices, including Bishoprics and the Holy Roman Emperor, are legally bound by "Election Capitulations" which limit their power. These contracts are defended as a necessary check against tyranny and the influence of poor advisors.</summary>

# On the Mixed Form of Government.

...in the same way—as the words are found in German in Hortleder <note>original: *Hortledern*; Friedrich Hortleder (1579–1640), a German historian and jurist who documented the constitutional history of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, and slightly differently in Latin in Goldast <note>original: *Goldasto*; Melchior Goldast (1578–1635), a Swiss jurist and collector of imperial constitutional documents</note>—is to be lamented. I willingly submit to his judgment. However, the discourse of Arumæus <note>Dominicus Arumæus (1579–1637), a pioneer in the study of public law in Germany</note> is relevant here; where he proves against Arnisaeus and Florentinus von Venningen that the Emperor, and any other elected Prince, can be bound by an oath, and that his power is limited by it, and he must absolutely keep such an oath.

### CHAPTER VI.
### On subjects: contractual, exempt, and privileged.

Furthermore, based on their origin, the laws I am discussing here (which namely restrict absolute power) are many. Because of them, it is not irrelevant to divide subjects into groups, where some are called *contractual* [*pactitii*], others *exempt* [*exemptitii*], and others *privileged* [*privilegiarii*]; following Johann Dauth in his *Hypotyposis*. Andreas Knichen disagrees in his *Epopsi*, number 130. See also Joachim Cluten in his *Collection of Daily Matters*, thesis 27, letters f, g, h, and Bruning in his *Disputation on the Types of Universities*, thesis 15.

II. *Contractual subjects* are those who were once free, but submitted themselves through certain agreements, a form of "contractual subjection." For those who came into submission through specific treaties, or reserved certain conditions, their own laws, and privileges for themselves during an election, are not called "subjects" in terms of the ruler's full power <note>This suggests they are more like partners in a contract than subordinates to an absolute monarch</note>. See Alberico Gentilis <note>An Italian jurist and one of the founders of international law</note>, *Royal Disputations*, 1, page 14. These pacts, since they were made with those not yet subjects, must be observed in every way, as Vincentius Cabotius notes in book 2, chapter 11.

III. They are called *exempt subjects* because they were once under municipal [local] jurisdiction, but through contracts or <term>prescription</term> <note>original: *præſcriptione*; a legal principle where a right or status is gained through long-standing custom or the passage of time</note>, they are exempt regarding certain rights. I am not speaking here of total exemption, for that creates a separate state entirely. For this reason, the Venetians, the Swiss, etc., do not wish to admit that they are members of the Empire; see Schönborner, *Politics*, book 5, chapter 7, and as I have already said in my *Treatise on Appeals*, chapter 2, number 6.

IV. They are called *privileged subjects* because of the privileges they hold. However, some privileges create a <term>mixed state</term> <note>original: *ſtatum mixtum*; a form of government where power is shared between a monarch, the nobility, and/or the people</note>, while others do not hinder the ruler's <term>sovereignty</term> <note>original: *ſuperioritati*; the supreme authority or 'superiority' of a ruler over their territory</note>. In this latter sense, almost all subjects are privileged: for there is no village in existence that does not shine with its own privileges, which it asserts as often as it sees fit. Privileges of this second kind change according to the differences of the times and the variety of circumstances. For no less than privileges—or private laws—universal laws are said to be in the hand of the Ruler. And it is a common tradition among jurists that Princes...
