## A Political-Legal Dissertation
<meta>catchword: made</meta>

...favors and privileges, granted by themselves or their predecessors, as it seems fit to them. Marcantonio Peregrinus, book 1, *On the Right of the Treasury* <note>original: *de Iure Fisci*</note>, the chapter on those having fiscal rights, whether they can, etc., number 19. Ludovico Moditius, in the section "The Decrees of Princes," <note>original: *Principum placita*</note> doubt 18. Rauchbar, volume 2, question 11. See also Maullius, *On Homage* <note>original: *de homagio*</note>, chapter 9, number 105, etc., and also 123, etc. Hence, you may find clauses scattered throughout laws, rescripts, pragmatic sanctions, and even new privileges that expressly revoke old privileges. Because of this, privileges not confirmed by a successor are considered to be of no value, according to Suetonius in his life of *Titus*, chapter 8. See, however, Johannes Buxtorf on the *Golden Bull* <note>original: *ad Auream Bullam*; the Golden Bull of 1356 was a decree that fixed important aspects of the constitutional structure of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, thesis 37.

Truly, I add here in passing, that those Princes who attempt to diminish or take away privileges granted by their ancestors to subjects or others for good service are like the Pharaoh who "did not know Joseph." Exodus 1, verse 8. Therefore, such privileges ought not to be revoked without a great cause. Guetta, counsel 13. Lehman, the last part of chapter 41. And this view pleases me more than the advice of Isabella in *Parnassus*, second report 7: "that one allows them to be violated <note>original German: *daß man sie vergreiffen laß*</note>, so that afterward they can be dragged into servitude." For even Saul was punished because he did not keep the promise to the Gibeonites that Joshua had made many years before by mistake. Joshua 9 and 2 Samuel 21, as I have already warned above. See also the Illustrious Georgius Enenckel, in the treatise *On Privileges* <note>original: *de privileg.*</note>, book 3, throughout, where he deals extensively with the remission and revocation of privileges. And add Rauchbar, volume 2, question 12, on whether they are lost through non-use.

The common opinion of legal interpreters is that a privilege granted by a Prince passes to his successors and binds them. Specifically, the order of justice and reason suggests that those who desire their own commands to be observed by their successors should preserve the will of their predecessor—unless, however, the privilege is enormously prejudicial to the dignity of the office itself. Pieter Peck, on the chapter "it is fitting" <note>original: *c. decet concessum*</note>, regarding the rules of law in the sixth book of the Decretals, 7 and 8. Add Giovanni Cravetta, counsel 732. The same author, in counsel 731, investigates whether the "good pleasure" of a Prince is ended by death; and in counsel 909, he treats when a Prince can revoke a privilege.

Certainly, if ownership <note>original: *dominium*</note> has been given to someone through a privilege, then it cannot be taken away without cause: for example, if someone is elevated to the nobility, etc. Thus, some privileges are precarious <note>term: *precario*—something held by the will of another and revocable at any time</note>, while others have the force of a gift. Emperor Louis IV also confirmed privileges given by the Bishops to the City of Speyer. Lehman, book 7, chapter 21, page 758; and on the same page, second column, he grants "eternal privileges." Likewise, privileges cannot be revoked if they have transitioned into a contract: Dominicus Arumæus, on the *Golden Bull*, discourse 5, thesis 23. Georg Everhard, volume 1, counsel 18 (where he discusses by what legal action they may be defended).

Furthermore, they are considered to obtain the force of a contract when they are given to a non-subject, or even when they are granted to subjects for a price paid. Peregrinus, in the said chapter, number 28. Moditius, in the said section "The Decrees of Princes," doubts 37 and 43. Lelio Zecchi, book 2, chapter 1, under number 6, the verse "furthermore." And in such cases, they are "exempt," as I believe. It is also not shameful for a Prince to enter into a treaty or contract with his subjects. For God Himself made this with men.

The author emphasizes that a ruler's integrity is mirrored in their commitment to honor existing agreements, citing both legal scholars and biblical precedents.</summary>

### On the Mixed State of the Commonwealth
<sig>Gg 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: ELEN-</meta>

...made. *Genesis 6:18, Genesis 9:8 and following, Genesis 15:18, Genesis 17:2, 4, 7, Exodus 34:27.* Molanus, *On Keeping Faith with Heretics* <note>original: *de fide heretic. fervandâ*</note>, book 4, chapter 12. Truly, in no way can privileges of the former kind—those which alter the state of the empire and are counted among the fundamental laws—be violated or revoked by a Prince without the consent of the other party. This is because, through mutual stipulation and contract, they almost always transform into agreed-upon pacts <note>original: *pacta conventa*; these were formal agreements between a ruler and their subjects, often a condition of taking the throne</note>. To this point belong the words of Eberhard von Weihe in his *Treatise on Succession and Election* <note>original: *tractat. de succeß. & election.*</note>, when he says: he holds the "heresy" <note>here meaning a controversial but firm opinion</note> that a solid obligation exists between Princes and subjects, and it is not permitted for a Prince to withdraw from it at his own whim, etc. Therefore, it is not permitted for a King or his successor to interpret such an irrevocable privilege—even one granted as a reward for good service—in a way that restricts or "corrects" it, provided the intent is clear (either from the nature of the words, the reasoning expressed within it, or through silent deduction). See Schrader, *Counsel 21, number 45 and 104, and volume 2*; Rosenthal, *chapter 7, conclusion 9, number 18*; and beautifully by Gomesius, *volume 2, chapter 1, number 1*. Indeed, for some advisors, it was a capital offense to have broken the privileges of the Estates <note>original: *privilegia Ordinum*; the "Estates" were the representative classes like the nobility, clergy, and commons</note>; see Comines, *book 5, chapter 17*. 

Yet, wherever one looks, there are those (who delight in being called "Court-politicians" <note>original: *Aulicopolitici*</note>) who deem such privileges to be ruinous, as noted by Boccalini in *Reports from Parnassus* <note>original: *de Parnaß.*</note>. They advise that these privileges should be abolished as the "seeds of litigation" and banished beyond the Garamantes <note>a phrase meaning to the ends of the earth</note>. See Comines, *chapter 16 and 17*. To others, these privileges are like toys <note>original: *crepundiorum*</note>, fit only for appeasing infants when they begin to cry. Boccalini, *book 2, chapter 1*. And certainly, it has long been common among the powerful to restrict, hate, and fail to keep privileges. In this way, even the Athenians oppressed those who had surrendered to them, acting against their own pacts. Aristotle, *Politics, book 3, chapter 9*.

V. Finally, this leads to the discussion of forms of government that are "confused" rather than "mixed." These occur where jurisdictions are torn apart and separated by privilege or custom, such that one person holds one type of power and another holds a different type; for instance, one holds criminal jurisdiction and another civil. Reinkingk, *page 161*; Leipold, *On Concurrent Jurisdiction* <note>original: *de concurr. juris d.*</note>; Killinger, *Discourse 8, number 9, etc.* In these cases, the "guiding star" <note>original: *cynosura*</note> is that when someone is in general possession of a jurisdiction, another is not thought to have claimed more by prescription than exactly what they have possessed. Wesenbeck, *On the Digest: Jurisdiction* <note>original: *ff. de juris dict.*</note>. This is seen in the Imperial Cities <note>original: *Civitatibus Imperio immediatè addictis*; cities that were subject only to the Emperor and not to local lords</note>; Bishops and neighboring Princes may hold many rights there, which are nonetheless not considered to imply a state of subjection. See the legal counsel in the case of **the City of Friedberg** against its **Burgrave** <note>a Burgrave was a military governor or count of a castle</note>. Likewise, Cologne swears an oath to the Bishop, and appeals are made to him from certain courts. **The Statutes of Cologne**, *pages 8 and 10*.
